• are constructed from balanced transfer operators,
• admit self-adjoint realizations,
• determine spectral and dynamical behavior,
• culminate naturally in the SMRK Hamiltonian.

They represent the conceptual and mathematical core of the QFM framework.

6 Spectral Theory of QFM Hamiltonians

6.1 Why Spectrum Matters

In Quansistor Field Mathematics, spectral theory is not an auxiliary tool but the primary lens
through which structure, stability, and meaning are revealed.
By Axiom V (Spectral Sovereignty), the long-term behavior of any QFM system is fully determined
by the spectrum of its Hamiltonian. Eigenvalues correspond to stable modes of computation,
resonance patterns, and invariant arithmetic or physical structures.

6.2 Basic Spectral Notions

Let H be a (possibly unbounded) QFM Hamiltonian on HQFM.

Definition 6.1 (Spectrum). The spectrum of H, denoted σ(H), is the set of λ ∈ C for which
H − λI fails to be invertible.

The spectrum decomposes into:
• point spectrum (eigenvalues),
• continuous spectrum,
• residual spectrum.

For self-adjoint QFM Hamiltonians, the residual spectrum is empty and σ(H) ⊂ R.

45



6.3 Eigenstates as Arithmetic or Computational Modes

An eigenstate ψλ satisfies
Hψλ = λψλ.

In QFM, eigenstates represent:
• stable computational attractors,
• arithmetic resonance patterns,
• stationary information distributions,
• invariant reasoning states in QVM.

Unlike finite-dimensional quantum systems, QFM eigenstates may be delocalized over Q and
exhibit hierarchical or fractal support.

6.4 Spectral Measures and Decomposition

For self-adjoint H, the spectral theorem yield∫s a projection-valued measure E(λ) such that

H = λ dE(λ).
R

Time evolution is then expressed as ∫
e−tH = e−tλ dE(λ).

R

This representation underlies:
• stability analysis,
• filtering and feature extraction,
• spectral learning dynamics,
• heat-kernel analogies.

6.5 Discrete vs. Continuous Spectrum

QFM Hamiltonians typically exhibit mixed spectra.

• Discrete eigenvalues correspond to isolated arithmetic or computational structures.
• Continuous components arise from infinite branching, multiplicative diffusion, or scale

invariance.

The coexistence of both is a defining feature distinguishing QFM from standard quantum lattice
systems.

6.6 Spectral Properties of Balanced Prime Operators

Recall the balanced prime operator

Kp = 1
Ap + pBp.
p

46



Proposition 6.1. Each Kp is self-adjoint and generates a symmetric multiplicative diffusion on
N.

The spectrum of Kp exhibits:
• accumulation at zero,
• logarithmic scaling behavior,
• nontrivial continuous components.

These properties reflect the infinite branching induced by prime multiplication and division.

6.7 Spectral Structure of the SMRK Hamiltonian

The SMRK Hamiltonian ∑
HSMRK = Kp + αΛ(n) + β logn

p∈P

combines infinitely many balanced operators with a diagonal arithmetic potential.

Heuristic Spectral Picture

Heuristically, σ(HSMRK) is expected to exhibit:
• a continuous bulk spectrum generated by multiplicative diffusion,
• arithmetic resonances induced by the von Mangoldt potential,
• logarithmic spectral drift.

The competition between diffusion and potential mirrors that of Schrödinger operators on
non-Euclidean spaces.

6.8 Spectral Gaps and Stability

Definition 6.2 (Spectral Gap). A spectral gap is an interval (a, b) ⊂ R such that (a, b)∩σ(H) = ∅.

Spectral gaps imply:
• dynamical stability,
• resistance to perturbations,
• robustness of computational modes.

In arithmetic QFM systems, gaps correspond to forbidden multiplicative regimes.

6.9 Resonances and Arithmetic Interference

Noncommutativity among transfer operators induces spectral resonances.
These resonances manifest as:

• quasi-eigenstates,
• slow-decaying modes,

47



• interference patterns in arithmetic propagation.
Such structures are invisible to purely combinatorial models and require the operator-spectral
framework of QFM.

6.10 Trace Formulas and Spectral Invariants

Formally, traces of functions of H encode global ∑arithmetic data:
Tr f(H) = f(λ).

λ∈σ(H)

While rigorous trace-class conditions require care, these expressions motivate:
• spectral invariants,
• partition functions,
• arithmetic trace formulas.

This perspective aligns QFM with Hilbert–Pólya-type operator conjectures.

6.11 Perturbation Theory

Small perturbations H 7→ H + εV model:
• arithmetic noise,
• computational uncertainty,
• learning or adaptation processes.

Standard results from self-adjoint perturbation theory apply locally, while global effects reflect
the infinite-dimensional and arithmetic nature of QFM.

6.12 Spectral Flow and Renormalization

As parameters α, β vary, eigenvalues undergo spectral flow.
This flow defines:

• phase transitions in arithmetic dynamics,
• renormalization trajectories,
• operator fixed points.

Such flows are central to understanding universality classes within QFM.

6.13 Computational Interpretation

In QVM implementations:
• eigenvalues represent inference scores,
• eigenstates encode learned structures,
• spectral filtering performs reasoning.

Learning corresponds to shaping the Hamiltonian to induce desired spectral features.

48



6.14 Summary

Spectral theory in QFM:
• governs stability and long-term behavior,
• encodes arithmetic and computational structure,
• unifies diffusion, potential, and resonance effects,
• provides a bridge to number theory and physics,
• establishes spectrum as the ultimate carrier of meaning.

This chapter prepares the ground for distributed realization, arithmetic applications, and falsifiable
predictions developed in subsequent sections.

7 Distributed Realization and the Quantum Virtual Machine

7.1 From Formalism to Machine

The previous chapters established QFM as a complete operator-theoretic framework. This chapter
addresses the crucial question: how can such a framework be realized as a concrete, distributed
computational system?
The answer is the Quantum Virtual Machine (QVM): an execution architecture in which quansistor
fields, transfer operators, and Hamiltonians are mapped onto distributed computational resources
while preserving locality, composability, and spectral meaning.

7.2 Principles of Distributed Realization

A QFM realization must satisfy the following constraints:
• locality of operator action,
• deterministic composability,
• parallel execution,
• reproducibility and verifiability,
• spectral fidelity.

These requirements are incompatible with monolithic architectures but align naturally with
distributed systems.

7.3 Quansistors as Computational Units

In the QVM, a quansistor is instantiated as a minimal computational unit representing a local
amplitude ψ(q) and its neighborhood N(q).
Each quansistor:

• stores local amplitude data,
• exposes interfaces for forward and backward transfer,
• applies local potential operators,

49



• participates in operator composition.
Quansistors are agnostic to global system size and interact only with neighbors.

7.4 Partitioning the Quansistor Field

Let Q be partitioned into subsets: ⊔M
Q = Qi.

i=1

Each subset Qi is assigned to a comput∑ational shard (node, canister, process). Operators
decompose as: ∑

H = Hi + Hij ,
i i̸=j

where Hi acts locally and Hij represents boundary interactions.

7.5 Execution of Transfer Operators

Forward Operators

A forward operator Af is executed by:
• reading ψ(f(q)) from the appropriate shard,
• updating ψ(q) locally.

This operation is stateless and parallelizable.

Backward Operators

Backward operators require aggregation:
• each shard emits partial contributions,
• boundary contributions are exchanged,
• aggregation is deterministic and order-independent.

This mirrors reduce operations in distributed computing.

7.6 Local Hamiltonian Updates

Time evolution proceeds via local Hamiltonian fragments:

ψi(t+ ∆t) = ψi(t)−∆tHiψi(t)

with boundary synchronization steps for Hij .
This supports:

• explicit time stepping,
• asynchronous updates,
• fault-tolerant recovery.

50



7.7 Spectral Consistency Across Shards

Spectral meaning must survive distribution.
This is ensured by:

• deterministic operator decomposition,
• reproducible aggregation order,
• global checkpointing of operator states.

Eigenmodes emerge as global correlations across shards rather than localized states.

7.8 QVM Execution Model

The QVM execution loop consists of:
1. local operator application,
2. boundary message exchange,
3. aggregation and normalization,
4. checkpointing and verification.

This loop is invariant under scaling and supports elastic resource allocation.

7.9 Fault Tolerance and Reproducibility

Because QFM operators are linear and decomposable:
• partial failures do not corrupt global state,
• lost shards can be recomputed,
• execution traces are replayable.

This property is essential for scientific verification and long-running arithmetic experiments.

7.10 Cryptographic and Verifiable Execution

Operator execution logs can be:
• hashed,
• time-stamped,
• independently verified.

Thus, QVM execution supports cryptographic proof of computation and scientific auditability.

7.11 Relationship to Existing Paradigms

Paradigm QVM Interpretation
Classical VM operator scheduler
Quantum circuit static operator fragment
MapReduce backward transfer aggregation
Blockchain VM deterministic replay

51



QVM subsumes these paradigms within a unified operator-based execution model.

7.12 Learning and Adaptation

Learning in QVM corresponds to modifying Hamiltonian parameters to shape spectral structure.
This includes:

• tuning potentials,

• enabling or disabling transfer paths,

• adjusting operator weights.
Learning is therefore a form of spectral engineering.

7.13 Scalability

Because all interactions are local, QVM scales with:
• size of Q,

• number of shards,

• available parallelism.
No global synchronization barrier is required except for optional checkpoints.

7.14 Interpretation

The QVM is not a simulator of a different machine. It is the natural execution substrate implied
by QFM itself.
In this sense, QFM is not merely a theory of computation, but a theory that becomes computation
when instantiated.

7.15 Summary

This chapter established:
• how quansistors map to computational units,

• how QFM operators execute in distributed environments,

• how Hamiltonian dynamics are preserved across shards,

• how spectral meaning survives scaling,

• how QVM realizes QFM as a concrete machine.
The QVM provides the bridge from abstract operator mathematics to executable, verifiable, and
scalable computation.

9 Physical Analogies and Simulation

9.1 Motivation

Although Quansistor Field Mathematics is formulated abstractly, its operator structure closely
parallels models found in mathematical physics. This chapter clarifies these analogies, not as
metaphors, but as precise correspondences between QFM operators and physical simulation
frameworks.
Such analogies serve two purposes:

• to provide intuition for QFM dynamics,
• to enable direct numerical simulation techniques.

9.2 Quansistor Fields as Discrete Physical Fields

A quansistor field
ψ : Q → A

56



is analogous to a discrete physical field defined on a non-Euclidean lattice.
Key correspondences:

Physics QFM
Lattice site quansistor index q
Field value amplitude ψ(q)
Adjacency neighborhood N(q)
Energy density potential V (q)

The essential difference is that Q need not be spatial—it may be arithmetic, logical, or abstract.

9.3 Diffusion and Transport

Balanced transfer operators induce diffusion-like dynamics.
For a Hamiltonian H, the evolution equation

∂tψ = −Hψ

resembles a heat equation on a generalized lattice.

• forward operators correspond to transport,
• backward operators correspond to aggregation,
• balance ensures reversibility-like behavior.

This analogy allows QFM systems to be simulated using established numerical methods for
diffusion processes.

9.4 Wave Phenomena

When Hamiltonians contain competing noncommuting transfer operators, oscillatory behavior
emerges.
Such dynamics correspond to:

• wave propagation,
• interference,
• standing modes (eigenstates).

Eigenstates of QFM Hamiltonians thus play the role of stationary waves on abstract spaces.

9.5 Potential Landscapes

Diagonal potential operators act as energy landscapes.
In arithmetic systems:

• Λ(n) creates localized arithmetic barriers,
• logn induces scale-dependent drift.

In physical analogies, these correspond to spatially varying potentials that trap or repel field
amplitude.

57



9.6 Comparison with Schrödinger Operators

The QFM Hamiltonian ∑
H = Ki + V

i

is structurally analogous to a Schrödinger operator

−∆ + V (x),

where:
• Ki act as generalized Laplacians,
• V is an external potential,
• Q replaces Euclidean space.

This analogy enables the transfer of intuition and techniques from quantum mechanics to QFM.

9.7 Simulation Techniques

QFM systems may be simulated using:
• explicit time stepping,
• implicit solvers for stiff operators,
• spectral decomposition when available,
• Monte Carlo sampling of transfer paths.

Locality ensures simulations scale efficiently in distributed environments.

9.8 Boundary Conditions

Boundary conditions arise naturally when Q is truncated or restricted.
Typical conditions include:

• absorbing boundaries,
• reflecting boundaries,
• periodic identifications.

Boundary choice influences spectral properties and must be considered carefully in simulations.

9.9 Emergence of Macroscopic Behavior

Large-scale QFM systems exhibit emergent phenomena:
• effective diffusion constants,
• collective oscillations,
• phase-like transitions under parameter changes.

These behaviors mirror macroscopic physics arising from microscopic laws.

58



9.10 Physical Interpretation of Arithmetic Dynamics

Arithmetic diffusion on N corresponds to transport on a highly irregular space.
This explains why:

• arithmetic statistics resemble random processes,

• deterministic operators produce stochastic-looking outcomes,

• physical analogies are mathematically justified.

9.11 Visualization and Experimentation

QFM simulations may be visualized as:
• heat maps over index sets,

• spectral density plots,

• mode decomposition animations.
Such visualizations are essential for hypothesis generation and falsification.

9.12 Limits of the Physical Analogy

While powerful, physical analogies must not be overstated.
QFM:

• does not assume physical spacetime,

• does not rely on quantum measurement postulates,

• remains an abstract operator theory.
Analogies are tools, not claims of physical identity.

9.13 Summary

This chapter demonstrated that:
• QFM Hamiltonians correspond naturally to physical operators,

• diffusion, waves, and potentials emerge generically,

• established simulation methods apply directly,

• arithmetic dynamics admit precise physical interpretation,

• QFM provides a unified simulation framework across domains.
QFM thus bridges abstract operator mathematics and concrete, computable dynamics.

10 Falsifiability, Experiments, and Predictions

10.1 Scientific Status of QFM

Quansistor Field Mathematics is proposed as a mathematical and computational framework, not
as a metaphysical theory. As such, it must satisfy the criteria of scientific falsifiability.
This chapter identifies concrete predictions, numerical experiments, and failure modes by which
QFM—and in particular arithmetic Hamiltonians such as HSMRK—can be tested, refined, or
rejected.

10.2 What Would Falsify QFM

QFM would be falsified if one or more of the following were demonstrated:

• QFM Hamiltonians cannot be defined as self-adjoint operators on any reasonable domain.
• Spectral properties predicted by balanced transfer operators are absent in numerical

realizations.
• Operator-based dynamics fail to reproduce known arithmetic statistics even qualitatively.
• Distributed execution destroys spectral invariants in an irreparable way.

These criteria distinguish QFM from purely formal or unfalsifiable frameworks.

10.3 Numerical Spectral Experiments

The primary experimental probe of QFM is numerical spectral analysis.
Concrete experiments include:

• truncation of Q = N to [1, N ],
• construction of finite-dimensional approximations of HSMRK,
• numerical diagonalization and spectral density estimation.

Observed spectra can be compared across increasing N to detect convergence or systematic
deviation.

10.4 Predicted Spectral Features

QFM predicts the following qualitative spectral features:

• presence of a continuous spectral bulk,
• clustering near arithmetic resonances,
• sensitivity to the von Mangoldt potential,
• logarithmic scaling effects.

Absence of these features would challenge the framework.

60



10.5 Dynamical Experiments

Time evolution experiments involve initializing a localized state ψ0 and observing

ψ(t) = e−tHψ0.

Predictions include:
• multiplicative diffusion over N,
• partial localization near prime powers,
• slow decay modes corresponding to spectral resonances.

10.6 Comparison with Random Models

To test whether observed phenomena are nontrivial, QFM simulations should be compared
against:

• random graph Hamiltonians,
• shuffled prime transfer models,
• purely stochastic diffusion processes.

QFM predicts statistically distinguishable behavior from such controls.

10.7 Robustness under Perturbation

Perturbation experiments probe stability:

H 7→ H + εV.

Predictions:
• small perturbations cause continuous spectral deformation,
• large perturbations destroy arithmetic structure,
• certain spectral invariants persist under noise.

Failure of robustness would indicate overfitting to idealized operators.

10.8 Distributed Execution Tests

QVM implementations allow falsification via distributed execution:
• compare spectra computed on different partitions,
• verify reproducibility under reordering,
• test fault recovery consistency.

Loss of invariants under distribution would contradict QFM’s locality axioms.

61



10.9 Predictions Beyond Arithmetic

Although motivated by arithmetic, QFM predicts similar phenomena in:
• graph dynamics,
• symbolic computation,
• learning systems modeled by operator flows.

Cross-domain consistency strengthens the framework; inconsistency weakens it.

10.10 Negative Results and Scope

Negative results are admissible and expected.
QFM does not claim:

• a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,
• universality over all mathematical systems,
• physical realization as a quantum theory.

Its claims are limited to providing a coherent operator framework whose validity depends on
experimental outcomes.

10.11 Reproducibility and Open Verification

All experiments described are reproducible using:
• published operator definitions,
• open-source numerical code,
• deterministic execution traces.

This openness is essential to scientific credibility.

10.12 Long-Term Research Program

If supported by evidence, QFM suggests a research program including:
• refined operator domains and rigor,
• deeper spectral analysis,
• large-scale distributed arithmetic experiments,
• connections to established number-theoretic conjectures.

If falsified, it still provides a useful negative result clarifying the limits of operator-based arithmetic
modeling.

10.13 Summary

This chapter established that:
• QFM is explicitly falsifiable,

62



• concrete numerical and distributed experiments are available,
• clear predictions and failure modes exist,
• negative outcomes are scientifically meaningful,
• the framework stands or falls by empirical and computational evidence.

QFM is thus presented not as a belief system, but as a testable, evolving scientific theory.

represents transport of amplitude from f(q) to q.

A.1.4 Backward Flow and Aggregation

Backward transfer operators induce convergent flow.

(Bfψ)(q) = ψ(r)

r:f(r)=q

This represents:
• aggregation of influences,

A.1.5 Balanced Dynamics

Balanced operators such as

Kp = 1

p

induce neither pure expansion nor pure contraction, but a form of multiplicative diffusion.
This balance:

Under repeated application of QFM operators, certain field configurations may emerge as

A.1.7 Locality and Causality

Although time is not a primitive object in QFM, iterative operator application induces an

Appendix B

B.1 Extended Operator Calculus

B.1.1 Role of Operator Calculus in QFM

The main text introduced the operator algebra of QFM as a formal framework for defining
dynamics on quansistor fields. This appendix extends that discussion by exploring operator
calculus at a more structural and interpretative level.
The purpose is not to introduce new axioms, but to clarify how operators may be combined,
transformed, and interpreted as higher-level computational or mathematical objects.

B.1.2 Operators as Programs

In QFM, operators can be viewed as programs acting on a distributed state space.

• forward transfer operators act as data fetch instructions,
• backward operators act as aggregation or reduction instructions,
• potential operators act as local modifiers or weights.

Operator composition corresponds to program composition, while linear combination corresponds
to parallel execution paths.

B.1.3 Normal Forms and Operator Decomposition

Every operator T ∈ O(Q) admits a d∑ecompositio∑n of the form

T = αiAf + β V

i j

as discussed in Chapter 3.
From a calculus perspective, this decomposition plays the role of a normal form, analogous to:

• canonical circuits in logic,
• normal forms in lambda calculus,
• basis expansions in functional analysis.

B.1.4 Commutation Relations

Noncommutativity is a defining feature of QFM operator calculus.
Given two transfer maps f and g, in general

[Af , Ag] ̸= 0, [Af , Bg] ̸= 0.

These commutation relations encode ordering sensitivity and give rise to interference effects,
even in purely arithmetic settings.

68



B.1.5 Operator Scaling and Renormalization

Operators may be rescaled or grouped into effective operators.
For example, a family of prime operators {Kp}p≤P may be approximated by an effective diffusion
operator acting on a truncated region of Q.
Such constructions resemble renormalization procedures in physics, where microscopic degrees of
freedom are absorbed into macroscopic effective laws.

B.1.6 Functional Calculus

Given a self-adjoint Hamiltonian H, one m∫ay formally define

f(H) = f(λ) dE(λ),
σ(H)

where E(λ) is the spectral measure.
In QFM, functional calculus enables:

• spectral filtering,
• time evolution via e−tH ,
• construction of resolvents and Green-type operators.

This elevates operators from transition rules to manipulable analytical objects.

B.1.7 Iterated and Nested Operators

Nested operator expressions such as
T = Af1Bf2Af3

represent multi-stage processes.
Iterated application defines discrete flows, while limits of iteration yield continuous dynamics.
Such constructions unify algorithmic iteration with operator semigroup theory.

B.1.8 Operator Flows

Parameter-dependent families of operators
H(θ) = H0 + θV

define operator flows.
As θ varies, spectral properties evolve continuously, producing bifurcations, resonances, or phase-
like transitions. This concept underlies both learning dynamics in QVM and perturbative analysis
in arithmetic Hamiltonians.

B.1.9 Symmetries and Invariants

Symmetries of Q induce symmetries of the operator algebra.
If U is a unitary (or invertible) symmetry operator commuting with H, then spectral degeneracies
and invariant subspaces arise.
Such symmetries correspond to arithmetic constraints, graph automorphisms, or conservation
laws.

69



B.1.10 Operator Metrics and Distances

One may introduce metrics on the space of operators, for example via operator norms or spectral
distances.
These metrics quantify:

• similarity between Hamiltonians,
• stability under perturbation,
• learning progress in adaptive QVM systems.

B.1.11 Limits of the Calculus

The extended operator calculus remains formal in several respects:
• convergence of infinite sums,
• domain subtleties for unbounded operators,
• trace-class conditions.

These issues are addressed rigorously only in restricted settings and are not assumed globally.

B.1.12 Summary

This appendix expanded the operator calculus of QFM by:
• interpreting operators as programs,
• clarifying normal forms and decomposition,
• emphasizing noncommutativity and scaling,
• introducing functional and flow-based viewpoints,
• outlining limits and open technical issues.

Together with Appendix A, this calculus-oriented perspective deepens intuition while preserving
the formal integrity of the main theory.

C.1 Hamiltonians and Spectral Intuition

C.1.1 Purpose and Scope

This appendix provides an interpretative layer for QFM Hamiltonians and their spectra. All formal

Nothing in this appendix is required for the logical consistency of the main text.

C.1.2 Hamiltonians as Generators of Meaning

In QFM, Hamiltonians generate more than temporal evolution. They generate structure.
Each Hamiltonian encodes:

• which transitions are allowed,
• how strongly they are weighted,
• how local interactions combine into global behavior.

From this perspective, a Hamiltonian functions as a semantic rule governing the field.

C.1.3 Eigenstates as Stable Concepts

Eigenstates of a Hamiltonian
Hψ = λψ

represent configurations that remain invariant (up to scale) under the action of H.
Intuitively, eigenstates correspond to:

• stable computational patterns,
• persistent arithmetic structures,
• invariant modes of reasoning.

In QVM terms, they act as “concepts” or “attractors” of computation.

C.1.4 Eigenvalues as Relevance Measures

Eigenvalues quantify the response of a state to Hamiltonian dynamics.
Larger eigenvalues correspond to:

• stronger participation in dynamics,
• higher energetic or computational relevance,
• faster decay or amplification under evolution.

Thus, the spectrum of a Hamiltonian provides a ranking of structural importance.

71



C.1.5 Spectral Decomposition as Field Analysis

The spectral decomposition ∫
ψ = dE(λ)ψ

can be viewed as decomposing a field into elementary semantic components.
Each spectral component isolates a mode with distinct dynamical behavior. This mirrors Fourier
analysis, but on abstract, non-Euclidean index spaces.

C.1.6 Spectral Bands and Structural Classes

Continuous spectral bands correspond to families of related structures rather than isolated
objects.
In arithmetic systems:

• bands may encode classes of integers with similar multiplicative behavior,
• gaps indicate forbidden or unstable configurations.

Such structures have no direct analogue in classical combinatorial number theory.

C.1.7 Resonances and Near-Eigenstates

Not all meaningful states are exact eigenstates.
Resonant or quasi-eigenstates:

• persist for long but finite times,
• encode approximate invariants,
• play a central role in arithmetic diffusion.

These states often dominate observable dynamics.

C.1.8 SMRK Hamiltonian: An Intuitive View

The SMRK Hamiltonian combines:
• multiplicative expansion,
• divisive aggregation,
• arithmetic potential shaping.

Intuitively, it defines a balance between growth and collapse on N, producing structured diffusion
rather than chaos.
Eigenstates reflect global arithmetic patterns rather than individual numbers.

C.1.9 Spectral Flow and Parameter Tuning

Varying parameters such as α and β induces spectral flow.
This flow:

• reorganizes eigenmodes,

72



• reveals phase-like transitions,
• provides a mechanism for learning and adaptation.

In QVM implementations, tuning parameters corresponds to spectral engineering.

C.1.10 Spectrum as Fingerprint

The spectrum of a Hamiltonian acts as a fingerprint of the underlying system.
Two Hamiltonians with similar spectra produce qualitatively similar dynamics, even if their
microscopic definitions differ.
This supports the use of spectral metrics for comparison and classification.

C.1.11 Relation to Physical and Cognitive Models

In physics, spectra encode energy levels.
In QFM, spectra encode:

• dynamical stability,
• computational relevance,
• semantic persistence.

This suggests a unifying role for spectral analysis across physics, computation, and cognition.

C.1.12 Interpretational Limits

The interpretations presented here are heuristic.
No claim is made that:

• Hamiltonians possess intrinsic meaning,
• spectra imply consciousness,
• arithmetic systems are physical substrates.

Meaning arises from interpretation layered atop formal structure.

Appendix D

D.1 Distributed Architecture and QVM Execution

D.1.1 Purpose of This Appendix

This appendix provides technical and architectural details of how Quansistor Field Mathematics
(QFM) can be instantiated as a distributed execution system, referred to as the Quantum Virtual
Machine (QVM).
The material here supplements Chapter 7 by specifying execution models, data layouts, de-
terminism guarantees, and implementation strategies. It is intended for system designers and
implementers.

D.1.2 Architectural Overview

A QVM realization consists of:
• a global quansistor index set Q,
• a partitioning of Q into shards,
• local execution engines applying operator fragments,
• a deterministic communication and aggregation protocol.

Each shard operates independently except for boundary interactions explicitly defined by transfer
operators.

D.1.3 Sharding Model

Let ⊔M
Q = Qi

i=1

be a partition of the index set.
Each shard Qi:

• stores amplitudes ψ(q) for q ∈ Qi,
• executes local operator components Hi,
• exchanges boundary data with neighboring shards.

Shard boundaries are determined by the neighborhood relation N(q).

D.1.4 Local Execution Engine

Each shard runs a local execution loop:
1. read current local amplitudes,
2. apply forward transfer operators,

74



3. emit backward contributions,
4. apply potential operators,
5. update local state.

This loop is deterministic and side-effect free.

D.1.5 Boundary Communication Protocol

Boundary interactions arise when f(q) ∈ Qj for q ∈ Qi, i ̸= j.
The protocol:

• collects outbound messages,
• exchanges them between shards,
• aggregates inbound contributions deterministically.

Ordering of messages does not affect results due to linearity.

D.1.6 Backward Aggregation Semantics

Backward operators require summation over preim∑ages:

(Bfψ)(q) = ψ(r).
r:f(r)=q

In distributed settings:
• each shard computes partial sums,
• partial results are merged,
• final values are written atomically.

This mirrors reduce operations in distributed computing frameworks.

D.1.7 Time Stepping and Scheduling

QVM supports multiple scheduling strategies:
• synchronous global steps,
• asynchronous local steps with barriers,
• event-driven updates for sparse dynamics.

All strategies preserve determinism when executed with fixed scheduling rules.

D.1.8 Determinism and Replay

Determinism is ensured by:
• fixed operator ordering,
• deterministic aggregation rules,

75



• explicit versioning of Hamiltonians.
Execution traces may be replayed exactly, enabling verification and debugging.

D.1.9 Fault Tolerance

Because operator execution is linear and local:
• shard failure affects only local state,
• failed shards can be recomputed from checkpoints,
• no global rollback is required.

This property enables long-running arithmetic and spectral experiments.

D.1.10 Checkpointing and State Persistence

Periodic checkpoints record:
• shard-local amplitudes,
• operator parameters,
• execution metadata.

Checkpoints enable:
• recovery from failure,
• migration across hardware,
• reproducible experimentation.

D.1.11 Cryptographic Verification

QVM execution can be made verifiable by:
• hashing operator definitions,
• hashing checkpoint states,
• time-stamping execution milestones.

This enables independent verification of results without rerunning the entire computation.

D.1.12 Mapping to Existing Platforms

The QVM model maps naturally to:
• containerized microservices,
• actor-based systems,
• deterministic blockchain-based compute platforms.

Each shard corresponds to a logical actor executing operator fragments.

D.1.14 Scalability Considerations

Scalability is governed by:

D.1.15 Security and Isolation

Shards operate in isolation:

• decisions affecting individuals must be auditable,
• misuse or misinterpretation must be actively prevented.

These constraints apply regardless of system scale or sophistication.

F.1.10 Long-Term Perspective

As operator-based systems grow in complexity, their societal impact may increase.
A responsible long-term approach requires:

• continuous evaluation of assumptions,
• openness to critique and revision,
• separation of formal results from speculative interpretation.

Scientific progress must be accompanied by ethical maturity.

F.1.11 Summary

This appendix emphasized that:
• meaning in QFM is emergent and relational,
• intelligence-like behavior can be described without strong metaphysical claims,
• responsibility remains with human designers and users,
• transparency and interpretability are essential,
• ethical constraints must guide deployment.

QFM is thus framed not as a doctrine, but as a formal tool whose significance depends on
evidence, interpretation, and responsible use.

Chapter 3

Spectral Foundations in
Operator-First Quantum Theory
From State Space to Spectral Topology:

An Operator-First Foundation
Enter Yourname

Abstract
This book develops an operator-first, spectral foundation for quantum
theory, emphasizing that the essential physical content of quantum
systems is not carried by state vectors or time-domain trajectories, but
by the spectral structure of operators acting on an appropriate state
space.
The exposition begins by reinterpreting the notion of state space itself.
Rather than treating states as primary objects, states are understood as
spectral configurations defined relative to families of operators and their
projection structures. This shift naturally leads to a framework in which
observables, measurement, and physical reality are encoded in spectral
properties rather than in particular linear representations.
Spectral decomposition and functional calculus are then presented not
merely as technical tools, but as structural principles. Operators are
shown to act on systems primarily by organizing and transforming their
spectra, with dynamics emerging as spectral action rather than as the
solution of differential equations in time. This viewpoint unifies measure-
ment, evolution, and stability within a single spectral language.
Special attention is devoted to unbounded operators, whose domains,
closures, and self-adjoint extensions are treated as integral components of
physical theory rather than as mathematical subtleties. Self-adjointness is
interpreted as a structural condition that guarantees spectral legitimacy,
while different self-adjoint realizations correspond to distinct physical
models.
The resolvent is introduced as a central analytic object and interpreted as
a spectral microscope: a probe that reveals fine-grained spectral topology
through its singularities, analytic behavior, and norm growth. Spectral
projections, stability, and sensitivity to perturbations are derived from
the resolvent’s structure, establishing it as the primary carrier of spectral
information.
Perturbation theory is reformulated as spectral deformation. Rather
than focusing on eigenvalue shifts or state corrections, perturbations are



understood as geometric and analytic deformations of spectral topology.
This perspective clarifies the distinction between stable discrete structures
and fragile continuous components, and prepares the ground for the
analysis of resonances and irreversible phenomena.
Resonances, decay, and instability are treated as intrinsic spectral features
arising from the analytic continuation of the resolvent. Unstable states
are not anomalies of the formal theory, but natural expressions of spectral
singularities governing long-time behavior. Scattering theory is finally
incorporated as a statement about spectral invariance and connectivity:
asymptotic behavior emerges from the global organization of spectral
components rather than from explicit state trajectories.
Taken together, Chapters 1–7 establish a unified operator-first and spec-
tral framework in which quantum theory is understood as the study of
spectral topology, analytic structure, and operator-defined invariants.
This foundation prepares the conceptual and mathematical ground for
subsequent developments, including arithmetic operators, spectral geom-
etry, and the SMRK program, while remaining fully consistent with the
standard formalism of quantum mechanics.

1 Operators and the State Space of Quantum Mechanics

1.1 State Space

The fundamental mathematical object of quantum mechanics is the state space, which is modeled
as a complex Hilbert space H. This space serves as the carrier of the states of a physical system
and provides a natural framework for the definition of the inner product, norm, and convergence.
From the physical point of view, a vector in H is not itself a physical state, but rather a
representation of a state. A physical state is determined by an equivalence class of vectors
differing by a nonzero complex scalar. Already at this level it becomes apparent that the essential
information is not contained in a particular linear representation, but in structures that are
invariant under this choice.
From a more modern perspective, a state can be understood not merely as a point in a linear
space, but as an object characterized by its projection properties with respect to the spectral
decompositions of relevant operators. The state space thus does not function merely as a linear
container, but as an environment in which spectral relations between operators and measurable
quantities are realized.

1.2 Linear Operators as Physical Observables

In quantum mechanics, physical observables are represented by linear operators acting on the state
space H. The requirement of linearity ensures compatibility with the principle of superposition,
while further properties of operators are dictated by their physical interpretation.
A central role is played by self-adjoint operators, whose spectra are real and allow a direct
interpretation of eigenvalues as possible outcomes of measurements. Eigenvectors (or, more
precisely, eigenspaces) determine the projection structure through which the state of the system
is reduced during measurement.
It is important to emphasize that the physical meaning of an operator is not determined by its
explicit algebraic form, but by the structure of its spectrum and the associated projections. The

85



linear action of the operator is a technical means, whereas the carrier of physical information is
the spectral decomposition.

1.3 The Spectrum as the Carrier of Physical Information

To every self-adjoint operator A one associates a spectrum σ(A), which may be discrete, continu-
ous, or of mixed type. This spectrum determines not only the possible measurement outcomes,
but also the manner in which the state space decomposes into invariant subspaces.
From this viewpoint, an operator is best understood as a spectral object: its action is fully
characterized by its spectral measure and the associated projection-valued decomposition. The
linear-algebraic representation is secondary and often basis-dependent, whereas the spectral
structure is invariant.
This perspective becomes particularly important in the case of unbounded operators, where
questions of domain, closure, and self-adjointness cannot be separated from spectral analysis.
Here it becomes clear that the spectrum is not an auxiliary notion, but the central object of the
theory.

1.4 Measurement and Projection Structure

The process of measurement can be described mathematically using projection operators associ-
ated with the spectral decomposition of the measured observable. The probability of individual
outcomes is determined by projecting the state vector onto the corresponding spectral subspaces.
State reduction after measurement is therefore not a general property of linear operators, but
a direct consequence of their spectral structure. The collapse of the state can be understood
as a loss of coherence between different spectral components, rather than as a violation of the
linearity of the dynamical equations.

1.5 Remark on the Spectral Interpretation

Although quantum mechanics is traditionally formulated in the language of linear operators on a
Hilbert space, a deeper analysis reveals that the decisive role is played by their spectra and the
associated projection structures. The linear formalism serves as a technical apparatus, while the
physical content is carried by the spectral properties of operators.
This viewpoint does not contradict the classical formulation of quantum mechanics, but rather
refines and unifies it, especially in the context of unbounded operators, continuous spectra, and
general measurement schemes.

2 Spectral Decomposition of Operators and Functional Calculus

2.1 Motivation for Spectral Decomposition

In quantum mechanics, many fundamental problems reduce to the study of self-adjoint operators.
These operators represent physical observables, and their spectra determine the possible outcomes
of measurements. For this reason, spectral analysis occupies a central position both in the
mathematical formalism and in the physical interpretation of the theory.
Spectral decomposition allows an operator to be decomposed into elementary components
corresponding to different parts of its spectrum. This decomposition provides a unified framework

86



for describing both discrete and continuous spectra and forms a natural bridge between abstract
operator theory and experimentally measurable quantities.

2.2 The Spectral Theorem for Self-Adjoint Operators

The fundamental result of the theory is the spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators. It
guarantees that to every self-adjoint operato∫r A on a Hilbert space there corresponds a projection-
valued measure E(λ) such that

A = λ dE(λ).
σ(A)

This representation does not merely express a formal decomposition of the operator, but reveals
its intrinsic structure: the operator is completely determined by its spectrum and the associated
projections. The linear action of the operator on state vectors arises from the integration of
elementary spectral contributions.
From a physical point of view, the projections E(∆) correspond to measurable events, namely the
statement that the result of a measurement lies within a given set ∆ ⊂ R. The spectral theorem
thus provides a precise mathematical formulation of the postulates of quantum measurement.

2.3 Discrete and Continuous Spectrum

The spectrum of an operator may exhibit different characteristics. A discrete spectrum consists
of isolated eigenvalues with corresponding eigenvectors, while a continuous spectrum manifests
itself through the absence of normalizable eigenstates and requires a description in terms of
generalized eigenfunctions.
From the perspective of spectral decomposition, both types of spectrum are treated in a unified
manner through the projection-valued measure. The distinction lies not in the principle of
decomposition, but in the analytic properties of the projections and the topology of the state
space.
This unified viewpoint emphasizes that the distinction between discrete and continuous spectrum
is not fundamental from the structural point of view, but reflects specific physical properties of
the system under consideration.

2.4 Functional Calculus

Spectral decomposition enables the introduction of functional calculus for self-adjoint operators.
Given a suitable function f , one can define∫the operator

f(A) = f(λ) dE(λ),
σ(A)

which admits a clear physical interpretation.
This apparatus is particularly important for the description of time evolution, where the exponen-
tial of the Hamiltonian appears in the form of a unitary evolution operator. Functional calculus
thus shows that the dynamics of a quantum system is naturally expressible as a transformation
of the spectrum, rather than merely as a formal solution of differential equations.

2.5 Spectral Interpretation of Dynamics

The time evolution of states is generated by the Hamiltonian, whose spectral properties determine
the character of the system’s dynamics. A discrete spectrum leads to quasiperiodic behavior,

87



whereas a continuous spectrum is associated with dissipative or scattering phenomena.
From this perspective, dynamics can be understood as a flow of phases assigned to individual
spectral components. The evolution of a state is therefore not primarily a motion of vectors in a
linear space, but a coordinated transformation of the spectral contributions from which the state
is composed.

2.6 Remark on the Spectral Viewpoint

Spectral decomposition and functional calculus demonstrate that the essential physical information
is contained in the spectrum of operators and in its projection structure. The linear-algebraic
apparatus serves as a means for manipulating these objects, whereas the substantive content of
the theory is determined by spectral properties.
This viewpoint provides a unified explanation of measurement, dynamics, and stability of quantum
systems, and prepares the ground for the study of more advanced structures such as unbounded
operators, resolvents, and spectral singularities.

3 Unbounded Operators, Domains, and Self-Adjointness

3.1 Unbounded Operators in Quantum Mechanics

In quantum mechanics, one naturally encounters operators that are not bounded on the entire
Hilbert space. Typical examples include the position and momentum operators, as well as
Hamiltonians of realistic physical systems. Such operators cannot be understood as everywhere-
defined linear maps, but rather as objects acting on suitably chosen subspaces of the state
space.
From the mathematical point of view, it is therefore essential to distinguish clearly between an
operator and its domain. An unbounded operator A is defined only on a dense subset D(A) ⊂ H,
and its properties cannot be studied independently of this choice.
From the physical perspective, this fact reflects the reality that not all vectors in the Hilbert space
correspond to physically admissible states for a given observable. The domain of an operator is
thus not a technical detail, but an integral part of the physical specification of the system.

3.2 Closedness and Closability

For unbounded operators, the notion of closedness plays a fundamental role. An operator is
called closed if its graph is a closed subset of the Cartesian product H×H. This property ensures
stability under limiting processes and is indispensable for a consistent spectral analysis.
Many physically relevant operators are not closed, but are closable. This means that they admit
a closure, which extends the original operator to a closed one. In practice, one therefore works
not with the original operator, but with its closure, which carries the physically meaningful
spectral information.
From this viewpoint, closedness can be regarded as a condition for the existence of a well-defined
spectrum. An operator that is neither closed nor closable cannot be interpreted as a physical
observable.

88



3.3 Symmetry and Self-Adjointness

The symmetry of an operator, defined by the relation

⟨Aψ, ϕ⟩ = ⟨ψ,Aϕ⟩ for all ψ, ϕ ∈ D(A),

is a necessary, but not sufficient, condition for the physical interpretation of an operator as an
observable.
The decisive property is self-adjointness, which guarantees the reality of the spectrum and the
existence of a spectral decomposition. For unbounded operators, self-adjointness is not merely
an algebraic property, but is intimately tied to the choice of domain. Two different self-adjoint
extensions of the same symmetric operator may lead to different spectral properties.
This fact has a direct physical consequence: the choice of a self-adjoint extension corresponds to
the choice of boundary conditions or, more generally, to the specification of the physical model.

3.4 Deficiency Indices and Spectral Structure

The theory of deficiency indices provides a systematic tool for studying self-adjoint extensions of
symmetric operators. These indices determine whether self-adjoint extensions exist and, if so,
how many such extensions there are.
From the spectral point of view, deficiency indices can be interpreted as a measure of indeterminacy
in the specification of the spectral structure of an operator. If the indices vanish, the spectral
structure is uniquely determined. Otherwise, there exists a family of possible spectra, each
corresponding to a different physical realization of the system.
This perspective emphasizes that the spectrum is not solely determined by the algebraic properties
of an operator, but depends sensitively on its domain and on the manner in which it is closed.

3.5 Self-Adjointness and Time Evolution

The self-adjointness of the Hamiltonian is a crucial condition for the existence of unitary time
evolution. Stone’s theorem guarantees that to every self-adjoint operator there corresponds a
one-parameter group of unitary operators describing the temporal evolution of the system.
From the viewpoint of spectral decomposition, this evolution is realized through phase factors
associated with individual spectral components. The stability and reversibility of the dynamics
are therefore direct consequences of the spectral properties of the Hamiltonian.
This relation once again confirms that the dynamics of a quantum system is fundamentally a
spectral phenomenon, while differential equations serve as its formal representation.

3.6 Remark on the Spectral Role of Domains

The analysis of unbounded operators shows that the domain of an operator is an essential part
of its physical interpretation. Spectrum, self-adjointness, and time evolution cannot be separated
from the question of the space on which the operator acts.
From this perspective, an operator can be said to “live” not merely in the Hilbert space, but in
the refined structure formed by its domain, its closure, and its spectral properties. The linear
formalism provides the framework, but the actual content of the theory is determined by the
spectral topology of these objects.

89



4 Resolvent, Spectral Projections, and Stability

4.1 The Resolvent Operator

Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H. For complex numbers z not belonging to
the spectrum σ(A), the operator (A− zI) is invertible, and its inverse

R(z) = (A− zI)−1

is called the resolvent of A at the point z.
Although A may be unbounded, the resolvent R(z) is a bounded operator for all z ∈ C \ σ(A).
This fact allows unbounded operators to be studied through families of bounded operators
parameterized by the complex spectral variable.
From the operator-first viewpoint, the resolvent is not a secondary construction, but a primary
analytic object through which the operator reveals its spectral organization.

4.2 Analytic Structure and Spectral Detection

The resolvent is an analytic operator-valued function on the resolvent set ρ(A) = C \ σ(A).
Singularities of this function correspond precisely to spectral points of the operator.
In this sense, the resolvent functions as a spectral microscope: by probing the operator with
complex spectral parameters, one detects fine-grained spectral features that are not accessible
through direct inspection of eigenvectors or algebraic expressions.
Isolated poles of the resolvent correspond to discrete eigenvalues, while branch cuts and non-
isolated singular behavior reflect continuous or unstable spectral components. The local behavior
of the resolvent thus encodes detailed information about the spectral topology of the operator.

4.3 Spectral Projections from the Resolvent

Spectral projections can be constructed directly from the resolvent by contour integration in the
complex plane. For a closed contour Γ enclo∮sing a portion of the spectrum, one defines

PΓ = 1 (A− zI)−1

This formula shows that projections are derived from the analytic structure of the resolvent. In
the operator-first interpretation, projections are not primitive objects but spectral summaries
extracted from the resolvent.
Physically, these projections correspond to idealized measurements that isolate spectral regions.
Conceptually, they demonstrate how measurement theory emerges from the analytic properties
of operators rather than being imposed independently.

4.4 Resolvent Norms and Spectral Stability

The stability of spectral features under perturbations is closely linked to the behavior of the
resolvent norm. Regions where the resolvent remains uniformly bounded correspond to stable
spectral configurations, while large resolvent norms signal spectral sensitivity or instability.
From the perspective of the spectral microscope, instability appears as a magnification effect:
small perturbations of the operator lead to large changes in the resolvent near certain spectral
regions. This behavior is particularly pronounced near continuous spectra and spectral thresholds.

90



Stability is therefore not characterized solely by the persistence of eigenvalues, but by the global
analytic behavior of the resolvent as a function of the spectral parameter.

4.5 Physical Interpretation of Resolvent-Based Stability

In physical terms, sharply localized spectral features correspond to well-isolated resolvent
singularities, indicating robust and long-lived states. Diffuse or unstable phenomena are reflected
in broad or highly sensitive resolvent behavior.
This interpretation is especially relevant in contexts such as scattering theory and resonance
phenomena, where the resolvent encodes decay rates, lifetimes, and transition structures that are
invisible at the level of static spectra.

4.6 Remark on the Spectral-Microscopic Viewpoint

The interpretation of the resolvent as a spectral microscope unifies spectral analysis, stability
theory, and physical interpretation within a single operator-theoretic framework. Rather than
cataloging spectral values, one studies how spectral structures respond to analytic probing.
This viewpoint prepares the conceptual ground for the analysis of resonances, scattering, and
spectral deformation, where the resolvent becomes the primary carrier of both mathematical and
physical information.

5 Resolvent, Spectral Projections, and Stability

5.1 The Resolvent Operator

Let A be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H. For complex numbers z not belonging to
the spectrum σ(A), the operator (A− zI) is invertible, and its inverse

R(z) = (A− zI)−1

is called the resolvent of A at the point z.
The resolvent is a bounded operator for all z ∈ C \ σ(A), even when A itself is unbounded.
This property makes the resolvent a powerful analytical tool, allowing one to study unbounded
operators through families of bounded ones.
From a spectral perspective, the resolvent encodes complete information about the spectrum
of the operator. Singularities of the resolvent correspond precisely to spectral points, and the
behavior of R(z) near the spectrum reflects its local structure.

5.2 Analytic Properties of the Resolvent

The resolvent is an analytic operator-valued function of the complex parameter z on the resolvent
set ρ(A) = C \ σ(A). This analyticity plays a crucial role in spectral theory, enabling the use of
complex-analytic techniques in the study of operators.
In particular, the growth behavior of the resolvent near the real axis provides insight into the
nature of the spectrum. Isolated poles correspond to discrete eigenvalues, while branch-type
singularities are associated with continuous spectral components.
The resolvent identity further reveals the internal coherence of the theory by relating the resolvents
at different spectral parameters. This identity forms the algebraic basis for perturbative and
stability analyses.

From the physical point of view, these projections correspond to idealized measurements that

5.4 Stability of the Spectrum

The stability of the spectrum under perturbations is a central issue in both mathematics
and physics. Small changes in the operator may lead to significant changes in the spectrum,
particularly in the presence of continuous spectral components.
The resolvent provides a natural framework for analyzing stability. If the resolvent varies
continuously with respect to perturbations, one can infer stability properties of the spectrum.
Conversely, instability often manifests itself through the emergence of large resolvent norms near
certain spectral regions.
This viewpoint highlights that spectral stability is not merely a question of eigenvalues, but of
the global behavior of the resolvent as an analytic object.

5.5 Physical Interpretation of Resolvent Stability

In physical terms, stability of the resolvent is closely related to the robustness of observed
phenomena. Sharp spectral features correspond to well-isolated poles of the resolvent, while
broad or unstable features are reflected in diffuse or highly sensitive resolvent behavior.
This interpretation is particularly relevant in scattering theory and resonance phenomena, where
the resolvent encodes information about transient states and decay processes.
Thus, the resolvent serves not only as a mathematical device, but as a conceptual tool for
understanding the stability and instability of physical systems.

5.6 Remark on the Resolvent-Centered Viewpoint

The resolvent-centered approach emphasizes that spectral properties are best understood through
analytic structures rather than purely algebraic ones. Projections, spectra, and stability properties
all emerge naturally from the behavior of the resolvent.
This perspective prepares the ground for the study of resonances, scattering theory, and non-self-
adjoint extensions, where the resolvent becomes the primary carrier of physical and mathematical
information.

6 Resolvents, Resonances, and Unstable States

6.1 Operator-First Viewpoint

In the operator-first formulation of quantum theory, physical phenomena are not described
primarily in terms of trajectories, wavefunctions, or time-dependent amplitudes, but as structural
properties of operators acting on a state space. Within this viewpoint, the resolvent of an
operator plays a privileged role, as it encodes the full spectral and dynamical content of the
system in a single analytic object.
Rather than treating the resolvent as a secondary construction derived from an operator, the
operator-first perspective regards the resolvent as a primary probe of physical behavior. Spectral
points, resonances, and instabilities are revealed directly through the analytic structure of the
resolvent, without reference to explicit eigenstates.

6.2 Resonances as Spectral Singularities

Resonances arise in systems where bound states interact with a continuum. From the operator-first
perspective, resonances are not eigenvalues in the traditional sense, but manifest as singularities
of the analytically continued resolvent.
These singularities typically appear as poles located off the real axis on unphysical sheets of
the complex energy plane. Their position encodes both the energy and the decay rate of the
associated unstable state.
This description emphasizes that resonances are inherently spectral phenomena. They are
defined not by vectors in the Hilbert space, but by the analytic behavior of the resolvent as an
operator-valued function.

6.3 Analytic Continuation of the Resolvent

To access resonances, one extends the resolvent beyond the real axis through analytic continuation.
This procedure reveals spectral structures that are invisible in the self-adjoint framework restricted
to real energies.
In the operator-first language, analytic continuation is not an auxiliary trick, but a natural
extension of spectral analysis. It allows the operator to be probed beyond its stable spectral
regime and exposes latent dynamical features encoded in its structure.
The resulting complex spectral data provide a unified description of scattering, metastability,
and decay within a single operator-theoretic framework.

6.4 Unstable States and Spectral Decay

Unstable states correspond to spectral components that do not persist under time evolution. In
the operator-first picture, instability is not defined by the failure of a state vector to remain
normalized, but by the presence of non-real spectral singularities governing the long-time behavior
of observables.
Time evolution generated by the Hamiltonian can be analyzed spectrally through the resolvent.
Exponential decay laws arise from isolated resonance poles, while more complex decay patterns
reflect branch cuts and continuous spectral components.
Thus, decay and irreversibility are not imposed externally, but emerge from the spectral topology
of the operator.

93



6.5 Scattering and Resolvent Structure

Scattering theory finds a natural formulation in terms of the resolvent. Incoming and outgoing
asymptotic behavior is encoded in boundary values of the resolvent near the continuous spectrum.
From the operator-first standpoint, scattering is a manifestation of how the resolvent connects
different spectral regions. The scattering matrix can be understood as a derived object, obtained
from the resolvent rather than introduced as an independent construct.
This reinforces the idea that the resolvent serves as the central carrier of physical information,
while other quantities are secondary projections of its structure.

6.6 SMRK-Oriented Interpretation

In the SMRK framework, operators are treated as fundamental spectral generators rather than
as mere quantizations of classical observables. Resonances and unstable states are interpreted as
intrinsic features of the operator’s spectral geometry.
The resolvent acts as a spectral microscope, revealing fine-grained structures that govern dynamics,
stability, and decay. In this sense, unstable states are not anomalies or pathologies, but natural
expressions of spectral complexity.
This interpretation aligns with a broader operator-first philosophy in which physical laws are
encoded in spectral relations and analytic structures, rather than in explicit time-domain evolution
equations.

6.7 Remark on Spectral Irreversibility

The operator-first analysis of resonances clarifies the origin of irreversibility in quantum systems.
While the underlying operator may be self-adjoint, its analytically continued resolvent exhibits
structures that break time-reversal symmetry at the spectral level.
Irreversibility thus emerges not from a modification of the dynamical laws, but from the spectral
organization of the operator. This viewpoint provides a coherent framework for understanding
decay, dissipation, and the arrow of time within a rigorously operator-based theory.

7 Scattering Theory and Spectral Invariance

7.1 Scattering in the Operator-First Framework

In the operator-first formulation, scattering theory is not introduced as a separate dynamical
scheme, but arises naturally from the spectral topology of operators. Physical processes tradi-
tionally described by asymptotic states and wave packets are reinterpreted as relations between
spectral regions encoded by the resolvent.
From this viewpoint, scattering does not primarily concern trajectories or time-domain evolution,
but the manner in which the operator connects incoming and outgoing spectral components.
The emphasis shifts from states to operators, and from temporal evolution to spectral structure.

7.2 Resolvent as a Spectral Probe

Throughout the preceding chapters, the resolvent has emerged as a central analytic object. In
scattering theory, its role becomes explicit: the resolvent acts as a spectral probe, interrogating
how perturbations deform the spectral topology of the operator.

94



Boundary values of the resolvent near the continuous spectrum encode the asymptotic behavior
of physical processes. Scattering amplitudes and transition probabilities are derived quantities,
obtained from the analytic structure of the resolvent rather than postulated independently.
This perspective unifies scattering with resonance theory and spectral stability within a single
operator-theoretic framework.

7.3 Wave Operators and Spectral Relations

Wave operators are traditionally introduced to compare the dynamics of an interacting system
with a reference free system. In the operator-first language, they express spectral relations
between two operators rather than mappings between explicit state trajectories.
Their existence and completeness are determined by spectral properties such as absolute continuity
and the absence of singular spectral components. Thus, wave operators reflect the compatibility
of spectral topologies between different operator realizations.

7.4 Spectral Invariance under Scattering

A central result of scattering theory is the invariance of certain spectral components under
interaction. In particular, the absolutely continuous part of the spectrum often remains stable
under a broad class of perturbations.
From the operator-first perspective, spectral invariance is not a coincidence but a structural
property of the resolvent. Perturbations that do not alter the global spectral topology preserve
scattering channels, even though local spectral features may be deformed.
This invariance explains why scattering phenomena exhibit universal characteristics largely
independent of microscopic details.

7.5 Operator-First Dynamics and Asymptotic Behavior

Asymptotic dynamics emerges from the long-range spectral organization of the operator. Instead
of tracking the time evolution of individual states, operator-first dynamics examines how spectral
components separate, persist, or interfere at infinity.
Scattering processes thus correspond to stable spectral pathways encoded in the resolvent. The
arrow from incoming to outgoing configurations is a manifestation of spectral organization rather
than an imposed temporal boundary condition.

7.6 SMRK-Calibrated Interpretation

Within the SMRK framework, scattering theory is interpreted as a statement about spectral
connectivity. Operators act as generators of spectral relations, and scattering reveals how these
relations remain invariant under admissible deformations.
The resolvent, functioning as a spectral probe, exposes invariant structures that govern transport,
interaction, and stability. This interpretation aligns scattering theory with the broader operator-
first philosophy developed throughout the preceding chapters.

7.7 Remark on Unified Spectral Topology

Taken together, the analysis of resolvents, resonances, perturbations, and scattering demonstrates
that spectral topology provides a unifying language for quantum theory. Dynamics, stability,

95



and asymptotic behavior are all expressions of how operators organize their spectra.
In this unified view, scattering theory does not introduce new principles, but completes the
operator-first narrative by revealing the invariant spectral structures that persist across interac-
tions.
