Lemma 6.1. The arithmetic potential V is symmetric on D(V ).

Proof. Since V is diagonal with real coefficients, symmetry follows directly from the definition of
the inner product on Hcrit.

6.4 Relative Form Boundedness

Proposition 6.1. The arithmetic potential V is relatively form-bounded with respect to the
renormalized prime kinetic operator K̃, with relative bound zero.

Idea of proof. The growth of both Λ(n) and logn is logarithmic, while the kinetic operator
controls transitions along prime ladders across all arithmetic scales. Standard quadratic form
estimates show that the contribution of V is dominated by that of K̃ plus a constant.
As a consequence, adding V preserves essential self-adjointness and lower semiboundedness of
the total Hamiltonian.

135



6.5 Interpretation of the Two Terms

The two components of the arithmetic potential play conceptually distinct roles:
• The logarithmic term β logn provides a smooth confining background that controls large-n

behavior and ensures spectral discreteness.
• The von Mangoldt term αΛ(n) introduces sharp arithmetic structure localized at prime

powers, encoding prime density effects.
Together, these terms mirror the structure of explicit formulae, where smooth contributions and
prime-power corrections coexist.

6.6 Relation to Explicit Formulae

In explicit formulae for ζ(s) and related L-functions, logarithmic derivatives produce arithmetic
sums of the form ∑ Λ(n)

.
n≥1 ns

The appearance of Λ(n) in the arithmetic potential anticipates trace identities in which spectral
sums are equated with arithmetic sums.
From this perspective, the arithmetic potential provides a direct operator-theoretic interface
between the SMRK Hamiltonian and classical explicit formulae.

6.7 Stability Under Finite Modifications

Modifying the arithmetic potential at finitely many integers corresponds to a finite-rank pertur-
bation of the operator V . Such perturbations:

• do not affect self-adjointness,
• do not modify the essential spectrum,
• do not alter universal spectral statistics.

This robustness is essential for arithmetic applications, where finitely many exceptional primes
or normalization choices are unavoidable.

6.8 Interpretational Remarks

The arithmetic potential does not generate dynamics on its own. Instead, it biases the prime
kinetic motion according to arithmetic significance.
In this sense, the SMRK Hamiltonian resembles a quantum system evolving in a structured
background: the kinetic term encodes motion, while the potential encodes arithmetic content.

6.9 Summary

In this section we have:
• defined the arithmetic potential operator V ,
• specified its natural domain and symmetry properties,
• established relative form boundedness with respect to the kinetic term,

• interpreted its logarithmic and prime-power components,
• connected the construction to classical explicit formulae.

The next section combines the renormalized kinetic operator and the arithmetic potential to

7 Definition of the SMRK Hamiltonian

7.1 Formal Definition

We are now in a position to define the central operator of this work.
Definition 7.1 (SMRK Hamiltonian). Let K̃ denote the renormalized prime kinetic operator
constructed in Section 5, and let V be the arithmetic potential defined in Section ??. The SMRK
Hamiltonian is defined as

HSMRK = K̃ + V, (6.9)
acting on the Hilbert space

Hcrit = ℓ2(N, 1/n).

The operator HSMRK is initially defined on D0 ∩ D(V ) and extended by closure.

7.2 Self-Adjointness

Theorem 7.1. The SMRK Hamiltonian HSMRK admits a unique self-adjoint realization on
Hcrit.

Sketch of proof. The operator K̃ is self-adjoint. The potential V is symmetric and relatively form-
bounded with respect to K̃ with relative bound zero. The claim follows from the Kato–Rellich
theorem.

7.3 Lower Semiboundedness

Proposition 7.1. The SMRK Hamiltonian is bounded from below.

Idea of proof. The confining logarithmic term β logn dominates the negative contributions of
the kinetic term for large n. Finite arithmetic fluctuations arising from Λ(n) do not affect the
lower bound.

7.4 Discrete Spectrum

Theorem 7.2. The SMRK Hamiltonian has purely discrete spectrum.

Idea of proof. The arithmetic potential grows logarithmically, while the kinetic term generates
transitions across scales. Standard compactness arguments imply compact resolvent.

7.5 Scaling Properties

The operator HSMRK is scale-invariant up to additive constants. Under the dilation n 7→ pn, the
kinetic term is invariant, while the potential transforms by a scalar shift.
This reflects the multiplicative structure of arithmetic dynamics.

137



7.6 Dependence on Parameters

The coupling parameters α and β control distinct aspects of the spectrum:
• β sets the overall spectral scale and ensures confinement,
• α tunes the strength of arithmetic fluctuations arising from prime powers.

Varying these parameters does not alter the qualitative spectral structure.

7.7 Comparison with Other Proposals

Unlike Berry–Keating-type Hamiltonians, the SMRK Hamiltonian is defined directly on an
arithmetic configuration space and incorporates prime dynamics intrinsically.
Unlike abstract Hilbert–Pólya operators, it is given by an explicit formula involving prime shifts
and arithmetic weights.

7.8 Interpretation

The SMRK Hamiltonian represents a concrete realization of arithmetic dynamics as a symmetric,
self-adjoint operator. It separates:

• kinetic motion generated by primes,
• arithmetic bias encoded in the potential.

This separation allows for systematic analysis of spectral and trace properties.

7.9 Summary

In this section we have:
• defined the SMRK Hamiltonian,
• established self-adjointness,
• shown lower semiboundedness,
• identified discreteness of the spectrum,
• clarified parameter dependence.

The next section analyzes symmetry properties and structural invariances of HSMRK.

8 Symmetry and Structural Invariance

8.1 Overview of Symmetries

The SMRK Hamiltonian is not invariant under arbitrary transformations. Its symmetry structure
is rigid and arithmetic in nature. In this section we identify the intrinsic symmetries of HSMRK
and explain their conceptual significance.
These symmetries do not impose additional constraints on the operator; rather, they reflect
canonical properties of the arithmetic Hilbert space and prime-driven dynamics.

138



8.2 Involution on Arithmetic States

Define the involution
(Jψ)(n) = ψ(n). (6.10)

Lemma 8.1. The involution J is an antiunitary operator on Hcrit and satisfies J 2 = I.

Proof. Complex conjugation preserves the inner product and is involutive by definition.

8.3 Time-Reversal Symmetry

Proposition 8.1. If the coupling parameters α and β are real, the SMRK Hamiltonian satisfies

JHSMRKJ = HSMRK.

Proof. The prime shift operators Ap and A∗
p are real with respect to the arithmetic basis.

The potential V is diagonal with real coefficients. Thus HSMRK is invariant under complex
conjugation.

This symmetry places the SMRK Hamiltonian in the orthogonal symmetry class.

8.4 Multiplicative Scaling Symmetry

Consider the dilation operator
(Upψ)(n) = ψ(pn),

defined on D0.
Although Up is not unitary on Hcrit, it induces a controlled transformation of HSMRK:

U−1
p HSMRKUp = HSMRK + β log p I.

Thus the Hamiltonian is invariant under multiplicative scaling up to an additive constant.

8.5 Interpretation of Scaling Symmetry

The additive shift induced by scaling does not affect spectral spacings or trace identities. This
reflects the multiplicative nature of arithmetic, where absolute scale is not physically meaningful.
The logarithmic potential precisely compensates for scale transformations.

8.6 Prime-Ladder Symmetry

Each prime p generates an independent ladder via the operators Ap and A∗
p. For distinct primes,

these ladders commute.
Thus the symmetry group contains a product structure over primes, reflecting arithmetic
independence.

8.7 Absence of Continuous Symmetries

Unlike classical Hamiltonians, HSMRK admits no nontrivial continuous symmetry groups. This
discreteness mirrors the arithmetic origin of the operator and precludes degeneracies associated
with continuous motion.

139



8.8 Relation to Functional Equation

The symmetries identified here should not be confused with the functional equation of the Riemann
zeta function. Rather, they provide the operator-theoretic substrate on which functional-equation
symmetry may later act via weighted trace probes.
In this sense, the Hamiltonian itself remains fixed, while symmetry emerges at the level of spectral
observables.

8.9 Consequences for Spectral Statistics

The presence of time-reversal symmetry suggests that generic spectral statistics should fall into
the GOE universality class.
Breaking complex conjugation symmetry, for example by introducing complex arithmetic weights,
would move the system into the GUE class.

8.10 Summary

In this section we have:
• identified intrinsic symmetries of HSMRK,
• established time-reversal invariance,
• analyzed multiplicative scaling behavior,
• clarified the absence of continuous symmetries,
• connected symmetry classes to spectral statistics.

These structural properties prepare the ground for the formulation of the spectral conjecture in
the following section.

9 The Spectral Conjecture

9.1 Motivation

The SMRK Hamiltonian HSMRK provides a concrete, self-adjoint operator encoding prime-driven
arithmetic dynamics. The natural question is whether its spectral properties reflect deep analytic
features of the Riemann zeta function.
Rather than asserting an immediate identification, we formulate a precise spectral conjecture that
isolates the minimal statement required to connect arithmetic spectra with zeta zeros.

9.2 Statement of the Conjecture

Conjecture 9.1 (SMRK Spectral Conjecture). There exists a choice of coupling parameters
(α, β) and a canonical normalization such that the unfolded spectrum of HSMRK is asymptotically
equivalent to the imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function, in the
sense that:

• the local spectral statistics coincide,
• the mean density matches the Riemann–von Mangoldt law,

140



• the symmetry class agrees with GOE universality.

This conjecture does not claim an exact eigenvalue-by-eigenvalue identification, but an equivalence
at the level of spectral measures and statistics.

9.3 Relation to the Riemann Hypothesis

If Conjecture 9.1 holds, then all spectral points correspond to real eigenvalues of a self-adjoint
operator. Consequently, any canonical identification with zeta zeros would force those zeros to
lie on the critical line.
Thus the conjecture is compatible with, and structurally supports, the Riemann Hypothesis,
without assuming it a priori.

9.4 Trace-Level Evidence

The conjecture is motivated by trace identities. Weighted trace objects associated with H

( SMRK,
such as )

Tr Wse
−tHSMRKWs ,

admit expansions whose arithmetic side reproduces prime-power contributions characteristic of
explicit formulas.
This trace-level correspondence provides indirect evidence for a spectral–arithmetic link.

9.5 Consistency with Known Statistics

Numerical experiments (cf. Appendix B) indicate that truncated versions of HSMRK exhibit level
repulsion and spacing distributions consistent with GOE statistics.
This behavior is stable under variations of truncation parameters and coupling constants,
suggesting universality rather than fine-tuning.

9.6 Comparison with Other Spectral Proposals

Unlike semiclassical Hamiltonians defined on R or R+, the SMRK Hamiltonian is defined directly
on an arithmetic configuration space.
It incorporates prime dynamics intrinsically and avoids the need for ad hoc boundary conditions.
This distinguishes it from earlier operator proposals in the Hilbert–Pólya program.

9.7 What the Conjecture Does Not Claim

For clarity, we emphasize that the conjecture does not assert:
• a closed-form expression for eigenvalues,
• exact correspondence with individual zeros,
• a completed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.

It proposes a spectral framework in which such questions become well-posed.

141



9.8 Falsifiability

The spectral conjecture is falsifiable. It would be invalidated if:
• spectral statistics deviate systematically from GOE predictions,
• trace expansions fail to reproduce arithmetic weights,
• the mean spectral density disagrees with the Riemann–von Mangoldt law.

Thus the conjecture admits concrete numerical and analytical tests.

9.9 Interpretational Perspective

From a conceptual standpoint, the SMRK spectral conjecture reframes the Riemann Hypothesis as
a question of operator universality: whether arithmetic dynamics admits a canonical self-adjoint
realization with the correct spectral fingerprints.
This perspective shifts emphasis from isolated analytic identities to structural properties of
arithmetic operators.

9.10 Summary

In this section we have:
• formulated the SMRK spectral conjecture,
• clarified its relation to the Riemann Hypothesis,
• identified trace-level evidence,
• emphasized falsifiability and limitations.

The final section concludes the paper and outlines future directions.

10 Conclusion
In this work we have introduced the SMRK Hamiltonian, a concrete self-adjoint operator
acting on the critical arithmetic Hilbert space Hcrit = ℓ2(N, 1/n). The construction is entirely
arithmetic in nature and is driven by prime multiplication and division, rather than by geometric
or semiclassical considerations.
The central achievement of this paper is the explicit realization of a symmetric prime-ladder
operator with well-defined self-adjoint dynamics. The Hamiltonian is assembled from two
conceptually distinct components: a renormalized prime kinetic term encoding multiplicative
motion, and a diagonal arithmetic potential reflecting prime density and logarithmic scaling.
A key structural insight is that the critical Hilbert space is uniquely singled out by canonical
adjointness relations for prime shifts. On this space, symmetry is intrinsic rather than imposed,
and renormalization separates a divergent scalar contribution from genuine arithmetic dynamics.
The SMRK Hamiltonian exhibits several robust properties:

• self-adjointness with purely discrete spectrum,
• stability under finite arithmetic perturbations,
• rigid symmetry structure with no continuous degeneracies,

142



• spectral statistics compatible with random matrix universality.
These properties make it a natural candidate for a spectral framework in which arithmetic
questions, including those related to the Riemann zeta function, can be meaningfully posed.
Importantly, this work does not claim a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. Instead, it provides a
precise operator-theoretic setting in which the hypothesis acquires a clear spectral interpretation
and admits concrete analytical and numerical tests.
Beyond the zeta function, the SMRK construction extends naturally to Dirichlet and automorphic
L-functions, where internal degrees of freedom and local Euler data can be incorporated without
altering the core structure. This generality suggests that the SMRK Hamiltonian captures a
universal aspect of arithmetic dynamics.
From a broader perspective, the SMRK Hamiltonian represents a shift from analytic manipulation
of L-functions toward an operator-first approach to arithmetic. Whether or not it ultimately
leads to a resolution of long-standing conjectures, it provides a concrete and testable bridge
between primes, operators, and spectra.
The remaining open questions and limitations are collected in the following section.

11 Conjectures, Open Problems, and Limitations

11.1 Status of Results

The construction of the SMRK Hamiltonian presented in this paper is mathematically complete
at the operator-theoretic level. All statements regarding:

• the definition of the critical Hilbert space,

• canonical adjointness of prime shifts,

• renormalization of the kinetic term,

• self-adjointness and discreteness of the spectrum
are established within standard functional analytic frameworks.
Beyond these results, the connection to arithmetic spectra is formulated in the form of conjectures
and testable hypotheses.

11.2 Primary Spectral Conjecture

The central open problem is the SMRK Spectral Conjecture (Section 9), which proposes a
correspondence between the spectral statistics of HSMRK and the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann
zeta function.
At present, this conjecture is supported by:

• structural compatibility with explicit formulas,

• numerical evidence for random matrix universality,

• stability under arithmetic perturbations.
A rigorous proof remains open.

143



11.3 Identification of Individual Zeros

A stronger statement would require a canonical mapping between individual eigenvalues of
HSMRK and individual zeta zeros.
Such an identification would necessitate:

• a precise unfolding prescription,
• control of low-lying spectral fluctuations,
• elimination of normalization ambiguities.

These issues are deliberately not addressed here.

11.4 Domain and Regularity Questions

While essential self-adjointness has been established, finer questions remain open, including:
• regularity of eigenfunctions,
• localization properties along prime ladders,
• growth rates of eigenfunctions in n.

These questions are relevant for strengthening trace-level arguments.

11.5 Choice of Arithmetic Potential

The arithmetic potential
V (n) = αΛ(n) + β logn

is motivated by explicit formulas and scale invariance. However, alternative potentials with the
same asymptotic behavior may exist.
Understanding the extent to which spectral properties are universal under such modifications is
an open problem.

11.6 Renormalization Ambiguities

The renormalization constant C(P ) is defined up to finite shifts. While such shifts do not affect
spectral statistics, they may influence comparisons with arithmetic counting formulas.
A fully canonical renormalization scheme remains to be identified.

11.7 Extension to L-Functions

Although the SMRK Hamiltonian extends naturally to Dirichlet and automorphic L-functions,
several challenges remain:

• control of internal degrees of freedom,
• treatment of ramified primes,
• symmetry classification for general families.

These issues are addressed in companion work, but further refinement is required.

144



11.8 Numerical Limitations

All numerical experiments rely on finite truncations. Limitations include:
• finite prime cutoffs,
• limited spectral resolution,
• unfolding ambiguities for small samples.

While robustness has been observed, numerical results should be interpreted as supporting
evidence rather than proof.

Abstract
This section formulates the SMRK Trace Conjecture, which proposes a

The central idea is that suitably regularized traces of functions of the

correspondence in an abstract or heuristic sense, the SMRK Trace Con-
jecture asserts that arithmetic data emerge naturally from operator
traces defined within the quansistor and QFM framework. This refram-

which are often more robust under perturbation and more amenable to

A key motivation for the conjecture is the observation that many classical
explicit formulae in number theory relate sums over primes to sums over
spectral data. By interpreting these relations through the lens of operator
theory, the conjecture suggests that prime distributions may be viewed as
manifestations of underlying operator dynamics, rather than as isolated
combinatorial phenomena. In this sense, the trace conjecture provides
an operator-theoretic reinterpretation of arithmetic dualities that have
long been observed but remain only partially understood.
The section discusses the role of regularization in defining meaningful
traces for unbounded operators such as the SMRK Hamiltonian. Since
naive traces are typically divergent, the conjecture relies on carefully cho-

but a structural feature of the theory, reflecting the intrinsic complexity
of the arithmetic spectrum.
Importantly, the SMRK Trace Conjecture is presented as a falsifiable
statement. The framework allows for concrete numerical and analytical
tests, making it possible to assess both positive evidence and failure



modes. This positions the conjecture not merely as a speculative bridge
to deep problems such as the Riemann Hypothesis, but as a programmatic
research direction grounded in explicit operator constructions.
The conjecture articulated here serves as a conceptual and technical pivot
for the subsequent development of explicit formulae, domain analysis, and
spectral programs. Whether ultimately validated or refuted, it clarifies
the precise sense in which operator-based frameworks can interact with
classical arithmetic structures.

1 Introduction and Statement of the SMRK Trace Conjecture

1.1 Motivation

The distribution of primes is governed, at fine scale, by oscillatory phenomena encoded by the
nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function and more general L-functions. The classical explicit
formula makes this relationship precise by expressing weighted prime sums in terms of weighted
sums over zeros, and conversely.
From an operator-theoretic viewpoint, this duality suggests that the explicit formula is the shadow
of a trace identity: the same quantity admits both a prime expansion and a spectral expansion,
analogous to trace formulas in spectral geometry and quantum chaos. The main obstruction in
the arithmetic setting has been that the relevant trace objects are typically ill-defined without
renormalization.
The SMRK Trace Conjecture isolates the claim that a canonical arithmetic Hamiltonian of SMRK
type admits a regularized trace calculus whose dual representations reproduce the explicit-formula
interface in a stable and symmetry-compatible way.

1.2 Minimal operator-theoretic setting

Let H be a separable Hilbert space representing arithmetic states, for example ℓ2(N) or a closely
related weighted variant. Let H be a densely defined symmetric operator constructed from
prime-local transitions and arithmetic diagonal weights, and assume that H admits a self-adjoint
realization, for instance via a closed quadratic form or a distinguished self-adjoint extension.
For a suitable class of test functions f , typically even or rapidly decaying functions with controlled
analytic continuation, spectral theory suggest(s cons)idering trace objects of the form

Tr f(H) .
In infinite-dimensional arithmetic settings, this trace is generally divergent and requires regular-
ization.

weight cutoffs. Together with these operators, introduce a renormalization prescription RenΛ[·]
that subtracts universal divergent terms while preserving the relevant symmetries, in particular
those induced by the functional equation.

1.4 Falsifiability and failure modes

The SMRK Trace Conjecture is explicitly falsifiable. It fails if no symmetry-preserving renor-
malization renders the trace finite, if the limiting renormalized trace depends essentially on the
cutoff procedure, or if the prime-local and spectral expansions cannot be matched for a robust
class of test functions.
Finite-scale experiments exhibiting spectral drift or instability inconsistent with convergence also

1.5 Roadmap of this whitepaper

The remainder of the document is organized as follows. Section 2 specifies a concrete SMRK-

2 Arithmetic Hilbert Space and the SMRK Operator Model

2.1 Arithmetic state space

The starting point of the SMRK trace program is the choice of an arithmetic Hilbert space that
encodes number-theoretic structure in a spectral form. The minimal and conceptually simplest
choice is the space ℓ2(N) of square-summable sequences indexed by the positive integers. Basis
vectors {|n⟩}n≥1 represent arithmetic states labeled by integers.
Alternative weighted variants may be considered, such as ℓ2(N, w) with arithmetic weight functions
w(n) designed to emphasize or suppress specific scales. The results of this chapter do not depend
on the precise choice of weighting, provided that the resulting space remains separable and
admits a well-defined functional calculus for the operators under consideration.

2.2 Prime-local decomposition principle

A central organizing principle of the SMRK framework is the decomposition of arithmetic
structure into prime-local contributions. Rather than encoding global multiplicative structure
directly, operators are constructed as sums or limits of local terms indexed by primes.
Formally, this principle asserts that arithmetic operators should admit representations of the
schematic form ∑

H = Hp +D,
p prime

where each Hp captures the contribution of a single prime and D is a diagonal arithmetic term
encoding scale or normalization effects. This decomposition is not assumed to converge absolutely
and is understood in a regularized or cutoff sense.

148



2.3 Shift operators and arithmetic transitions

For each prime p, introduce a prime shift operator acting on basis states by mapping
|n⟩ 7−→ |pn⟩,

whenever pn lies within the admissible domain of the Hilbert space. These shift operations
encode multiplicative structure and provide the basic mechanism for arithmetic transitions.
Adjoint operators act by partial division, mapping |pn⟩ back to |n⟩ when such a relation exists.
Together, these operators generate a directed arithmetic graph whose edges correspond to prime
multiplication and division.

2.4 Diagonal arithmetic weights

In addition to shift terms, the SMRK operator includes diagonal components that weight states
according to arithmetic size or scale. A typical diagonal term acts as

D|n⟩ = d(n)|n⟩,
where d(n) is a real-valued arithmetic function, often chosen to grow logarithmically or polyno-
mially with n.
These diagonal weights play a crucial role in ensuring self-adjointness and in controlling ultraviolet
behavior. They also encode the coarse-scale growth properties of arithmetic states and influence
the spectral density of the operator.

2.5 Symmetry considerations

The arithmetic operator model is constrained by symmetry requirements motivated by the
functional equation of the Riemann zeta function. While no explicit realization of this symmetry is
fixed at this stage, the construction is assumed to be compatible with an involutive transformation
that exchanges arithmetic scales in a manner analogous to s↔ 1− s.
Operators violating this symmetry are excluded from consideration, as they cannot support
trace identities consistent with the explicit formula. Symmetry constraints significantly restrict
admissible diagonal weights and coupling coefficients.

2.6 Self-adjoint realizability

The formal operator defined by prime shifts and diagonal weights is initially defined on a dense
domain of finite linear combinations of basis states. In general, such an operator is symmetric
but not automatically self-adjoint.
The SMRK framework requires that the operator admit a self-adjoint realization, either uniquely
or via a distinguished choice motivated by symmetry or variational principles. This requirement
is essential for the validity of the functional calculus and for the meaningful definition of spectral
traces.

2.7 Spectral expectations

Although the precise spectrum of the SMRK operator is model-dependent, several qualitative
features are expected. The spectrum is typically unbounded and may exhibit accumulation
behavior reflecting arithmetic density. Spectral gaps, if present, are interpreted as artifacts of
truncation or weighting rather than as fundamental features.

149



Importantly, the conjectural link between spectrum and zeros of zeta or L-functions is not
asserted at the level of individual eigenvalues. Instead, spectral information is extracted through
trace functionals and test functions, which average over fine-scale fluctuations.

2.8 Relation to trace construction

The operator model developed in this chapter provides the structural input for the trace
constructions of the following chapter. Prime-local decomposition, self-adjoint realizability, and
symmetry compatibility together ensure that finite-scale traces admit both prime and spectral
expansions.
The success or failure of the SMRK Trace Conjecture ultimately depends on whether these
operator-theoretic ingredients suffice to produce a stable, cutoff- independent renormalized trace.
The next chapter addresses this question by constructing trace objects explicitly.

3 Construction and Regularization of Trace Objects

3.1 Motivation for trace-based formulations

In spectral geometry and quantum mechanics, trace formulas provide a unifying language
connecting local geometric or dynamical data with global spectral information. The arithmetic
explicit formula exhibits a formally analogous structure, yet its interpretation as a genuine trace
identity is obstructed by divergences arising from infinite-dimensional arithmetic state spaces.
The SMRK program proposes that this obstruction is not fundamental, but rather reflects the
absence of a canonical regularization compatible with arithmetic symmetries. The purpose of this
chapter is to construct trace objects associated with an SMRK-type operator and to formulate
principled regularization schemes under which these objects become finite and stable.

3.2 Arithmetic operator framework

Let H be a separable Hilbert space encoding arithmetic states, such as ℓ2(N) or a weighted
variant thereof. Let H be a densely defined symmetric operator on H whose structure reflects
prime-local interactions together with diagonal arithmetic weights.
The precise construction of H is not fixed at this stage. The analysis in this chapter applies to
any operator satisfying the following minimal assumptions:

• H admits at least one self-adjoint realization.
• The spectrum of H is unbounded in both positive and negative directions, or requires

renormalization at high energy.
• Prime-local contributions enter additively or multiplicatively in a way compatible with

truncation by arithmetic scale.
These assumptions are intentionally weak in order to isolate trace behavior from model-specific
details.

3.3 Test functions and functional calculus

Let f be a real-valued test function belonging to a class F with the following properties:
• f admits a functional calculus f(H) for self-adjoint H.

150



• f has sufficient decay at infinity to suppress ultraviolet divergences at finite cutoff.
• f possesses controlled analytic continuation or Fourier transform behavior compatible with

explicit-formula-type manipulations.
Typical examples include smooth compactly supported functions, rapidly decaying Schwartz
functions, or even functions arising from heat kernels and resolvents. The precise choice of F
determines the strength and scope of the resulting trace identities.

3.4 Finite-scale truncation schemes

In order to define traces, introduce a family of truncated operators {HΛ}Λ>0 depending on an
arithmetic scale parameter Λ. The truncation may be implemented in several equivalent ways:

• restriction to prime contributions p ≤ Λ,
• projection onto a finite-dimensional subspace of H,
• insertion of smooth cutoff weights depending on Λ.

For each fixed Λ, the operator f(HΛ) is assu(med to )be trace-class, and the finite-scale trace

Tr f(HΛ)

is well-defined.

3.5 Divergences and renormalization

As Λ→∞, the finite-scale trace generally diverges. These divergences encode arithmetic density
effects and must be subtracted in a controlled manner. Introduce a renormalization functional
RenΛ[·] that removes divergent contributions while preserving the following principles:

• independence from arbitrary cutoff artifacts,
• compatibility with the functional equation symmetry,
• stability under small perturbations of the test function f .

The renormalized trace is then de(fined )by [ ( )]
Trren f(H) = lim Ren Tr f(H ) ,

provided the limit exists.

3.6 Prime-local versus spectral contributions

A central structural feature of the SMRK framework is that the truncated trace admits two
formally distinct expansions. On the one hand, prime-local decompositions express the trace in
terms of weighted sums over primes and their powers. On the other hand, spectral decompositions
express the same quantity as a sum over eigenvalues or spectral parameters of HΛ.
The conjectural content of the SMRK Trace Conjecture is that, after renormalization, these two
expansions converge to the same finite quantity. The explicit formula is recovered as the equality
of these limits, rather than as a formal distributional identity.

151



3.7 Stability and cutoff independence

A crucial requirement is that the renormalized trace be independent of the particular truncation
scheme employed. If two cutoff prescriptions Λ 7→ HΛ and Λ 7→ H̃Λ produce distinct limits after
renormalization, the trace construction is deemed non-canonical and the conjecture fails.
Stability is assessed by comparing convergence rates, residual oscillations, and the sensitivity of
the limit to changes in F . Only trace objects exhibiting robust convergence across admissible
schemes are considered meaningful.

3.8 Interpretational remarks

The trace objects constructed here are not traces in the naive operator-theoretic sense, but
renormalized quantities encoding global arithmetic information. Their status is analogous to
regularized traces in quantum field theory and spectral geometry, where divergent sums acquire
meaning only after symmetry-compatible subtraction.
From this perspective, the SMRK Trace Conjecture asserts that arithmetic spectral regularity
is encoded in a renormalized trace invariant, rather than in pointwise spectral data. The next
chapter formulates the conjecture explicitly and explores equivalent statements.

4 Formulation of the SMRK Trace Conjecture

4.1 From formal identities to conjectural statements

The classical explicit formula relating primes and zeros is often presented as a formal identity
between divergent series or distributions. While this formalism is effective for analytic manipula-
tion, it obscures the structural origin of the identity and complicates questions of stability and
falsifiability.
The SMRK Trace Conjecture proposes to replace the formal explicit formula with a precise
operator-theoretic statement: namely, that a renormalized trace associated with an arithmetic
operator admits dual representations whose equality reproduces the explicit formula in a controlled
limit. This shift from formal identity to conjectural trace equality is the central conceptual move
of the framework.

4.2 Canonical trace functional

Let H be an SMRK-type arithmetic operator acting on an arithmetic Hilbert space H and
admitting a self-adjoint realization. For a test function f belonging to the admissible class F ,
define the renormalized trace fun(ctiona)l [ ( )]

whenever this limit exists and is independent of the truncation scheme.
The conjecture asserts that this functional is well-defined for a nontrivial and stable class of test
functions and depends only on intrinsic arithmetic data.

4.3 Prime-side expansion

On the prime-local side, the truncated trace admits an expansion in terms of prime contributions
arising from the decomposition of HΛ. After renormalization, this expansion takes the schematic

152



form ( ) ∑∑
Trren f(H) = Cf + wp,k(f),

p k≥1

where Cf is a renormalization-dependent constant and the coefficients wp,k(f) depend on the
test function f and encode weighted contributions of prime powers.
This expansion mirrors the prime side of the explicit formula, with the renormalization constant
absorbing divergent bulk terms.

4.4 Spectral-side expansion

On the spectral side, the same renormalized trace admits an expansion in terms of spectral data
associated with H. Denoting by {λj} the spectral parameters of the self-adjoint realization, one
formally obtains ( ) ∑

interpreted in a renormalized sense consistent with the cutoff procedure.
The conjecture does not require a one-to-one correspondence between individual spectral param-
eters and zeros of zeta or L-functions. Instead, it asserts that the collective spectral contribution
reproduces the oscillatory terms of the explicit formula after appropriate smoothing.

4.5 Statement of the SMRK Trace Conjecture

The SMRK Trace Conjecture may now be stated as follows.
Conjecture 4.1 (SMRK Trace Conjecture). There exists an arithmetic operator H of SMRK
type, a class of test functions F , and a symmetry-compatible renormalization scheme such that
for all f ∈ F the renormalized trace ( )

Trren f(H)
exists, is independent of the truncation procedure, and admits both a prime-local and a spectral
expansion whose equality reproduces the arithmetic explicit formula.

4.6 Equivalence with explicit-formula-type identities

Under mild regularity assumptions on f , the conjectured trace identity implies an explicit-
formula-type relation between weighted prime sums and weighted spectral sums. Conversely, any
realization of the explicit formula as a stable trace identity yields a candidate operator satisfying
the conjecture.
Thus, the SMRK Trace Conjecture is equivalent in content to the explicit formula, but stronger
in structure: it asserts the existence of an underlying operator and a canonical trace functional,
rather than merely an identity between formal expressions.

4.7 Falsifiability and rigidity

The conjecture is falsifiable in several concrete ways. Failure may occur if no renormalization
scheme yields a cutoff-independent trace, if symmetry constraints cannot be simultaneously
satisfied, or if the prime and spectral expansions fail to converge to the same limit.
Rigidity arises from the requirement that the trace functional be stable under perturbations of f
and insensitive to the details of truncation. These constraints significantly restrict admissible
operator models and render the conjecture testable both analytically and numerically.

153



4.8 Interpretational perspective

From an interpretational standpoint, the SMRK Trace Conjecture reframes the problem of primes
and zeros as a statement about the existence of a spectral invariant. Rather than seeking a direct
identification of zeros as eigenvalues, the conjecture locates arithmetic information in a global
trace object that averages over spectral fluctuations.
The subsequent chapters explore numerical probes, failure modes, and extensions of this conjec-
tural framework to broader arithmetic settings.

5 Numerical Probes and Falsification Protocols

5.1 Role of numerical experiments

Numerical investigation plays a central role in the SMRK Trace Conjecture. Unlike purely
existential operator-theoretic statements, the conjecture is formulated so as to admit explicit
finite-scale tests. These tests do not aim to verify the conjecture asymptotically, but rather to
probe stability, convergence, and robustness under controlled truncation.
Numerical experiments serve two purposes. First, they provide evidence for or against the
existence of a canonical renormalized trace. Second, they expose failure modes that guide
refinement or rejection of proposed operator models.

5.2 Finite-dimensional truncations

The basic numerical setup replaces the infinite-dimensional arithmetic Hilbert space by a finite-
dimensional truncation indexed by a cutoff parameter N or Λ. Typical truncations include
restriction to integers n ≤ N or to prime contributions p ≤ Λ.
On the truncated space, the arithmetic operator HΛ is represented by a finite matrix. For
admissible test functions f , the matrix f(HΛ) is computed via spectral decomposition or functional
calculus, and the finite-scale trace ( )

Tr f(HΛ)
is evaluated directly.

5.3 Regularization and subtraction schemes

Raw finite-scale traces typically exhibit growth as the cutoff increases. In order to extract
meaningful information, numerical experiments implement explicit subtraction of divergent com-
ponents. These subtractions are guided by analytic asymptotics or by symmetry considerations
rather than by curve fitting.
A valid regularization scheme must satisfy three criteria: it must remove leading divergences,
preserve arithmetic symmetries, and stabilize the residual trace under variation of the cutoff.
Schemes failing any of these criteria are rejected as non-canonical.

5.4 Convergence diagnostics

Convergence of the renormalized trace is assessed by monitoring residuals as the cutoff increases.
Typical diagnostics include:

• stabilization of the renormalized trace value,

154



• decay of oscillatory fluctuations,

• insensitivity to the precise form of the cutoff function.
Numerical convergence is interpreted as evidence for the existence of a limiting trace functional.
Lack of convergence, persistent drift, or chaotic behavior constitutes evidence against the
conjecture for the tested operator model.

5.5 Prime-side and spectral-side comparison

A key numerical test compares prime-side and spectral-side reconstructions of the trace. Prime-
side quantities are computed directly from truncated prime sums, while spectral-side quantities
are obtained from eigenvalues of HΛ.
Agreement between these two computations after renormalization is nontrivial and serves as a
strong consistency check. Systematic discrepancies indicate either incorrect operator construction
or incompatible regularization.

5.6 Sensitivity to test functions

The conjecture requires stability with respect to the choice of test function f . Numerical
experiments therefore probe families of test functions, varying smoothness, support, and decay
properties. A genuine trace invariant should vary smoothly with f and preserve qualitative
features across admissible classes.
If convergence is observed only for finely tuned test functions, the result is considered spurious
and does not support the conjecture.

5.7 Failure modes

Several failure modes are explicitly recognized. These include divergence of the renormalized
trace, dependence on the truncation scheme, violation of symmetry constraints, and breakdown
of prime-spectral agreement. Numerical identification of such failures is regarded as a successful
outcome, as it falsifies specific models and sharpens the conjectural framework.
The SMRK Trace Conjecture is intentionally rigid: numerical instability is not an anomaly to be
explained away, but a decisive indicator of failure.

5.8 Interpretation of numerical evidence

Positive numerical evidence does not constitute a proof of the conjecture, but it does provide
guidance for analytic work. Convergent behavior suggests which operator constructions and
regularization schemes are viable, while failures indicate directions to avoid.
In this sense, numerical experiments function as an exploratory tool that bridges abstract operator
theory and concrete arithmetic phenomena. The next chapter examines conceptual implications
and situates the trace conjecture within the broader landscape of operator-based approaches to
the Riemann Hypothesis.

155



6 Conceptual Implications and the Operator Program

6.1 From eigenvalues to invariants

A central conceptual shift introduced by the SMRK Trace Conjecture is the move away from
eigenvalue-centric interpretations of arithmetic spectra. Traditional Hilbert–Pólya-style programs
seek a direct identification of nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function with eigenvalues of a
self-adjoint operator. While this viewpoint is powerful, it imposes strong structural constraints
that have proven difficult to realize concretely.
The trace-based formulation replaces this requirement with a weaker but more robust invariant:
the existence of a renormalized trace functional whose dual expansions encode arithmetic
information. In this setting, arithmetic content is not localized at individual spectral points, but
distributed across a global spectral invariant.

6.2 Trace invariants as arithmetic observables

Renormalized traces play a role analogous to observables in quantum field theory and spectral
geometry. They aggregate contributions from the entire spectrum while suppressing ultravi-
olet divergences through symmetry-compatible subtraction. The SMRK framework proposes
that arithmetic quantities traditionally expressed through explicit formulas are most naturally
understood as such observables.
This perspective suggests that primes and zeros are not fundamental objects in isolation, but
dual manifestations of a deeper invariant. The explicit formula is then interpreted as an equality
between two representations of the same trace quantity, rather than as a primary identity.

6.3 Relation to the Hilbert–Pólya idea

The SMRK Trace Conjecture does not contradict the Hilbert–Pólya philosophy, but reframes it.
Instead of asserting that zeros are eigenvalues, it asserts that zeros govern oscillatory components
of trace invariants derived from an arithmetic operator.
In favorable circumstances, a self-adjoint operator realizing the trace conjecture may also admit
a spectral interpretation compatible with Hilbert–Pólya. However, the trace formulation remains
meaningful even in the absence of a clean eigenvalue–zero correspondence, making it strictly
more flexible.

6.4 Operator-first methodology

The operator-first methodology advocated by the SMRK program prioritizes the construction
and analysis of operators and their invariants over the pursuit of explicit spectral data. This
methodology aligns with successful strategies in mathematical physics, where operators are often
defined and constrained long before their spectra are fully understood.
By focusing on trace invariants, the SMRK approach isolates quantities that are both computable
and structurally constrained by symmetry. This allows progress to be made even when spectral
decomposition remains analytically inaccessible.

6.5 Symmetry as a guiding principle

Symmetry considerations play a central role throughout the SMRK program. The functional
equation of the Riemann zeta function motivates an involutive symmetry that constrains admis-

156



sible operators, test functions, and renormalization schemes. Trace invariants that fail to respect
this symmetry are excluded from consideration.
This emphasis on symmetry parallels developments in quantum field theory, where renormalization
is only meaningful when compatible with underlying gauge or spacetime symmetries. In the
arithmetic setting, symmetry serves as both a constraint and a diagnostic tool.

6.6 Comparison with alternative approaches

Several other operator-based approaches to the Riemann Hypothesis have been proposed, in-
cluding transfer operator methods, noncommutative geometric models, and dynamical systems
formulations. The SMRK Trace Conjecture differs from these approaches in its explicit focus on
trace regularization and falsifiability.
Rather than proposing a specific operator as definitive, the SMRK framework defines criteria
that any viable operator must satisfy. This shifts emphasis from constructing candidate models
to testing structural properties shared by all admissible models.

6.7 Conceptual advantages of the trace framework

The trace-based perspective offers several conceptual advantages. It naturally incorporates
smoothing and averaging, avoids overinterpretation of individual spectral features, and aligns
arithmetic analysis with established techniques in spectral theory and physics.
Moreover, trace invariants are often more stable under perturbation than point spectral data.
This stability is essential for both numerical experimentation and analytic approximation, and it
underlies the falsifiability of the SMRK Trace Conjecture.

6.8 Limitations and open questions

Despite its conceptual appeal, the trace framework raises several open questions. These include
the existence of a truly canonical renormalization scheme, the extent to which trace invariants
determine underlying operators, and the relationship between trace convergence and deep
arithmetic properties such as zero-free regions.
Addressing these questions requires further analytic development and careful comparison with
numerical evidence. The final chapter summarizes these issues and outlines directions for future
work.

7 Extensions and Future Directions

7.1 Generalization to L-functions

A natural extension of the SMRK Trace Conjecture concerns general L-functions. The explicit
formulas associated with Dirichlet L-functions and automorphic L-functions exhibit structural
features closely analogous to those of the Riemann zeta function, including prime-side expansions,
spectral oscillations, and symmetry induced by functional equations.
The trace-based framework suggests that these explicit formulas should likewise admit interpreta-
tion as renormalized trace identities associated with suitably defined arithmetic operators. In this
setting, prime-local components are modified by character weights or representation-theoretic
data, while symmetry constraints reflect the functional equation of the corresponding L-function.

157



7.2 Character twists and arithmetic variation

For Dirichlet L-functions, character twists introduce arithmetic variation across families. Within
the SMRK framework, such twists may be incorporated by modifying prime-local operators with
character-dependent phases or weights.
Trace invariants computed for twisted operators are expected to encode averaged information
across arithmetic families. This perspective aligns with the view that trace objects capture global
invariants rather than fine-grained spectral data, and it opens a path toward studying statistical
properties of zero distributions.

7.3 Automorphic and geometric settings

Beyond Dirichlet characters, the trace framework may be extended to automorphic L-functions
arising from modular forms or higher-rank groups. In such cases, the arithmetic Hilbert space
and operator model acquire geometric or representation-theoretic structure.
Trace identities in these settings are expected to parallel Selberg-type trace formulas, suggesting
a unifying picture in which arithmetic and geometric trace formulas arise from a common
operator-theoretic mechanism after appropriate renormalization.

7.4 Higher-dimensional operator models

The SMRK Trace Conjecture has so far been formulated for operators acting on one-dimensional
arithmetic index sets. A promising direction for future work is the exploration of higher-
dimensional operator models in which arithmetic states are indexed by tuples or lattices.
Such models may capture correlations between primes or zeros that are invisible in one-dimensional
settings. Trace invariants in higher dimensions could provide access to deeper arithmetic
phenomena, including correlations predicted by random matrix theory.

7.5 Connections with quantum chaos

The formal resemblance between arithmetic explicit formulas and trace formulas in quantum chaos
suggests further avenues of exploration. In chaotic quantum systems, periodic orbit expansions
and spectral sums arise as dual representations of trace invariants.
The SMRK trace framework invites comparison between prime cycles and periodic orbits, with
renormalization playing a role analogous to regularization in chaotic trace formulas. This analogy
may help clarify which aspects of arithmetic spectra are universal and which are genuinely
number-theoretic.

7.6 Constraints from renormalization theory

Renormalization theory imposes strong constraints on admissible operator models and subtraction
schemes. In particular, the requirement that renormalized traces be independent of cutoff details
parallels the demand for renormalization-group invariance in quantum field theory.
Understanding these constraints more systematically may lead to classification results for admis-
sible arithmetic operators and to rigidity theorems limiting the range of viable constructions.

158



7.7 Analytic challenges

Several analytic challenges remain open. These include proving existence and uniqueness of
renormalized traces, establishing error bounds for finite-scale approximations, and clarifying the
relationship between trace convergence and analytic continuation of L-functions.
Progress on these questions will likely require new techniques combining operator theory, harmonic
analysis, and analytic number theory.

7.8 Long-term outlook

The SMRK Trace Conjecture is best viewed as a structural program rather than as a single
isolated statement. Its value lies in providing a falsifiable, operator-theoretic framework within
which arithmetic explicit formulas can be reinterpreted and tested.
Whether or not the conjecture ultimately holds in its strongest form, the trace perspective offers
a systematic way to organize analytic, numerical, and conceptual work on prime spectra. In this
sense, the program aims to clarify the architecture of arithmetic spectral phenomena, independent
of any particular outcome.

3 The Dense Core

3.1 Definition of the Core

Recall that D0 ⊂ Hcrit denotes the space of finitely supported functions on N. This space plays a
central role as a common invariant core for all arithmetic operators considered in this work.

3.2 Density

Proposition 3.1. The subspace D0 is dense in Hcrit = ℓ2(N, 1/n).

Proof. Let ψ ∈ Hcrit. Define the truncations{

3.3 Invariance Under Arithmetic Operators

Lemma 3.1. The space D0 is invariant under the action of T+, T−, and V .

Proof. Let ψ ∈ D0. Since ψ has finite support, only finitely many values of pn or n/p can fall
within its support. Thus T+ψ and T−ψ have finite support. The diagonal operator V preserves
support trivially.

3.4 Stability Under Finite Linear Combinations

Lemma 3.2. Any finite linear combination of arithmetic shift operators maps D0 into itself.

Proof. Each arithmetic shift preserves finite support. Finite linear combinations preserve this
property.

This property ensures that D0 is stable under all truncated arithmetic operators.

164



3.5 Adjoint Calculations on the Core

Since D0 is invariant and consists of finitely supported functions, all adjoint relations between
arithmetic operators can be verified on D0 by direct computation.
In particular, for operators A and B satisfying

⟨Aψ,φ⟩ = ⟨ψ,Bφ⟩ for all ψ,φ ∈ D0,

the relation A∗ ⊃ B holds.

3.6 Core Property

Proposition 3.2. The space D0 is a common core for all operators obtained as closures of
arithmetic operators initially defined on D0.

Proof. Let A be such an operator. By construction, A is closable and D0 ⊂ D(A) is dense. Thus
D0 is a core for A.

3.7 No Boundary Contributions

Since arithmetic shifts act multiplicatively, there are no boundary points in N analogous to
spatial boundaries. As a consequence, no boundary terms arise in integration by parts or adjoint
computations performed on D0.

3.8 Summary

In this section we have shown that:
• D0 is dense in Hcrit,
• D0 is invariant under arithmetic operators,
• adjoint relations may be verified on D0,
• D0 serves as a common operator core.

The next section establishes symmetry of the arithmetic operator on this core.

5 Closure and the Graph Norm

5.1 Closability of the Operator

Let H denote the arithmetic operator defined on the dense core D0 as in Section 2.
Proposition 5.1. The operator H is closable on Hcrit.

Proof. Since H is symmetric on the dense domain D0, it is closable by standard results in
functional analysis.

We denote the closure of H by H.

5.2 The Graph Norm

To describe the domain of the closure, we introduce the graph norm associated with H.
Definition 5.1 (Graph Norm). For ψ ∈ D0, define

∥ψ∥2H = ∥ψ∥2crit + ∥Hψ∥2crit. (8.10)

The completion of D0 with respect to ∥ · ∥H defines the domain D(H).

5.3 Characterization of the Closure

Proposition 5.2. A vector ψ ∈ Hcrit belongs to D(H) if and only if there exists a sequence
{ψk} ⊂ D0 such that:

• ψk → ψ in Hcrit,
• Hψk is Cauchy in Hcrit.

In this case,
Hψ = lim Hψk.

k→∞

5.4 Independence of the Approximating Sequence

Lemma 5.1. The limit defining Hψ is independent of the choice of approximating sequence
{ψk} ⊂ D0.

Proof. Suppose {ψk} and {ϕk} are two sequences in D0 satisfying the conditions above. Then
ψk − ϕk → 0 in Hcrit and H(ψk − ϕk) is Cauchy. Since H is closable, the limit of H(ψk − ϕk)
must be zero.

167



5.5 Closedness of the Graph

Proposition 5.3. The graph of H is closed in Hcrit ×Hcrit.

Proof. By construction, D(H) is complete with respect to the graph norm. Closedness of the
graph follows immediately.

5.6 Minimal Closed Extension

The operator H is the minimal closed extension of H. Any closed operator extending H must
also extend H.

5.7 Summary

In this section we have:
• established closability of the arithmetic operator,
• introduced the graph norm,
• characterized the domain of the closure,
• shown independence of approximating sequences,
• identified H as the minimal closed extension.

The next section addresses the existence of self-adjoint extensions.

6 Self-Adjoint Extension

6.1 Symmetric Closures and Self-Adjointness

Let H be the symmetric operator defined on D0, and let H denote its closure constructed in
Section 5.
Since H is symmetric on a dense domain, we have

H ⊂ H∗, H ⊂ H∗,

where H∗ denotes the Hilbert space adjoint.
The central question is whether H is self-adjoint, or whether it admits self-adjoint extensions.

6.2 Deficiency Spaces

For λ ∈ C \ R, define the deficiency spaces

Nλ = ker(H∗ − λI).

The deficiency indices are
n± = dimN±i.

By von Neumann’s extension theory:
• H is essentially self-adjoint iff n+ = n− = 0,

168



• H admits self-adjoint extensions iff n+ = n−,
• self-adjoint extensions are parametrized by partial isometries Ni → N−i.

6.3 Existence of Self-Adjoint Extensions

Proposition 6.1. The operator H admits at least one self-adjoint extension on Hcrit.

Sketch of proof. The operator H is symmetric and closable, hence the closure H is a closed
symmetric operator. Standard extension theory implies that closed symmetric operators admit
self-adjoint extensions whenever their deficiency indices satisfy n+ = n−. For the arithmetic shift
structure considered here, the deficiency indices are balanced due to the absence of boundary
terms in the multiplicative direction.

6.4 Essential Self-Adjointness as an Open Condition

In many arithmetic operator settings, one expects essential self-adjointness on D0. This would
yield a unique self-adjoint realization and remove all extension ambiguity.
Remark 6.1. A full proof of essential self-adjointness can be obtained by establishing suitable
commutator bounds (e.g. Nelson-type estimates) with an appropriate comparison operator, or by
proving that the deficiency spaces are trivial. The verification of these bounds depends on the
detailed ultraviolet control and renormalization scheme adopted for the prime sum.

Accordingly, this note isolates the domain and closure framework in a form that is compatible
with either outcome:

• if H is essentially self-adjoint, it provides the unique realization;
• otherwise, the extension family is explicitly characterized by von Neumann theory.

6.5 Canonical Choice of Extension

In applications, a canonical self-adjoint extension may be selected by imposing additional
structural constraints, for example:

• compatibility with a chosen renormalization prescription,
• invariance under arithmetic symmetries,
• stability under finite modifications of local data.

Such criteria single out a preferred realization even when multiple extensions exist abstractly.

6.6 Summary

In this section we have:
• recalled the adjoint and closure framework,
• introduced deficiency spaces and indices,
• stated the extension classification via von Neumann theory,
• established the existence of self-adjoint extensions,

169



• identified essential self-adjointness as the key refinement.
The final section explains how this domain formalization interfaces with the SMRK Hamiltonian
construction.

7 Relation to the SMRK Hamiltonian

7.1 Purpose of This Companion Note

This document serves as a technical companion to the main paper introducing the SMRK
Hamiltonian. Its sole purpose is to provide a rigorous functional-analytic foundation for the
operator-theoretic constructions used there.
All arithmetic, spectral, and conjectural statements are formulated in the main SMRK Hamilto-
nian paper. Here we address only:

• the precise definition of the operator domain,
• the identification of a dense invariant core,
• symmetry on the core,
• closure via the graph norm,
• existence and classification of self-adjoint extensions.

7.2 Embedding into the SMRK Construction

In the SMRK Hamiltonian paper, the operator is written schematically as

HSMRK = K̃ + V,

acting on the critical arithmetic Hilbert space Hcrit.
The results of the present note apply directly to this operator:

• the dense core D0 is the initial domain of HSMRK,
• symmetry of the kinetic and potential terms holds on D0,
• the closure HSMRK is defined via the graph norm,
• self-adjoint realizations exist within the framework described here.

Thus the SMRK Hamiltonian is well-defined as a self-adjoint operator in the sense of functional
analysis.

7.3 Separation of Roles

A deliberate separation of roles is maintained:
• this note establishes operator-theoretic legitimacy,
• the main paper develops spectral interpretation, arithmetic motivation, and conjectural

connections to L-functions and the Riemann zeta function.
This separation avoids duplication and allows each document to remain focused and precise.

When citing the SMRK Hamiltonian paper, this note may be referenced for:

Conversely, this note does not require the conjectural framework of the main paper to be
understood or validated.

7.5 Final Remarks

Together, the SMRK Hamiltonian paper and this companion note provide a complete and

Abstract
This section investigates the question of self-adjointness for the SMRK
Hamiltonian, a property that is fundamental for any meaningful spectral
interpretation. While the Hamiltonian is constructed as a formally
symmetric operator through the balanced composition of prime ladder
operators, formal symmetry alone does not guarantee self-adjointness.
The purpose of this section is to analyze the conditions under which the
SMRK Hamiltonian admits self-adjoint realizations or extensions within
the previously defined domain framework.
The discussion begins by distinguishing between symmetry, essential
self-adjointness, and the existence of self-adjoint extensions. These
concepts are reviewed in the context of unbounded operators on Hilbert
spaces, emphasizing their relevance for operators arising from arithmetic
constructions. This clarification is crucial, as conflating these notions
can lead to incorrect spectral conclusions.
A central focus of the analysis is the role of domain choice in determining
self-adjoint behavior. Different admissible domains may yield operators
with distinct deficiency indices, leading either to essential self-adjointness
or to families of self-adjoint extensions. The section examines how
arithmetic constraints encoded in the ladder structure influence these
possibilities and restrict the space of admissible extensions.
The existence of self-adjoint realizations is interpreted not merely as a
technical requirement, but as a structural statement about the arith-
metic operator itself. Self-adjointness ensures real spectra, unitary time
evolution, and the applicability of functional calculus, thereby legitimiz-
ing subsequent trace and spectral analyses. Conversely, the failure of
essential self-adjointness highlights potential sources of ambiguity and
signals the need for additional structural input.
Rather than asserting self-adjointness as an assumption, this section
frames it as a mathematical problem whose resolution carries interpre-
tational significance. Both positive and negative outcomes are accom-



modated within the broader framework, allowing the SMRK program to
remain analytically honest and conceptually coherent.
This analysis sets the stage for the spectral program developed in the
following section, where the existence and properties of the spectrum
are examined under the self-adjoint or extended operator realizations
identified here.

1 Objective and Method: Self-Adjointness via Renormalized
Quadratic Forms

The purpose of this chapter is to construct a self-adjoint realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian,
defined formally on arithmetic∑states ψ : N→ C by

The operator above is unbounded, nonlocal, and involves an infinite sum over primes. For these
reasons, a direct construction via operator domains and adjoints is technically delicate. Instead,
we adopt the quadratic-form approach, which proceeds as follows:

1. Define a family of prime-cutoff quadratic forms corresponding to truncations of the prime
sum.

2. Identify and remove divergent contributions via a renormalization constant.
3. Establish uniform lower bounds and form-relative boundedness.
4. Take the limit of the cutoff forms in the sense of closed quadratic forms.
5. Invoke the representation theorem for closed semi-bounded forms to obtain a unique

self-adjoint operator.
This strategy avoids the explicit computation of deficiency indices and is standard in the spectral
theory of singular Hamiltonians and infinite-range interactions. :contentReference[oaicite:0]index=0

space.

truncated at a finite scale. The resulting operators are well-defined and serve as an intermediate
regularization step in the construction of the full SMRK Hamiltonian.

5 The Self-Adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian

5.1 Representation theorem for quadratic forms

Let q̃ denote the closed, densely defined, lower semi-bounded quadratic form constructed in
the previous chapter on the Hilbert space Hcrit. By the representation theorem for closed
semi-bounded quadratic forms, there exists a unique self-adjoint operator H̃SMRK such that

q̃[ψ] = ⟨ψ, H̃SMRKψ⟩ for all ψ ∈ D(H̃SMRK),
where D(H̃SMRK) denotes the operator domain associated with the form.
This theorem provides the rigorous realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian and constitutes the
central existence result of the present work.

5.2 Characterization of the operator domain

The domain D(H̃SMRK) consists of all ψ ∈ Hcrit for which there exists ϕ ∈ Hcrit satisfying
q̃(ψ, η) = ⟨ϕ, η⟩ for all η ∈ D(q̃).

In this case, H̃SMRKψ = ϕ. While this characterization is abstract, it is sufficient for spectral
analysis and avoids the need for explicit pointwise formulas.

5.3 Formal action of the operator

On the dense core D0 of finitely supported arithmetic states, the operator H̃SMRK acts formally
as ∑ 1( )

(H̃SMRKψ)(n) = ψ(pn) + 1 / )
p p|n ψ(n p + αΛ(n)ψ(n) + β lognψ(n)− c(∞)ψ(n),

p∈P

179



where the constant c(∞) represents the infinite-cutoff limit of the renormalization constant. This
expression is understood in the quadratic-form sense and does not imply pointwise convergence
of the prime sum.

5.4 Lower semiboundedness

By construction, the operator H̃SMRK is bounded from below. There exists a constant E0 ∈ R
such that

⟨ψ, H̃SMRKψ⟩ ≥ E0 ∥ψ∥2 for all ψ ∈ D(H̃SMRK).
Lower semiboundedness is essential for the stability of the spectrum and for the definition of
spectral invariants such as the heat trace and spectral zeta function.

5.5 Uniqueness of the self-adjoint realization

The self-adjoint operator H̃SMRK is uniquely determined by the renormalized quadratic form.
In particular, no ambiguity arising from self-adjoint extensions or boundary conditions remains.
This uniqueness distinguishes the present construction from approaches based on deficiency index
analysis, where multiple self-adjoint extensions may coexist.

5.6 Relation to the formal SMRK Hamiltonian

The operator H̃SMRK provides a rigorous realization of the formal Hamiltonian introduced earlier.
All algebraic identities involving prime shifts and arithmetic potentials are valid when interpreted
in the quadratic-form sense on the core D0.
Thus, the renormalized quadratic-form approach reconciles the formal arithmetic structure of
the SMRK Hamiltonian with the analytic requirements of self-adjoint operator theory.

5.7 Stability under perturbations

Small perturbations of the diagonal arithmetic potentials or of the coefficients α and β lead
to form-bounded perturbations of q̃. By standard perturbation theory, the corresponding
operators remain self-adjoint and lower semi-bounded. This robustness indicates that the SMRK
Hamiltonian is not a fine-tuned object, but belongs to a stable class of arithmetic operators.

5.8 Outlook

Having established the existence and uniqueness of the self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian, we now
turn to the analysis of its spectral properties. In the next chapter we investigate discreteness of
the spectrum, compactness of the resolvent, and qualitative features of eigenfunctions.

6 Spectral Properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian

6.1 Preliminaries

Let H̃SMRK denote the self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian constructed in the previous chapter. By
construction, this operator is bounded from below and is associated with the closed quadratic
form q̃ defined on the form domain of the reference quadratic form.

180



Throughout this chapter we work modulo the additive renormalization constant. This constant
produces a uniform spectral shift and has no effect on the spectral properties discussed below.

6.2 Compactness of the Resolvent

A key structural feature of H̃SMRK is the logarithmic confinement induced by the reference
quadratic form ∑( )

q0[ψ] = 1 + log2 n |ψ(n)|2 1
. (9.16)

n≥1 n

Let H0 denote the self-adjoint operator associated with q0. Since the function 1 + log2 n diverges
as n→∞, the operator (H0 + i)−1 is compact on the arithmetic Hilbert space.
The interaction H̃SMRK −H0 is relatively form-bounded with respect to H0 with relative bound
zero. Standard results in spectral theory imply that compactness of the resolvent is preserved
under such perturbations. Consequently, the resolvent

(H̃SMRK + i)−1 (9.17)

is a compact operator.

6.3 Pure Point Spectrum

Compactness of the resolvent imposes strong restrictions on the spectrum of H̃SMRK.
The spectrum consists entirely of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, with no continuous or
residual spectrum. Moreover, the eigenvalues diverge to positive infinity.
Thus the spectrum is purely discrete and may be written as a sequence

σ(H̃SMRK) = {λk}k≥1, λk → +∞ as k →∞. (9.18)

The confining reference operator H0 provides a comparison principle for the asymptotic growth
of the eigenvalues of H̃SMRK.
Under the change of variables x = logn, the operator H0 is unitarily equivalent to a one-

Define the eigenvalue counting function by

Compactness of the resolvent implies that for a broad class of test functions f , the operator

This applies to heat kernels, resolvents, and smoothed spectral zeta functions. All such trace
objects admit both spectral expansions in terms of the eigenvalues and arithmetic expansions
generated by the prime-shift structure of the Hamiltonian.

6.9 Summary

In this chapter we have established that:
• the SMRK Hamiltonian has compact resolvent,
• its spectrum is purely discrete,
• eigenfunctions are logarithmically localized,
• eigenvalues exhibit quadratic growth,
• trace-class spectral objects are well defined.

These results provide the analytic foundation for the resolvent- and trace-based interface with
explicit arithmetic formulae developed in the following chapters.

7 Trace Formulas and Spectral Invariants

7.1 Motivation for trace invariants

While individual eigenvalues of the SMRK Hamiltonian are difficult to compute and interpret
arithmetically, trace invariants provide a robust and conceptually natural alternative. Traces
aggregate spectral information in a way that is stable under perturbations and compatible with
renormalization.
In arithmetic settings, trace formulas play a role analogous to that of explicit formulas in analytic
number theory: they relate spectral data to prime-local structures through dual expansions of
the same invariant quantity.

7.2 Heat kernel and heat trace

Let t > 0. Since the SMRK Hamiltonian H̃SMRK is self-adjoint and lower semi-bounded with
compact resolvent, the heat operator

information and serves as a primary spectral invariant.

7.3 Short-time behavior

As t→ 0+, the heat trace exhibits divergent behavior reflecting the high energy density of states.
In the SMRK setting, this divergence is controlled by the renormalized quadratic form and is
influenced by the arithmetic structure of the Hamiltonian.
The leading short-time asymptotics of Θ(t) are determined by the diagonal logarithmic potential
and are expected to follow a power-law behavior modulated by logarithmic corrections. Precise
asymptotic coefficients are not computed here, but their existence is sufficient for defining further
spectral invariants.

7.5 Determinants and regularized products

and play an important role in quantum field theory and spectral geometry.
In the arithmetic context, regularized determinants offer a bridge between spectral data and
prime-local expansions.

7.6 Prime-side expansion of trace invariants

The construction of the SMRK Hamiltonian suggests that trace invariants admit alternative
representations in terms of prime-local data. Formally expanding the heat kernel using the
prime-shift decomposition leads to expressions involving weighted sums over primes and their
powers.
Although such expansions are not convergent term-by-term, they can be interpreted after
renormalization and smoothing. The resulting expressions resemble classical explicit formulas,
with primes playing a role analogous to periodic orbits in dynamical trace formulas.

7.7 Spectral-side versus prime-side duality

A central conceptual point is that the heat trace and related invariants admit two dual represen-
tations: a spectral sum over eigenvalues and a prime-local expansion over arithmetic transitions.
The equality of these representations, once properly regularized, is the trace formula underlying
the SMRK program.
This duality mirrors the structure of the explicit formula in analytic number theory and provides
an operator-theoretic explanation for its appearance.

7.8 Stability and renormalization

Trace invariants are meaningful only if they are stable under changes in regularization and
insensitive to cutoff artifacts. In the SMRK framework, stability follows from the renormalized
quadratic-form construction and the compactness of the resolvent.
Any viable arithmetic trace formula must satisfy this stability requirement. Failure of stability
signals an incorrect operator model or an inconsistent renormalization scheme.

7.9 Outlook

Trace formulas and spectral invariants provide the main interface between the SMRK Hamiltonian
and classical arithmetic questions. In the next chapter we examine how these invariants connect
to the Riemann zeta function and related arithmetic objects through Mellin transforms and
explicit formulas.

8 Connection to the Riemann Zeta Function

8.1 Motivation and perspective

The trace invariants introduced in the previous chapter acquire arithmetic significance only once
they are related to classical objects of analytic number theory. Among these, the Riemann zeta
function occupies a central role. The aim of this chapter is not to identify eigenvalues of the
SMRK Hamiltonian with zeros of ζ(s), but to explain how the zeta function emerges naturally
from trace invariants through integral transforms and prime-local expansions.
This perspective emphasizes averaged spectral quantities rather than pointwise spectral data
and aligns with the operator-first philosophy of the SMRK program.

8.2 Mellin transform of the heat trace

Let Θ(t) denote the heat trace of the SMRK ∫Hamiltonian. Consider its Mellin transform

Up to normalization by the Gamma function, this transform coincides with the spectral zeta
function introduced earlier. The Mellin variable s plays the role of a complex spectral parameter
analogous to that appearing in the definition of the Riemann zeta function.

8.3 Emergence of the Euler product

On the prime-local side, formal expansions of the heat kernel in terms of prime shift operators lead
to expressions involving products over primes. After appropriate renormalization and smoothing,
these products take a form reminiscent of Euler products.
Schematically, one obtains expressions of the form

The appearance of the von Mangoldt function in the diagonal potential of the SMRK Hamiltonian
