zeta function.

185



8.5 Spectral interpretation of the explicit formula

Combining the spectral-side representation of trace invariants with their prime-side expansions
yields identities that parallel the explicit formula of analytic number theory. Zeros of the zeta
function appear not as individual eigenvalues, but as oscillatory components in the spectral
representation of the trace.
From this viewpoint, the explicit formula is interpreted as a statement about the equality of two
representations of the same renormalized trace invariant, rather than as a direct spectral identity.

8.6 Critical line considerations

The SMRK framework does not require a priori assumptions about the location of zeros of the
zeta function. However, the symmetry properties of the Hamiltonian and of the associated trace
invariants suggest a natural reflection symmetry in Mellin space corresponding to s↔ 1− s.
This symmetry is inherited from the arithmetic structure of the operator and provides a conceptual
explanation for the appearance of the critical line in explicit formulas, without asserting a direct
identification of zeros with eigenvalues.

8.7 Analytic continuation and regularization

Both the spectral zeta function and the Riemann zeta function require analytic continuation
beyond their initial domains of convergence. In the SMRK setting, analytic continuation arises
from the subtraction of short-time divergences in the heat trace and from the renormalized
definition of trace invariants.
This parallel highlights the role of renormalization as a unifying mechanism in both spectral
theory and analytic number theory.

8.8 Limitations of the correspondence

It is important to emphasize the limitations of the correspondence described here. The SMRK
Hamiltonian does not provide a direct spectral realization of the zeros of the Riemann zeta
function. Instead, it offers a framework in which arithmetic information encoded by the zeta
function emerges naturally at the level of trace invariants.
This distinction avoids overinterpretation of the operator model and clarifies the precise scope of
the claims being made.

8.9 Outlook

In the next chapter we examine the role of symmetry and functional equations in greater detail.
We show how reflection symmetries of trace invariants mirror the functional equation of the
Riemann zeta function and constrain admissible operator models.

9 Functional Equation and Symmetry

9.1 Symmetry as a structural principle

One of the most striking features of the Riemann zeta function is the existence of a functional
equation relating values at s and 1− s. Any operator-theoretic framework intended to interface

186



with arithmetic explicit formulas must account for this symmetry at a structural level.
In the SMRK program, symmetry is not imposed post hoc on spectral data, but is built into the
operator construction and the associated trace invariants. This chapter analyzes how functional-
equation-type symmetries emerge naturally from the arithmetic structure of the Hamiltonian.

9.2 Reflection symmetry in Mellin space

Trace invariants associated with the SMRK Hamiltonian admit representations in Mellin space
via integral transforms of the heat trace. In this representation, the natural involution s 7→ 1− s
arises as a reflection symmetry of the Mellin variable.
This symmetry is linked to the logarithmic weighting of arithmetic states and to the invariance
of the underlying Hilbert space under multiplicative inversion at the level of scales. As a result,
trace expressions exhibit paired contributions at s and 1 − s, mirroring the structure of the
functional equation.

9.3 Prime-shift symmetry

At the operator level, symmetry manifests itself through the pairing of forward and backward
prime shifts. The operators Sp and S∗

p appear on equal footing in the symmetrized kinetic terms
of the SMRK Hamiltonian.
This pairing ensures that prime multiplication and division contribute symmetrically to trace
invariants. It is this symmetry that ultimately gives rise to balanced prime-side expansions and
prevents the emergence of spurious asymmetries in the arithmetic trace formulas.

9.4 Diagonal potentials and scale duality

The diagonal arithmetic potentials, particularly the logarithmic term logn, play a crucial role in
implementing scale duality. Under Mellin transformation, multiplication by logn corresponds to
differentiation with respect to the spectral parameter s.
This correspondence is essential for reproducing the structure of the functional equation and for
ensuring that renormalized trace invariants transform covariantly under s 7→ 1− s.

9.5 Symmetry of the renormalization scheme

Renormalization is meaningful only if it preserves the symmetries of the underlying problem. In
the SMRK framework, the subtraction of divergent terms is designed to be invariant under the
same involutions that govern the trace invariants themselves.
Any renormalization scheme that breaks reflection symmetry would lead to inconsistent trace
identities and is therefore excluded. This requirement significantly restricts admissible subtraction
procedures and reinforces the rigidity of the framework.

9.6 Consequences for trace invariants

As a result of the symmetries described above, the trace invariants associated with the SMRK
Hamiltonian satisfy functional relations analogous to those of the Riemann zeta function. While
these relations do not imply a direct spectral realization of zeta zeros, they ensure that trace
formulas respect the same global constraints as the classical explicit formula.

187



Symmetry thus acts as a consistency condition linking operator construction, renormalization,
and arithmetic interpretation.

9.7 Comparison with classical functional equations

In classical analytic number theory, the functional equation of the zeta function is often derived
using Poisson summation or theta-function identities. The SMRK approach replaces these
analytic tools with operator-theoretic symmetry principles.
This shift in perspective highlights the universality of functional equations as manifestations of
deeper symmetries, rather than as isolated analytic accidents.

9.8 Limitations and scope

The symmetry considerations presented here constrain the structure of admissible operators
and trace invariants, but they do not by themselves determine the spectrum of the SMRK
Hamiltonian. Additional analytic input would be required to extract fine-grained information
about zeros or to establish stronger arithmetic consequences.
The role of symmetry in the SMRK program is therefore structural rather than deterministic.

9.9 Outlook

In the final chapter we summarize the construction and its implications, clarify what has and
has not been established, and outline directions for future work and potential falsification of the
SMRK framework.

10 Conclusion and Future Directions

10.1 Summary of the construction

In this work we have constructed a self-adjoint realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian acting
on an arithmetic Hilbert space. The operator arises from symmetrized prime shift interactions
combined with diagonal arithmetic potentials and is defined rigorously through a renormalized
quadratic-form approach.
The construction proceeds in a sequence of conceptually transparent steps: prime cutoffs
regularize the kinetic terms, divergent contributions are removed by a canonical subtraction,
and the resulting closed quadratic form uniquely determines a self-adjoint operator. This
approach avoids ambiguities associated with self-adjoint extensions and ensures stability under
perturbations.

10.2 Spectral and arithmetic features

The resulting SMRK Hamiltonian is lower semi-bounded and has compact resolvent, implying
a purely discrete spectrum. While individual eigenvalues are not identified with arithmetic
quantities, the operator admits a rich family of trace invariants that encode arithmetic information
in an averaged and renormalization-stable manner.
These trace invariants exhibit a dual structure: on the spectral side they are expressed as sums
over eigenvalues, while on the arithmetic side they admit expansions involving primes and prime
powers. This duality mirrors the structure of explicit formulas in analytic number theory.

188



10.3 Relation to the Riemann zeta function

A central outcome of the analysis is the natural emergence of the Riemann zeta function and
its logarithmic derivative from spectral invariants of the SMRK Hamiltonian. This emergence
occurs through Mellin transforms of the heat trace and through the presence of the von Mangoldt
function in the diagonal arithmetic potential.
The correspondence is structural rather than literal: zeros of the zeta function are not claimed
to coincide with eigenvalues of the Hamiltonian. Instead, the operator framework reproduces the
architecture of the explicit formula at the level of renormalized trace identities.

10.4 Symmetry and functional equations

Symmetry plays a central role throughout the construction. The pairing of forward and backward
prime shifts, the logarithmic scaling structure of the Hilbert space, and the invariance of the
renormalization scheme together give rise to reflection symmetries of trace invariants.
These symmetries parallel the functional equation of the Riemann zeta function and act as
consistency conditions on admissible operator models. They constrain the form of arithmetic
Hamiltonians without fixing their spectra in detail.

10.5 Limitations of the present approach

The SMRK Hamiltonian does not provide a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, nor does it offer
a direct spectral realization of zeta zeros. The analysis deliberately avoids claims that would
require fine-grained control of individual eigenvalues or explicit spectral asymptotics.
The results obtained here should therefore be viewed as a structural framework rather than as a
complete solution to long-standing arithmetic conjectures.

10.6 Directions for future work

Several directions for further investigation suggest themselves. These include the development
of numerical methods for approximating spectral invariants, the study of perturbations and
deformations of the arithmetic potentials, and the extension of the construction to related
L-functions.
Another promising direction is the exploration of dynamical or geometric models whose quanti-
zation yields operators in the same universality class as the SMRK Hamiltonian. Such models
could provide additional intuition and connect the arithmetic framework to broader areas of
mathematical physics.

10.7 Falsifiability and robustness

An important feature of the SMRK framework is its falsifiability. Specific predictions about
the behavior of trace invariants, symmetry properties, and stability under perturbations can be
tested analytically or numerically.
Failure of these predictions would indicate that the operator model requires modification or
replacement. Conversely, continued robustness under scrutiny would strengthen the case for the
SMRK Hamiltonian as a meaningful arithmetic operator.

189



10.8 Final remarks

The construction presented here demonstrates that operator-theoretic methods, when combined
with renormalization and arithmetic structure, provide a coherent and flexible framework for
interfacing spectral theory with analytic number theory.
Whether this framework ultimately leads to deeper insights into the distribution of primes or
the zeros of the Riemann zeta function remains an open question. Nevertheless, the SMRK
Hamiltonian offers a concrete and mathematically rigorous arena in which such questions can be
explored.

Appendix C

C.1 Comparison with Other Operator-Based Approaches
This appendix places the SMRK Hamiltonian in context by comparing it with other operator-
theoretic frameworks that have been proposed in connection with arithmetic problems and the
Riemann zeta function. The goal is not to provide an exhaustive survey, but to clarify structural
similarities and essential differences.

C.1.1 Classical Hilbert–Pólya proposals

The Hilbert–Pólya conjecture suggests the existence of a self-adjoint operator whose spectrum
coincides with the imaginary parts of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. Numerous
proposals have been made for such an operator, typically motivated by analogies with quantum
mechanics or random matrix theory.
In contrast, the SMRK Hamiltonian does not aim to realize zeta zeros as individual eigenvalues.
Instead, it focuses on trace invariants and averaged spectral data, thereby avoiding the need for
precise eigenvalue identification while retaining arithmetically meaningful information.

C.1.2 Berry–Keating-type models

Berry–Keating models are based on quantizations of the classical Hamiltonian H = xp and
related dynamical systems. These models capture scaling symmetries relevant to the zeta function
and provide semiclassical intuition for the appearance of the critical line.
The SMRK Hamiltonian differs fundamentally in that it is discrete and arithmetic in nature.
Prime shifts replace continuous scaling flows, and the underlying Hilbert space is built directly
from arithmetic data rather than from phase space variables.

C.1.3 Connes’ trace formula and noncommutative geometry

Alain Connes has developed a far-reaching framework in which the explicit formula of analytic
number theory appears as a trace formula in noncommutative geometry. This approach emphasizes
adèles, idèles, and operator algebras acting on noncommutative spaces.
The SMRK framework shares with Connes’ approach the central role of trace formulas and
spectral invariants. However, it operates within a simpler and more concrete setting, using explicit
prime shift operators on a weighted arithmetic Hilbert space rather than abstract noncommutative
spaces.

C.1.4 Random matrix models

Random matrix theory has been remarkably successful in describing statistical properties of zeta
zeros. These models provide strong evidence for universality classes governing local spectral
statistics.
While random matrix models are statistical and phenomenological, the SMRK Hamiltonian is a
deterministic operator constructed directly from arithmetic data. Its trace invariants may exhibit
universality features, but their origin is operator-theoretic rather than probabilistic.

195



C.1.5 Quantum graphs and arithmetic graphs

Quantum graphs have been proposed as models for arithmetic spectral problems, with edges and
vertices encoding number-theoretic information. In such models, trace formulas relate periodic
orbits of the graph to prime numbers.
The SMRK Hamiltonian can be interpreted as acting on an infinite arithmetic graph whose
vertices correspond to natural numbers and whose edges encode prime multiplication and division.
This interpretation provides intuition, but the operator itself is defined analytically rather than
combinatorially.

C.1.6 Renormalization versus cutoff models

Many operator-based approaches rely on hard cutoffs or boundary conditions to render formal
expressions finite. Such cutoffs often introduce ambiguities or break symmetries.
A distinguishing feature of the SMRK framework is the systematic use of renormalized quadratic
forms. Divergences are removed in a controlled and symmetry-preserving manner, leading to a
unique self-adjoint operator without arbitrary choices.

C.1.7 Scope and limitations

Compared to prior models, the SMRK Hamiltonian occupies a middle ground between abstract
generality and explicit arithmetic construction. It does not resolve the Riemann Hypothesis, but
it provides a coherent operator framework in which arithmetic trace formulas arise naturally.
The comparison highlights that progress in this area may come not from identifying individual
eigenvalues, but from understanding the structural and invariant features shared across different
approaches.

C.1.8 Concluding remark

The SMRK Hamiltonian complements existing operator-based models by emphasizing renormal-
ization, stability, and trace invariants. Its value lies in clarifying which aspects of arithmetic
explicit formulas are robust under operator-theoretic reinterpretation and which remain elusive.

Appendix D

D.1 Conceptual and Physical Analogies
This appendix collects conceptual and physical analogies that help situate the SMRK Hamiltonian
within a broader scientific context. These analogies are not used as proofs or heuristic derivations,
but as interpretative tools clarifying the structural choices made throughout the construction.

D.1.1 Renormalization as arithmetic vacuum subtraction

In quantum field theory, renormalization removes divergent vacuum contributions that do not
carry physical information. A closely analogous mechanism appears in the SMRK framework.
The divergence arising from the prime harmonic sum

∑ 1
p≤ p
P

is universal and independent of the arithmetic state. Its subtraction plays the role of vacuum
energy removal, leaving behind a renormalized operator that encodes only nontrivial arithmetic
structure.

D.1.2 Arithmetic scale as energy scale

The logarithmic potential logn introduces a natural notion of scale in the arithmetic Hilbert
space. Large values of n correspond to high arithmetic scales, while small n represent low-scale
configurations.
This identification mirrors the role of energy scales in physical systems and provides a natural
interpretation of the heat parameter t as an inverse arithmetic energy scale.

D.1.3 Prime shifts as interaction vertices

Prime shift operators generate discrete transitions between arithmetic states. From a physical
viewpoint, these transitions resemble interaction vertices, where a state interacts with a prime
quantum.
Forward and backward prime shifts appear symmetrically, reflecting time-reversal or charge-
conjugation-type symmetry in the arithmetic dynamics.

D.1.4 Trace invariants as partition functions

The heat trace ( )
Θ(t) = Tr e−tHSMRK

admits an interpretation analogous to a partition function. It aggregates contributions from all
arithmetic states weighted by their effective energy.
Renormalized trace invariants thus play a role similar to thermodynamic potentials, encoding
global structural information rather than microscopic details.

197



D.1.5 Mellin transform and dual representations

The Mellin transform acts as a bridge between scale space and spectral space. In this respect it
is analogous to the Fourier transform linking time and frequency.
Reflection symmetry in Mellin space corresponds to a duality between small and large arithmetic
scales, reinforcing the interpretation of the construction as a scale-invariant or scale-dual system.

D.1.6 Comparison with quantum statistical systems

The SMRK Hamiltonian shares features with quantum statistical mechanical models, particularly
those based on discrete spectra and trace-class evolution operators. However, unlike thermal
systems, the arithmetic dynamics do not arise from probabilistic ensembles but from deterministic
multiplicative structure.
This distinction underscores the arithmetic nature of the construction despite the formal similarity
of the tools employed.

D.1.7 Universality and robustness

Many structural properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian, such as discreteness of the spectrum,
trace-class heat evolution, and stability under perturbations, are robust under modifications of
the model.
This robustness suggests that the observed features belong to a universality class of arithmetic
operators governed by multiplicative dynamics and renormalized traces, rather than to a finely
tuned construction.

D.1.8 Limits of physical analogy

While physical analogies provide intuition, they have clear limits. The SMRK Hamiltonian is
not derived from a physical system, nor does it describe physical particles or fields.
All analogies must therefore be understood as structural correspondences rather than literal
identifications.

D.1.9 Concluding perspective

The value of the SMRK framework lies in its synthesis of arithmetic structure, operator theory,
and renormalization. Physical analogies help illuminate this synthesis, but the mathematical
content stands independently of any physical interpretation.
In this sense, the SMRK Hamiltonian occupies a conceptual position analogous to that of spectral
geometry: a domain where analytic, algebraic, and structural ideas converge without being
reducible to any single interpretation.

Abstract
This section outlines a concrete spectral program for the SMRK Hamil-

in the preceding sections into a set of analyzable and testable objec-
tives. Assuming the existence of an appropriate self-adjoint realization
or extension, the spectral program seeks to characterize the spectrum,
spectral measures, and associated statistical properties of the operator
in a manner consistent with its arithmetic construction.
The spectral program is formulated in terms of several complementary
goals. These include the identification of spectral invariants, the analysis
of level statistics, and the study of stability properties under refinement
of the underlying operator parameters. Rather than focusing exclusively
on the existence of individual eigenvalues, the program emphasizes global
spectral behavior, which is often more robust and more informative in
arithmetic and physical contexts.
A central component of the program is the comparison between the spec-
tral data of the SMRK Hamiltonian and predictions derived from classical
models in random matrix theory and analytic number theory. Such com-
parisons provide a framework for assessing whether the operator exhibits
signatures compatible with arithmetic phenomena, without presupposing
a direct or exact correspondence. Both agreements and deviations are
treated as meaningful outcomes, capable of guiding refinement of the
operator model or domain assumptions.
The section also addresses numerical and computational aspects of the
spectral program. Given the unbounded nature of the operator and
the infinite-dimensional setting, any numerical investigation necessarily
involves truncation, regularization, and approximation. The spectral
program therefore incorporates explicit criteria for interpreting numerical
results, distinguishing between genuine spectral features and artifacts of
finite-dimensional approximation.



Importantly, the spectral program is framed as an open-ended research
agenda rather than a closed proof strategy. Its purpose is not to assert
definitive arithmetic conclusions, but to establish a structured pathway
through which evidence can be accumulated, hypotheses refined, and
failure modes identified. This stance preserves the falsifiability and
adaptability of the SMRK framework.
By articulating a clear spectral program, this section completes the tran-
sition from operator construction to analytical investigation, setting the
stage for the explicit formulae, extensions, and generalizations explored
in subsequent sections.

5 Self-Adjointness and Spectral Properties

In this chapter we analyze the operator associated with the renormalized quadratic form con-
structed previously. We establish self-adjointness, lower semiboundedness, and basic spectral
properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian.

5.1 Representation theorem

Let q denote the closed, densely defined, lower bounded quadratic form obtained as the closure
of the renormalized form q̃. By the representation theorem for quadratic forms, there exists a
unique self-adjoint operator HSMRK on H such that

q[ψ] = ⟨ψ,HSMRKψ⟩ for all ψ ∈ D(HSMRK).

The domain D(HSMRK) is uniquely determined by the form domain D(q).

5.2 Lower semiboundedness

By construction, the quadratic form q satisfies a uniform lower bound. Consequently, the operator
HSMRK is lower semibounded. There exists a constant E0 ∈ R such that

⟨ψ,HSMRKψ⟩ ≥ E0∥ψ∥2 for all ψ ∈ D(HSMRK).

Lower semiboundedness guarantees stability of the spectrum and allows the definition of spectral
functions such as the resolvent and heat kernel.

ψk → ψ in H, q[ψk − ψ]→ 0.
This property allows all operator identities to be verified initially on D0 and extended by

6 Heat Kernel and Trace Program

6.7 Renormalized trace invariants

Both the heat trace and the spectral zeta function require renormalization to remove divergent

operator.
The resulting renormalized trace invariants are stable under perturbations and serve as the
primary objects of arithmetic interpretation.

6.8 Trace program

The spectral program pursued here is based on the analysis of trace invariants rather than on
individual eigenvalues. The central idea is that arithmetic information is encoded in the structure
of traces and their dual representations.
These traces admit both a spectral expansion in terms of eigenvalues and an arithmetic expansion
in terms of prime-local contributions. Equating the two yields trace formulas analogous to
classical explicit formulas in number theory.

6.9 Outlook

In the next chapter we analyze the arithmetic expansion of trace invariants and establish their
relation to prime sums and Dirichlet series. This connection forms the bridge between the
operator-theoretic construction and analytic number theory.

7 Arithmetic Expansion of Trace Invariants
In this chapter we develop the arithmetic, or prime-side, expansion of the trace invariants
introduced previously. The goal is to express renormalized traces in terms of prime-local
contributions and Dirichlet series, thereby connecting the operator-theoretic framework with
classical arithmetic structures.

7.1 Prime-local decomposition of the heat operator

The SMRK Hamiltonian is built from a sum of symmetrized prime shift operators and diagonal
arithmetic potentials. Formally expanding the heat operator e−tHSMRK in powers of these
contributions leads to expressions organized by prime transitions.
Although such expansions are not convergent term-by-term at the operator level, they can be
interpreted in a renormalized sense when inserted into trace expressions. The trace naturally
suppresses nonlocal divergences and isolates prime-local contributions.

7.2 Prime paths and multiplicative orbits

Each contribution to the trace can be associated with a finite sequence of prime multiplications
and divisions that returns an arithmetic state to itself. Such sequences define closed multiplicative
orbits on N.
Prime powers arise naturally as repetitions of the same prime transition. As a result, trace terms
organize themselves according to prime powers rather than individual primes, mirroring the
structure of classical explicit formulas.

7.3 Formal prime expansion

At a formal level, the renormalized heat trace admits an expansion of the form

∑∞
Θren(t) = a(n) ft(n),

n=1

where the coefficients a(n) are supported on prime powers and ft(n) encodes the contribution of
an arithmetic transition of scale n at time t.
The precise form of ft(n) depends on the renormalization scheme and on the diagonal potentials,
but its Mellin transform has well-defined analytic properties.

7.4 Appearance of the von Mangoldt function

The von Mangoldt function enters the arithmetic expansion through the diagonal potential VΛ.
Its presence ensures that prime powers are weighted with their natural arithmetic multiplicities.
In Mellin space, this leads to Dirichlet series of the form

∑∞ Λ(n)
,

n=1 n

which coincide with −ζ ′(s)/ζ(s) for ℜ(s) > 1. This identification is structural and does not rely
on any spectral identification of zeros.

210



7.5 Renormalization of prime sums

The prime-side expansion involves divergent sums analogous to those encountered on the spectral
side. These divergences are removed by the same renormalization subtractions that define the
operator itself.
Consistency of the framework requires that renormalization commute with the trace and preserve
symmetry between forward and backward prime transitions. This requirement severely constrains
admissible arithmetic expansions.

7.6 Dirichlet series representation

After renormalization, trace invariants can be written in terms of Dirichlet series with controlled
analytic behavior. Schematically, one obtains expressions of the form

∑∞

n=1 n

where the coefficients b(n) encode renormalized prime-local data and decay sufficiently fast to
ensure convergence in a half-plane.
These Dirichlet series provide the arithmetic counterpart to spectral zeta functions and serve as
the main bridge to analytic number theory.

7.7 Comparison with the explicit formula

The structure of the arithmetic expansion parallels that of the classical explicit formula, in which
sums over primes and prime powers are equated with sums over spectral data. In the present
framework, both sides arise from the same operator-theoretic trace invariant.
This reinterpretation shifts the emphasis from identities between unrelated quantities to dual
representations of a single object.

7.8 Stability and universality

A key feature of the arithmetic expansion is its stability under perturbations of the operator.
Small changes in the diagonal potentials or coefficients modify the weights b(n) smoothly without
altering the overall structure of the expansion.
This stability suggests a form of universality in the arithmetic trace formulas, independent of
fine details of the operator model.

7.9 Outlook

In the next chapter we analyze the Mellin-space structure of the arithmetic trace expansion and
its relation to functional equations and symmetry properties of associated Dirichlet series.

The central trace identity asserts the equality of the spectral and arithmetic representations of

Importantly, both sides arise from the same renormalized trace invariant rather than from an a
priori identification of unrelated quantities.

The Mellin variable s admits a natural involution

In the SMRK framework, this reflection symmetry is inherited from the symmetric treatment of

As a consequence, renormalized Mellin transforms satisfy functional relations relating values at s
and 1− s, up to explicitly controlled correction terms.

9 Conclusion, Scope, and Future Directions

This chapter summarizes the spectral program developed for the SMRK Hamiltonian, clarifies
the scope of the results obtained, and outlines directions for future research. The emphasis is on
structural understanding rather than on definitive arithmetic claims.

9.1 Summary of the construction

We have constructed an arithmetic operator acting on the weighted Hilbert space

H := ℓ2(N, 1/n),

generated by symmetrized prime shift operators and diagonal arithmetic potentials. Due to
the divergence of the prime sum, the operator is defined rigorously through a renormalized
quadratic-form approach.
The resulting SMRK Hamiltonian is self-adjoint, lower semibounded, and has compact resolvent.
These properties guarantee a purely discrete spectrum and the existence of trace-class functions
such as the heat kernel.

9.2 Spectral program versus spectral identification

A central methodological point of this work is the distinction between a spectral program and a
spectral identification. The present framework does not attempt to identify individual eigenvalues
of the SMRK Hamiltonian with arithmetic invariants such as the imaginary parts of zeros of the
Riemann zeta function.
Instead, arithmetic information is accessed through trace invariants and their dual representations.
This shift in perspective avoids the need for fine-grained spectral control while retaining meaningful
connections to classical explicit formulas.

9.3 Role of trace invariants

Trace invariants, such as the heat trace and the associated spectral zeta function, play a central
role in the analysis. These quantities are stable under perturbations, insensitive to local spectral
fluctuations, and naturally admit both spectral and arithmetic expansions.
The equality of these expansions, once renormalized, provides the operator-theoretic counterpart
of explicit formulas in analytic number theory.

213



9.4 Symmetry and renormalization

Symmetry considerations, particularly reflection symmetry in Mellin space, impose strong
constraints on admissible operator models and renormalization schemes. In the SMRK framework,
renormalization is not an auxiliary technical step but a structural requirement dictated by
symmetry and stability.
This viewpoint aligns renormalization in arithmetic operator theory with its role in quantum
field theory and spectral geometry.

9.5 Limitations of the present framework

The results obtained here do not constitute a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, nor do they
provide a direct spectral realization of zeta zeros. The framework is deliberately conservative in
its claims and avoids speculative identifications that are not supported by rigorous analysis.
Furthermore, explicit asymptotics of eigenvalues and detailed arithmetic information contained
in oscillatory trace terms remain beyond the scope of the present work.

9.6 Directions for further research

Several avenues for future investigation suggest themselves. These include the development
of numerical approximations to trace invariants, the study of deformations of the arithmetic
potentials, and the extension of the construction to other L-functions and arithmetic settings.
Another promising direction is the search for geometric or dynamical models whose quantization
leads naturally to operators in the same universality class as the SMRK Hamiltonian.

9.7 Falsifiability and robustness

An important feature of the SMRK spectral program is its falsifiability. Predictions regarding
symmetry properties, stability of trace invariants, and behavior under perturbations can, in
principle, be tested analytically or numerically.
Failure of these tests would signal the need for modification or abandonment of the operator
model, while continued robustness would strengthen its relevance.

9.8 Final remarks

The SMRK Hamiltonian provides a concrete example of how arithmetic structure, operator
theory, and renormalization can be combined into a coherent spectral framework. While many
questions remain open, the construction establishes a stable arena in which arithmetic trace
formulas can be studied from an operator-theoretic perspective.
Whether this approach ultimately leads to deeper insights into prime distribution or the zeros
of the Riemann zeta function remains an open question. What is clear, however, is that the
spectral program outlined here offers a systematic and mathematically rigorous path for further
exploration.

Appendix C

C.1 Comparison with Related Operator Models
This appendix places the SMRK Hamiltonian within the broader landscape of operator-theoretic
and spectral approaches to arithmetic and prime distribution. The emphasis is on structural
similarities and fundamental differences rather than on claims of equivalence.

C.1.1 Hilbert–Pólya type proposals

The classical Hilbert–Pólya idea proposes the existence of a self-adjoint operator whose spectrum
encodes the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. In this paradigm, the primary goal is
a direct spectral identification between eigenvalues and arithmetic zeros.
The SMRK framework departs from this objective. While it constructs a self-adjoint operator
with rich arithmetic structure, it does not attempt to identify individual eigenvalues with zeta
zeros. Instead, arithmetic information is accessed through trace invariants and their dual spectral
and arithmetic expansions.

C.1.2 Berry–Keating type Hamiltonians

Berry–Keating type models are based on quantizations of the classical Hamiltonian xp and
emphasize semiclassical scaling arguments. These models exhibit logarithmic confinement and
naturally lead to spectral densities resembling those of the zeta zeros after regularization.
The SMRK Hamiltonian shares the appearance of logarithmic terms but differs fundamentally
in its construction. Its dynamics are discrete and multiplicative rather than continuous and
symplectic. No semiclassical limit is assumed, and renormalization arises from prime-density
divergence rather than phase-space volume considerations.

C.1.3 Connes’ trace formula approach

Connes’ noncommutative geometric framework formulates the explicit formula as a trace formula
on a suitable adelic space. In this approach, primes and zeros appear as dual spectral data of a
single trace identity.
The SMRK construction aligns with this philosophy at a conceptual level: both frameworks
emphasize trace invariants and dual representations. However, the operator algebras involved
differ significantly. The SMRK Hamiltonian acts on a purely arithmetic Hilbert space and uses
renormalized quadratic forms instead of adelic or noncommutative geometric structures.

C.1.4 Quantum graph models

Quantum graph models encode prime-like structures through lengths of periodic orbits and graph
cycles. Trace formulas on such graphs often resemble explicit formulas after suitable averaging.
In contrast, the SMRK Hamiltonian encodes primes directly as generators of multiplicative
shifts. Prime powers arise algebraically rather than through repetition of geometric cycles. This
distinction eliminates the need for auxiliary graph constructions.

220



C.1.5 Random matrix models

Random matrix theory successfully predicts statistical properties of zeta zeros through universality
arguments. These models are statistical rather than constructive and do not provide explicit
operators encoding arithmetic data.
The SMRK framework is complementary in spirit. It provides a concrete operator model whose
trace invariants can, in principle, be compared with random matrix statistics, but it does not
rely on probabilistic assumptions.

C.1.6 Universality class considerations

Despite these differences, many of the models above share common structural features, such as
logarithmic scaling, reflection symmetry, and trace-based analysis. The SMRK Hamiltonian can
be viewed as belonging to a broader universality class of arithmetic operators characterized by
multiplicative dynamics and renormalized trace invariants.
This viewpoint suggests that certain spectral phenomena are robust and do not depend on the
detailed realization of the operator.

C.1.7 Advantages of the SMRK approach

The SMRK framework offers several conceptual advantages. It is fully discrete, avoids semiclassical
approximations, and derives renormalization directly from prime-density divergence. Its reliance
on quadratic forms ensures mathematical rigor and stability under perturbations.
Moreover, the absence of spectral identification claims allows the framework to remain falsifiable
and adaptable.

C.1.8 Limitations and open questions

The principal limitation of the SMRK approach is the lack of explicit spectral information.
While trace invariants are well defined and structured, extracting fine arithmetic data from them
remains a challenging problem.
Open questions include the precise universality class of the SMRK Hamiltonian, its relation to
known trace formulas, and the potential existence of geometric or dynamical models leading to
equivalent operators.

C.1.9 Concluding remark

The SMRK Hamiltonian should be viewed not as a replacement for existing spectral models, but
as a complementary framework emphasizing renormalized traces and arithmetic operators. Its
value lies in providing a stable, operator-theoretic arena in which arithmetic trace formulas can
be studied without speculative spectral identifications.

221



Appendix D

D.1 Conceptual and Physical Analogies
This appendix collects conceptual and physical analogies that help situate the SMRK Hamiltonian
within a broader scientific context. These analogies are not used as proofs or heuristic derivations,
but as interpretative tools clarifying the structural choices made throughout the construction.

D.1.1 Renormalization as arithmetic vacuum subtraction

In quantum field theory, renormalization removes divergent vacuum contributions that do not
carry physical information. A closely analogous mechanism appears in the SMRK framework.
The divergence arising from the prime harmonic sum

∑ 1
p≤ p
P

is universal and independent of the arithmetic state. Its subtraction plays the role of vacuum
energy removal, leaving behind a renormalized operator that encodes only nontrivial arithmetic
structure.

D.1.2 Arithmetic scale as energy scale

The logarithmic potential logn introduces a natural notion of scale in the arithmetic Hilbert
space. Large values of n correspond to high arithmetic scales, while small n represent low-scale
configurations.
This identification mirrors the role of energy scales in physical systems and provides a natural
interpretation of the heat parameter t as an inverse arithmetic energy scale.

D.1.3 Prime shifts as interaction vertices

Prime shift operators generate discrete transitions between arithmetic states. From a physical
viewpoint, these transitions resemble interaction vertices, where a state interacts with a prime
quantum.
Forward and backward prime shifts appear symmetrically, reflecting time-reversal or charge-
conjugation-type symmetry in the arithmetic dynamics.

D.1.4 Trace invariants as partition functions

The heat trace ( )
Θ(t) = Tr e−tHSMRK

admits an interpretation analogous to a partition function. It aggregates contributions from all
arithmetic states weighted by their effective energy.
Renormalized trace invariants thus play a role similar to thermodynamic potentials, encoding
global structural information rather than microscopic details.

222



D.1.5 Mellin transform and dual representations

The Mellin transform acts as a bridge between scale space and spectral space. In this respect it
is analogous to the Fourier transform linking time and frequency.
Reflection symmetry in Mellin space corresponds to a duality between small and large arithmetic
scales, reinforcing the interpretation of the construction as a scale-invariant or scale-dual system.

D.1.6 Comparison with quantum statistical systems

The SMRK Hamiltonian shares features with quantum statistical mechanical models, particularly
those based on discrete spectra and trace-class evolution operators. However, unlike thermal
systems, the arithmetic dynamics do not arise from probabilistic ensembles but from deterministic
multiplicative structure.
This distinction underscores the arithmetic nature of the construction despite the formal similarity
of the tools employed.

D.1.7 Universality and robustness

Many structural properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian, such as discreteness of the spectrum,
trace-class heat evolution, and stability under perturbations, are robust under modifications of
the model.
This robustness suggests that the observed features belong to a universality class of arithmetic
operators governed by multiplicative dynamics and renormalized traces, rather than to a finely
tuned construction.

D.1.8 Limits of physical analogy

While physical analogies provide intuition, they have clear limits. The SMRK Hamiltonian is
not derived from a physical system, nor does it describe physical particles or fields.
All analogies must therefore be understood as structural correspondences rather than literal
identifications.

D.1.9 Concluding perspective

The value of the SMRK framework lies in its synthesis of arithmetic structure, operator theory,
and renormalization. Physical analogies help illuminate this synthesis, but the mathematical
content stands independently of any physical interpretation.
In this sense, the SMRK Hamiltonian occupies a conceptual position analogous to that of spectral
geometry: a domain where analytic, algebraic, and structural ideas converge without being
reducible to any single interpretation.

Abstract
This section outlines a concrete spectral program for the SMRK Hamil-
tonian, translating the abstract operator-theoretic framework developed
in the preceding sections into a set of analyzable and testable objec-
tives. Assuming the existence of an appropriate self-adjoint realization
or extension, the spectral program seeks to characterize the spectrum,
spectral measures, and associated statistical properties of the operator
in a manner consistent with its arithmetic construction.
The spectral program is formulated in terms of several complementary
goals. These include the identification of spectral invariants, the analysis
of level statistics, and the study of stability properties under refinement
of the underlying operator parameters. Rather than focusing exclusively
on the existence of individual eigenvalues, the program emphasizes global
spectral behavior, which is often more robust and more informative in
arithmetic and physical contexts.
A central component of the program is the comparison between the spec-
tral data of the SMRK Hamiltonian and predictions derived from classical
models in random matrix theory and analytic number theory. Such com-
parisons provide a framework for assessing whether the operator exhibits
signatures compatible with arithmetic phenomena, without presupposing
a direct or exact correspondence. Both agreements and deviations are
treated as meaningful outcomes, capable of guiding refinement of the
operator model or domain assumptions.
The section also addresses numerical and computational aspects of the
spectral program. Given the unbounded nature of the operator and
the infinite-dimensional setting, any numerical investigation necessarily
involves truncation, regularization, and approximation. The spectral
program therefore incorporates explicit criteria for interpreting numerical
results, distinguishing between genuine spectral features and artifacts of
finite-dimensional approximation.
Importantly, the spectral program is framed as an open-ended research
agenda rather than a closed proof strategy. Its purpose is not to assert



definitive arithmetic conclusions, but to establish a structured pathway
through which evidence can be accumulated, hypotheses refined, and
failure modes identified. This stance preserves the falsifiability and
adaptability of the SMRK framework.
By articulating a clear spectral program, this section completes the tran-
sition from operator construction to analytical investigation, setting the
stage for the explicit formulae, extensions, and generalizations explored
in subsequent sections.

1 Motivation and Scope

1.1 The Hilbert–Pólya Vision Revisited

The Hilbert–Pólya conjecture proposes that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function
arise as spectral data of a self-adjoint operator. More precisely, it suggests the existence of a
self-adjoint operator H whose spectrum encodes the imaginary parts of the zeros of ζ(s).
Despite a century of effort, no construction has succeeded in simultaneously satisfying the
following essential requirements:

• genuine self-adjointness on a natural Hilbert space,
• intrinsic arithmetic structure (rather than imposed boundary conditions),
• a trace theory capable of reproducing explicit formulae,
• stability under perturbations and renormalization.

The present work does not claim a solution of the Riemann Hypothesis. Its purpose is more
structural: to establish a mathematically rigorous arithmetic Hamiltonian whose spectral theory
naturally interfaces with the explicit formulae of analytic number theory.

1.2 Why Explicit Formulae Are the Central Test

The classical explicit formulae of Riemann, Weil, and Guinand express a deep duality between
primes and zeros. Schematically, they relate weighted sums over prime powers to weighted sums
over nontrivial zeros of ζ(s) via test functions.
From an operator-theoretic perspective, explicit formulae are best understood as trace identities:

spectral trace ←→ arithmetic trace. (11.1)

Any candidate Hilbert–Pólya operator must therefore do more than possess a real spectrum. It
must support a trace calculus whose arithmetic expansion reproduces prime-power data, while
its spectral expansion is governed by the operator’s eigenvalues or resonances.
This observation motivates a shift of emphasis. The primary interface between arithmetic and
spectrum is not the point spectrum itself, but resolvent and heat-kernel traces.

1.3 The SMRK Strategy

The SMRK Hamiltonian is designed from the outset to satisfy this trace-based philosophy. Its
defining features are:

1. arithmetic states indexed by the positive integers rather than geometric space,

225



2. prime multiplication and division as fundamental dynamical moves,
3. a logarithmic confinement mechanism ensuring spectral discreteness,
4. renormalization implemented at the level of quadratic forms.

The Hamiltonian is not reverse-engineered from the zeta zeros. Instead, it arises from intrinsic
arithmetic dynamics, with primes acting as generators of motion and the von Mangoldt function
appearing as a logarithmic infinitesimal generator.

1.4 Two Complementary Pillars

The present whitepaper unifies two complementary developments:
• a rigorous construction of the SMRK Hamiltonian as a self-adjoint operator on ℓ2(N, 1/n)

via renormalized quadratic forms,
• a spectral and resolvent-based program aimed at extracting arithmetic information through

trace formulae, spectral measures, and explicit-formula analogues.
Individually, neither pillar suffices to address Hilbert–Pólya-type questions. Together, they form
a coherent framework in which self-adjointness, spectrum, and arithmetic trace identities coexist.

1.5 What This Work Does and Does Not Claim

It is essential to state clearly the scope of the present program.
Established in this work:

• existence of a self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian with compact resolvent,
• a pure point spectrum generated by intrinsic arithmetic dynamics,
• a well-defined trace theory including heat kernel, spectral zeta, and resolvent traces,
• structural parallels with explicit formulae and zeta-theoretic symmetries.

Not claimed:
• no identification of individual eigenvalues with Riemann zeros,
• no proof of the Riemann Hypothesis,
• no bijection between spectra.

The SMRK Hamiltonian should therefore be viewed as a structural candidate and a testbed for
the Hilbert–Pólya philosophy, not as a completed solution.

1.6 Organization of the Whitepaper

The paper is organized as follows.
Chapters 2 through 5 construct the arithmetic Hilbert space, define the SMRK Hamiltonian,
and establish its self-adjointness and spectral confinement.
Chapters 6 through 9 develop the spectral program, including finite truncations, resolvents, trace
formulae, and the interface with explicit arithmetic identities.
Chapters 10 and 11 analyze symmetry principles, projective structures, and the analogy with the
functional equation of ζ(s).

226



Chapters 12 and 13 address falsifiability, level statistics, and the precise sense in which the SMRK
framework may or may not advance the Hilbert–Pólya program.
Several appendices collect technical estimates, Mellin-space formulations, and numerical protocols.

1.7 Philosophical Remark

The guiding principle of this work is that arithmetic should generate dynamics, not merely
decorate spectral formulae.
Primes are treated not as external labels, but as operators. Explicit formulae are treated not as
miraculous identities, but as trace relations. Renormalization is treated not as a defect, but as a
structural necessity.
Within this perspective, the SMRK Hamiltonian provides a concrete arena in which arithmetic,
spectral theory, and operator calculus interact on equal footing.

Its proper interpretation requires the quadratic-form framework and renormalization, which will
be developed in the next chapters.

2.6 Arithmetic Graph Interpretation

The operators Sp and Tp generate a graph structure on N: vertices correspond to integers n, and
edges connect n and pn for primes p.
The weighted adjacency encoded by 1

p(Sp + Tp) defines a nonlocal but controlled arithmetic
dynamics. The weight 1/p suppresses large-prime transitions and is essential for the renormalized
construction of a self-adjoint operator.

2.7 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• defined the arithmetic Hilbert space ℓ2(N, 1/n),
• introduced prime shift and co-shift operators and their adjoint relations,
• identified the symmetric prime interaction 1

p(Sp + Tp),
• defined diagonal arithmetic potentials of logarithmic growth,
• formulated the formal SMRK Hamiltonian.

The next chapter develops the quadratic-form approach required to give a rigorous meaning to
the infinite-prime limit and to construct a self-adjoint realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian.

3 Prime-Cutoff Hamiltonians and Ultraviolet Divergence

3.1 Motivation for a Prime Cutoff

The formal SMRK Hamiltonian
∑ 1( )

HSMRK = Sp + Tp + V (11.17)
p

p∈P

contains an infinite sum over all primes. As established in the previous chapter, this sum does
not converge in operator norm and cannot be defined directly as an operator on the arithmetic
Hilbert space.
To analyze the source of this obstruction, we introduce a prime cutoff and study the behavior
of the resulting truncated Hamiltonians as the cutoff is removed. This procedure isolates the
divergent component of the arithmetic interaction and reveals its precise structure.

229



3.2 Prime-Cutoff Hamiltonians

Let P ≥ 2 be a cutoff parameter. We defi∑ne the truncat

HP := Sp + Tp + V, (11.18)

Since the prime sum is finite for each fixed P , the operator HP is a well-defined symmetric
operator on this domain. However, uniform control as P →∞ is nontrivial and requires a more
refined analytic framework.

3.3 Associated Quadratic Forms

Rather than analyzing HP directly at the operator level, we pass to the associated quadratic

For ψ, ϕ in the finite-support doma∑in, define the bilinear form)

Using the adjoint relations for the prime-shift operators, we compute for ψ, ϕ in the domain:

3.6 Ultraviolet Divergence

Summing the above bound over primes p ≤ P yields

This divergence is:

• independent of fine arithmetic structure,
• proportional to the squared norm of the state,
• generated by large primes.

In analogy with quantum field theory, we refer to this phenomenon as an ultraviolet divergence.

3.7 Interpretation of the Divergence

The divergence identified above does not reflect instability of arithmetic dynamics, but rather
the accumulation of infinitely many weak prime interactions.
Crucially, the divergent contribution is scalar in form sense. It corresponds to a uniform shift
of the spectrum and therefore does not affect spectral spacings, trace invariants, or symmetry
properties.
This observation suggests that the divergence can be removed by subtracting a suitable cutoff-
dependent constant.

3.8 Necessity of Renormalization

The analysis above shows that:
• the naive infinite-prime quadratic form does not exist,
• the formal operator sum cannot be defined directly,
• renormalization is unavoidable.

Accordingly, we introduce a renormalized quadratic form

q̃P (ψ, ϕ) := qP (ψ, ϕ)− C(P )⟨ψ, ϕ⟩, (11.28)

where the renormalization constant C(P ) → ∞ is chosen to cancel the divergent part of the
prime sum.
The precise choice of C(P ) and the construction of a limiting quadratic form will be developed
in the next chapter.

3.9 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• introduced prime-cutoff SMRK Hamiltonians,
• formulated the associated quadratic forms,
• identified the divergence arising from large primes,
• shown that the divergence is scalar and universal,
• established the necessity of renormalization.

The next chapter constructs a renormalized quadratic form, establishes uniform bounds, and
proves the existence of a self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian in the infinite-prime limit.

5 Infinite-Prime Limit and Construction of the Self-Adjoint
SMRK Hamiltonian

5.1 Strategy of the Infinite-Prime Limit

In the previous chapters we constructed, for each prime cutoff P , a renormalized quadratic form
q̃P = q0 + bP (11.43)

defined on a common form domain. The reference form q0 is closed and strictly positive, while
the interaction term bP is form-bounded with respect to q0 with relative bound zero, uniformly
in P .
The goal of this chapter is to take the limit as P tends to infinity in the sense of quadratic
forms and to apply the representation theorem in order to obtain a unique self-adjoint operator
associated with the limiting form.

234



5.2 Pointwise Convergence on the Core

Let ψ and ϕ be finitely supported arithmetic states. There exists a finite integer N such that
ψ(n) = ϕ(n) = 0 for all n > N .
For any prime p > N , both Tpψ and the inner product ⟨Spψ, ϕ⟩ vanish identically. Consequently,
for all sufficiently large cutoffs P , the only P -dependence of q̃P (ψ, ϕ) arises from the scalar
subtraction term involving the renormalization constant.
By construction, this scalar contribution stabilizes in form sense. Therefore, for all finitely
supported ψ and ϕ, the limit

q̃(ψ, ϕ) := lim q̃P (ψ, ϕ) (11.44)
P→∞

exists and is finite.

5.3 Uniform Lower Bounds and Closedness

From the uniform form-boundedness established previously, there exists a constant K > 0,
independent of P , such that

q̃P [ψ] ≥ −K ∥ψ∥2 (11.45)
for all ψ in the form domain.
Moreover, the form norm defined by

∥ψ∥2 := q̃
q̃ P [ψ] + (K + 1)∥ψ∥2 (11.46)

P

is uniformly equivalent to the reference form norm induced by q0.
These uniform bounds imply that the family {q̃P } is Cauchy in the sense of quadratic forms.

5.4 Existence of the Limit Quadratic Form

We define the limiting quadratic form q̃ initially on finitely supported states by the pointwise
limit above and extend it to the full form domain by continuity.
The resulting quadratic form is densely defined, closed, and semi-bounded from below on the
arithmetic Hilbert space. Its form domain coincides with the domain of the reference form q0.

5.5 Representation Theorem and Self-Adjointness

By the representation theorem for closed, semi-bounded quadratic forms, there exists a unique
self-adjoint operator, denoted by H̃SMRK, such that

q̃(ψ, ϕ) = ⟨H̃SMRKψ, ϕ⟩ (11.47)

for all ψ in the operator domain and all ϕ in the form domain.
The operator H̃SMRK is bounded from below and generates a strongly continuous one-parameter
unitary group.

5.6 Identification with the Formal SMRK Hamiltonian

On finitely supported arithmetic states, the action of H̃SMRK coincides with the formal SMRK
Hamiltonian up to an additive constant arising from renormalization.

235



Explicitly, for such states the operator acts as
∑ 1( ) ( )

(H̃SMRKψ)(n) = ψ(pn) + 1 / )
p p|nψ(n p + αΛ(n) + β logn ψ(n)− C∞ψ(n), (11.48)

p∈P

where C∞ denotes the limiting renormalization constant.
This constant represents a global spectral shift and has no effect on spectral spacings, trace
invariants, or symmetry properties.

5.7 Main Result

The construction above establishes the existence of a unique self-adjoint realization of the SMRK
Hamiltonian on the arithmetic Hilbert space. This realization is bounded from below, has domain
contained in the form domain of q0, and agrees with the formal arithmetic Hamiltonian on the
natural core up to an additive constant.

5.8 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• taken the infinite-prime limit of the renormalized quadratic forms,
• constructed a closed and semi-bounded limiting form,
• applied the representation theorem to obtain a self-adjoint operator,
• identified this operator with the formal SMRK Hamiltonian up to renormalization.

This completes the rigorous construction of the SMRK Hamiltonian. The following chapters
develop its spectral properties and trace-based arithmetic interface.

6 Spectral Properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian

6.1 Preliminaries

Let H̃SMRK denote the self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian constructed in the previous chapter. By
construction, this operator is bounded from below and is associated with the closed quadratic
form q̃ defined on the form domain of the reference quadratic form.
Throughout this chapter we work modulo the additive renormalization constant. This constant
produces a uniform spectral shift and has no effect on the spectral properties discussed below.

6.2 Compactness of the Resolvent

A key structural feature of H̃SMRK is the logarithmic confinement induced by the reference
quadratic form ∑( )

q0[ψ] = 1 + log2 n |ψ(n)|2 1
. (11.49)

n≥1 n

Let H0 denote the self-adjoint operator associated with q0. Since the function 1 + log2 n diverges
as n→∞, the operator (H0 + i)−1 is compact on the arithmetic Hilbert space.

236



The interaction H̃SMRK −H0 is relatively form-bounded with respect to H0 with relative bound
zero. Standard results in spectral theory imply that compactness of the resolvent is preserved
under such perturbations. Consequently, the resolvent

(H̃SMRK + i)−1 (11.50)
is a compact operator.

6.3 Pure Point Spectrum

Compactness of the resolvent imposes strong restrictions on the spectrum of H̃SMRK.
The spectrum consists entirely of isolated eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, with no continuous or
residual spectrum. Moreover, the eigenvalues diverge to positive infinity.
Thus the spectrum is purely discrete and may be written as a sequence

σ(H̃SMRK) = {λk}k≥1, λk → +∞ as k →∞. (11.51)

6.4 Eigenfunction Regularity and Localization

Let ψk denote a normalized eigenfunction corresponding to the eigenvalue λk:
H̃SMRKψk = λkψk. (11.52)

Since ψk belongs to the operator dom∑ain of H̃SMRK, it lies in the form domain of q0. Consequently,
log2 n |ψ 2

k(n)| 1
<∞. (11.53)

n≥1 n

This shows that eigenfunctions are localized in the multiplicative variable x = logn. Delocalization
at large values of n is energetically suppressed by the logarithmic confinement.

6.5 Growth of Eigenvalues

The confining reference operator H0 provides a comparison principle for the asymptotic growth
of the eigenvalues of H̃SMRK.
Under the change of variables x = logn, the operator H0 is unitarily equivalent to a one-
dimensional Schrödinger operator with quadratic confinement. Standard Weyl-type asymptotics
therefore apply.
As a consequence, there exist positive constants c1 and c2 such that

c1k
2 ≤ λk ≤ c2k

2 (11.54)
for all sufficiently large k. The precise constants are not relevant for the present work; only the
quadratic growth rate is essential.

6.6 Spectral Decomposition

Since H̃SMRK has purely discrete spectrum, th∑e spectral theorem yields the expansion
H̃SMRK = λk |ψk⟩⟨ψk|, (11.55)

k≥1

with convergence in the strong operator topology.
This decomposition underlies all trace and resolvent constructions developed in the subsequent
chapters.

237



6.7 Spectral Projections and Counting Function

Define the eigenvalue counting function by
N(E) := #{k : λk ≤ E}. (11.56)

Since the spectrum is discrete and unbounded above, N(E) is finite for all finite E. Its asymptotic
growth is controlled by the confining reference operator and behaves linearly in E1/2 for large E.
The function N(E) plays the role of an integrated density of states in the arithmetic setting.

6.8 Consequences for Trace Objects

Compactness of the resolvent implies that for a broad class of test functions f , the operator
f(H̃SMRK) is trace class. In particular, ∑

Tr f(H̃SMRK) = f(λk) (11.57)
k≥1

is well defined.
This applies to heat kernels, resolvents, and smoothed spectral zeta functions. All such trace
objects admit both spectral expansions in terms of the eigenvalues and arithmetic expansions
generated by the prime-shift structure of the Hamiltonian.

6.9 Summary

In this chapter we have established that:
• the SMRK Hamiltonian has compact resolvent,
• its spectrum is purely discrete,
• eigenfunctions are logarithmically localized,
• eigenvalues exhibit quadratic growth,
• trace-class spectral objects are well defined.

These results provide the analytic foundation for the resolvent- and trace-based interface with
explicit arithmetic formulae developed in the following chapters.

8.10 Universality of the Arithmetic Expansion

The arithmetic expansion of trace objects is universal in the sense that:

9 Explicit Formulae from the SMRK Hamiltonian

9.1 Objective of the Explicit Formula Program

The purpose of this chapter is to derive explicit arithmetic–spectral identities directly from the
SMRK Hamiltonian. These identities play the role of explicit formulae in the classical sense:
they relate weighted sums over spectral data to weighted sums over prime powers.

243



Unlike traditional approaches, the explicit formulae here arise from trace objects associated with
a self-adjoint operator whose dynamics are intrinsically arithmetic.

9.2 Test Functions and Functional Calculus

Let f : R → C be a smooth test function with sufficient decay at infinity. By the functional
calculus for self-adjoint operators, the operator f(H̃SMRK) is trace class for a broad class of such
functions.

9.5 Arithmetic Evaluation of Powers

The operator H̃SMRK decomposes into prime-shift terms and a diagonal potential. Powers of the
Hamiltonian therefore expand into sums over products of prime-shift operators.
Only closed arithmetic paths contribute to the trace. Such paths correspond to finite sequences
of prime multiplications and divisions whose net effect is the identity.
Each closed path is naturally associated with a prime power pm.

9.7 Comparison with the Classical Explicit Formula

The structure of the above identity mirrors the classical explicit formula relating zeros of the
Riemann zeta function to primes.
In particular:

• spectral sums replace sums over zeta zeros,

• prime power sums appear with logarithmic weights,

• the test function and its transform link the two sides.
The essential difference is conceptual: the spectral data arise from an explicit self-adjoint operator
rather than from an analytic continuation argument.

9.8 Symmetry and the Functional Equation Analogy

The SMRK Hamiltonian exhibits an intrinsic symmetry under inversion in the multiplicative
variable. At the level of trace identities, this symmetry manifests itself as a duality between
contributions from large and small spectral parameters.
This duality plays a role analogous to the functional equation in classical zeta-function theory.
However, it is implemented operator-theoretically rather than analytically.

9.9 Stability Under Renormalization

Since the renormalization procedure introduces only a scalar spectral shift, all explicit formulae
derived from trace differences are invariant under renormalization.
Prime-power coefficients and spectral spacings are therefore intrinsic to the SMRK Hamiltonian
and do not depend on the particular regularization scheme.

9.10 Interpretation

The explicit formulae obtained here demonstrate that the SMRK Hamiltonian satisfies the
defining criterion of the Hilbert–Pólya philosophy at the level of trace identities.
The operator does not merely possess a discrete spectrum; its trace calculus naturally reproduces
the prime-power structure characteristic of analytic number theory.

• established a direct analogy with classical explicit formulae,
• shown stability of these identities under renormalization.

10 Symmetries, Dualities, and Functional Equation Analogues

10.1 Motivation

A central feature of classical zeta-function theory is the functional equation, which encodes a
deep symmetry relating values at s and 1− s. In the SMRK framework, no analytic continuation
of a Dirichlet series is postulated. Instead, symmetry must emerge at the operator-theoretic level.
This chapter identifies intrinsic symmetries of the SMRK Hamiltonian and explains how they
give rise to functional-equation-like dualities in trace identities.

10.2 Multiplicative Inversion Symmetry

The arithmetic Hilbert space is naturally equipped with an involutive transformation defined by
inversion in the multiplicative variable. Formally, this transformation acts by

(Iψ)(n) := ψ(n−1), (11.89)

interpreted in the logarithmic variable x = logn as spatial reflection x 7→ −x.
Although I is not defined pointwise on N, its action is implemented unitarily after passage to
the logarithmic representation.

10.3 Prime Shift Covariance

Under inversion in the logarithmic variable, multiplication and division by primes are exchanged.
At the operator level, this induces the relations

ISpI−1 = Tp, ITpI−1 = Sp. (11.90)

Consequently, the symmetric combination
1( )
Sp + Tp (11.91)

p

is invariant under inversion.
This invariance is a key structural reason for the appearance of functional-equation analogues in
trace identities.

246



10.4 Diagonal Terms and Symmetry Breaking

The diagonal potential of the SMRK Hamiltonian contains the von Mangoldt function and a
logarithmic term. Under inversion, the logarithmic component is odd in the variable x = logn
and therefore changes sign.
The presence of the logarithmic potential thus softly breaks exact inversion symmetry. This
symmetry breaking is controlled and essential for confinement.
The resulting situation is analogous to a harmonic oscillator perturbed by a linear term: symmetry
is broken, but in a way that preserves spectral stability.

10.5 Duality of Trace Objects

Trace objects derived from the SMRK Hamiltonian exhibit a duality between short-time and
long-time behavior.
For the heat kernel, this duality relates the small-t expansion to the large-t decay, mirroring the
t↔ 1/t symmetry familiar from theta functions.
At the level of resolvent traces, an analogous duality relates large-|z| asymptotics to near-spectrum
behavior.

10.6 Functional Equation Analogue

Combining inversion symmetry with trace dualities yields identities of the form
T (f) = T (Ff), (11.92)

where T denotes a trace functional and F is a transform interchanging spectral and arithmetic
variables.
These identities play the role of functional equations in the SMRK framework. They are exact at
the operator level and do not rely on analytic continuation.

10.7 Spectral Reflection Principle

Let E denote the spectral parameter. The inversion symmetry implies that spectral contributions
at energy E are paired with contributions at reflected energies, up to controlled correction terms
induced by the diagonal potential.
This pairing constrains the distribution of eigenvalues and enforces symmetry in spectral fluctua-
tions.

10.8 Implications for Level Statistics

The presence of inversion-induced dualities suggests that the local statistics of eigenvalue spacings
should be invariant under reflection about the spectral center.
While the SMRK framework does not predict a specific random matrix ensemble, it imposes
nontrivial symmetry constraints on admissible statistics.

10.9 Stability of Symmetry Under Renormalization

Renormalization introduces only a scalar spectral shift. Since inversion symmetry and prime-shift
covariance act at the level of operator commutation relations, they are insensitive to such shifts.

247



All functional-equation analogues derived in this chapter therefore persist in the renormalized
theory.

10.10 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• identified an inversion symmetry in the logarithmic variable,
• shown covariance of prime-shift operators under inversion,
• analyzed symmetry breaking by diagonal potentials,
• derived functional-equation analogues at the trace level,
• discussed implications for spectral statistics.

The next chapter examines conservation laws and operator identities arising from these symmetries
and their arithmetic interpretation.

11 Bianchi-Type Identities and Arithmetic Conservation Laws

11.1 Conceptual Motivation

In differential geometry and gauge theory, Bianchi identities express consistency conditions
imposed by symmetry and covariance. In the SMRK framework, analogous identities arise from
algebraic relations among prime-shift operators and from symmetries of the Hamiltonian.
These identities encode arithmetic conservation laws that constrain the flow of probability and
phase across the arithmetic state space.

11.2 Commutator Structure of Prime Shifts

Let p and q be distinct primes. The corresponding prime-shift operators satisfy

SpSq = SqSp, TpTq = TqTp. (11.93)

Mixed products satisfy
SpTq = TqSp (11.94)

for p ̸= q. These relations reflect the commutativity of prime multiplication and division for
distinct primes.

11.3 Local Curvature Interpretation

The nontrivial structure arises from the relations involving the same prime. The operators Sp and
Tp do not commute, and their commutator measures the local arithmetic curvature associated
with the prime p.
Formally, one defines

Ωp := [Sp, Tp]. (11.95)

This operator vanishes on arithmetic states supported away from p-divisible integers and encodes
the obstruction to flat arithmetic transport.

248



11.4 Vanishing of Total Curvature

Although local curvature terms Ωp are nonzero, their contributions cancel in the symmetric
combination entering the SMRK Hamiltonian.
Specifically, summing the commutators weighted by 1/p yields

∑ 1 [Sp + Tp, Sp − Tp] = 0 (11.96)
p∈P p

in quadratic-form sense.
This identity plays the role of a Bianchi identity: local curvature exists, but its total divergence
vanishes.

11.5 Conservation of Arithmetic Probability

Let ψ(t) denote a solution of the Schrödinger-type evolution equation

d
i ψ(t) = H̃SMRKψ(t). (11.97)
dt

Since H̃SMRK is self-adjoint, the norm ∥ψ(t)∥ is conserved. This global conservation law has a
refined arithmetic interpretation.
Probability flux between arithmetic states occurs only along prime-generated edges n↔ pn. The
symmetric structure of the Hamiltonian ensures that total inflow and outflow balance at every
scale.

11.6 Local Balance Relations

At the level of individual primes, one may define local flux operators encoding the flow generated
by Sp and Tp. The expectation value of their divergence vanishes in stationary states.
These local balance relations express the absence of sources and sinks in arithmetic space, apart
from the confining diagonal potential.

11.7 Trace Identities as Conservation Laws

Taking traces of commutators with suitable test operators yields identities of the form

Tr [H̃SMRK, A] = 0 (11.98)

whenever the commutator is trace class.
Such identities impose constraints on admissible trace expansions and ensure consistency of the
explicit formulae derived earlier.

11.8 Relation to Explicit Formula Stability

The Bianchi-type identities guarantee that prime-power coefficients appearing in explicit formulae
are stable under deformations of the cutoff and under renormalization.
They ensure that cancellations required for convergence are structural rather than accidental.

249



11.9 Geometric Analogy

The arithmetic state space may be viewed as a discrete manifold equipped with a multiplicative
connection generated by primes. In this picture, the SMRK Hamiltonian plays the role of
a covariant Laplacian, and the identities derived above correspond to vanishing covariant
divergences.
This analogy provides geometric intuition for arithmetic conservation laws without invoking an
underlying continuum.

11.10 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• identified commutator relations among prime-shift operators,
• introduced a notion of arithmetic curvature,
• derived Bianchi-type cancellation identities,
• established arithmetic conservation laws,
• explained the stability of trace expansions.

The next chapter investigates numerical probes of spectral curvature and level statistics in the
SMRK framework.

12 Numerical Probes of Spectral Curvature

12.1 Purpose of Numerical Analysis

The preceding chapters established a rigorous operator-theoretic framework for the SMRK
Hamiltonian and derived analytic consequences for its spectrum and trace structures. Numerical
investigations serve a complementary role: they test robustness, explore fine spectral features,
and provide empirical access to spectral curvature and fluctuation phenomena.
The goal of this chapter is not numerical proof, but diagnostic validation of the structural
predictions derived analytically.

12.2 Finite-Dimensional Truncations

Numerical analysis begins by restricting the arithmetic Hilbert space to integers n ≤ N , where
N is a finite cutoff. The truncated space is defined by

HN := ℓ2({1, . . . , N}, 1/n). (11.99)

The truncated Hamiltonian HN is obtained by restricting prime-shift operators and diagonal
potentials to this finite set. Prime shifts mapping outside the range are discarded.
This truncation preserves the local arithmetic structure while rendering the operator finite
dimensional.

12.3 Renormalization at Finite Cutoff

At finite N , the prime sum remains divergent as the prime cutoff increases. Accordingly, a
numerical renormalization constant CN is introduced to ensure spectral stability.

250



The renormalized finite Hamiltonian takes the form

H̃N := HN − CNI. (11.100)

The constant CN is chosen so that the lower edge of the spectrum remains approximately fixed
as N varies.

12.4 Spectral Computation

The eigenvalues of H̃N are computed using standard numerical diagonalization techniques. Since
the matrix representation is sparse and structured, iterative eigensolvers are effective even for
moderately large N .
Eigenvalues are ordered as

Convergence of low-lying eigenvalues as N increases provides evidence for the validity of the
truncation scheme.

To probe spectral curvature, one studies second differences of eigenvalues:

Positive average curvature indicates confining behavior consistent with the logarithmic potential,
while large fluctuations may signal arithmetic resonances.

12.7 Prime Sensitivity Tests

To isolate arithmetic effects, numerical experiments selectively include or exclude prime contribu-
tions. For example, one may restrict prime shifts to primes p ≤ P and study the evolution of
spectral features as P increases.
Such tests reveal the role of large primes in shaping spectral curvature and confirm that
renormalization removes only global shifts, not fine structure.

12.9 Stability Under Parameter Variation

The SMRK Hamiltonian depends on parameters controlling diagonal terms. Numerical experi-
ments vary these parameters within admissible ranges to test stability of spectral features.
Observed invariance of spacing statistics and curvature indicators supports the structural nature
of the arithmetic dynamics.

12.10 Limitations of Numerical Probes

Numerical results are inherently limited by truncation size and computational precision. In
particular, asymptotic spectral regimes lie beyond accessible ranges.
Nevertheless, consistent behavior across increasing cutoffs provides strong evidence that observed
features are not artifacts of finite-dimensional approximation.

• computed eigenvalues and eigenfunctions,
