• tested sensitivity to prime contributions and parameters.
The numerical probes support the analytic framework and motivate the final comparison with
classical number-theoretic structures developed in the next chapter.

13 Comparison with Classical Number Theory

13.1 Scope of the Comparison

The SMRK framework introduces an operator-theoretic setting in which arithmetic structure
generates dynamics and spectral data. The purpose of this chapter is to compare this framework
with classical constructions in analytic number theory and to clarify points of contact, agreement,
and divergence.
The comparison is structural rather than identificatory: no direct equivalence between spectra
and classical zero sets is asserted.

252



13.2 Explicit Formulae Revisited

Classical explicit formulae relate weighted sums over primes to weighted sums over nontrivial
zeros of the Riemann zeta function. In the SMRK framework, analogous identities arise from
trace expansions of a self-adjoint operator.
The correspondence may be summarized as follows:

• spectral sums replace sums over zeta zeros,
• trace functionals replace contour integrals of logarithmic derivatives,
• prime-power weights arise from closed arithmetic paths.

In both settings, test functions mediate the relation between arithmetic and spectral data.

13.3 Role of the von Mangoldt Function

In classical theory, the von Mangoldt function appears as the coefficient governing prime powers
in explicit formulae. Within the SMRK Hamiltonian, the same function enters as a diagonal
potential generating logarithmic arithmetic forces.
This dual role clarifies the origin of logarithmic prime weights in trace expansions and provides a
dynamical interpretation of the von Mangoldt function.

13.4 Dirichlet Series versus Operator Traces

Classical zeta functions are defined as Dirichlet series and extended by analytic continuation.
In contrast, the SMRK framework begins with a self-adjoint operator and defines trace objects
directly.
While both approaches yield meromorphic functions encoding arithmetic data, their foundations
differ fundamentally:

• Dirichlet series rely on analytic continuation,
• operator traces rely on spectral theory and compactness.

This distinction allows the SMRK framework to avoid assumptions about analytic continuation
while retaining access to explicit-formula-type identities.

13.5 Functional Equation versus Operator Symmetry

The functional equation of the Riemann zeta function encodes a symmetry exchanging s and
1− s. In the SMRK framework, analogous symmetry arises from inversion in the logarithmic
variable and covariance of prime-shift operators.
Both mechanisms impose duality constraints on arithmetic–spectral relations. The difference lies
in implementation: analytic symmetry versus operator-theoretic symmetry.

13.6 Zero Sets and Spectral Data

Classical number theory focuses on the location of zeros of zeta and L-functions. The SMRK
framework produces a discrete spectrum with well-defined eigenvalues and eigenfunctions.

253



No claim is made that these eigenvalues coincide with classical zeros. Instead, the comparison
highlights a shared organizing principle: arithmetic information is encoded in spectral distributions
subject to symmetry and trace constraints.

13.7 Trace Formulae and Weil-Type Analogues

Weil’s explicit formula may be interpreted as a trace formula on an adelic space. The SMRK
framework realizes a trace formula on a purely arithmetic Hilbert space indexed by the natural
numbers.
Both settings involve:

• a global trace identity,
• local contributions indexed by primes,
• symmetry-induced cancellations.

The SMRK construction may thus be viewed as a non-adelic, operator-based analogue of Weil-type
trace formulae.

13.8 Spectral Statistics and Random Matrix Theory

Classical conjectures relate zero statistics of zeta functions to random matrix ensembles. The
SMRK framework does not impose a specific ensemble but predicts structural constraints on
spectral statistics derived from arithmetic symmetry.
Numerical probes suggest nontrivial correlations distinct from purely random spectra, highlighting
the influence of prime-generated dynamics.

13.9 Limitations of the Comparison

The comparison with classical number theory has clear limits:
• no analytic continuation of zeta functions is derived,
• no identification of SMRK eigenvalues with classical zeros is established,
• no proof of classical conjectures is claimed.

The SMRK framework should therefore be regarded as complementary rather than substitutive.

13.10 Conceptual Synthesis

Despite foundational differences, both classical number theory and the SMRK framework share
a common philosophy: arithmetic structure manifests through spectral and trace phenomena
governed by symmetry.
The SMRK Hamiltonian provides a concrete realization of this philosophy within a self-adjoint
operator setting.

13.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• compared SMRK trace identities with classical explicit formulae,

254



• analyzed the role of the von Mangoldt function,
• contrasted operator traces with Dirichlet series,
• examined symmetry principles and functional equation analogues,
• clarified the scope and limitations of the comparison.

This concludes the main body of the work. The appendices collect technical details, auxiliary
constructions, and numerical protocols supporting the framework developed here.

B.1 Mellin Space and Weighted Trace Constructions

B.1.1 Motivation

Weighted trace constructions play a central role in connecting spectral data of the SMRK Hamil-

B.1.2 Mellin Transform on Arithmetic States

Let ψ be an arithmetic state. Its Mellin transfo∑rm is formally defined by

n≥1

B.1.3 Weighted Operators

For real s > 0, define the diagonal weight operator by
(Wsψ)(n) := n−sψ(n). (11.2)

The operator Ws is Hilbert–Schmidt for s > 1/2 and trace class for s > 1.

For nonreal z, the weighted resolvent trace( is defined by )

The function R(z; s) is analytic in z away from the real axis and analytic in s for Re s > 1/2.
This joint analyticity allows contour deformation and Mellin inversion techniques analogous to
those used in classical analytic number theory.

B.1.6 Connection with Explicit Formulae

Weighted traces provide the natural test-function framework for explicit-formula-type identities.
The Mellin parameter s controls arithmetic weights, while the spectral parameter z controls
smoothing in energy space.
Their interplay replaces the role of complex variable shifts in classical zeta functions.

Abstract
This section extends the SMRK Hamiltonian framework beyond the clas-
sical setting of the Riemann zeta function to encompass more general L-
functions. The objective is to investigate whether the operator-theoretic
principles developed in the preceding sections admit natural general-
izations that reflect broader arithmetic contexts, including Dirichlet
L-functions and related families.
The extension is formulated at the level of operator construction rather
than as a direct translation of known analytic results. Instead of modify-
ing explicit formulae by hand, the approach seeks to adapt the underlying
operator fields, ladder structures, and arithmetic weights so that the
resulting Hamiltonians encode the additional symmetries and arithmetic
data associated with general L-functions. This preserves the conceptual
integrity of the SMRK framework while allowing for greater expressive
power.
A central challenge addressed in this section is the incorporation of
characters, conductors, and arithmetic twists into the operator dynamics.
These features introduce new layers of structure that must be reflected
both in the definition of the arithmetic state space and in the interaction
rules of the ladder operators. The section discusses how such data can
be embedded into the operator formalism without sacrificing analytic
control or spectral interpretability.
The implications of this generalization are explored at the level of traces,
explicit formulae, and spectral programs. While the existence of a uni-
versal operator capturing all L-functions is not assumed, the framework
demonstrates how families of related operators may be studied within a
common mathematical language. This perspective emphasizes structural
relationships rather than isolated cases, aligning with the operator-field
philosophy underlying QFM.
The section also highlights limitations and open problems. Not all features
of general L-functions admit immediate operator-theoretic interpretation,
and the extension of domain and self-adjointness results remains subtle
in more complex arithmetic settings. These challenges are presented

263



as intrinsic aspects of the theory, guiding future research rather than
detracting from the coherence of the framework.
By situating general L-functions within the SMRK operator program,
this section demonstrates the scalability of the approach and delineates
its current boundaries. It marks the conceptual completion of the math-
ematical foundation developed in Part I and prepares the transition to
computational, architectural, and applied considerations in subsequent
parts of this compendium.

1 From the Riemann Zeta Function to General L-Functions

1.1 Motivation

The SMRK Hamiltonian was initially formulated in direct correspondence with the arithmetic
structure underlying the Riemann zeta function. While this setting already captures essential
features of prime dynamics, it represents only the simplest member of a much broader family of
arithmetic objects.
The natural next step is to extend the construction from the Riemann zeta function to general
L-functions. This extension is not an afterthought but a structural necessity: the operator-
theoretic framework should be flexible enough to accommodate local data, internal symmetries,
and representation-theoretic input.

1.2 What Changes Beyond the Zeta Function

The Riemann zeta function corresponds to the trivial representation at every prime. General
L-functions introduce additional local structure:

• local Euler factors with multiple parameters,
• internal degrees of freedom indexed by representation dimension,
• nontrivial local symmetries and phases,
• arithmetic weights beyond simple prime powers.

From the operator perspective, this means that arithmetic states can no longer be described
solely by integers. Additional internal labels must be incorporated.

1.3 Arithmetic States with Internal Structure

To accommodate general L-functions, arithmetic states are extended from scalar functions ψ(n)
to vector-valued objects

ψ(n) ∈ Cd(n), (12.1)
where the internal dimension d(n) depends on the local data attached to n.
In the simplest cases, d(n) is constant and equal to the degree of the L-function. More generally,
it reflects multiplicative composition of local representations.

1.4 Prime Locality as a Guiding Principle

A defining feature of L-functions is locality at primes. Each prime contributes an independent local
factor to the Euler product, and global structure emerges from their multiplicative combination.

264



The SMRK framework respects this principle by associating to each prime p a local operator
acting on the internal degrees of freedom. Global operators are obtained by assembling these
local actions across all primes.

1.5 Euler Products as Operator Factorizations

Classically, an L-function is defined by an Eule∏r product of the form
L(s) = Lp(s), (12.2)

p

where each Lp(s) encodes local arithmetic data.
In the operator framework, this structure is mirrored by factorization of the Hamiltonian
interaction into prime-local contributions. Each prime-shift operator is decorated with a finite-
dimensional matrix encoding the corresponding local Euler factor.

1.6 From Scalars to Matrix-Valued Prime Shifts

For the Riemann zeta function, prime shifts act as scalar operators. For general L-functions,
each prime p is associated with a matrix

Ap ∈ Matd×d(C), (12.3)
encoding local arithmetic data.
Prime multiplication and division are accompanied by multiplication with Ap or its adjoint,
producing a coupled arithmetic–internal dynamics.

1.7 Preservation of the SMRK Core Principles

Despite the added complexity, the core principles of the SMRK framework remain intact:
• arithmetic dynamics is generated by primes,
• interactions are local in the prime index,
• the Hamiltonian is constructed from symmetric prime-shift combinations,
• renormalization removes only scalar divergences.

The generalization to L-functions therefore represents an enrichment rather than a conceptual
departure.

1.8 Why the Extension Is Nontrivial

Extending the SMRK Hamiltonian to general L-functions introduces genuine new challenges:
• internal spaces must be consistently assembled over composite integers,
• prime-shift operators become matrix-valued,
• self-adjointness requires compatibility conditions on local data,
• trace expansions involve generalized von Mangoldt weights.

These issues require careful formulation and are addressed systematically in the chapters that
follow.

265



1.9 Organization of This Document

The remainder of this document proceeds as follows. We first formalize Euler products and local
arithmetic data. We then construct arithmetic Hilbert spaces with internal degrees of freedom
and define prime-shift operators carrying local representations.
Subsequent chapters establish renormalization, self-adjointness, spectral properties, and trace
expansions. Special cases, including Dirichlet and automorphic L-functions, are treated explicitly.

1.10 Summary

This chapter has:
• motivated the extension of the SMRK Hamiltonian beyond the zeta function,
• identified the new arithmetic and operator-theoretic ingredients,
• outlined the role of local prime data and internal degrees of freedom,
• set the stage for a unified operator framework for general L-functions.

The next chapter introduces Euler products and local parameter data in a form suitable for
operator-theoretic implementation.

2 Euler Products and Local Arithmetic Data

2.1 Local–Global Decomposition

A defining feature of L-functions is their decomposition into independent local factors indexed
by primes. This decomposition expresses a global arithmetic object as a product of prime-local
contributions, each encoding finite-dimensional data.
From the operator-theoretic perspective, this locality principle dictates that the global Hamilto-
nian must be assembled from prime-indexed building blocks, with no direct coupling between
distinct primes.

2.2 General Euler Factors

Let L(s) be an L-function of degree d. Its Eule∏r product is written formally as

L(s) = Lp(s), (12.4)
p

where each local factor takes the form (
Lp(s) = det I −Ap p−s)−1

Here Ap ∈ Matd×d(C) is a matrix encoding the local arithmetic data at the prime p.

2.3 Local Parameters and Eigenvalues

The matrix Ap is assumed to be diagonalizable over C with eigenvalues

{αp,1, . . . , αp,d}. (12.6)

The parameters αp,j play the role of local spectral data and govern the contribution of prime
powers in explicit formulae.

2.4 Ramified and Unramified Primes

For most primes, the local data are unramified and satisfy uniform bounds on αp,j . A finite set
of primes may be ramified, at which the local factor deviates from the generic form.
In the SMRK framework, ramified primes are treated by modifying the corresponding local
operators without altering the global structure. Since only finitely many primes are affected, this
does not influence renormalization or asymptotic spectral properties.

2.5 Multiplicativity and Composite Integers

Local data at primes determine arithmetic dat∏a at composite integers via multiplicativity. For
an integer

n = pνp , (12.8)
p

the associated local space is constructed as a tensor product over primes dividing n.
This multiplicative assembly ensures consistency between prime-local operators and global
arithmetic states.

2.6 Generalized von Mangoldt Functions

Associated with the local parameters αp,j is a generalized von Mangoldt function defined by

∑d
ΛL(pm) := αmp,j log p, (12.9)

j=1

and extended by zero to integers that are not prime powers.
These weights replace the classical von Mangoldt function in trace expansions and explicit
formulae.

2.7 Local Admissibility Conditions

For the operator construction to be well defined, the local data must satisfy basic admissibility
conditions:

• boundedness of αp,j uniformly in p,
• compatibility with adjoint operations,
• finite-dimensionality of local spaces.

These conditions ensure that prime-shift operators decorated with local matrices are uniformly
form-bounded and admit a common renormalization scheme.

267



2.8 Operator Interpretation of Euler Factors

In the SMRK framework, Euler factors are not treated as analytic objects but as operator-
theoretic data. Each factor Lp(s) corresponds to a local interaction term acting on internal
degrees of freedom and coupled to arithmetic prime shifts.
The determinant structure of Lp(s) is reflected in traces over the internal spaces associated with
prime-power loops.

2.9 Universality of the Local Data Formalism

The formalism introduced here applies uniformly to:
• Dirichlet L-functions,

• Artin L-functions,

• automorphic L-functions,

• finite products and twists thereof.
Only the specification of the local matrices Ap changes; the global operator architecture remains
fixed.

2.10 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• introduced general Euler products in operator-ready form,

• described local arithmetic parameters and eigenvalues,

• defined generalized von Mangoldt functions,

• explained multiplicative assembly over composite integers,

• established admissibility conditions for local data.
The next chapter constructs arithmetic Hilbert spaces carrying internal degrees of freedom
compatible with this local–global structure.

3 Arithmetic Hilbert Spaces with Internal Degrees of Freedom

3.1 Motivation

To accommodate general L-functions, arithmetic states must carry internal degrees of freedom
reflecting local representation data at primes. This chapter constructs arithmetic Hilbert spaces
that combine multiplicative structure in the integer variable with finite-dimensional internal
spaces.
The construction preserves the core SMRK principle: arithmetic dynamics is driven by prime
shifts, while internal structure evolves locally at each prime.

268



3.2 Local Internal Spaces

Fix an L-function of degree d. To each prime p we associate a finite-dimensional complex vector
space

V ∼= Cdp , (12.10)
carrying the local arithmetic data encoded by the matrix Ap.
At unramified primes, these spaces are canonically identified. At ramified primes, Vp may differ,
but only finitely many such primes occur.

3.3 Internal Spaces for Composite Integers

For a positive integer ∏

This definition reflects the multiplicative assembly of local data and ensures compatibility with
Euler products.

3.4 Arithmetic States

An arithmetic state is a collection

ψ = {ψ(n)}n≥1, ψ(n) ∈ Vn, (12.13)

with finite norm defined below.
Such states may be viewed as vector-valued arithmetic functions equipped with a prime-
factorization-dependent internal structure.

3.5 Inner Product and Norm

The arithmetic Hilbert space HL is defined by the inner product
∑

⟨ψ, ϕ⟩ := 1 ⟨ψ(n), ϕ(n)⟩V ,

where the inner product on Vn is induced from the tensor product of the local spaces.
The weight 1/n ensures compatibility with multiplicative shifts and guarantees that prime-shift
operators admit simple adjoint relations.

3.6 Dense Subspace and Core

The set of arithmetic states with finite support in n and finite-dimensional support in internal
indices forms a dense subspace of HL.
This subspace serves as a common invariant core for all operators introduced in subsequent
chapters.

269



3.7 Canonical Identification of Tensor Factors

For integers n and m with coprime factorizations, the internal spaces satisfy

V ∼
nm = Vn ⊗ Vm. (12.15)

This canonical identification is essential for defining prime-shift operators that act consistently
across composite integers.

3.8 Normalization Conventions

The choice of inner product on each Vp is fixed so that the local matrices Ap act as bounded
operators with uniformly controlled norms.
This normalization ensures that global operators constructed from prime-local data are uniformly
form-bounded.

3.9 Comparison with the Scalar Case

When d = 1 and Ap = 1 for all primes, the internal spaces Vn reduce to C for all n. In this case,
HL coincides with the arithmetic Hilbert space used for the Riemann zeta function.
Thus the present construction is a strict generalization of the scalar SMRK setting.

3.10 Structural Properties

The arithmetic Hilbert space with internal degrees of freedom satisfies:
• separability,
• multiplicative tensor-factor structure,
• compatibility with prime shifts,
• existence of a natural dense core.

These properties form the foundation for defining Hamiltonians and trace objects in the generalized
setting.

3.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• constructed arithmetic Hilbert spaces with internal structure,
• defined arithmetic states as vector-valued functions,
• established the weighted inner product,
• ensured multiplicative compatibility across primes,
• related the construction to the scalar SMRK case.

The next chapter defines prime-shift operators decorated with local representations acting on
these spaces.

4 Prime-Shift Operators with Local Representations

4.1 Purpose of Prime-Shift Operators

Prime-shift operators generate arithmetic dynamics by implementing multiplication and division
by primes. In the generalized L-function setting, these shifts must be decorated with local
representation data acting on internal degrees of freedom.
This chapter defines such operators and establishes their fundamental algebraic and adjoint
properties.

4.2 Multiplicative Prime Shifts

Let p be a prime. The multiplicative prim{e-shift operator Sp acts on arithmetic states by

(Spψ)(n) := Ap ψ(n/p), p | n, (12.16)
0, otherwise.

Here Ap acts on the internal space Vn/p and is transported to Vn via the canonical tensor
identification.

4.3 Divisive Prime Shifts

The divisive prime-shift operator Tp acts by

(Tpψ)(n) := ψ(pn), (12.17)

where the internal space Vpn is identified with Vp ⊗ Vn.
In this action, no matrix multiplication is applied; the internal structure is extended by tensoring
with the identity on Vp.

4.4 Adjoint Relations

With respect to the weighted inner product on HL, the operators Sp and Tp satisfy

This relation generalizes the scalar adjoint identity and ensures symmetric construction of the
Hamiltonian.

4.5 Boundedness Properties

Under the admissibility assumptions on the local matrices Ap, the operators Sp and Tp are
bounded on the dense core of finitely supported arithmetic states.
Moreover, their operator norms grow at most polynomially in p, which is sufficient for form-
boundedness after weighting by 1/p.

271



4.6 Commutation Relations

For distinct primes p and q, the prime-shift operators commute:

SpSq = SqSp, TpTq = TqTp, SpTq = TqSp. (12.19)

These relations reflect the independence of prime factors and ensure consistency of multiplicative
assembly.

4.7 Local Noncommutativity

For a fixed prime p, the operators Sp and Tp do not commute. Their noncommutativity encodes
local arithmetic curvature associated with the prime p and is controlled by the local matrix Ap.
This local structure plays a key role in trace expansions and curvature identities.

4.8 Ramified Primes

At ramified primes, the definition of Ap and the identification of internal spaces may differ from
the unramified case. Since only finitely many primes are ramified, these modifications introduce
only finite-rank perturbations.
Such perturbations do not affect renormalization, self-adjointness, or asymptotic spectral proper-
ties.

4.9 Consistency with Multiplicativity

The definitions of Sp and Tp are compatible with multiplicativity in the sense that their combined
action on composite integers respects the tensor-product structure of internal spaces.
This consistency ensures that global arithmetic dynamics is entirely determined by prime-local
data.

4.10 Reduction to the Scalar Case

When all local matrices Ap are equal to the identity, the decorated prime-shift operators reduce
to the scalar shifts used in the zeta-function case.
Thus the present construction is a strict generalization of the original SMRK prime-shift operators.

4.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• defined prime-shift operators carrying local representation data,
• established their adjoint and boundedness properties,
• analyzed their commutation relations,
• treated the role of ramified primes,
• connected the construction to the scalar SMRK case.

The next chapter defines the generalized SMRK Hamiltonian for L-functions using these opera-
tors.

5 Definition of the SMRK Hamiltonian for General L-Functions

5.1 Guiding Principles

The construction of the SMRK Hamiltonian for general L-functions follows the same principles
as in the scalar case:

• arithmetic dynamics is generated by prime shifts,
• interactions are local in the prime index,
• symmetry between multiplication and division by primes is enforced,
• divergences arise only from infinite prime sums and are removable by renormalization.

The presence of internal degrees of freedom modifies the operator structure but not the underlying
philosophy.

5.2 Formal Definition

The formal SMRK Hamiltonian associated with an L-function is defined by
∑ 1( )

HL := Sp + S∗ + 2 2
p p VL, (1 . 0)

p∈P

where Sp denotes the decorated prime-shift operator defined previously, and VL is a diagonal
potential acting on arithmetic states.

5.3 Diagonal Potential

The diagonal potential VL encodes generalized von Mangoldt weights and logarithmic confinement:
( )

(VLψ)(n) := αΛL(n) + β logn ψ(n). (12.21)

Here ΛL denotes the generalized von Mangoldt function associated with the local parameters αp,j ,
and α, β are real constants controlling the relative strength of arithmetic forcing and confinement.

5.4 Symmetric Prime Interaction

The combination Sp+S∗
p ensures that the prime interaction is symmetric and formally self-adjoint.

This symmetry is essential for constructing a self-adjoint realization of the Hamiltonian.
In contrast, unsymmetrized prime shifts would generate irreversible arithmetic flows and are
therefore excluded.

5.5 Domain of Definition

The operator HL is initially defined on the dense core of finitely supported arithmetic states with
finite internal support.
On this domain, all sums over primes are finite and the action of HL is well defined.

273



5.6 Divergence of the Prime Sum

As in the scalar case, the sum over primes in the definition of HL diverges when taken over all
primes. This divergence arises from the accumulation of infinitely many weak prime interactions
and is independent of the internal representation data.
The divergence is scalar in form sense and therefore removable by renormalization.

5.7 Quadratic Form Associated with the Hamiltonian

To prepare for renormalization, we∑introduce the quadratic form
1( )

qL(ψ, ϕ) := ⟨Spψ, ϕ⟩+ ⟨S∗ψ, ϕ⟩
p p + ⟨VLψ, ϕ⟩, (12.22)

p∈P

initially defined on the dense core.
This form captures the essential features of the formal Hamiltonian while providing a suitable
framework for analytic control.

5.8 Hermiticity

Using the adjoint relations established previously, one verifies that

qL(ψ, ϕ) = qL(ϕ, ψ) (12.23)

for all ψ and ϕ in the domain.
Thus the quadratic form is Hermitian, even though the formal operator sum is divergent.

5.9 Reduction to the Scalar Case

When the degree d = 1 and all local matrices Ap are trivial, the Hamiltonian HL reduces exactly
to the original SMRK Hamiltonian associated with the Riemann zeta function.
This confirms that the generalized construction is a true extension of the scalar framework.

5.10 Interpretation

The SMRK Hamiltonian for general L-functions describes arithmetic dynamics on a state space
enriched by internal representation data. Prime shifts transport both arithmetic position and
internal state, while the diagonal potential imposes logarithmic confinement and arithmetic
forcing.
This operator encodes, in a single object, the global arithmetic content of the underlying
L-function.

5.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• defined the formal SMRK Hamiltonian for general L-functions,
• introduced the diagonal potential with generalized von Mangoldt weights,
• analyzed symmetry and divergence of the prime interaction,

274



• formulated the associated quadratic form,
• related the construction to the scalar case.

The next chapter performs renormalization and constructs a self-adjoint realization of the
Hamiltonian.

6 Renormalization and Self-Adjointness

6.1 Need for Renormalization

The formal SMRK Hamiltonian for general L-functions contains an infinite sum over prime-
indexed interactions. As in the scalar case, this sum diverges in operator norm and cannot be
interpreted directly as a self-adjoint operator.
The divergence originates from the accumulation of infinitely many weak prime interactions and
is independent of the internal representation data. Consequently, renormalization is unavoidable.

6.2 Prime Cutoff and Truncated Hamiltonians

Let P ≥ 2 be a prime cutoff. We define th∑e truncated Hamiltonian by

6.6 Uniform Form Bounds

There exists a reference quadratic form q0, incorporating logarithmic confinement, such that for

6.7 Existence of the Limit Form

The uniform bounds imply that the family {q̃L,P }P is Cauchy in the sense of quadratic forms.
Consequently, there exists a limiting quadratic form

The limiting form is closed, densely defined, and bounded from below.

6.8 Self-Adjoint Hamiltonian

By the representation theorem for closed quadratic forms, there exists a unique self-adjoint
operator H̃L such that

q̃L(ψ, ϕ) = ⟨H̃Lψ, ϕ⟩ (12.30)

for all ψ in the operator domain and all ϕ in the form domain.
The operator H̃L is bounded from below and generates a strongly continuous unitary time
evolution.

6.9 Identification with the Formal Hamiltonian

On the dense core of finitely supported arithmetic states, the action of H̃L coincides with that of
the formal Hamiltonian HL up to an additive constant arising from renormalization.
This constant produces a uniform spectral shift and has no effect on spectral spacings or trace
identities.

6.10 Stability under Local Data Variation

Since renormalization removes only a scalar divergence, the construction of H̃L is stable under
variation of the local matrices Ap, provided they satisfy the admissibility conditions.
In particular, changing finitely many local factors produces only finite-rank perturbations.

• obtained a self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian for general L-functions.

7 Spectral Properties and Compactness

7.1 Preliminaries

Let H̃L denote the self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian associated with a general L-function, con-
structed in the previous chapter. By construction, H̃L is bounded from below and defined via a
closed quadratic form on the arithmetic Hilbert space with internal degrees of freedom.
All spectral statements in this chapter are understood modulo the additive renormalization
constant.

7.2 Reference Operator and Confinement

The reference quadratic form q0 incorporates a logarithmic confining potential of the form
∑

q0[ψ] = (1 + log2 n) ∥ψ(n)∥2 1
. (12.31)

n≥1 n

This confinement suppresses delocalization in the arithmetic variable and plays the role of an
effective potential growing at infinity.

7.3 Compactness of the Resolvent

Let H0 denote the self-adjoint operator associated with q0. Since the confining term diverges as
n→∞, the resolvent (H0 + i)−1 is compact.
The difference H̃L−H0 is relatively form-bounded with relative bound zero. By standard results
in spectral theory, compactness of the resolvent is preserved under such perturbations.
Therefore, the resolvent

(H̃L + i)−1 (12.32)
is compact on the arithmetic Hilbert space.

7.4 Pure Point Spectrum

Compactness of the resolvent implies that the spectrum of H̃L consists entirely of isolated
eigenvalues of finite multiplicity.

277



There is no continuous or residual spectrum. The eigenvalues form a sequence

σ(H̃L) = {λk}k≥1, λk → +∞ as k →∞. (12.33)

7.5 Eigenfunction Regularity

Let ψk be an eigenfunction associated with the eigenvalue λk. Since ψk lies in the form domain
of q0, it satisfies ∑

log2 n ∥ψk(n)∥2 1
<∞. (12.34)

n≥1 n

Thus eigenfunctions are localized in the logarithmic variable and decay rapidly at large arithmetic
scales.

7.6 Growth of Eigenvalues

The confining nature of the reference operator provides a comparison principle for the asymptotic
growth of eigenvalues.
Under the change of variables x = logn, the operator H0 becomes unitarily equivalent to a one-
dimensional Schrödinger operator with quadratic confinement. Standard Weyl-type arguments
then imply quadratic growth of eigenvalues:

c1k
2 ≤ λk ≤ c2k

for sufficiently large k and positive constants c1, c2.

7.7 Internal Degrees of Freedom

The presence of finite-dimensional internal spaces does not alter compactness or discreteness of
the spectrum. Internal multiplicities are absorbed into the finite multiplicity of eigenvalues.
Thus the essential spectral behavior is governed by arithmetic confinement rather than representation-
theoretic complexity.

7.8 Spectral Decomposition

The spectral theorem yields the expansion ∑
H̃L = λk |ψk⟩⟨ψk|, (12.36)

k≥1

with convergence in the strong operator topology.
This decomposition underlies all trace and resolvent constructions in subsequent chapters.

7.9 Stability under Local Perturbations

Finite modifications of local data at ramified primes correspond to finite-rank perturbations of
H̃L. Such perturbations do not affect compactness of the resolvent or the asymptotic growth of
eigenvalues.
Therefore, the spectral properties established here are stable under admissible variations of local
arithmetic data.

8 Trace Objects and Generalized von Mangoldt Functions

8.1 Purpose of Trace Objects

Trace objects provide the principal bridge between the spectral data of the SMRK Hamiltonian
and arithmetic structures encoded by general L-functions. In the operator-theoretic framework,
traces replace Dirichlet series and contour integrals as the primary analytic tools.
This chapter introduces the relevant trace objects and explains how generalized von Mangoldt
functions emerge naturally from their arithmetic expansions.

8.2 Spectral Traces

Let H̃L be the self-adjoint SMRK Hamiltonian constructed previously. For a suitable test
function f : R → C with sufficient decay, the o∑perator f(H̃L) is trace class and admits the
spectral expansion

Tr f(H̃L) = f(λk), (12.37)
k≥1

where {λk} are the eigenvalues of H̃L.

8.3 Heat Kernel Trace

A fundamental example is the heat kernel trace, defin∑ed for t > 0 by

KL(t) := Tr e−tH̃L = e−tλk . (12.38)
k≥1

Quadratic growth of the eigenvalues guarantees convergence for all positive t. The heat kernel
encodes global spectral information and admits both short-time and long-time asymptotic regimes.

8.7 Arithmetic Expansion Strategy

An alternative evaluation of trace objects proceeds by expanding the operator f(H̃L) in terms of
the prime-shift structure of the Hamiltonian.
Closed arithmetic paths, formed by sequences of prime multiplications and divisions that return
to the same integer, contribute to the trace. Each such path is naturally associated with a prime
power.

8.8 Emergence of Generalized von Mangoldt Functions

Evaluating the contribution of a prime power pm yields weights proportional to

8.10 Universality of the Construction

The appearance of generalized von Mangoldt functions is independent of the specific choice of
trace object. Heat kernels, resolvents, and smoothed spectral zeta functions all produce the same
prime-power weights.
This universality reflects the intrinsic encoding of arithmetic data in the prime-shift operators
rather than in analytic continuation procedures.

8.11 Interpretation

In the SMRK framework, generalized von Mangoldt functions are not inserted by hand. They
emerge dynamically as the weights of closed arithmetic loops generated by the Hamiltonian.
Trace objects therefore provide a direct operator-theoretic realization of arithmetic explicit-
formula structures for general L-functions.

9 Explicit Formula Interface for General L-Functions

9.1 Objective

The purpose of this chapter is to derive explicit arithmetic–spectral identities for general L-
functions within the SMRK framework. These identities play the role of explicit formulae: they
relate weighted sums over spectral data of a self-adjoint operator to weighted sums over prime
powers governed by generalized von Mangoldt functions.
Unlike classical approaches, no analytic continuation of Dirichlet series is assumed. All identities
arise from operator-theoretic trace calculus.

9.2 Test Functions and Functional Calculus

Let f : R → C be a smooth test function with sufficient decay at infinity. By the functional
calculus for self-adjoint operators, the operator f(H̃L) is trace class.
Its trace admits the spectral representation ∑

The goal is to compute this trace in an alternative, arithmetic form.

prime-shift structure.

9.5 Closed Arithmetic Paths

Powers of the Hamiltonian expand into sums over products of decorated prime-shift operators.
Only closed arithmetic paths contribute to the trace.
Such paths correspond to finite sequences of prime multiplications and divisions whose net effect
on the arithmetic variable is trivial. Each closed path is canonically associated with a prime
power pm.

9.7 Explicit Formula Structure

This identity constitutes the explicit formula interface for general L-functions.

9.8 Comparison with Classical Explicit Formulae

The structure mirrors that of classical explicit formulae:
• spectral sums replace sums over zeros of L-functions,
• prime-power sums appear with generalized von Mangoldt weights,
• test functions and their transforms mediate the correspondence.

The essential distinction is foundational: the SMRK formula arises from a self-adjoint operator
rather than from analytic continuation of a Dirichlet series.

9.9 Stability under Renormalization

Renormalization introduces only an additive scalar shift in the spectrum. Since explicit formulae
involve trace differences or test functions with sufficient decay, they are invariant under such
shifts.
Therefore, the explicit formula interface is intrinsic to the SMRK Hamiltonian and independent
of regularization choices.

9.10 Scope and Limitations

The explicit formula interface derived here:
• applies uniformly to broad classes of L-functions,
• does not assume functional equations or analytic continuation,
• does not identify SMRK eigenvalues with classical zero sets.

It should be viewed as an operator-theoretic analogue rather than a replacement of classical
explicit formulae.

9.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• derived explicit arithmetic–spectral identities from trace calculus,
• identified generalized von Mangoldt functions as prime-power weights,
• established a direct analogy with classical explicit formulae,
• demonstrated invariance under renormalization.

10 Functional Equation and Gauge Symmetry

10.1 Motivation

In classical analytic number theory, the functional equation of an L-function expresses a deep
duality relating values at complementary arguments. Within the SMRK framework, no analytic
continuation is assumed. Instead, functional-equation-like behavior must arise from intrinsic
operator symmetries.
This chapter identifies the relevant symmetries of the generalized SMRK Hamiltonian and
explains how they induce functional-equation analogues at the level of trace identities.

10.2 Logarithmic Inversion

The arithmetic variable admits a natural logarithmic parametrization x = logn. In this represen-
tation, inversion corresponds to reflection

x 7→ −x. (12.51)

At the operator level, this transformation is implemented by a unitary involution I acting on
arithmetic states, defined abstractly by its action on the logarithmic variable.

10.3 Gauge Action on Internal Degrees of Freedom

General L-functions carry local representation data at each prime. This introduces a natural
gauge freedom: internal bases at different primes may be independently rotated without altering
arithmetic content.
Formally, let Up be a unitary operator acting on the local space Vp. Gauge transformations act
on arithmetic states by

10.6 Diagonal Potential and Symmetry Breaking

The diagonal potential contains a logarithmic term logn, which is odd under inversion in the
logarithmic variable. This term therefore breaks exact inversion symmetry.
The symmetry breaking is controlled and essential for confinement. It plays a role analogous to
a linear perturbation in a symmetric confining potential.

10.7 Functional Equation Analogue

Combining inversion symmetry of the prime interaction with gauge invariance yields identities of
the form

Tr f(H̃L) = Tr (Ff)(H̃L), (12.56)
where F denotes a transform intertwining inversion in the logarithmic variable with internal
gauge action.
These identities serve as functional-equation analogues within the SMRK framework. They are
exact at the operator level and do not rely on analytic continuation.

10.8 Gauge-Invariant Trace Objects

All trace objects introduced previously are invariant under local gauge transformations. In
particular, weighted resolvent traces and heat kernel traces depend only on the eigenvalues of
local matrices Ap, not on their choice of basis.
This invariance reflects the representation-theoretic nature of the arithmetic data and ensures
consistency across different realizations of the same L-function.

10.9 Spectral Duality

The inversion symmetry induces a duality between spectral contributions associated with large
and small arithmetic scales. At the level of trace expansions, this duality pairs prime-power
contributions in a manner reminiscent of classical functional equations.
While no direct relation between spectral parameters and complex arguments of L-functions is
asserted, the structural analogy is exact.

10.10 Stability under Renormalization

Renormalization introduces only a scalar spectral shift. Since both inversion symmetry and
gauge invariance act through unitary conjugation, all functional-equation analogues derived here
are invariant under renormalization.

• identified logarithmic inversion as a fundamental symmetry,

• established gauge covariance of prime-shift operators,

• derived functional-equation analogues from operator symmetries,

• demonstrated stability under renormalization.

11 Dirichlet L-Functions

11.1 Role as a Canonical Test Case

Dirichlet L-functions provide the simplest nontrivial generalization of the Riemann zeta function.
They introduce genuine local phases while retaining a scalar internal structure. As such, they
serve as an ideal testing ground for the generalized SMRK framework.
In this chapter we specialize the general construction to Dirichlet characters and analyze the
resulting operator-theoretic features.

11.2 Dirichlet Characters

Let χ be a Dirichlet character modulo q. The associated Dirichlet L-function is defined formally
by ∑ χ(n) ∏(

In this setting, the degree of the L-function is one, but local data are nontrivial due to the
presence of phases.

11.3 Local Data for Dirichlet Characters

For primes p ∤ q, the local matrix reduces to the scalar

Ap = χ(p). (12.58)

For primes p | q, the local factor is trivial and contributes no prime shift. These primes are
ramified and require special treatment.

11.4 Arithmetic Hilbert Space

Since the degree is one, internal spaces Vp and Vn are one-dimensional for all n. Arithmetic
states are therefore scalar-valued functions ψ(n), as in the zeta-function case.
However, the action of prime shifts is modified by character values.

11.9 Spectral Properties

All spectral properties established for the general SMRK Hamiltonian apply to H̃χ:

• purely discrete spectrum,

11.11 Interpretation

Dirichlet characters introduce arithmetic phases into prime dynamics without altering the
dimensionality of the internal space. This highlights the flexibility of the SMRK framework:
nontrivial arithmetic information can be encoded purely through decorated prime shifts.

12 Automorphic L-Functions

12.1 Motivation

Automorphic L-functions represent the most structured and representation-theoretic class within
the landscape of L-functions. Their local data arise from automorphic representations of reductive
groups and carry genuinely higher-dimensional internal degrees of freedom.
This chapter explains how automorphic L-functions fit naturally into the SMRK framework and
how their rich local structure is reflected in operator dynamics.

12.2 Automorphic Representations and Local Factors

Let π be an automorphic representation of a reductive group over the adeles. The associated
standard L-function admits an Euler product ∏

Here Ap(π) is a matrix whose eigenvalues encode the Satake parameters of the representation at
the prime p.

12.3 Internal Spaces and Satake Parameters

For automorphic L-functions of degree d, the local internal spaces
V ∼p = Cd (12.66)

carry an action of the local matrix Ap(π).
The eigenvalues of Ap(π), often denoted by {αp,1, . . . , αp,d}, determine both the Euler factors
and the generalized von Mangoldt weights.

12.4 Ramification and Local Modification

At almost all primes, the representation π is unramified and the local data are uniformly bounded.
At ramified primes, the structure of Ap(π) may change and the local internal space may differ.
Within the SMRK framework, ramified primes produce only finite-rank modifications of the
Hamiltonian. These do not affect renormalization, compactness, or asymptotic spectral behavior.

12.5 Prime Shifts with Automorphic Data

Decorated prime-shift operators act on arithmetic states by combining arithmetic multiplication
or division with the action of Ap(π) on internal degrees of freedom.
This action implements the local representation-theoretic content of π at the level of arithmetic
dynamics.

12.7 Renormalization and Self-Adjointness

Renormalization proceeds exactly as in the general L-function case. The divergence of the prime
sum is scalar and independent of the representation π.
The resulting renormalized operator H̃π is self-adjoint, bounded from below, and has compact
resolvent.

12.8 Spectral Structure

The spectrum of H̃π consists of discrete eigenvalues of finite multiplicity, diverging to infinity.
Internal multiplicities arising from the representation π contribute to degeneracies but do not
alter global spectral growth.
Eigenfunctions remain logarithmically localized in the arithmetic variable.

12.11 Representation-Theoretic Interpretation

Within the SMRK framework, automorphic L-functions are realized as arithmetic Hamiltonians
whose internal degrees of freedom carry representation-theoretic data.
This provides a concrete operator-theoretic interpretation of automorphic local data and unifies
them with prime-generated arithmetic dynamics.

13 Conclusion and Outlook

13.1 Summary of the Construction

In this document we have developed a unified operator-theoretic framework for L-functions
based on the SMRK Hamiltonian. Starting from the arithmetic structure of the Riemann zeta

290



function, we systematically extended the construction to general L-functions by incorporating
local representation data and internal degrees of freedom.
The resulting framework replaces Dirichlet series and analytic continuation by a self-adjoint
operator acting on an arithmetic Hilbert space. Prime dynamics are implemented by decorated
prime-shift operators, while diagonal potentials provide logarithmic confinement and arithmetic
forcing.

13.2 Renormalization and Self-Adjointness

A central technical result is that the divergence arising from infinite prime sums is scalar in form
sense and can be removed by renormalization. This leads to a closed, semi-bounded quadratic
form and a unique self-adjoint realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian.
The construction is robust: it is stable under variation of local arithmetic data, under inclusion
of ramified primes, and under changes of renormalization scheme up to unitary equivalence.

13.3 Spectral Structure

The renormalized SMRK Hamiltonian has compact resolvent and purely discrete spectrum. Eigen-
values diverge quadratically, and eigenfunctions are logarithmically localized in the arithmetic
variable.
These properties hold uniformly across the entire class of L-functions considered, from Dirichlet
characters to automorphic representations with higher-dimensional local data.

13.4 Trace Objects and Explicit Formulae

Trace objects associated with the SMRK Hamiltonian provide the primary analytic interface
between spectral and arithmetic data. Heat kernels, resolvents, and weighted traces admit both
spectral expansions and arithmetic expansions.
Generalized von Mangoldt functions emerge naturally as the weights of prime-power contributions
associated with closed arithmetic paths. This yields explicit-formula interfaces that mirror classical
explicit formulae, but arise purely from operator theory without analytic continuation.

13.5 Symmetry Principles

Functional-equation analogues appear as consequences of intrinsic operator symmetries, notably
logarithmic inversion and local gauge invariance of internal degrees of freedom. These symmetries
constrain trace identities and induce dualities between spectral and arithmetic contributions.
The framework thus realizes the spirit of the Hilbert–Pólya philosophy at the level of operator
dynamics and trace calculus, while remaining agnostic about the direct identification of spectral
parameters with classical zero sets.

13.6 Special Cases and Universality

Dirichlet L-functions and automorphic L-functions fit naturally into the same architecture.
Differences between these cases are encoded entirely in local matrices and internal spaces, while
the global operator structure remains fixed.
This universality suggests that the SMRK Hamiltonian captures a common arithmetic skeleton
underlying diverse classes of L-functions.

291



13.7 Limitations

The results presented here do not constitute proofs of classical conjectures such as the Riemann
Hypothesis. No claim is made that the spectrum of the SMRK Hamiltonian coincides with the
zero sets of L-functions.
Instead, the framework should be viewed as complementary: it provides a rigorous, self-adjoint
operator setting in which arithmetic explicit-formula structures arise naturally and transparently.

13.8 Future Directions

Several directions for further research emerge naturally:
• refinement of numerical probes and large-scale spectral experiments,
• investigation of level statistics and symmetry classes,
• extension to families of L-functions and parameter-dependent Hamiltonians,
• deeper analysis of gauge symmetries and representation-theoretic constraints,
• exploration of connections with adelic trace formulae and noncommutative geometric

frameworks.
These directions point toward a broader operator-based perspective on arithmetic spectral theory.

13.9 Final Remark

The SMRK Hamiltonian provides a concrete realization of arithmetic dynamics driven by prime
structure and local representation data. By placing L-functions within a self-adjoint operator
framework, it opens a pathway toward a spectral understanding of arithmetic that is both
conceptually transparent and analytically controlled.
This concludes the document.

B.1 Numerical Protocol for L-Functions

B.1.1 Scope and Purpose

This appendix describes a numerical protocol for probing spectral and arithmetic features of
the SMRK Hamiltonian associated with general L-functions. The protocol is designed to be
implementation-agnostic, reproducible, and compatible with the operator-theoretic framework
developed in the main text.
No analytic continuation of L-functions is assumed. All numerical procedures are based on finite
truncations of prime interactions and standard spectral algorithms.

B.1.2 Finite Prime Cutoff

Numerical computations begin by fixing a prime cutoff P . All prime-indexed sums and operators
are truncated to primes p ≤ P . The resulting truncated Hamiltonian is

∑ 1( )
H̃L,P = Sp + S∗ + VL − C(P ), (12.1)

p p
p∈P
p≤P

where C(P ) is the renormalization constant.
Increasing P improves approximation quality while increasing computational cost.

B.1.3 Arithmetic Truncation

In addition to the prime cutoff, arithmetic states are restricted to integers n ≤ N , where N
is a chosen arithmetic cutoff. The Hilbert space is thus replaced by a finite-dimensional space
spanned by basis vectors indexed by

{(n, α) : 1 ≤ n ≤ N, α ∈ Vn}. (12.2)

Boundary effects at n = N are controlled by discarding transitions that leave the truncated
domain.

B.1.4 Matrix Representation

Under the combined cutoffs (P,N), the operator H̃L,P becomes a finite Hermitian matrix. Its
entries are computed explicitly from:

• prime-shift transitions n↔ pn,
• internal matrix actions Ap,
• diagonal potential terms logn and ΛL(n).

Sparse matrix representations are recommended, as prime-shift interactions are local.

296



B.1.5 Eigenvalue Computation

Standard numerical linear algebra techniques may be used to compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors
of the truncated Hamiltonian. Suitable methods include:

• Lanczos or Arnoldi iterations for sparse matrices,
• shift-and-invert strategies for low-lying spectrum,
• block methods for handling internal degeneracies.

Only the lowest portion of the spectrum is typically stable under truncation.

B.1.6 Convergence Diagnostics

Convergence of spectral quantities is assessed by:
• increasing the prime cutoff P ,
• increasing the arithmetic cutoff N ,
• monitoring stability of low-lying eigenvalues,
• comparing spectral gaps across truncations.

Eigenvalues that stabilize under simultaneous increases of P and N are interpreted as approxi-
mations to the true spectrum.

B.1.7 Numerical Trace Objects

Trace objects are approximated numerically by finite sums over computed eigenvalues. For
example, the heat kernel trace is approximated by

B.1.8 Extraction of Prime-Power Signals

Arithmetic signatures are extracted by analyzing oscillatory components of trace objects as
functions of the spectral parameter or time variable t.
Fourier analysis in the logarithmic variable reveals peaks at frequencies m log p, corresponding to
prime powers. The amplitudes of these peaks approximate generalized von Mangoldt weights.

B.1.9 Normalization and Scaling

To compare numerical results across different truncations, it is essential to apply consistent
normalization conventions:

• subtract the same renormalization constant C(P ),
• rescale energies to account for finite-size effects,

297



• normalize eigenfunctions with respect to the weighted inner product.
These steps ensure meaningful comparison of spectral data.

B.1.10 Numerical Stability and Error Sources

Primary sources of numerical error include:
• truncation of prime sums,
• truncation of arithmetic domain,
• boundary effects at large n,
• finite precision in eigenvalue solvers.

Errors are controlled by systematic truncation studies and by focusing on robust spectral features.

B.1.11 Reproducibility Guidelines

For reproducibility, numerical experiments should record:
• prime cutoff P ,
• arithmetic cutoff N ,
• local data specification Ap,
• renormalization constant C(P ),
• numerical solver and precision.

This information suffices to reproduce all numerical results within the SMRK framework.

This appendix explains how the general SMRK Hamiltonian for L-functions reduces to the

The divergence structure of the prime sum is unchanged by the reduction. Renormalized quadratic

Thus the renormalization procedure is universal and independent of local representation data.

All spectral properties established in the general theory reduce to the known properties of the

from the classical theory.

C.1.9 Explicit Formula Interface

The explicit formula interface derived in the general case specializes to the zeta-function explicit
formula, with spectral sums over SMRK eigenvalues replacing sums over nontrivial zeros.
This specialization provides a clear bridge between the general operator framework and the
original SMRK formulation.

C.1.10 Conceptual Interpretation

The reduction shows that all additional structure in the general L-function case arises from
nontrivial local data. The arithmetic backbone—prime-generated dynamics, renormalization,
and confinement—remains unchanged.

300



This highlights the role of the Riemann zeta function as the universal base point of the SMRK
framework.

C.1.11 Summary

This appendix has:
• shown how the general SMRK Hamiltonian reduces to the zeta case,
• demonstrated collapse of internal spaces,
• recovered scalar prime-shift operators,
• verified consistency of renormalization and spectral properties,
• identified the classical von Mangoldt function as a special case.

D.1 Numerical Experiments for Automorphic Families

D.1.1 Objective

This appendix outlines numerical experiments designed to probe spectral and arithmetic features
of the SMRK Hamiltonian associated with automorphic L-functions. The focus is on family-level
behavior rather than on individual representations, with the goal of identifying stable patterns
under variation of local data.
All experiments follow the numerical protocol described in Appendix B.

D.1.2 Choice of Automorphic Families

Numerical studies are organized around families of automorphic representations {πκ} indexed by
a discrete parameter κ. Typical examples include:

• varying weight or level in GL(2) cusp forms,
• twists by finite-order characters,
• families with fixed degree and bounded conductor.

Within a family, local matrices Ap(πκ) vary coherently with κ, while the global operator archi-
tecture remains unchanged.

D.1.3 Local Data Sampling

For numerical feasibility, local data are specified explicitly for primes p ≤ P . At unramified
primes, the matrices Ap(πκ) are constructed from prescribed Satake parameters. At ramified
primes, local contributions are either omitted or modeled by finite-rank modifications.
Consistency across the family is ensured by fixing normalization conventions for all local matrices.

D.1.4 Truncated Hamiltonians

For each family member πκ, a truncated Hamiltonian
H̃πκ,P,N (12.1)

is constructed using the same prime cutoff P and arithmetic cutoff N .
This uniform truncation allows direct comparison of spectral data across different representations
within the family.

D.1.5 Low-Lying Spectrum

Numerical experiments focus primarily on the low-lying eigenvalues

λk }

K
k=1, (12.2)

where K is chosen such that eigenvalues are stable under truncation.

D.1.6 Spectral Statistics

To study collective behavior, spectral spacings are rescaled by local mean density and aggregated
across the family. Empirical distributions of nearest-neighbor spacings provide insight into
symmetry classes and correlations.
Such statistics are compared qualitatively across different automorphic families.

In addition to direct spectral analysis, trace objects are evaluated numerically. For each πκ,

Oscillatory components of trace objects are analyzed via Fourier methods in the logarithmic
variable. Peaks at frequencies m log p are identified and compared across family members.
The stability of peak locations and relative amplitudes across the family provides numerical
evidence for the universality of generalized von Mangoldt weights.

D.1.9 Family Averaging

To suppress noise and truncation artifacts, numerical quantities are averaged over the family index
κ. Averaged spectra and traces reveal structures that are not visible at the level of individual
representations.
This averaging procedure mirrors classical approaches to families of L-functions, but is imple-
mented entirely at the operator level.

D.1.10 Sensitivity to Local Variations

Experiments include controlled perturbations of local data at selected primes. The resulting
changes in spectral data are compared with theoretical expectations for finite-rank perturbations.
Observed stability of global spectral features under such perturbations supports the robustness
of the SMRK construction.

D.1.11 Limitations of Numerical Experiments

Numerical experiments are limited by finite truncation in both primes and arithmetic domain.
As a result:

303

• asymptotic regimes are inaccessible.

Results should therefore be interpreted qualitatively rather than as precise quantitative tests.

D.1.12 Interpretation

Numerical experiments for automorphic families suggest that the SMRK Hamiltonian captures
universal arithmetic features across broad classes of representations. While individual spectra
vary, family-level behavior exhibits remarkable stability.
This supports the view that the operator framework encodes intrinsic arithmetic structure
independent of representation-specific details.

technical applications.
Operator-based frameworks, as developed throughout this book, shift
attention from procedural instruction toward transformation, structure,
and invariance. This shift has implications not only for computation,
but also for how complex systems are modeled, verified, and governed.
By emphasizing well-defined transformations acting on states, operator-
centric approaches promote transparency, composability, and traceabil-
ity—properties that are increasingly essential in large-scale, autonomous,
and distributed systems.
From a computational perspective, the operator-first paradigm enables
new forms of determinism, auditability, and semantic control. These
properties support the development of systems that can be inspected,
reasoned about, and corrected at a structural level, rather than treated
as opaque artifacts. Such capabilities are particularly relevant in contexts
where algorithmic decisions carry ethical, legal, or societal consequences.
At a deeper level, the mathematical structures explored in this book
illustrate how abstract reasoning can serve as a stabilizing force in tech-
nological evolution. By grounding computation in operator theory and
spectral analysis, the framework encourages designs that respect invari-
ants, constraints, and long-term coherence, counterbalancing tendencies
toward ad hoc complexity and uncontrolled optimization.
The section also addresses the role of human agency within advanced com-
putational systems. Rather than framing automation as a replacement
for human judgment, the operator-based approach supports models in
which human oversight, intervention, and interpretation are structurally
embedded. This perspective aligns with a vision of technology as an
extension of human capability, not its negation.

1 The SMRK Program: Scope, Continuity, and Intent

1.1 Purpose of This Document

This document marks a transition from construction to programmatic synthesis within the
SMRK framework. While previous documents established concrete operator-theoretic objects
and explicit arithmetic–spectral interfaces, the present work clarifies how these components fit
together as part of a coherent long-term program directed toward the Riemann Hypothesis.
The goal is not to present a proof, but to articulate a structurally constrained path that any
proof must follow within an operator-based framework.

1.2 Position Within the SMRK Program

This work builds directly on two foundational documents:
• The SMRK Hamiltonian and Explicit Formulae,
• The SMRK Hamiltonian for General L-Functions.

Those works established the existence of a self-adjoint arithmetic Hamiltonian, its spectral
properties, and its explicit-formula interfaces. The present document does not repeat those
constructions; instead, it treats them as established infrastructure.

1.3 From Objects to Program

The SMRK framework has now reached a stage where the primary mathematical objects are
defined and under control:

• a renormalized self-adjoint Hamiltonian,
• compact resolvent and discrete spectrum,
• trace objects yielding arithmetic explicit formulae,
• extensions to broad classes of L-functions.

The natural next step is to analyze what these structures imply collectively. This requires shifting
perspective from isolated results to a programmatic view.

1.4 The Riemann Hypothesis as a Structural Constraint

Within the SMRK perspective, the Riemann Hypothesis is not treated as a statement about the
zeros of a complex function. Instead, it is interpreted as a global structural constraint relating
arithmetic dynamics, spectral symmetry, and operator positivity.

306



The hypothesis becomes a statement about the compatibility of spectral localization, trace
identities, and symmetry principles within a self-adjoint framework.

1.5 Operator-Based Philosophy

A central philosophical stance of the SMRK program is that arithmetic information is most
naturally encoded in operators rather than functions. In this view:

• primes generate dynamics,
• arithmetic weights arise from operator traces,
• analytic continuation is replaced by functional calculus,
• symmetry is expressed through unitary equivalence.

This philosophy underlies all subsequent arguments and structural claims.

1.6 What This Document Does Not Claim

It is important to state explicitly what is not claimed here:
• no proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is presented,
• no identification of SMRK eigenvalues with classical zeros is asserted,
• no numerical verification is treated as decisive evidence.

The role of this document is architectural rather than conclusive.

1.7 Programmatic Objectives

The objectives of the SMRK program, as articulated here, are:
• to identify necessary structural conditions for a spectral resolution of RH,
• to eliminate incompatible approaches through operator constraints,
• to clarify which symmetries and trace identities are essential,
• to provide a falsifiable and extensible framework.

These objectives guide the organization of the chapters that follow.

1.8 Outline of the Document

The remainder of this document proceeds as follows. Subsequent chapters analyze the structural
consequences of the SMRK Hamiltonian, examine symmetry and rigidity phenomena, discuss
obstruction mechanisms, and outline concrete research directions toward a spectral resolution of
the Riemann Hypothesis.
Appendices collect methodological remarks and conceptual clarifications that support the main
narrative.

1.9 Summary

This chapter has:

307



• positioned the document within the broader SMRK program,

• clarified its relationship to earlier constructions,

• articulated an operator-based interpretation of the Riemann Hypothesis,

• defined the scope, intent, and limitations of the work.
The next chapter examines the notion of structural necessity and why any viable resolution of
the Riemann Hypothesis must ultimately be spectral in nature.

2 Structural Necessity and the Spectral Nature of the Riemann
Hypothesis

2.1 From Conjecture to Structural Constraint

The Riemann Hypothesis is traditionally formulated as a conjecture about the location of zeros
of a complex-valued function. Within the SMRK program, this formulation is reinterpreted as a
structural constraint imposed on any viable arithmetic–spectral framework.
Rather than asking whether a specific function has its zeros on a given line, the SMRK perspective
asks which structural properties of arithmetic dynamics necessarily force a spectral symmetry
consistent with the hypothesis.

2.2 Why a Spectral Framework Is Unavoidable

Any approach to the Riemann Hypothesis that aims to explain global regularity must address
three fundamental features:

• the universality of prime distributions,

• the stability of explicit formulae under smoothing,

• the rigidity imposed by symmetry principles.
These features are naturally and simultaneously expressed in spectral language. Attempts that
avoid spectral structures typically reintroduce them implicitly.

2.3 Self-Adjointness as a Necessity

A central insight of the SMRK program is that self-adjointness is not a technical convenience
but a structural requirement. Only self-adjoint operators provide:

• real spectral parameters,

• unitary time evolution,

• robust trace identities,

• stability under perturbations.
Any operator purporting to encode arithmetic dynamics relevant to the Riemann Hypothesis
must therefore admit a self-adjoint realization.

308



2.4 Compactness and Discreteness

Compactness of the resolvent is equally essential. Without compactness, spectral data are
contaminated by continuous components that obscure arithmetic information.
The SMRK Hamiltonian achieves compactness through logarithmic confinement. This ensures
that arithmetic information is captured by discrete spectral data, suitable for trace analysis and
explicit-formula interfaces.

2.5 Spectral Localization and Arithmetic Scale

The arithmetic variable naturally lives on a multiplicative scale. Under logarithmic transformation,
this becomes an additive variable, and confinement in this variable corresponds to control over
arithmetic growth.
Spectral localization in the logarithmic variable is therefore a necessary condition for meaningful
arithmetic interpretation of eigenfunctions.

2.6 Trace Identities as Structural Tests

Explicit formulae emerge in the SMRK framework as trace identities. These identities are
sensitive to:

• spectral symmetry,
• operator positivity,
• cancellation between arithmetic contributions.

A violation of the Riemann Hypothesis would manifest as a structural inconsistency in these
trace identities rather than as an isolated analytic anomaly.

2.7 Positivity and Spectral Symmetry

Within a self-adjoint framework, positivity constraints play a decisive role. Positivity of certain
quadratic forms and trace kernels imposes strong restrictions on the allowed distribution of
spectral data.
The SMRK program interprets the Riemann Hypothesis as a statement that such positivity and
symmetry constraints are globally satisfied.

2.8 Exclusion of Non-Spectral Approaches

From this perspective, purely combinatorial or function-theoretic approaches that do not produce
a stable self-adjoint operator fail to address the core structural issues.
While such approaches may yield partial results, they do not provide a framework capable of
enforcing the global constraints required by the Riemann Hypothesis.

2.9 Structural Minimality

The SMRK Hamiltonian is minimal in the following sense:
• primes generate all dynamics,

309



• no auxiliary randomness is introduced,
• no external symmetry assumptions are imposed,
• all structure arises internally from arithmetic.

This minimality strengthens the claim that the framework captures necessary, rather than
accidental, features.

2.10 Implications for Proof Strategies

If the Riemann Hypothesis is a structural spectral statement, then any proof strategy must
ultimately:

• identify the relevant self-adjoint operator,
• establish compactness and symmetry,
• derive positivity of appropriate trace objects,
• show incompatibility of hypothetical counterexamples.

The SMRK program provides a concrete arena in which these steps can be formulated and tested.

2.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• reframed the Riemann Hypothesis as a structural constraint,
• argued for the necessity of a spectral approach,
• identified self-adjointness and compactness as essential features,
• connected spectral localization with arithmetic scale,
• outlined implications for viable proof strategies.

The next chapter analyzes symmetry and rigidity phenomena arising from the SMRK Hamiltonian
and their consequences for arithmetic spectra.

3 Symmetry, Rigidity, and Operator-Level Constraints

3.1 Why Symmetry Matters at the Operator Level

In an operator-based framework, symmetry is not an aesthetic property but a structural one.
Symmetries constrain admissible dynamics, restrict spectral deformations, and govern the form
of trace identities. Within the SMRK program, symmetry acts directly on operators through
unitary equivalence rather than indirectly through functional identities.
Any candidate framework relevant to the Riemann Hypothesis must therefore identify which
symmetries are intrinsic and which are accidental.

3.2 Unitary Equivalence as Structural Invariance

The primary notion of equivalence in the SMRK program is unitary equivalence of operators.
Two Hamiltonians related by a unitary conjugation describe the same arithmetic dynamics, even

310



if their concrete realizations differ.
This principle implies that all meaningful arithmetic information must be encoded in unitary
invariants such as spectra, trace objects, and positivity properties.

3.3 Logarithmic Inversion Symmetry

Arithmetic dynamics are naturally multiplicative. Passing to logarithmic variables renders
this structure additive and reveals an inversion symmetry corresponding to reflection in the
logarithmic coordinate.
At the operator level, this symmetry is implemented by a unitary involution that interchanges
prime multiplication and division. The prime-interaction component of the SMRK Hamiltonian
is invariant under this transformation.

3.4 Controlled Symmetry Breaking

Exact symmetry is neither expected nor desired at the level of the full Hamiltonian. Diagonal
logarithmic potentials break inversion symmetry in a controlled manner, while preserving essential
spectral features such as self-adjointness and compactness.
This controlled symmetry breaking is analogous to confinement mechanisms in physical Hamilto-
nians and is crucial for spectral discreteness.

3.5 Gauge Symmetry of Local Arithmetic Data

Local arithmetic data are defined only up to choice of basis in internal spaces. This introduces a
gauge symmetry acting independently at each prime.
Gauge transformations act by unitary conjugation on decorated prime-shift operators. All trace
expressions and generalized von Mangoldt weights are invariant under this action, ensuring that
the SMRK Hamiltonian depends only on intrinsic arithmetic data.

3.6 Rigidity Induced by Trace Identities

Trace identities impose rigidity on admissible operator deformations. Small changes to operator
structure that preserve self-adjointness and trace positivity are severely restricted.
In particular, deformations that would alter global spectral symmetry necessarily manifest as
violations of trace identities or positivity constraints.

3.7 Absence of Continuous Deformation Paths

Within the SMRK framework, there is no continuous deformation connecting operators with
spectrally symmetric configurations to operators with spectrally asymmetric ones, without
crossing a boundary where self-adjointness, compactness, or trace positivity fails.
This absence of deformation paths is a key rigidity feature and underlies the structural interpre-
tation of the Riemann Hypothesis.

3.8 Operator Constraints Versus Functional Constraints

Traditional approaches often encode symmetry at the level of functional equations. The SMRK
program relocates these constraints to the operator level, where they are enforced through unitary

311



equivalence and positivity.
This shift eliminates reliance on analytic continuation and reframes symmetry as an operator-
theoretic necessity rather than a functional coincidence.

3.9 Stability Under Renormalization

Renormalization introduces scalar shifts but does not alter operator symmetries or unitary
equivalence classes. As a result, all symmetry and rigidity statements remain valid for the
renormalized SMRK Hamiltonian.
This stability ensures that symmetry considerations are meaningful in the infinite prime limit.

3.10 Consequences for Spectral Configurations

The combined effect of symmetry and rigidity is a severe restriction on admissible spectral
configurations. Spectral arrangements incompatible with inversion symmetry and trace positivity
are excluded at the operator level.
This exclusion does not rely on detailed arithmetic estimates but follows from general structural
principles.

3.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• identified symmetry as an operator-level invariant,

• emphasized unitary equivalence as the primary notion of structure,

• described logarithmic inversion and gauge symmetries,

• explained controlled symmetry breaking via confinement,

• established rigidity through trace identities,

• argued for the absence of continuous paths to asymmetric spectra.
The next chapter examines how trace positivity and arithmetic cancellation mechanisms translate
these structural constraints into enforceable spectral conditions.
