5 Trace Positivity and Arithmetic Cancellation Mechanisms

5.1 Role of Trace Positivity

Trace objects lie at the core of the SMRK framework. They provide the interface between operator
theory and arithmetic structure. Among their properties, positivity plays a distinguished role:
it imposes global constraints on admissible spectral behavior that cannot be bypassed by local
adjustments.
Within the SMRK program, trace positivity is not an auxiliary assumption but a structural
requirement inherited from self-adjointness and functional calculus.

314



5.2 Positive Trace Kernels

Given a self-adjoint Hamiltonian H̃, trace kernels of the form
Tr f(H̃), (13.1)

where f is a nonnegative function, are manifestly nonnegative.
Examples include:

• heat kernel traces Tr e−tH̃ ,
• resolvent-based traces with positive spectral weights,
• smoothed spectral projectors.

These objects encode global spectral information while preserving positivity.

5.3 Spectral Decomposition and Positivity

Positivity at the trace level translates into constraints on the spectral decomposition. If {λk}
denotes the spectrum of H̃, then ∑

Tr f(H̃) = f(λk) ≥ 0 (13.2)
k

for all admissible nonnegative f .
Any hypothetical spectral configuration leading to negative contributions in such expressions is
excluded.

5.4 Arithmetic Expansion of Trace Objects

Trace objects admit parallel arithmetic expan∑sions expressed as sums over prime powers. Schemat-
ically, ∑

Tr f(H̃) = B(f) + ΛL(pm) f̂(m log p), (13.3)
p m≥1

where B(f) denotes the bulk contribution and f̂ is an appropriate transform of f .
This representation reveals how arithmetic data enter trace expressions.

5.5 Cancellation as a Structural Requirement

Prime-power contributions in the arithmetic expansion are oscillatory. Positivity of the total
trace therefore requires delicate cancellation between terms associated with different primes and
powers.
Such cancellation is not optional. It is enforced by the requirement that the spectral side remains
nonnegative for all admissible test functions.

5.6 Failure Modes of Cancellation

If arithmetic cancellation fails, trace positivity is violated. This manifests as:
• negative contributions for specific test functions,
• instability under smoothing,

315



• sensitivity to small perturbations of arithmetic weights.
Within the SMRK framework, these failures signal incompatibility with a self-adjoint spectral
realization.

5.7 Relation to the Riemann Hypothesis

The Riemann Hypothesis may be interpreted as asserting that the arithmetic cancellation required
for trace positivity is globally consistent.
Rather than focusing on individual oscillatory terms, the SMRK program treats the hypothesis as
a statement that no admissible test function can expose a positivity violation in trace identities.

5.8 Operator-Level Enforcement

Because trace positivity is enforced at the operator level, it cannot be restored by adjusting
arithmetic weights alone. Any modification that disrupts cancellation must either:

• break self-adjointness,
• destroy compactness,
• or violate unitary invariance.

This makes trace positivity a powerful exclusion principle.

5.9 Robustness Under Renormalization

Renormalization affects trace objects only by adding or subtracting scalar terms that do not
compromise positivity. Consequently, all positivity arguments remain valid in the infinite prime
limit.
This robustness ensures that cancellation mechanisms are meaningful beyond finite truncations.

5.10 Structural Implications

Trace positivity converts spectral symmetry and operator rigidity into enforceable constraints. It
transforms abstract symmetry principles into concrete inequalities that must hold uniformly.
These inequalities severely restrict the space of admissible spectral configurations.

5.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• identified trace positivity as a core structural requirement,
• described positive trace kernels and their spectral meaning,
• analyzed arithmetic expansions of trace objects,
• explained cancellation as a necessary mechanism,
• linked positivity failure to structural incompatibility,
• interpreted the Riemann Hypothesis as global consistency of trace positivity.

316



The next chapter analyzes obstruction mechanisms and explains why non-critical spectral
configurations are incompatible with the SMRK operator framework.

6 Obstructions to Non-Critical Spectral Configurations

6.1 Meaning of Non-Critical Configurations

Within a spectral framework, a non-critical configuration refers to any arrangement of spectral
data that breaks the symmetry required by the Riemann Hypothesis. Such configurations may
arise hypothetically from asymmetries in spectral localization or from imbalance in arithmetic
trace contributions.
The purpose of this chapter is to explain why such configurations are structurally obstructed
within the SMRK framework.

6.2 Hypothetical Deformations of the Spectrum

Assume, for the sake of argument, that the spectrum of the SMRK Hamiltonian admits a
deformation that breaks critical symmetry while preserving basic analytic features.
Such a deformation would correspond to shifting spectral mass in a way that introduces asymmetry
without destroying discreteness or boundedness.

6.3 Breakdown of Trace Positivity

Any asymmetric spectral deformation immediately impacts trace objects. Since trace kernels
test the spectrum globally, asymmetry produces negative contributions for appropriately chosen
test functions.
This violates the trace positivity established in the previous chapter.

6.4 Incompatibility with Unitary Equivalence

Non-critical spectral configurations cannot be related to critical ones by unitary conjugation.
Consequently, they represent genuinely distinct operator classes.
Because all admissible arithmetic Hamiltonians must belong to a fixed unitary equivalence class,
such configurations are excluded.

6.5 Failure of Cancellation Mechanisms

Asymmetric spectral arrangements correspond, on the arithmetic side, to failure of prime-
power cancellation. This manifests as systematic bias in arithmetic expansions that cannot be
compensated by finite adjustments.
The failure persists under smoothing and truncation, indicating a fundamental structural defect.

6.6 Absence of Stable Perturbative Paths

There exists no perturbative path connecting a critical configuration to a non-critical one while
preserving self-adjointness, compactness, and trace positivity.
Any attempted interpolation necessarily crosses a boundary where one of these properties fails.

317



6.7 Renormalization Does Not Restore Admissibility

Renormalization affects only scalar components of the Hamiltonian. It cannot repair structural
defects caused by spectral asymmetry.
Thus non-critical configurations remain inadmissible even after renormalization.

6.8 Global Versus Local Obstructions

Local deviations at finitely many primes correspond to finite-rank perturbations and do not
alter global spectral structure. In contrast, non-critical spectral configurations require global
deformation across infinitely many arithmetic scales.
This distinction explains why localized anomalies do not threaten the SMRK framework, whereas
global asymmetry does.

6.9 Interpretation in Programmatic Terms

From a programmatic perspective, this chapter establishes an exclusion principle: any candidate
spectral configuration incompatible with trace positivity and symmetry is ruled out a priori.
This shifts the burden of proof away from checking individual configurations and toward estab-
lishing the structural properties of the operator.

6.10 Implications for Counterexample Strategies

Any attempt to construct a counterexample to the Riemann Hypothesis within a spectral
framework must therefore:

• violate self-adjointness,

• abandon compactness,

• or sacrifice trace positivity.
Such attempts fall outside the SMRK program.

6.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• defined non-critical spectral configurations,

• examined hypothetical spectral deformations,

• shown their incompatibility with trace positivity,

• explained the absence of admissible deformation paths,

• established an operator-level exclusion principle.
The next chapter explains how explicit formulae function as enforcement mechanisms that
translate these structural obstructions into spectral constraints.

318



7 From Explicit Formulae to Spectral Enforcement

7.1 Explicit Formulae as Structural Interfaces

Explicit formulae occupy a central position in analytic number theory as identities relating
spectral data to arithmetic sums over primes. Within the SMRK framework, explicit formulae
are reinterpreted as trace identities arising from functional calculus applied to a self-adjoint
arithmetic Hamiltonian.
This reinterpretation elevates explicit formulae from computational tools to structural interfaces
that enforce admissible spectral behavior.

7.2 Trace Identities and Functional Calculus

Given a self-adjoint Hamiltonian H̃ and a suitable test function f , functional calculus yields an
operator f(H̃) whose trace admits both a spectral and an arithmetic expansion.
The equality of these expansions is not an assumption but a consequence of operator theory.
Explicit formulae therefore inherit the rigidity and positivity constraints of trace objects.

7.3 Test Functions as Probes

The choice of test function f determines which aspects of the spectrum are probed. Smooth,
compactly supported, or rapidly decaying functions allow selective emphasis on specific spectral
scales while preserving positivity.
Within the SMRK program, admissible test functions form a controlled class designed to prevent
artificial violations of trace positivity.

7.4 Arithmetic Side as a Constraint, Not an Input

In traditional settings, explicit formulae are often used to extract information about primes
from spectral assumptions. In the SMRK framework, the direction is reversed: arithmetic
contributions constrain the spectrum through trace identities.
Prime-power terms enter with fixed weights determined by local operator data. They cannot be
tuned independently to accommodate arbitrary spectral configurations.

7.5 Enforcement Through Positivity

Trace positivity converts explicit formulae into enforcement mechanisms. If a spectral configura-
tion were incompatible with required arithmetic cancellation, there would exist a test function
for which the trace becomes negative.
Because such negativity is forbidden, incompatible spectra are excluded.

7.6 Universality of the Enforcement Mechanism

The enforcement role of explicit formulae does not depend on fine arithmetic details. It relies
only on:

• self-adjointness,
• compact resolvent,

319



• positivity of trace kernels,
• boundedness of local arithmetic data.

This universality explains why similar explicit-formula structures appear across different classes
of L-functions.

7.7 Comparison with Analytic Continuation

Classical approaches often rely on analytic continuation to extend explicit formulae beyond their
region of convergence. In contrast, the SMRK framework replaces analytic continuation by
functional calculus on a self-adjoint operator.
This shift removes ambiguity and places explicit formulae on firm operator-theoretic ground.

7.8 Spectral Symmetry as an Outcome

Within this perspective, spectral symmetry is not postulated but enforced. Any asymmetry
incompatible with explicit-formula trace identities is ruled out by positivity and rigidity.
The Riemann Hypothesis thus emerges as the statement that the enforced spectral configuration
is globally symmetric.

7.9 Stability Under Approximation

Finite truncations of primes or arithmetic domain produce approximate explicit formulae. While
truncation introduces errors, the enforcement mechanism remains visible in the stability of
low-lying spectral data.
This stability provides practical support for numerical exploration without elevating numerical
results to the status of proof.

7.10 Programmatic Significance

By reinterpreting explicit formulae as enforcement mechanisms, the SMRK program shifts the
focus of the Riemann Hypothesis from verification to inevitability. The hypothesis becomes the
only configuration compatible with the full set of operator constraints.

7.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• reframed explicit formulae as trace identities,
• explained the role of functional calculus,
• described test functions as spectral probes,
• shown how positivity enforces admissible spectra,
• contrasted operator enforcement with analytic continuation,
• interpreted the Riemann Hypothesis as an enforced outcome.

8 Universality Across Families of L-Functions

8.1 Why Universality Matters

A credible structural approach to the Riemann Hypothesis must not depend on accidental
features of a single arithmetic object. Instead, it must exhibit universality across broad classes of
L-functions, reflecting common underlying mechanisms rather than case-specific coincidences.
Within the SMRK program, universality is a consequence of operator architecture rather than of
shared analytic properties.

8.2 Common Operator Backbone

All L-functions treated in the SMRK framework share the same global operator backbone:
• arithmetic Hilbert space organized by multiplicative structure,
• prime-generated dynamics via shift operators,
• logarithmic confinement ensuring compact resolvent,
• renormalized self-adjoint realization.

Differences between families appear only through local data decorating the prime shifts.

8.3 Local Data as Controlled Variations

Dirichlet characters, automorphic representations, and higher-degree L-functions introduce local
matrices Ap acting on internal spaces. These variations modify prime-power weights but do not
alter the global structure of the Hamiltonian.
As a result, universality is preserved at the operator level even as arithmetic detail varies.

8.4 Trace Structure Across Families

Trace objects retain the same formal structur∑e ac∑ross all families:

Only the coefficients ΛL(pm) depend on the specific L-function. The functional form of the trace
identity is universal.

8.5 Universality of Positivity Constraints

Positivity of trace kernels imposes identical constraints across families. Regardless of degree or
conductor, any admissible L-function must satisfy the same global positivity conditions.
This explains why the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalizations appear as a single phenomenon
rather than as independent conjectures.

8.6 Families and Deformation Stability

Continuous variation within families—such as twisting by characters or changing weights—induces
continuous changes in local data. These variations correspond to bounded perturbations of the

321



Hamiltonian and preserve spectral admissibility.
The absence of admissible paths to non-critical configurations persists uniformly across families.

8.7 Ramification as a Finite-Rank Effect

Ramified primes differ between families, but they contribute only finite-rank perturbations to the
Hamiltonian. Such perturbations do not affect compactness, self-adjointness, or global spectral
symmetry.
This explains why universality is not disrupted by local arithmetic complexity.

8.8 Comparison with Random Matrix Heuristics

Random matrix models capture certain universal statistical features of zeros of L-functions. In
contrast, the SMRK framework derives universality from deterministic operator constraints.
The two perspectives are complementary: random matrix statistics may emerge as a secondary
consequence of the rigid operator structure.

8.9 Implications for Generalized Riemann Hypotheses

The SMRK program suggests that generalized Riemann Hypotheses for families of L-functions
are not independent conjectures. They reflect the same underlying operator-level enforcement
applied to different local data.
This unification reduces the conceptual complexity of the problem.

8.10 Programmatic Consequences

Universality shifts the emphasis from individual proofs to structural analysis. Once the operator
framework is established, the same enforcement mechanisms apply uniformly across families.
This perspective clarifies why progress on one class of L-functions often informs others.

8.11 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• identified a common operator backbone across L-function families,

• described local data as controlled variations,

• demonstrated universality of trace identities,

• established family-independent positivity constraints,

• explained stability under deformation and ramification,

• interpreted generalized RH as a single structural phenomenon.

9 Numerical Evidence as Structural Validation

9.1 Role of Numerics in the SMRK Program

Numerical investigations play a carefully delimited role within the SMRK program. They are
not treated as sources of proof, but as instruments for validating structural claims derived from
operator theory.
In particular, numerics serve to test stability, consistency, and universality of the spectral
framework under controlled approximations.

9.2 Distinction Between Proof and Validation

A fundamental distinction must be maintained between mathematical proof and numerical
evidence. Proof establishes necessity, whereas numerics provide empirical support that a proposed
structure behaves as expected.
The SMRK program relies on numerics only in the latter sense. Numerical results are interpreted
as confirmation that operator-level constraints are not artifacts of idealized constructions.

9.3 Finite Truncations as Experimental Proxies

All numerical implementations of the SMRK Hamiltonian necessarily involve truncations:
• restriction to finitely many primes,
• restriction to a finite arithmetic domain,
• finite-dimensional internal spaces.

These truncations define experimental proxies for the infinite operator. Structural features that
persist across increasing truncation scales are interpreted as robust.

9.4 Stability of Low-Lying Spectrum

One of the most informative numerical indicators is the stability of low-lying eigenvalues under
increasing truncation parameters. Persistent eigenvalue patterns suggest that the underlying
infinite operator has a well-defined discrete spectrum.
Instabilities, by contrast, signal either insufficient truncation or structural incompatibility.

9.5 Trace Objects and Smoothing

Numerical evaluation of trace objects, such as heat kernel traces, provides a smoothed view of the
spectrum that suppresses truncation noise. These traces are particularly well suited for numerical
study because they emphasize global spectral features rather than individual eigenvalues.
Consistency of trace behavior across truncation scales supports the validity of the operator
framework.

9.6 Detection of Arithmetic Signatures

Even under heavy truncation, numerical trace objects exhibit oscillatory components associated
with prime powers. The appearance of these signatures confirms that arithmetic information is

323



encoded at the operator level rather than inserted artificially.
The persistence of such signatures across different L-function families further supports universality
claims.

9.7 Numerics and Positivity Constraints

Numerical experiments also probe trace positivity. While finite truncations may introduce small
numerical artifacts, systematic violation of positivity would indicate a breakdown of the operator
framework.
Observed numerical behavior is consistent with positivity constraints predicted by theory.

9.8 Limits of Numerical Resolution

Numerical studies are inherently limited in their ability to access asymptotic regimes. Fine
spectral correlations and extreme arithmetic scales remain beyond reach.
Accordingly, numerical evidence is interpreted qualitatively, with emphasis on structural trends
rather than precise quantitative agreement.

9.9 Numerics as Falsifiability Tools

A strength of the SMRK program is that it is falsifiable. Numerical experiments can, in principle,
expose structural inconsistencies by revealing instability, loss of positivity, or breakdown of
universality.
That no such inconsistencies have been observed under systematic numerical probing provides
indirect support for the framework.

9.10 Relation to Other Numerical Approaches

Classical numerical studies of zeros of L-functions focus on verifying hypotheses for finite ranges.
In contrast, SMRK numerics investigate the behavior of an operator whose spectrum is conjectured
to encode the same structural constraints.
The two approaches address complementary aspects of the same problem.

9.11 Interpretive Caution

Numerical agreement should not be mistaken for proof, nor should numerical anomalies be
overinterpreted. The SMRK program emphasizes conceptual clarity and structural necessity over
numerical confirmation.
This caution preserves the logical integrity of the framework.

9.12 Summary

In this chapter we have:
• clarified the role of numerical evidence as validation rather than proof,
• described truncation-based numerical proxies,
• discussed stability of low-lying spectral data,

324



• analyzed numerical trace objects and arithmetic signatures,
• emphasized positivity and universality checks,
• articulated limits and interpretive principles for numerics.

10 What a Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis Must Ultimately
Establish

10.1 From Verification to Necessity

A proof of the Riemann Hypothesis must go beyond verification of individual cases or asymptotic
regimes. Within the SMRK program, proof is understood as establishing necessity: the impos-
sibility of any alternative spectral configuration compatible with the full set of operator-level
constraints.
The question is therefore not whether the critical configuration occurs, but whether any other
configuration can exist.

10.2 Existence of a Canonical Self-Adjoint Operator

The first requirement is the existence of a canonically defined self-adjoint operator encoding
arithmetic dynamics. This operator must:

• arise intrinsically from prime structure,
• admit a renormalized self-adjoint realization,
• possess compact resolvent.

Without such an operator, spectral language remains metaphorical rather than rigorous.

10.3 Uniqueness up to Unitary Equivalence

A viable proof must establish that the relevant operator is unique up to unitary equivalence.
Apparent freedom in construction must reduce to gauge choices or finite-rank modifications that
do not alter spectral invariants.
This uniqueness ensures that spectral conclusions are not artifacts of representation.

10.4 Enforcement of Spectral Symmetry

The proof must demonstrate that spectral symmetry is enforced by the operator itself. Symmetry
should follow from:

• intrinsic operator symmetries,
• trace positivity,
• rigidity under admissible perturbations.

Symmetry assumed as an external condition does not constitute proof.

325



10.5 Positivity of All Admissible Trace Objects

A decisive element is the global positivity of all admissible trace kernels derived from the operator.
This includes traces associated with a broad class of nonnegative test functions.
Any hypothetical counterexample must produce a violation of positivity for some trace object.
Demonstrating the impossibility of such violations is therefore central.

10.6 Control of Arithmetic Cancellation

The proof must account for arithmetic cancellation at all relevant scales. This requires showing
that prime-power contributions necessarily cancel in a manner compatible with trace positivity
and spectral symmetry.
Partial or scale-dependent cancellation is insufficient.

10.7 Stability Under Renormalization and Limits

All arguments must remain valid under renormalization and in the infinite prime limit. Depen-
dence on finite cutoffs or auxiliary parameters undermines necessity.
A proof must therefore be robust under all limiting procedures intrinsic to the framework.

10.8 Exclusion of Non-Critical Configurations

The final step is an explicit exclusion principle: a demonstration that any non-critical spectral
configuration is incompatible with at least one essential operator-level requirement.
This exclusion must be global and structural rather than case-by-case.

10.9 Role of Numerical Evidence

Numerical evidence plays no direct role in proof, but it can inform intuition and suggest which
structural properties are decisive. A proof must stand independently of numerical confirmation.
The SMRK program treats numerics as supportive but logically nonessential.

10.10 Minimality of Assumptions

An effective proof should rely on minimal assumptions. Each assumption must be shown to be
unavoidable within the operator-based perspective.
Redundant or ad hoc assumptions weaken the structural force of the argument.

10.11 Programmatic Synthesis

Taken together, these requirements form a coherent checklist. Any approach claiming to resolve
the Riemann Hypothesis must address each item explicitly or implicitly.
The SMRK program provides a framework in which all these requirements can be formulated
precisely and examined systematically.

10.12 Summary

In this chapter we have:

326



• reframed proof as establishment of necessity,
• identified essential operator-level requirements,
• emphasized uniqueness and symmetry enforcement,
• highlighted the role of trace positivity and cancellation,
• articulated robustness under renormalization,
• formulated a global exclusion principle.

The final chapter concludes the document by synthesizing these insights and outlining the
remaining path toward a spectral resolution of the Riemann Hypothesis.

11 Conclusion: Toward a Spectral Resolution of the Riemann
Hypothesis

11.1 From Construction to Program

The SMRK program began with the construction of a concrete arithmetic Hamiltonian and
its extension to general classes of L-functions. In this document, the focus has shifted from
construction to synthesis: from defining objects to understanding the structural consequences of
their existence.
This transition reflects a maturation of the framework from technical development to program-
matic clarity.

11.2 Structural Interpretation of the Riemann Hypothesis

Within the SMRK perspective, the Riemann Hypothesis is not viewed as an isolated analytic
statement but as a global structural constraint imposed by self-adjointness, symmetry, and
positivity.
The hypothesis becomes a statement about what spectral configurations are compatible with
arithmetic dynamics governed by prime-generated operators.

11.3 Role of Operator-Level Constraints

Operator-level constraints—self-adjointness, compactness, unitary invariance, and trace posi-
tivity—form the backbone of the SMRK program. These constraints are not adjustable; they
arise naturally from the requirement that arithmetic information be encoded coherently at the
operator level.
Their combined effect severely restricts admissible spectral behavior.

11.4 Explicit Formulae as Enforcement Mechanisms

Explicit formulae, traditionally viewed as analytic identities, are reinterpreted here as enforcement
mechanisms. Through trace identities and positivity constraints, they convert arithmetic structure
into spectral necessity.
This reinterpretation is a central conceptual shift of the SMRK program.

327



11.5 Universality and Robustness

A striking feature of the framework is its universality across families of L-functions. Variations in
local arithmetic data do not alter the global enforcement mechanism, highlighting the robustness
of the operator architecture.
This universality supports the view that the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalizations are
manifestations of a single underlying principle.

11.6 Limits of the Present Work

This document does not present a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. Instead, it clarifies the
structural landscape in which such a proof must reside.
By identifying necessary operator-level conditions and exclusion principles, the SMRK program
narrows the space of viable approaches.

11.7 Toward a Proof

A spectral resolution of the Riemann Hypothesis requires demonstrating that the SMRK Hamil-
tonian satisfies all enforcement criteria globally and without exception.
The work presented here lays out the conceptual and structural components required for such a
demonstration, providing a roadmap rather than a conclusion.

11.8 Open Directions

Several directions remain open within the SMRK program:
• refinement of operator-level positivity arguments,
• deeper analysis of symmetry and rigidity mechanisms,
• extension of numerical validation to broader families,
• exploration of connections with other spectral programs.

These directions indicate where further progress is both possible and meaningful.

11.9 Final Perspective

The SMRK program proposes that the Riemann Hypothesis is best understood not as a mysterious
property of a special function, but as a necessary outcome of arithmetic dynamics encoded in a
self-adjoint operator framework.
Whether this perspective ultimately yields a complete proof remains to be seen. What it already
provides is a coherent, rigorous, and falsifiable path toward a spectral resolution of one of
mathematics’ most enduring problems.

Appendix B

B.1 Relation to Hilbert–Pólya and Other Spectral Programs

B.1.1 Historical Context

The Hilbert–Pólya idea proposes that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function arise as
spectral data of a self-adjoint operator. While no explicit operator was identified in the original
proposal, the idea established a lasting connection between number theory and spectral theory.
The SMRK program may be viewed as a concrete realization of this philosophical direction,
formulated in a modern operator-theoretic language.

B.1.2 Hilbert–Pólya as a Guiding Principle

Within the SMRK framework, the Hilbert–Pólya idea is interpreted not as a literal spectral
identification of zeros, but as a requirement that arithmetic information be encoded in a self-
adjoint operator whose spectral properties reflect deep arithmetic constraints.
The emphasis is on structural enforcement rather than direct correspondence.

B.1.3 Differences in Operator Construction

Traditional Hilbert–Pólya approaches often seek an operator whose spectrum coincides explicitly
with the imaginary parts of zeta zeros. The SMRK program departs from this goal in several
key ways:

• the operator is constructed from prime-generated dynamics rather than analytic continua-
tion,

• spectral parameters are not identified with zeros directly,
• enforcement of symmetry arises through trace positivity rather than spectral matching.

These differences shift the focus from identification to necessity.

B.1.4 Role of Self-Adjointness

Both the Hilbert–Pólya idea and the SMRK program place self-adjointness at the center. In
the SMRK framework, self-adjointness is achieved through renormalized quadratic forms and
logarithmic confinement, ensuring mathematical rigor.
This provides a concrete realization of a key Hilbert–Pólya requirement.

B.1.5 Comparison with Connes’ Spectral Approach

Noncommutative geometric approaches, notably those developed by Connes, interpret the explicit
formula as a trace formula on a spectral triple. These approaches share with SMRK an emphasis
on operator theory and trace identities.
The SMRK program differs by:

• avoiding reliance on noncommutative geometry,

332



• constructing an explicit arithmetic Hamiltonian,
• emphasizing positivity and enforcement mechanisms.

The two perspectives are complementary rather than contradictory.

B.1.6 Relation to Quantum Chaos Models

Models inspired by quantum chaos and random matrix theory propose statistical correspondence
between zeros of L-functions and spectra of random operators. The SMRK program does not
posit randomness at the operator level.
Instead, any random-matrix-like statistics are viewed as emergent phenomena arising from rigid
deterministic operator constraints.

B.1.7 Comparison with Trace Formula Programs

Classical trace formulae relate spectral data of automorphic operators to sums over geometric
or arithmetic objects. The SMRK program parallels this structure but operates in a purely
arithmetic setting, with primes generating the dynamics.
This highlights a shared structural theme while maintaining a distinct framework.

B.1.8 Advantages of the SMRK Perspective

The SMRK program offers several advantages over earlier spectral approaches:
• explicit self-adjoint operator construction,
• built-in renormalization handling infinite prime sums,
• universal applicability across L-function families,
• clear falsifiability criteria.

These features strengthen the programmatic value of the framework.

B.1.9 Limitations and Open Comparisons

Despite its strengths, the SMRK program does not subsume all spectral approaches. Connections
to noncommutative geometry, quantum chaos, and classical trace formulae remain to be explored
in detail.
These connections represent opportunities rather than deficiencies.

B.1.10 Interpretive Summary

The SMRK program can be viewed as a modern, operator-theoretic descendant of the Hilbert–
Pólya idea. It preserves the core insight—that arithmetic regularity should have a spectral
origin—while replacing speculative identification with structural enforcement.

B.1.11 Summary

This appendix has:

333



• placed the SMRK program in the context of Hilbert–Pólya,
• clarified similarities and differences with other spectral approaches,
• emphasized the role of self-adjointness and trace identities,
• highlighted the distinctive features of the SMRK framework.

Appendix C

C.1 Falsifiability and Failure Modes

C.1.1 Falsifiability as a Programmatic Requirement

A distinguishing feature of the SMRK program is its explicit commitment to falsifiability. The
framework is constructed so that its core claims impose concrete, testable structural constraints
at the operator level.
If these constraints fail, the program is not weakened but invalidated. This distinguishes the
SMRK approach from heuristic or purely interpretive frameworks.

C.1.2 What Would Constitute Failure

Failure of the SMRK program would occur if any of the following were demonstrated:
• nonexistence of a renormalized self-adjoint Hamiltonian consistent with arithmetic dynamics,
• unavoidable loss of compact resolvent in the infinite prime limit,
• violation of trace positivity for an admissible class of test functions,
• existence of a stable non-critical spectral configuration compatible with all operator con-

straints.
Each item represents a sharp structural criterion rather than a numerical anomaly.

C.1.3 Operator-Level Failure Modes

At the operator level, failure may arise through:
• breakdown of self-adjointness under renormalization,
• uncontrolled growth of off-diagonal prime-shift terms,
• loss of confinement in the logarithmic variable,
• emergence of continuous spectrum incompatible with trace analysis.

Such failures would undermine the spectral interpretation of arithmetic dynamics.

C.1.4 Trace-Level Failure Modes

Trace identities provide a sensitive diagnostic. Potential failure modes include:
• existence of a nonnegative test function yielding a negative trace,
• instability of trace values under smoothing,
• inconsistency between spectral and arithmetic expansions.

Any of these outcomes would signal incompatibility with the SMRK framework.

335



C.1.5 Failure of Arithmetic Cancellation

The SMRK program relies on global arithmetic cancellation enforced by trace positivity. Failure
would manifest as persistent imbalance in prime-power contributions that cannot be compensated
by spectral symmetry.
Such imbalance would indicate that arithmetic dynamics cannot be encoded in a single self-adjoint
operator.

C.1.6 Robustness Against Finite Perturbations

Finite-rank perturbations arising from ramified primes or local modifications are explicitly allowed.
Failure occurs only if global structural properties are affected.
This distinction ensures that falsifiability targets genuine structural defects rather than technical
irregularities.

C.1.7 Numerical Signals of Failure

While numerical evidence cannot prove validity, it can suggest failure. Warning signs include:
• instability of low-lying spectrum under increasing truncation,
• systematic violation of approximate trace positivity,
• loss of universality across families.

Such signals would motivate closer analytical scrutiny.

C.1.8 Conceptual Failure Modes

Beyond technical issues, conceptual failure could arise if:
• operator-level constraints fail to capture known arithmetic phenomena,
• enforcement mechanisms prove too weak to exclude non-critical configurations,
• the framework requires ad hoc assumptions lacking intrinsic justification.

These failures would call into question the foundational philosophy of the program.

C.1.9 Distinction from Proof Failure

It is important to distinguish failure of the SMRK program from failure to complete a proof.
The former implies that the structural approach itself is flawed; the latter may reflect incomplete
development or missing techniques.
The SMRK program is designed so that genuine failure can be clearly identified.

C.1.10 Value of Falsifiability

Falsifiability strengthens the program by clarifying its logical status. A framework that cannot
fail cannot meaningfully succeed.
By articulating precise failure modes, the SMRK program invites rigorous scrutiny and engagement
from the broader mathematical community.

336



C.1.11 Summary

This appendix has:
• defined falsifiability criteria for the SMRK program,
• identified operator-level and trace-level failure modes,
• distinguished local perturbations from global defects,
• clarified the role of numerical signals,
• emphasized the conceptual value of explicit failure conditions.

D.1 Open Problems and Research Directions

D.1.1 Purpose of This Appendix

This appendix collects open problems and research directions that naturally arise from the SMRK
program. The emphasis is not on conjectural claims, but on concrete questions whose resolution
would clarify, strengthen, or delimit the operator-based approach to the Riemann Hypothesis.
The problems listed here are intended to be accessible entry points for further work, both
analytical and numerical.

D.1.2 Global Positivity Proofs

A central open problem is the establishment of global trace positivity for the full class of admissible
test functions. While positivity follows formally from self-adjointness, a detailed characterization
of admissible test classes remains open.
Clarifying this issue would significantly strengthen the enforcement mechanism at the heart of
the SMRK program.

D.1.3 Rigidity Beyond Symmetry

The rigidity arguments presented rely on symmetry and trace identities. An important direction
is to identify additional rigidity mechanisms that operate independently of explicit symmetry
assumptions.
Such mechanisms could further restrict admissible operator deformations and reduce the concep-
tual distance to a complete proof.

D.1.4 Quantitative Bounds on Cancellation

While the framework establishes the necessity of arithmetic cancellation, quantitative bounds on
the rate and uniformity of cancellation remain to be developed.
Obtaining such bounds at the operator level could bridge the gap between qualitative structural
arguments and quantitative analytic results.

D.1.5 Operator Uniqueness

Although uniqueness up to unitary equivalence is strongly suggested, a fully explicit proof of
uniqueness for the SMRK Hamiltonian remains open.
Such a result would eliminate residual ambiguity in operator construction and further solidify
the spectral interpretation.

D.1.6 Extension to Broader Arithmetic Settings

An important direction is the extension of the SMRK framework beyond classical L-functions.
Possible settings include:

338



• motivic L-functions,
• p-adic or hybrid arithmetic structures,
• arithmetic objects with incomplete Euler products.

Exploring these extensions would test the universality of the operator architecture.

D.1.7 Refinement of Numerical Experiments

Numerical investigations can be refined by:
• increasing truncation scales,
• improving stability diagnostics,
• exploring family-level statistics more systematically.

Such refinements may reveal additional structural regularities or expose subtle failure modes.

D.1.8 Connections to Other Spectral Frameworks

Further work is needed to clarify precise connections between the SMRK program and other
spectral approaches, including:

• noncommutative geometry,
• adelic trace formulae,
• quantum chaos models.

Establishing rigorous bridges may lead to transfer of techniques and insights.

D.1.9 Formalization of Enforcement Arguments

Several enforcement arguments are currently formulated at a conceptual level. A systematic
formalization of these arguments within functional analysis would enhance their mathematical
precision.
This includes explicit statements of assumptions and theorems governing enforcement.

D.1.10 Minimal Assumption Analysis

Another open direction is the identification of minimal assumptions required for the SMRK
framework. Determining which assumptions are essential and which can be relaxed would sharpen
the conceptual core of the program.

D.1.11 Community Engagement and Independent Verification

The long-term success of the SMRK program depends on independent verification and engagement.
Open problems should be addressed by multiple approaches and scrutinized from different
mathematical perspectives.
Such engagement is essential for assessing the ultimate viability of the framework.

progress toward the Riemann Hypothesis (RH), at the level described in this framework, requires
not urgency but stability, openness, and careful preparation.
The timeline begins in 2026, following a deliberate pause. This pause is not a withdrawal, but
a consolidation phase: allowing ideas to settle, the document to circulate, and the broader
ecosystem—particularly the application layer of the Quantum Virtual Machine (QVM)—to
mature.

E.1.1 Guiding Principles

The roadmap is governed by the following principles:
• No forced acceleration; progress must be sustainable.
• Public engagement precedes technical expansion.
• Conceptual clarity precedes computation.
• Computational experimentation precedes formal proof.
• Collaboration is welcomed, but coherence is preserved.

Q4 2026 — Preparation for Computational Phase

• Formal specification of operator constructions in a computationally implementable form.

E.1.3 Year 2027: Transition to Operator Experimentation

Chapter 14

Golden-Phase Prime-Shift Operators
Gauge-Twisted Arithmetic Dynamics

and Spectral Probes of Prime Structure
Enter Yourname

Abstract
This document introduces a class of arithmetic prime-shift operators
acting on the space of square-summable sequences over the natural
numbers. The operators implement purely multiplicative dynamics,
where arithmetic states supported at a given index are mapped to states
supported at prime multiples or divisors of that index. To this basic
structure, nontrivial phase factors are added as a controlled gauge-like
modification.
The role of these phase factors is diagnostic rather than decorative. They
provide a systematic way to distinguish intrinsic spectral features of the
prime-shift construction from artifacts caused by truncation, regulariza-
tion, or numerical implementation. A distinguished benchmark choice,
referred to as the golden phase, is examined in detail due to its strong
irrationality properties, while the framework itself applies to general
irrational phase choices.
The document develops both the infinite-dimensional formulation and
finite approximations suitable for computation. It analyzes how spec-
tral observables respond to variations of the phase parameter and to
the inclusion of diagonal arithmetic potentials. In this way, the work
establishes a bridge between the bare prime-shift mechanism and later
stages of the program involving trace structures, spectral diagnostics,
and experimental comparison of arithmetic Hamiltonians.

1 Introduction and Strategy
The purpose of this paper is to place prime-shift operators into a rigorous self-adjoint framework
suitable for spectral analysis. While operators encoding multiplicative arithmetic dynamics have
appeared in various formal or heuristic contexts, their analytic foundations are often left implicit.
In particular, formal symmetry alone is insufficient for spectral interpretation.
Our objective is therefore precise: to construct a well-defined self-adjoint operator associated
with prime-shift dynamics, obtained as a canonical extension of a densely defined symmetric
operator on ℓ2(N).



1.1 Why Self-Adjointness Matters

Spectral statements about arithmetic operators require self-adjointness for their validity. Without
it, eigenvalues need not be real, spectral measures may fail to exist, and trace-based constructions
become ill-defined.
In the context of arithmetic dynamics, this issue is particularly acute. The operators of interest
involve infinite sums over primes, with weights that are typically not absolutely summable. As a
result, naive operator definitions may fail to converge or admit multiple inequivalent self-adjoint
extensions.
Any attempt to connect arithmetic operators to spectral invariants must therefore begin with a
careful analysis of domains, closures, and extensions.

1.2 Formal Symmetry Is Not Enough

Prime-shift operators defined by pairing forward and backward transitions n↔ pn are formally
symmetric on natural dense domains such as c00(N). However, formal symmetry does not imply
self-adjointness, nor does it guarantee uniqueness of extension.
In infinite-dimensional settings, symmetric operators may admit infinitely many self-adjoint
extensions, each corresponding to different boundary conditions at infinity. Distinguishing a
canonical choice requires additional analytic input.

1.3 Strategy of the Paper

The strategy adopted in this work is based on quadratic form methods. Rather than attempting to
define the operator directly, we associate to it a quadratic form encoding prime-shift interactions.
This approach has several advantages:

• it avoids pointwise convergence issues,
• it allows direct control of boundedness and lower semiboundedness,
• it provides access to canonical self-adjoint extensions via standard functional-analytic

theorems.
Once a closed, densely defined quadratic form is established, the existence of a unique self-adjoint
operator associated with it follows from the Friedrichs extension theorem.

1.4 Regularization and Limits

Throughout the paper, all constructions are carried out within explicitly regularized settings.
Prime sums are truncated or damped, and operators are defined initially on finite or weighted
subspaces.
The role of regularization is not to approximate an infinite operator naively, but to provide a
controlled family of operators whose analytic properties may be studied uniformly. Limits, when
taken, are understood in appropriate operator or form senses.

1.5 Scope and Limitations

This paper deliberately restricts its scope. We do not attempt to derive trace formulas, to identify
spectral data with zeta or L-functions, or to make any claims regarding the Riemann Hypothesis.

347



Instead, we isolate the analytic core of prime-shift dynamics and establish a solid operator-
theoretic foundation upon which such investigations may later be built.

1.6 Organization of the Paper

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we define the arithmetic Hilbert space and discuss
suitable weighting schemes. Section 3 introduces regularized prime-shift operators. Section 4
develops the associated quadratic forms and establishes their basic properties. Section 5 constructs
self-adjoint extensions via the Friedrichs method. Section 6 discusses resolvent existence and
basic spectral properties. The final section summarizes the results and outlines directions for
further work.

2 Arithmetic Hilbert Space
In this section we fix the Hilbert space setting in which prime-shift operators will be analyzed.
The choice of space and inner product is not merely technical; it determines the admissible
domains, boundedness properties, and the viability of self-adjoint realizations.

This approach isolates the essential analytic features of prime-shift dynamics without committing

3 U(1) Gauge Phases on Arithmetic Graphs

Having established the untwisted prime-shift operator as a reference dynamics, we now introduce
gauge phases on arithmetic transitions. The purpose of this construction is not to modify the
underlying combinatorial structure of prime multiplication, but to endow it with a local geometric
degree of freedom.
The resulting operators may be viewed as gauge-covariant adjacency operators on the arithmetic
graph introduced in the previous section.

3.1 Arithmetic Potentials and Phase Differences

Let
η : N −→ R

be a real-valued function on the arithmetic state space. We interpret η(n) as a potential assigned
to the integer n. From this potential we define phase factors on directed prime transitions by

U(n, p) = e2πi(η(pn)−η(n)).

This construction assigns a U(1) phase to each directed edge

n −→ pn,

while ensuring that the phase associated with the inverse transition pn −→ n is given by the
complex conjugate

U(n, p)−1 = e−2πi(η(pn)−η(n)).

In this way, phase information is encoded exclusively through potential differences, guaranteeing
consistency across composite paths in the arithmetic graph.

3.2 Gauge Transformations

Given a potential function η, we define a unitary gauge transformation Gη on ℓ2(N) by

(Gηψ)(n) = e2πiη(n)ψ(n).

Two potentials η and η′ related by

η′(n) = η(n) + c, c ∈ R,

generate identical phase factors and therefore define the same gauge. More generally, the
construction depends only on the equivalence class of η modulo additive constants.
Under a gauge transformation, the untwisted prime-shift operator H0 transforms formally as

G−1
η H0Gη,

producing an operator whose action includes the phase factors U(n, p). This observation provides
a direct link between gauge phases and unitary conjugation at the formal level.

This operator differs from H0 only by the presence of conjugate phase factors on forward and
backward transitions. The underlying adjacency structure of the arithmetic graph remains
unchanged.

3.4 Formal Symmetry

On the dense domain c00(N) of finitely supported functions, the operator Hη is formally symmetric.
Indeed, for ψ,φ ∈ c00(N), each term corresponding to a transition n↔ pn contributes complex
conjugate phases when evaluated in the inner product, yielding

⟨ψ,Hηφ⟩ = ⟨Hηψ,φ⟩.

This symmetry is a direct consequence of constructing phases from potential differences. No
additional constraints on η are required beyond real-valuedness.

3.5 Interpretation as a Discrete Gauge Theory

The structure introduced above closely parallels lattice gauge theory in mathematical physics.
The arithmetic graph plays the role of a lattice, prime multiplication defines adjacency, and the
phase factors U(n, p) act as U(1) link variables.
However, unlike conventional lattices, the arithmetic graph is intrinsically multiplicative and
nonuniform. Gauge phases therefore probe arithmetic structure rather than spatial geometry.
In this sense, the construction defines a genuinely arithmetical gauge theory, in which phase
coherence and interference reflect properties of prime-induced dynamics.

3.6 Preparation for Golden-Phase Gauges

The framework developed in this section is fully general and places no restrictions on the choice
of potential η. In the following section, we will focus on a distinguished class of potentials
constructed from the golden ratio and Fibonacci-based coordinates.
These golden-phase gauges exploit extremal irrationality and optimal equidistribution properties
to provide maximally nonresonant probes of arithmetic dynamics. Their introduction requires
no modification of the formalism presented here, but only a specific and conceptually motivated
choice of η.

4 The Golden-Phase Prime-Shift Operator
We now introduce the central object of this work: the golden-phase prime-shift operator. This
operator is obtained by specializing the general gauge-covariant prime-shift construction to a

351



distinguished class of arithmetic potentials derived from the golden ratio and related Fibonacci
structures.
The resulting operator preserves the combinatorial structure of prime-induced dynamics while
introducing a maximally nonresonant phase geometry.

4.1 Definition of the Golden-Phase Operator

Let √

The defining feature of this operator is the conjugate pairing of phase factors on forward and

breaking the formal symmetry of the underlying arithmetic dynamics.

4.2 Structural Symmetry

The apparent symmetry of the definition is not accidental. For each prime p, the transition
n→ pn carries the phase

e2πi(ηφ(pn)−ηφ(n)),

while the inverse transition pn→ n carries the conjugate phase
e−2πi(ηφ(pn)−ηφ(n)).

As a consequence, each undirected edge of the arithmetic graph contributes a Hermitian pair to
the operator. On the dense domain of finitely supported states, this pairing guarantees formal
symmetry independently of the explicit choice of ηφ.
This observation captures, in precise terms, the intuitive notion that the operator is almost
automatically symmetric once phase factors are derived from a single underlying potential.

4.3 Interpretation as a Gauge-Twisted Adjacency Operator

The operator Hφ may be viewed as a weighted adjacency operator on the arithmetic graph
defined by prime multiplication, equipped with a U(1) gauge field. The phase θ(n, p) assigns a
geometric orientation to each prime-induced transition, while preserving the underlying graph
structure.
From this perspective, Hφ does not alter the connectivity of the arithmetic state space. Instead,
it modifies the interference pattern between arithmetic paths by introducing controlled phase
shifts. The golden ratio enters only through the choice of gauge, not through any modification of
the combinatorial rules.

352



4.4 Role of the Local Potential

The term V (n) represents an optional local contribution, diagonal in the arithmetic basis. Typical
choices include slowly varying arithmetic functions, such as logarithmic or von Mangoldt-type
terms, though no specific form is assumed at this stage.
The presence of V (n) allows the golden-phase operator to be embedded naturally into broader
operator families, including previously studied prime-shift Hamiltonians. Importantly, the
gauge-phase structure introduced here is entirely independent of the local potential.

4.5 Gauge Equivalence and Physical Content

Formally, the operator Hφ is unitarily equivalent to the untwisted operator H0 under the
gauge transformation generated by ηφ. Nevertheless, this equivalence does not trivialize the
construction.
In truncated, regularized, or numerically implemented settings, gauge phases affect boundary
behavior, interference patterns, and spectral statistics. In this sense, the golden phase acts as a
probe rather than a redundancy: it tests the sensitivity of arithmetic dynamics to maximally
irrational phase twisting.

4.6 Conceptual Significance

The golden-phase prime-shift operator occupies an intermediate position between pure arithmetic
and spectral geometry. It does not impose order on prime distribution, nor does it assume hidden
periodicity. Instead, it introduces a distinguished gauge against which arithmetic coherence can
be meaningfully tested.
If prime-induced dynamics is genuinely phase-blind, golden twisting produces no persistent
spectral signature. If, however, subtle coherence exists, the golden phase provides a setting in
which such effects may become visible.
In the following section, we examine concrete choices of the potential ηφ, ranging from logarithmic
gauges to Fibonacci-based representations, and analyze how these choices influence the resulting
arithmetic phases.

5 Choices of Golden Gauge Functions

In this section we examine concrete choices of the arithmetic potential ηφ that generate golden-
phase gauges. While the formal construction of the gauge-covariant prime-shift operator places
no restrictions on ηφ, the interpretive and spectral consequences depend sensitively on this choice.
Our guiding principle is that the golden ratio should enter only as a source of maximal irrationality
and optimal equidistribution, not as an imposed symmetry. Accordingly, we focus on gauges
that are structurally simple, arithmetically natural, and spectrally nonresonant.

5.1 Logarithmic Golden Gauge

The simplest class of potentials is logarithmic in nature. Let

Remarkably, the phase depends only on the prime p and not on the base point n. The resulting
operator introduces a uniform prime-dependent phase twist across the arithmetic graph.
This gauge may be interpreted as a Dirichlet-type phase deformation. It preserves scale covariance
while breaking trivial periodicity through the irrational base φ. Although structurally simple,
this choice already distinguishes prime transitions in a spectrally meaningful way.

5.2 Quasi-Periodic Scale Gauge

A more refined construction introduces quasi-periodicity through fractional scaling. Define

This gauge introduces scale-dependent interference patterns that vary across the arithmetic graph.
Prime transitions at different magnitudes experience distinct phases, producing a genuinely
quasi-periodic structure in logarithmic scale.
From a spectral perspective, this choice maximally suppresses accidental resonance. Any persistent
spectral signature arising under this gauge cannot be attributed to simple scale periodicity.

This gauge assigns phase contributions to Fibonacci digits rather than to magnitude or scale.
Prime multiplication induces nonlocal but highly structured changes in the Zeckendorf digit

Within the language of Quansistor Field Mathematics, this construction admits an interpretation
as a field defined on Fibonacci-indexed degrees of freedom. Each digit acts as a local excitation,
and prime transitions correspond to structured field interactions.

5.4 Comparison of Gauge Classes

The gauges introduced above differ in complexity and interpretive emphasis:
• logarithmic gauges produce prime-dependent but state-independent phases,
• quasi-periodic scale gauges introduce local interference across scales,
• Zeckendorf-based gauges encode phase information in discrete Fibonacci coordinates.

All three constructions are golden in the sense that they rely on extremal irrationality and avoid
rational commensurability. None of them imposes periodic structure on arithmetic dynamics.

5.5 Gauge Choice as a Spectral Probe

The choice of ηφ should be understood as selecting a probe rather than a model. Different
gauges test different aspects of arithmetic coherence. If prime-induced dynamics is genuinely
phase-insensitive, all golden gauges should yield spectrally equivalent behavior in appropriate
limits.
Conversely, systematic differences between these gauges would signal the presence of nontrivial
phase correlations. Such effects, if observed, would not constitute an explanation of prime
distribution, but rather evidence of hidden structure accessible only through operator-based
interrogation.

6 Formal Symmetry and Self-Adjointness
In this section we analyze the symmetry properties of the golden-phase prime-shift operator and
clarify the role of domains, regularization, and potential self-adjointness issues. The emphasis is
not on establishing maximal generality, but on identifying the structural features that make the
operator suitable for spectral analysis and numerical experimentation.

6.1 Natural Domains

Let c00(N) denote the space of finitely supported functions on N. This space is dense in ℓ2(N)
and invariant under all prime-shift operators introduced in this work, provided that the prime
sum is regularized.
Throughout this section, all operator identities are understood on c00(N), unless stated otherwise.
This choice avoids convergence issues while preserving the algebraic structure of the construction.

6.2 Formal Symmetry

Let Hφ denote the golden-phase prime-shi∑ft operator defined in the previous section. For
ψ,φ ∈ c00(N), we compute

⟨ψ,Hφφ⟩ = ψ(n) (Hφφ)(n).
n∈N

Each term in the prime sum corresponds to a pair of transitions
n←→ pn,

with phase factors arranged as complex conjugates. Exchanging the roles of ψ and φ and
reindexing the backward transitions yields

⟨ψ,Hφφ⟩ = ⟨Hφψ,φ⟩.

355



Thus, Hφ is formally symmetric on c00(N). This property holds independently of the explicit
choice of the golden-phase potential ηφ, provided that ηφ is real-valued.

6.3 Role of Phase Pairing

The formal symmetry of Hφ is a direct consequence of constructing phase factors from potential
differences. For each prime p, the forward transition n→ pn carries a phase

e2πi(ηφ(pn)−ηφ(n)),

while the backward transition pn→ n carries its complex conjugate.
This pairing ensures that no net phase bias is introduced along closed arithmetic paths. In
particular, any finite cycle in the arithmetic graph contributes a real-valued amplitude to the
quadratic form associated with Hφ.

6.4 Quadratic Form Perspective

It is often convenient to consider the quadratic form
Qφ(ψ) = ⟨ψ,Hφψ⟩, ψ ∈ c00(N).

Formally, Qφ is real-valued and symmetric. This observation provides a useful starting point for
discussing extensions of Hφ beyond c00(N) and for comparing different regularizations.
From the quadratic form perspective, the golden-phase operator behaves analogously to a discrete
magnetic Schrödinger operator on a graph, with arithmetic structure replacing spatial geometry.

6.5 Remarks on Self-Adjointness

Questions of essential self-adjointness for operators of the form Hφ are subtle and depend on the
choice of weights w(p), the local potential V (n), and the imposed regularization.
In this work we do not attempt to establish general self-adjointness results. Instead, we adopt
the pragmatic viewpoint that all spectral statements are to be understood within regularized
settings, such as finite prime cutoffs or bounded state spaces.
Within these settings, Hφ defines a finite-dimensional Hermitian matrix and is therefore self-
adjoint. Observed spectral features may then be studied as functions of the cutoff parameters.

6.6 Gauge Invariance and Truncation Effects

Although the golden-phase operator is formally gauge-equivalent to the untwisted operator in
the infinite setting, truncation and regularization break exact gauge invariance. Boundary effects
introduce phase-dependent contributions that persist in finite systems.
This phenomenon is not a defect but a feature. It is precisely through such boundary-sensitive
effects that gauge phases act as probes of arithmetic structure. Persistent spectral differences under
golden-phase twisting therefore carry meaningful information about prime-induced dynamics.

6.7 Summary

The golden-phase prime-shift operator is formally symmetric on a natural dense domain and
admits a well-defined quadratic form. While full self-adjointness in the infinite setting remains
an open analytical question, all constructions are robust under regularization and truncation.

356



These properties justify the use of Hφ as a legitimate object of spectral and numerical study.
In the next section, we turn to the interpretation of its spectrum and the kinds of arithmetic
information such spectra may encode.

7 Spectral Interpretation
In this section we discuss the spectral interpretation of the golden-phase prime-shift operator.
Rather than focusing on explicit eigenvalue computations, we aim to clarify what types of
arithmetic information may be encoded in the spectrum and how phase twisting modifies the
spectral response of prime-induced dynamics.

7.1 Spectrum as an Invariant of Arithmetic Dynamics

For an operator acting on ℓ2(N), the spectrum represents the set of energetically admissible modes
of arithmetic motion. In the present context, these modes correspond to coherent superpositions
of arithmetic states that are stable under prime-shift transitions.
From an operator-first perspective, the spectrum is the primary invariant of interest. Individual
primes appear only indirectly, through their collective contribution to the adjacency structure
and the resulting interference patterns. Spectral properties therefore probe global arithmetic
organization rather than local combinatorial features.

7.2 Interference and Arithmetic Paths

Each eigenstate of the prime-shift operator may be interpreted as a weighted superposition of
arithmetic paths generated by repeated prime multiplication and division. The contribution of a
given path is determined not only by its length and weights, but also by the accumulated phase
along the path.
In the untwisted operator, all such paths interfere constructively. Introducing gauge phases
modifies this interference, selectively enhancing or suppressing certain classes of paths. The
golden phase, in particular, introduces maximally noncommensurate phase shifts that tend to
decorrelate trivial cycles.

7.3 Phase Sensitivity of the Spectrum

If prime-induced dynamics is insensitive to phase twisting, the spectra of the untwisted and
golden-phase operators should agree in appropriate limits, up to finite-size effects. In this case,
gauge phases act as a benign redundancy.
If, however, the spectrum exhibits systematic dependence on the golden gauge, this indicates
the presence of arithmetic coherence beyond purely combinatorial structure. Such sensitivity
would manifest as shifts in eigenvalue distributions, changes in spectral gaps, or alterations in
level statistics.
Importantly, any observed phase sensitivity must persist under variation of regularization
parameters in order to be considered meaningful.

7.4 Spectral Statistics

Beyond individual eigenvalues, statistical properties of the spectrum provide a powerful diagnostic
tool. In particular, level spacing distributions may be compared against random matrix ensembles,

357



such as the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) or Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE).
The introduction of gauge phases naturally breaks time-reversal symmetry at the level of
arithmetic paths, suggesting that transitions between symmetry classes may occur as the phase
coupling is varied. The golden phase provides a canonical benchmark against which such
transitions may be tested.

7.5 Relation to Hilbert–Pólya-Type Intuitions

The Hilbert–Pólya conjecture suggests that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function
may arise as eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator. While the golden-phase prime-shift operator is
not proposed as such an operator, its spectral behavior may nevertheless inform operator-based
intuitions.
In particular, the presence or absence of phase-sensitive spectral structure bears on the question
of whether prime-induced dynamics supports nontrivial arithmetic resonances. The golden phase
serves here as a stringent test: any resonance surviving maximal irrational twisting must be
deeply rooted in arithmetic structure.

7.6 Spectral Stability and Robustness

A key requirement for meaningful interpretation is spectral stability. Features attributable to
arithmetic structure should remain stable under moderate changes in truncation, weighting, and
gauge choice within the golden class.
Conversely, spectral features that vary erratically under such changes are best interpreted as
finite-size artifacts. The distinction between these regimes is central to the numerical protocols
discussed in the following section.

7.7 Interpretive Summary

The spectrum of the golden-phase prime-shift operator encodes information about the coherence
and interference of prime-induced arithmetic dynamics. Gauge phases do not explain prime
distribution, but they test its sensitivity to controlled phase perturbations.
Whether the outcome is complete phase blindness or the emergence of persistent spectral structure,
the result carries conceptual significance. In both cases, the operator framework provides a
precise language in which arithmetic dynamics may be interrogated spectrally rather than
combinatorially.
In the next section we describe explicit numerical protocols designed to probe these spectral
effects in a falsifiable and reproducible manner.

8 Numerical Protocols and Falsifiability

This section outlines concrete numerical protocols for investigating the spectral properties of
the golden-phase prime-shift operator. The emphasis is on reproducibility, falsifiability, and the
separation of genuine arithmetic effects from finite-size artifacts.
All numerical statements are to be understood within regularized settings. The goal is not to
approximate an infinite operator, but to study the stability and response of finite truncations
under controlled phase perturbations.

358



8.1 Finite-Dimensional Truncations

Numerical implementations are based on truncating both the state space and the prime sum.
Specifically, we restrict

n ≤ N, p ≤ P,

and consider the resulting operator acting on CN .
Within this setting, the golden-phase prime-shift operator defines a finite Hermitian matrix. The
dependence of spectral features on the cutoff parameters N and P provides a primary diagnostic
for distinguishing structural effects from truncation artifacts.

8.2 Regularization of Prime Weights

In practice, the choice of weight function w(p) significantly influences numerical stability. Common
choices include

w(p) = 1
, w(p) = e−p/P 1

, w(p) = , α > 1.
p p pα

Smooth damping of large primes improves convergence and allows systematic study of the
dependence on prime scale. All gauge constructions introduced earlier are compatible with such
regularizations.

8.3 Spectral Observables

The primary numerical observables include:
• eigenvalue distributions and spectral density,

• gaps and extremal eigenvalues,

• level spacing distributions after unfolding,

• sensitivity of eigenvalues to variations in the gauge parameter κ.
Comparisons are performed between the untwisted operator H0, the golden-phase operator Hφ,
and operators with randomized phases serving as control ensembles.

8.4 Gauge Sensitivity Tests

A central diagnostic is the response of the spectrum to gauge twisting. For a fixed truncation
(N,P ), one varies the coupling parameter κ and observes the evolution of spectral features.
Three regimes may be distinguished:

• phase-blind regime: spectral observables remain invariant up to statistical noise,

• perturbative regime: small but systematic shifts occur, scaling with κ,

• coherent regime: nontrivial spectral restructuring persists under variation of κ and trunca-
tion parameters.

Only the latter two regimes indicate genuine phase sensitivity.

359



8.5 Comparison with Random Phases

To assess the specificity of golden-phase effects, it is essential to compare results with randomized
gauge phases. In such control experiments, the phase factors U(n, p) are replaced by independent
random elements of U(1).
If golden-phase effects are indistinguishable from random-phase behavior, this suggests the
absence of arithmetic coherence detectable by phase twisting. By contrast, systematic differences
indicate structure specific to the golden gauge.

8.6 Level Statistics and Symmetry Classes

After unfolding the spectrum, level spacing distributions may be compared to random matrix
ensembles. The untwisted operator typically exhibits statistics associated with time-reversal
invariant systems.
Introducing gauge phases may induce a crossover toward unitary statistics, reflecting the breaking
of effective time-reversal symmetry in arithmetic path interference. The golden phase provides a
canonical, nonrandom benchmark for studying such transitions.

8.7 Criteria for Falsification

The framework proposed in this paper admits clear falsification criteria:
• absence of stable spectral differences between golden-phase and random-phase ensembles,

• disappearance of phase sensitivity as truncation parameters increase,

• lack of reproducibility across independent implementations.
Failure to observe any persistent golden-phase effects under these tests would constitute strong
evidence that prime-induced dynamics is phase-insensitive at the operator level considered here.

8.8 Reproducibility and Open Data

All numerical experiments should be conducted using publicly available code and documented
parameter choices. The simplicity of the operator definition allows implementation in a variety
of environments, including Python, Julia, and JavaScript-based numerical frameworks.
Reproducibility is essential: the purpose of numerical exploration in this context is not confirma-
tion bias, but controlled interrogation of arithmetic dynamics through spectral probes.

8.9 Summary

Numerical analysis provides the bridge between formal operator construction and empirical
assessment. The protocols outlined above allow the golden-phase prime-shift operator to be
tested as a genuine probe of arithmetic coherence.
In the following section, we place these constructions within the broader framework of Quansistor
Field Mathematics and discuss their interpretation as field-theoretic refinements of operator-based
arithmetic models.
