2.4 Dependence on truncation dimension

Spectral deviation is examined as a function of the truncation dimension N . As N increases, one
of the following behaviors is observed:

• monotone decrease of ∆(N),
• saturation at a finite error level,
• growth or oscillation indicating instability.

Only the first behavior is interpreted as evidence of asymptotic spectral correspondence. The
other behaviors signal truncation artifacts or structural incompatibility.

2.5 Low-lying versus higher eigenvalues

Low-lying eigenvalues often exhibit larger relative deviations, due to stronger sensitivity to
boundary conditions and diagonal potential terms.
For this reason, spectral agreement is evaluated separately for:

450



• low-index eigenvalues,
• intermediate spectral ranges,
• the highest reliably computed eigenvalues.

This stratification helps distinguish localized discrepancies from global spectral trends.

2.6 Robustness under parameter variation

The spectral comparison is repeated for multiple values of the parameters α, β, Pmax, and N .
Parameter regimes yielding qualitatively similar spectral alignment are identified.
Conversely, parameter choices that produce spurious agreement only within narrow tuning
windows are flagged as unstable. Such regimes are documented but not treated as evidence of
structural validity.

2.7 Summary of spectral findings

The results of this section demonstrate that the SMRK Hamiltonian can exhibit partial spectral
alignment with the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function over finite ranges and resolutions.
However, spectral matching alone is insufficient to establish relevance to the Riemann Hypothesis.
Accordingly, these results are interpreted as preliminary consistency checks, to be complemented
by statistical, arithmetic, and stability diagnostics in subsequent sections.

3 Level Spacing Statistics

3.1 Motivation for spacing analysis

While pointwise spectral matching tests whether individual eigenvalues approximate the imaginary
parts of zeta zeros, it does not capture the local statistical structure of the spectrum.
Level spacing statistics probe short-range correlations between neighboring eigenvalues. For the
nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function, extensive numerical evidence indicates agreement
with the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE) of random matrix theory.
In this section, we examine whether the spectrum of the SMRK Hamiltonian exhibits compatible
local statistics, independently of absolute alignment.

3.2 Nearest-neighbor spacings

Let
λ1 ≤ λ2 ≤ · · · ≤ λM

denote a sequence of reliably computed eigenvalues of the truncated SMRK Hamiltonian.
The nearest-neighbor spacings are defined as

sn = λn+1 − λn, n = 1, . . . ,M − 1.

Raw spacings depend on the local density of eigenvalues. To allow comparison across spectral
regions, the spectrum must be unfolded.

451



3.3 Spectral unfolding

Unfolding transforms the eigenvalues to a new sequence with approximately unit mean spacing.
Let N(λ) denote the integrated spectral density, estimated either empirically or via a smooth fit.
The unfolded eigenvalues are given by

λ̃n = N(λn),

and the unfolded spacings by
s̃n = λ̃n+1 − λ̃n.

Care is taken to ensure that the unfolding procedure does not artificially impose random-matrix-
like behavior. Multiple unfolding methods are tested to assess robustness.

3.4 Comparison with random matrix ensembles

The empirical distribution of unfolded spacings s̃n is compared with standard random matrix
ensembles. The primary reference is the Gaussian Unitary Ensemble (GUE), whose spacing
distribution is

PGUE(s) = 32
π2 s

2e−4s2/π.

Alternative ensembles, such as the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) and Poisson statistics,
are used as controls.
Deviation between the empirical distribution and reference distributions is quantified using the
Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance and related measures.

3.5 Finite-size and boundary effects

Spacing statistics are sensitive to finite-size effects, particularly for low-lying eigenvalues and
near truncation boundaries.
To mitigate these effects, statistics are computed only on interior spectral windows, excluding
regions strongly affected by truncation or diagonal dominance.
Results are reported for multiple window sizes to assess consistency.

3.6 Results and observed trends

Across tested parameter regimes, the spacing statistics of the SMRK Hamiltonian exhibit mixed
behavior.
In certain configurations, the unfolded spacings show partial agreement with GUE predictions
over limited spectral ranges. In other regimes, significant deviations are observed, including
excess level clustering or near-Poisson behavior.
These observations indicate that local spectral correlations are highly sensitive to parameter
choices and truncation details.

3.7 Interpretation and limitations

Agreement with GUE-like statistics is interpreted as supportive evidence of compatibility with
known zeta zero phenomenology, but not as confirmation of arithmetic relevance.

452



Conversely, failure to reproduce GUE statistics does not necessarily invalidate the SMRK
Hamiltonian. Finite-size effects, incomplete unfolding, or unresolved truncation artifacts may
obscure universal behavior.
Accordingly, level spacing statistics are treated as a diagnostic tool, to be considered alongside
spectral matching, explicit formula residuals, and stability tests.

3.8 Summary

Level spacing analysis provides an important statistical perspective on the SMRK Hamilto-
nian spectrum. While partial agreement with random matrix predictions can be observed in
selected regimes, the results emphasize the necessity of complementary diagnostics and careful
interpretation.

4 Explicit Formula Residual Results

4.1 Purpose of the explicit formula test

Spectral agreement and level spacing statistics do not by themselves guarantee arithmetic
relevance. The explicit formula provides a direct bridge between the distribution of primes and
the spectral data.
In this section, we evaluate the SMRK Hamiltonian using explicit formula diagnostics, comparing
prime-side quantities with zero-side reconstructions derived from the operator spectrum. The
resulting residuals serve as a stringent test of arithmetic compatibility.

4.2 Prime-side reference quantities

Let Λ(n) denote the von Mangoldt function. We consider smoothed prime-weighted sums of the
form ∑∞

Ψf (X) = Λ(n) f(logn− logX),
n=1

where f is a smooth test function with compact support or rapid decay.
In numerical implementations, the sum is truncated according to the support of f and recorded
with controlled error bounds. These quantities serve as independent arithmetic reference data.

4.3 Zero-side reconstruction from the SMRK spectrum

Given a finite set of eigenvalues {λn} of the truncated SMRK Hamiltonian, we construct the
zero-side approximation

∑

This construction mirrors the truncated explicit formula used for certified zeta zeros, with
operator eigenvalues playing the role of imaginary parts of nontrivial zeros.

4.4 Definition of residuals

The explicit formula residual associated with the SMRK Hamiltonian is defined as

RH(X) = Ψf (X)−Ψf,H(X).

Under ideal circumstances, RH(X) should consist primarily of truncation effects, smoothing arti-
facts, and controlled lower-order terms. Persistent structured deviations indicate incompatibility
between the operator-induced spectrum and the arithmetic data.

4.6 Stability under refinement

A central diagnostic is the behavior of residuals under refinement. Specifically, we examine
whether:

• residual magnitudes decrease as truncation dimension increases,
• residual structure remains stable under changes in the test function f ,
• oscillatory features persist across refinement levels.

Residual patterns that remain stable under refinement are interpreted as structural. Those that
diminish or change qualitatively are attributed to truncation artifacts.

4.7 Observed behavior

Numerical experiments reveal that explicit formula residuals for the SMRK Hamiltonian exhibit
nontrivial structure.
In certain parameter regimes, residual magnitudes decrease modestly with increasing resolution,
suggesting partial arithmetic compatibility. In other regimes, persistent oscillatory residuals
remain, indicating a mismatch between the operator spectrum and prime-weighted sums.
These findings demonstrate that explicit formula diagnostics are more discriminating than spectral
or spacing tests alone.

4.8 Interpretation and implications

The residual analysis confirms that arithmetic compatibility is a strong and restrictive constraint.
Even operators that perform well in spectral matching may fail explicit formula tests.
The SMRK Hamiltonian does not uniformly pass the explicit formula diagnostics across all
tested regimes. This outcome does not invalidate the operator-based approach, but highlights
the sensitivity of arithmetic structure to operator details.

454



4.9 Summary

Explicit formula residuals provide the most stringent numerical test applied in this study. They
reveal both promising behavior in selected regimes and clear failure modes in others.
These results underscore the necessity of combining spectral, statistical, and arithmetic diagnostics
when evaluating candidate operators for relevance to the Riemann Hypothesis.

5 Stability Under Refinement

5.1 Motivation

Numerical agreement observed at a fixed resolution may arise from truncation artifacts, parameter
tuning, or accidental cancellations. To distinguish such effects from structurally meaningful
behavior, it is essential to study stability under systematic refinement.
In this section, we examine how the numerical properties of the SMRK Hamiltonian evolve as
resolution parameters are varied. Only features that persist across multiple refinement levels are
treated as significant.

5.2 Refinement dimensions

Refinement is performed along several independent axes:
• truncation dimension N of the Hilbert space,
• prime cutoff parameter Pmax,
• numerical precision and solver tolerances,
• spectral window size used for diagnostics,
• smoothing parameters in explicit formula tests.

Each refinement dimension is varied independently and in selected coupled sweeps, allowing
interactions between parameters to be identified.

5.3 Spectral stability

Spectral stability is assessed by monitoring the behavior of eigenvalues (N)
λn as N increases.

For fixed index n, a stable spectral feature is characterized by convergence

λ(N)
n −→ λn as N →∞,

up to controlled numerical error.
In practice, convergence is evaluated by tracking relative changes

| (N2) N )

for increasing truncation levels N1 < N2.
Eigenvalues exhibiting erratic drift, splitting, or reordering under refinement are classified as
unstable and excluded from sensitive diagnostics.

455



5.4 Stability of spectral matching

The normalized spectral deviation defined in Section 2 is examined across refinement levels. A
stable matching regime is indicated by:

• decreasing or bounded deviation as N and Pmax increase,
• consistent ordering of matched eigenvalues,
• absence of abrupt error growth near truncation boundaries.

Failure of these conditions signals that apparent agreement at low resolution does not extrapolate.

5.5 Stability of level spacing statistics

Level spacing statistics are recomputed for increasing truncation dimensions and for different
interior spectral windows.
Stability is indicated by:

• similar unfolded spacing distributions across refinement levels,
• comparable goodness-of-fit metrics with respect to reference ensembles,
• robustness to moderate changes in unfolding procedures.

Strong dependence of spacing statistics on truncation size or window selection is interpreted as
evidence of finite-size dominance.

5.6 Stability of explicit formula residuals

Explicit formula residuals provide the most sensitive refinement test. Residual functions RH(X)
are examined for:

• reduction in overall magnitude with increasing resolution,
• persistence or decay of structured oscillatory components,
• qualitative similarity across smoothing parameter choices.

Residual features that remain stable under simultaneous refinement of truncation dimension,
prime cutoff, and smoothing scale are interpreted as intrinsic to the operator structure.

5.7 Cross-parameter interactions

Refinement along one axis may amplify or suppress instability along another. For example,
increasing Pmax without a corresponding increase in N can introduce boundary artifacts, while
increased N with insufficient prime coverage may underrepresent arithmetic structure.
Such interactions are explicitly monitored, and only parameter regimes exhibiting coherent
behavior across multiple axes are considered reliable.

5.8 Summary of refinement behavior

The refinement analysis reveals that the SMRK Hamiltonian exhibits a mixture of stable and
unstable features.

456



Certain spectral and statistical properties persist under refinement, suggesting genuine structural
behavior. Other apparent agreements degrade as resolution increases, indicating truncation-
induced artifacts.
These findings reinforce the necessity of refinement-based validation and motivate the careful
interpretation of numerical agreement as provisional rather than definitive.

6 Negative Results and Failure Cases

6.1 Role of negative results

Negative results play a central role in the experimental framework adopted in this work. Because
the objective is falsification rather than confirmation, documenting failure modes is as important
as reporting partial successes.
This section records parameter regimes, numerical configurations, and operator variants for which
the SMRK Hamiltonian fails to meet one or more diagnostic criteria. These results delimit the
space of plausible operator constructions and help prevent overinterpretation of isolated positive
findings.

6.2 Spectral overfitting at low truncation

In several parameter configurations, good spectral alignment with zeta zeros was observed only
at low truncation dimensions. As the truncation dimension N increased, spectral deviations grew
or eigenvalue ordering became unstable.
Such behavior is interpreted as overfitting to finite spectral data. Operators exhibiting this pattern
were excluded from further analysis, even if initial spectral comparisons appeared favorable.

6.3 Instability under prime cutoff variation

The prime cutoff parameter Pmax plays a critical role in shaping the arithmetic structure of the
SMRK Hamiltonian.
In some regimes, increasing Pmax without proportional increase in N led to pronounced boundary
effects, manifesting as spectral distortion and increased explicit formula residuals.
Conversely, overly restrictive prime cutoffs failed to capture sufficient arithmetic structure,
resulting in near-Poisson spectral statistics. These regimes were classified as inadequate.

6.4 Failure of explicit formula compatibility

Several operator variants exhibited acceptable spectral matching and level spacing statistics, yet
failed explicit formula diagnostics.
In these cases, explicit formula residuals remained large or structurally unstable under refinement,
indicating a fundamental mismatch between the operator-induced spectrum and prime-weighted
sums.
These failures demonstrate that explicit formula tests are strictly stronger than purely spectral
diagnostics.

457



6.5 Parameter sensitivity and fine tuning

Some configurations produced apparent agreement with diagnostics only within narrow parameter
windows. Small perturbations of parameters α, β, or Pmax resulted in rapid degradation of
spectral or arithmetic scores.
Such fine-tuned regimes are not considered structurally meaningful. The framework treats
robustness to moderate parameter variation as a necessary condition for relevance.

6.6 Numerical pathologies

Additional failure modes arose from numerical issues, including:
• loss of orthogonality in eigenvectors at large N ,
• sensitivity to solver tolerances,
• accumulation of round-off errors in explicit formula sums.

While these issues can sometimes be mitigated through increased precision or alternative algo-
rithms, they nonetheless impose practical limits on achievable resolution.

6.7 Implications for operator design

The documented failures highlight several lessons for future operator constructions:
• spectral matching alone is insufficient,
• arithmetic structure must be encoded robustly,
• stability under refinement is a non-negotiable requirement,
• fine tuning should be viewed with skepticism.

These observations inform the design of modified or alternative operators and motivate the
exploration of broader operator families.

6.8 Summary

The negative results reported here demonstrate the discriminating power of the experimental
framework. By explicitly recording failure cases, the study narrows the landscape of plausible
operator models and strengthens the credibility of any surviving candidates.

7 Discussion and Interpretation

7.1 Summary of numerical findings

The numerical experiments reported in this work provide a multifaceted assessment of the SMRK
Hamiltonian as a candidate operator within the Hilbert–Pólya program.
Across spectral matching, level spacing statistics, explicit formula diagnostics, and refinement
analysis, the results reveal a nuanced picture. The SMRK Hamiltonian exhibits partial com-
patibility with known properties of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function, but also
displays clear limitations and failure modes.

458



These findings underscore the importance of evaluating operator proposals along multiple
independent dimensions, rather than relying on a single diagnostic.

7.2 Interpretation of spectral agreement

The observed spectral alignment between SMRK eigenvalues and zeta zeros over finite ranges
suggests that arithmetic transfer operators can encode nontrivial spectral structure.
However, the lack of uniform convergence under refinement indicates that spectral agreement
alone does not establish relevance to the Riemann Hypothesis. Instead, such agreement should
be viewed as an initial filter: necessary, but far from sufficient.
This interpretation aligns with the broader understanding that many constructions can reproduce
finite spectral data without capturing the underlying arithmetic dynamics.

7.3 Statistical structure versus arithmetic content

Level spacing statistics provide insight into local spectral correlations. Partial agreement with
GUE-like behavior in selected regimes is consistent with known phenomenology of zeta zeros.
At the same time, the sensitivity of spacing statistics to truncation and parameter choices high-
lights their limited discriminating power. Statistical compatibility does not uniquely characterize
arithmetic origin and must be interpreted in conjunction with explicit arithmetic tests.

7.4 Explicit formula diagnostics as a decisive filter

Among all diagnostics employed, explicit formula residuals emerge as the most restrictive. They
directly test whether the operator-induced spectrum can reproduce prime-weighted sums, rather
than merely mimic spectral patterns.
The persistence of structured residuals in many parameter regimes demonstrates that encoding
arithmetic content is substantially more demanding than achieving spectral resemblance. This
observation reinforces the view that arithmetic compatibility is the defining constraint for any
operator relevant to the Riemann Hypothesis.

7.5 Stability and structural significance

Stability under refinement serves as a practical proxy for structural validity. Features that degrade
as resolution increases are unlikely to reflect intrinsic properties of the underlying operator.
The mixed stability behavior observed for the SMRK Hamiltonian suggests that certain aspects
of its construction capture meaningful structure, while others remain sensitive to truncation
artifacts or parameter tuning.
This distinction provides guidance for future refinements and modifications of arithmetic transfer
operators.

7.6 Implications for the Hilbert–Pólya program

The results presented here do not support the conclusion that the SMRK Hamiltonian realizes the
Hilbert–Pólya conjecture. They do, however, demonstrate that the conjecture can be approached
as a falsifiable experimental program.

459



By embedding candidate operators within a disciplined numerical framework, it becomes possible
to systematically exclude incompatible models and focus analytical effort on constructions that
survive stringent tests.
This shift from speculative construction to constrained evaluation represents a methodological
advance in operator-based research on RH.

7.7 Lessons for future operator constructions

Several general lessons emerge:
• arithmetic structure must be encoded robustly,
• spectral agreement must persist under refinement,
• explicit formula compatibility is essential,
• fine-tuned parameter regimes are suspect.

These lessons apply not only to the SMRK Hamiltonian, but to any future operator proposal
aimed at explaining zeta zero statistics.

7.8 Concluding perspective

The numerical study presented in this work illustrates both the promise and the limitations of
arithmetic Hamiltonian approaches to the Riemann Hypothesis.
While no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding RH itself, the framework succeeds in
transforming operator proposals into testable scientific objects. In doing so, it helps clarify which
directions merit deeper analytical investigation and which are unlikely to succeed.
The value of this work lies not in resolving the Riemann Hypothesis, but in advancing a
structured pathway toward understanding the interplay between arithmetic, operators, and
spectral phenomena.

Appendix A

A.1 Numerical Parameters and Configurations
This appendix records the numerical parameters used in the experiments reported in this work.
All results in Sections 2–6 should be interpreted relative to these configurations.
Unless stated otherwise, each parameter set corresponds to an independent reproducible run, as
defined by the reproducibility protocol referenced in Whitepaper IV.

A.1.1 Truncation Parameters

The SMRK Hamiltonian is truncated to finite-dimensional subspacesHN ⊂ ℓ2(N). The truncation
dimension N is varied to assess stability.
Typical values used in the experiments include:

N in {200, 400, 800, 1200, 2000}

Only interior spectral regions, sufficiently separated from truncation boundaries, are used for
sensitive diagnostics.

A.1.2 Prime Cutoff

The prime cutoff parameter Pmax limits the range of primes included in the transfer terms.
Representative values include:

P_max in {11, 23, 47, 97, 197}

For each truncation dimension N , Pmax is chosen such that prime-induced transitions do not
dominate boundary effects.

A.1.3 Diagonal Potential Coefficients

The diagonal arithmetic potential is parameterized by real coefficients α and β:
U(n) = αΛ(n) + β logn.

Explored parameter ranges include:

alpha in [0.0, 1.0]
beta in [-1.0, 1.0]

Parameter sweeps are performed with step sizes chosen to detect sensitivity without fine tuning.

A.1.4 Numerical Precision and Solvers

Eigenvalue computations are performed using symmetric eigensolvers, with numerical precision
adjusted according to truncation size.
Typical settings include:

461



- double precision for N <= 800
- extended precision for N > 800
- solver tolerance <= 1e-10

Precision settings are logged for each run and included in the reproducibility manifest.

A.1.5 Reference Zero Data

Certified nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are used as reference data.
For each truncation level, only as many zeros are used as can be reliably matched to stable
eigenvalues. Zero sets satisfy the certification criteria described in Whitepaper IV, including
checkpoint validation.

A.1.6 Explicit Formula Parameters

Explicit formula diagnostics use smoothed test functions f with compact support or rapid decay.
Representative choices include:

- Gaussian kernels with sigma in {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}
- compact bump functions with fixed width

Residuals are evaluated on logarithmic grids spanning multiple scales in X.

A.1.7 Run Identification

Each numerical run is assigned a deterministic run identifier, computed as a hash of:
• code revision identifier,
• serialized configuration parameters,
• environment summary.

This identifier is referenced by all output artifacts and manifests associated with the run.

A.1.8 Notes on Extensibility

The parameter ranges reported here are not intended to be exhaustive. They represent a baseline
configuration sufficient to reveal both partial agreement and failure modes.
Future studies may extend these ranges or introduce additional parameters, provided that
reproducibility and stability analysis are maintained.

Appendix B

B.1 Reproducibility and Data Integrity
This appendix specifies the minimal reproducibility standard for the experimental framework
introduced in Sections 2–3. The goal is to ensure that numerical claims (e.g. “certified zeros
up to height T” or “residual norms across scales”) can be independently re-run, verified, and
compared.

B.1.1 Principles

We adopt the following principles:
1. Determinism where possible. If an experiment uses randomness (e.g. randomized grids

or Monte Carlo probes), the random seed must be fixed and recorded.
2. Full provenance. Every produced dataset must carry enough metadata to uniquely

identify the code version, configuration, and environment.
3. Immutable artifacts. Primary outputs (zero lists, checkpoint tables, residual arrays) are

treated as immutable once published. Any change creates a new artifact with a new hash.
4. Comparability. Artifacts must be stored in stable formats with documented schemas, so

results can be compared across versions and implementations.

B.1.2 Version Control Requirements

All code used to generate numerical artifacts must be version controlled. A minimal record for
each run includes:

- repository URL / identifier
- git commit hash (or equivalent immutable revision id)
- dirty flag (whether local changes existed)
- branch / tag name (optional)

If the experiment is performed outside a version-controlled repository, a snapshot archive of the
code must be produced and hashed alongside the outputs.

B.1.3 Environment Capture

The computational environment can affect numerical results. For each run, record at minimum:

- OS name and version
- CPU architecture (and optional instruction set flags)
- language/runtime version (Python/Julia/C++ compiler, etc.)
- numerical library versions (mpmath, Arb, MPFR, FFT libraries, etc.)
- floating-point precision settings (binary64, mp.dps, Arb precision, etc.)

If containerization is used (Docker/Podman), the container image hash should be recorded and
preferred as a canonical environment reference.

463



B.1.4 Configuration Logging

All experiment parameters must be serialized and stored as part of the run. We recommend
using a plain text format such as JSON or YAML. A minimal configuration must include:

- T_max
- scan parameters: dt_init, dt_min, dt_max
- root refinement parameters: eps_root, max_refine_iter
- checkpoint heights and count tolerances
- smoothing parameters for explicit-formula tests
- grids used: X_grid specification, spacing, bounds

The configuration file itself must be hashed and referenced by that hash in every output file.

B.1.5 Artifact Formats and Schemas

To support long-term comparability, we recommend the following stable formats:
• Zeros: line-oriented text (CSV/TSV) or JSONL with one row per zero.
• Root intervals: CSV/TSV with columns (an, bn, γn) where γn = 1

2(an + bn).
• Checkpoint table: CSV/TSV with columns (Tj , found, predicted,∆).
• Residual arrays: CSV/TSV or binary formats (Parquet/NPY) with explicit column

names and units.
If binary formats are used, a text manifest must accompany them to document the schema and
the software required to read the file.

B.1.6 Cryptographic Hashing and Manifests

Every primary artifact produced by the framework must be hashed. Let H(·) denote a crypto-
graphic hash function (e.g. SHA-256). For each run, produce a manifest file containing:

- artifact filename
- artifact byte size
- SHA-256 hash
- creation timestamp (UTC)
- config hash reference
- code revision reference

A recommended minimal manifest structure is:

run_id: <string>
created_utc: <timestamp>
code_revision: <commit-hash>
config_sha256: <hash>
artifacts:
- name: zeros_Tmax_<...>.tsv

B.1.7 Run Identifiers and Naming Conventions

We recommend a deterministic run identifier:

run_id := H(code_revision ∥ config_hash ∥ environment_summary),

where ∥ denotes concatenation of canonicalized strings.
Artifact filenames should include at least:

• the run identifier (or a prefix of it),
• the maximum height Tmax for zero computations,
• the smoothing or test-function label for explicit-formula runs.

Example:

checkpoints_Tmax_1e6_run_ab12cd34.tsv
residuals_gauss_sigma0p2_Tmax_1e6_run_ab12cd34.tsv

B.1.8 Minimal Comparability Tests

To confirm that two runs are comparable, the following must match:
1. identical code revision (or documented differences),
2. identical configuration hash,
3. compatible numerical precision settings,
4. identical artifact schema versions.

If any of these differ, results may still be scientifically comparable, but should not be treated as
byte-identical reproductions. Such cases must be documented explicitly.

B.1.9 Integrity Notes on Timestamping

If third-party timestamping is used (e.g. OpenTimestamps), it should be applied to the manifest
file rather than to individual artifacts. This anchors the full run state (code revision, configuration,
and all output hashes) under a single immutable timestamp commitment.
Timestamping strengthens provenance claims but does not replace reproducibility requirements:
the experiment must remain runnable from the recorded code and configuration.

B.1.10 Summary

The reproducibility protocol above defines the minimum standard for treating numerical results
in this work as verifiable scientific artifacts. The intent is to support cumulative progress: future

operator models and refinements can be compared against prior results without ambiguity about
computational provenance or data integrity.

Abstract
This document formulates a strictly operator-theoretic framework for
arithmetic Hamiltonians of Hilbert–Pólya type and serves as the formal
entry point of the identification program. The construction begins with
a careful specification of the underlying Hilbert space, operator domains,
and elementary building blocks, prior to any discussion of symmetry,
closure, or spectral interpretation.
The state space is taken to be the space of square-summable sequences
over the natural numbers, equipped with its standard basis indexed
by n. On a dense core of finitely supported sequences, prime-indexed
shift operators are introduced. These operators implement multiplicative
arithmetic dynamics by mapping a state supported at n to a state
supported at pn, together with a corresponding inverse action when
divisibility allows. In addition, diagonal multiplication operators defined
by real-valued arithmetic functions are included as potential terms.
The principal contribution of the document is methodological. It demon-
strates how such arithmetic shift and potential operators can be assembled
into candidate Hamiltonians while systematically addressing the domain
problems inherent to unbounded operators. Conditions for symmetry,
closability, and canonical self-adjoint realization are discussed, providing
a rigorous foundation for subsequent analytic and numerical work.
At this stage, no claims are made regarding spectral identification or
the distribution of zeros of the Riemann zeta function. The objective
is instead to eliminate a central weakness of earlier Hilbert–Pólya-type
constructions, namely the reliance on formally defined operators lacking
controlled domains and well-defined self-adjoint status. The resulting
framework provides a clean and auditable operator foundation upon
which later developments of the program are built.

3 Essential Self-Adjointness
This section addresses the central structural question of the operator H: whether the symmetric

5.1 Finite Truncations

The operator H is approximated by finite-dimensional truncations acting on ℓ2({1, . . . , N}).

Numerical spectra of truncated operators exhibit:

5.3 Stability Tests

5.4 Limitations

Finite truncations cannot resolve:
• essential self-adjointness,
• deficiency indices,
• true spectral type.

Numerical experiments serve only as supporting evidence and motivation for further analysis.

5.5 Reproducibility

All numerical experiments are reproducible using deterministic algorithms and fixed parameter

6 Riemann Hypothesis as a Corollary
This section clarifies the precise logical relationship between the operator-theoretic framework
developed in this work and the Riemann Hypothesis. No new analytical results are introduced.
The purpose is solely to state conditional implications in a transparent, non-circular manner.

6.1 Statement of the Riemann Hypothesis

The Riemann Hypothesis asserts that all nontrivial zeros ρ of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s)
satisfy

ℜ(ρ) = 1
2 .

Equivalently, all nontrivial zeros may be written as

ρ = 1
2 + iγ, γ ∈ R.

6.2 Conditional Hilbert–Pólya Principle

The Hilbert–Pólya principle may be formulated abstractly as follows:

If there exists a self-adjoint operator whose spectral data encode the nontrivial zeros
of ζ(s), then the Riemann Hypothesis holds.

The validity of this principle rests entirely on two independent requirements:

475



1. the existence of a canonical self-adjoint operator,
2. a rigorous identification between its spectral data and the zeros of ζ(s).

6.3 Logical Structure of the Present Framework

Within the framework developed in this work, the following conditional chain is identified:

(A) The symmetric operator H defined on D is essentially self-adjoint.
(B) The spectrum (or suitably regularized spectral determinant) of the unique self-adjoint

extension H̃ coincides with the set of imaginary parts of nontrivial zeros of ζ(s).

Theorem 6.1 (Conditional Corollary). If conditions (A) and (B) hold, then the Riemann
Hypothesis is true.

Proof. Under condition (A), the operator H̃ is self-adjoint, hence its spectrum is real. Under
condition (B), this spectrum coincides with the set {γ} appearing in the nontrivial zeros ρ = 1

2 +iγ
of ζ(s). Therefore all such γ are real, which is exactly the Riemann Hypothesis.

6.4 Non-Circularity

It is essential to emphasize that neither condition (A) nor (B) assumes the Riemann Hypothesis.
In particular:

• essential self-adjointness is a purely operator-theoretic property,
• spectral identification must be derived independently of any a priori assumptions on the

location of zeros.
Thus the implication established above is strictly one-directional.

6.5 Status and Limitations

At present, neither condition (A) nor condition (B) has been established in full generality. The
present work isolates these conditions explicitly and demonstrates that no additional hidden
assumptions are required.
Consequently, the Riemann Hypothesis appears here not as a premise, but as a conditional
corollary of a well-defined analytical program.

6.6 Interpretational Remark

Whether or not the program ultimately succeeds, the reformulation of the Riemann Hypothesis
as a question of operator-theoretic uniqueness and spectral correspondence provides a concrete
and falsifiable pathway for further investigation.

• deficiency indices,
• true spectral type.

Numerical experiments serve only as supporting evidence and motivation for further analysis.

7.5 Reproducibility

All numerical experiments are reproducible using deterministic algorithms and fixed parameter
choices. Implementation details are documented separately.

8 Failure Modes and Limitations
This section summarizes the principal ways in which the program developed in this work could
fail. The purpose is to make all assumptions explicit and to delimit the scope of the conclusions.

477



8.1 Failure of Essential Self-Adjointness

If the deficiency equation admits nontrivial ℓ2 solutions, the operator H would admit multiple
self-adjoint extensions. In that case:

• no canonical spectrum exists,
• any arithmetic interpretation becomes extension-dependent,
• the Hilbert–Pólya framework collapses at the structural level.

8.2 Spectral Mismatch

Even if H is essentially self-adjoint, its spectrum may fail to correspond to arithmetic data.
Possible issues include:

• presence of continuous spectrum,
• absence of discrete spectral points,
• lack of trace-class properties needed for explicit formulas.

8.3 Regularization Ambiguities

Any use of spectral traces or determinants requires regularization. Different regularization
schemes may yield inequivalent results. Failure to control this dependence would undermine
arithmetic conclusions.

8.4 Parameter Dependence

The parameters α and β play a structural role. Certain choices may destroy lower semibounded-
ness, invalidate closability, or introduce pathological spectral behavior.

8.5 Logical Separation from the Riemann Hypothesis

No part of the present framework assumes the Riemann Hypothesis. Conversely, the failure of
this program would not constitute evidence against the truth of the Riemann Hypothesis itself.

8.6 Summary

The framework succeeds only if:
• essential self-adjointness is established,
• spectral quantities are well-defined and stable,
• arithmetic identification is derived, not imposed.

All other outcomes are explicitly acknowledged and documented.

9 Analysis of the Deficiency Equation
This section provides a preliminary analytical investigation of the deficiency equation introduced
in Section ??. The analysis is partial and exploratory, intended to clarify structure rather than

478



to deliver a complete proof.

9.1 Restatement of the Equation

9.2 Growth Considerations

The diagonal term β logn grows unboundedly with n. Formally, this suggests that any solution
ψ(n) must decay sufficiently rapidly to compensate for logarithmic growth.
In particular, polynomially decaying solutions are excluded for β ̸= 0.

9.3 Prime-Scale Coupling

The equation couples values of ψ across multiplicative scales. This destroys any simple local
recurrence and prevents reduction to standard one-dimensional difference equations.
Such non-locality is expected to suppress square-summable solutions, though a rigorous proof
remains open.

9.4 Heuristic Absence of ℓ2 Solutions

Assuming generic oscillatory behavior induced by the imaginary term ±i, and taking into account
logarithmic confinement, it is heuristically unlikely that nontrivial ℓ2 solutions exist.
This heuristic supports, but does not prove, the conjecture that the deficiency indices vanish.

9.5 Open Problem

Prove or disprove that equation (20.5) admits no nontrivial solutions in ℓ2(N).

This problem represents the central analytical challenge of the program.

10 Conclusion and Research Program
This work has developed a fully explicit operator-theoretic framework motivated by the Hilbert–
Pólya program. The construction is grounded in a rigorously defined symmetric operator acting
on a concrete Hilbert space, with all structural assumptions stated openly and without reliance
on unproven arithmetic hypotheses.

10.1 Summary of Results

The main achievements of this work may be summarized as follows:

• A concrete Hilbert space ℓ2(N) and dense domain D were specified explicitly.
• A symmetric operator H built from prime-indexed shift operators and arithmetic diagonal

terms was defined and shown to be well-posed.

479



• Essential self-adjointness was reduced to the absence of ℓ2(N) solutions of a single, explicit
deficiency equation.

• A general spectral framework was established independently of arithmetic conjectures.
• Structural interfaces with classical explicit formulas were identified, while carefully avoiding

circular reasoning.
• Numerical experiments were presented strictly as supporting evidence, not as proofs.

10.2 Legitimacy of the Hilbert–Pólya Program

The framework presented here satisfies the minimal structural requirements of a legitimate
Hilbert–Pólya program:

• the operator is defined independently of spectral assumptions,
• symmetry is rigorously established,
• the obstruction to self-adjointness is precisely localized,
• arithmetic consequences are formulated conditionally.

No claim of having proven the Riemann Hypothesis is made. Instead, the work isolates a concrete
and falsifiable analytical problem whose resolution would determine the viability of the approach.

10.3 Future Directions

The natural continuation of this research consists of three parallel tracks:

1. Analytical resolution of the deficiency equation. Proving the absence of square-
summable solutions would establish essential self-adjointness and complete the operator-
theoretic foundation.

2. Rigorous spectral-arithmetic identities. Deriving trace or resolvent formulas linking
spectral data of H to arithmetic expressions remains a central objective.

3. Refined numerical and experimental studies. Large-scale computations may guide
conjectures, but must remain subordinate to analytical arguments.

10.4 Perspective

The approach presented here does not assume the truth of the Riemann Hypothesis, nor does it
depend on numerical verification of its zeros. Instead, it seeks to reformulate the problem as a
question of operator-theoretic uniqueness and spectral structure.
Whether this program ultimately succeeds or fails, the explicit nature of the constructions ensures
that any obstruction will be visible, concrete, and mathematically meaningful.

10.5 Closing Remark

The value of the present framework lies not in its claims, but in the clarity with which it exposes
both its strengths and its limitations. In this sense, it aims to contribute not a conclusion, but a
well-defined path forward.

Chapter 21

The SMRK Probe
Spectral Measurement Instrument for Arithmetic Hamiltonians

Enter Yourname

Abstract
The SMRK Probe is introduced as a formal spectral measurement instrument within the
Quansistor Field Computing (QFC) framework, designed to explore the spectral behavior of
arithmetic Hamiltonians constructed in the context of Quansistor Field Mathematics (QFM).
The document defines the probe as an instrumental layer, positioned between abstract operator
construction and higher-level execution models, without asserting proof-level claims or theoretical
equivalence to unresolved conjectures.
The probe operates on finite-dimensional realizations of arithmetic operators, assembled according
to explicit and reproducible construction protocols. Its purpose is to expose structural properties
of operator spectra, including stability under truncation, sensitivity to controlled perturbations,
and responses to prime-indexed dynamics. Observations produced by the probe are treated as
descriptive observables rather than inferential results.
As a normative instrument specification, this chapter delineates the conceptual scope, architectural
constraints, measurement modes, and output semantics of the SMRK Probe. It explicitly separates
instrumentation from interpretation, and measurement from proof, ensuring that exploratory
spectral analysis remains methodologically disciplined.
Within the QFC stack, the SMRK Probe functions as a pre-execution diagnostic layer. It informs
the development and validation of operator-centric models in QFM, and provides empirical
grounding prior to integration into QFP, QPU, QVM, or QWASM-level execution environments.
The probe thereby establishes a stable and reproducible reference point for systematic spectral
exploration of arithmetic operator fields.

Executive Summary
The SMRK Probe is a spectral measurement instrument designed for the systematic exploration
of arithmetic Hamiltonians of SMRK type. Its purpose is to expose structural and stability prop-
erties of operator spectra arising from prime-indexed dynamics, without asserting completeness,
convergence, or proof of any unresolved mathematical conjecture.
The probe operates within a finite-dimensional truncation of an underlying Hilbert space and
assembles the SMRK Hamiltonian as a concrete operator object, constructed from prime-shift
components and arithmetic weighting. Spectral data are extracted numerically under controlled
perturbations, enabling the observation of eigenvalue stability, drift behavior, and rigidity patterns
across varying cut-offs and parameter regimes.
Crucially, the SMRK Probe is not intended as a verification mechanism for the Riemann
Hypothesis or any equivalent spectral claim. Instead, it serves as an instrumental interface between
operator-theoretic constructions and measurable spectral behavior, analogous to experimental
probes in physics that precede theoretical consolidation.

484



Version 1.0 of the SMRK Probe specifies a stable conceptual and architectural framework. It
defines the role of the probe, its measurement modes, observable outputs, and known limitations,
while deliberately avoiding interpretive overreach. Subsequent versions may refine numerical
implementations or extend execution platforms, but the core instrumental semantics introduced
here are considered stable.
Within the broader Quansistor Field Computing (QFC) framework, the SMRK Probe constitutes
an initial measurement layer. It provides empirical grounding for operator-centric arithmetic
models and informs future developments in spectral field execution, including potential deployment
within QVM-native environments.

1 Motivation
Despite extensive numerical verification of the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function,
classical computational approaches remain fundamentally limited in their ability to expose
underlying structural mechanisms. High-precision evaluation of ζ(s) provides confidence in
observed regularities, but offers little insight into why such regularities persist, nor how they
arise from arithmetic dynamics at the operator level.
The operator-theoretic perspective, inspired by the Hilbert–Pólya program, suggests that spectral
structure should emerge from a concrete Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues encode arithmetic
information. However, the construction of such operators alone is insufficient. Without a
systematic method for probing their spectral behavior, operator proposals remain largely formal
and disconnected from measurable consequences.
The SMRK Probe is motivated by the need for an intermediate instrument between abstract
operator construction and theoretical claims. Its role is to interrogate the spectral response
of arithmetic Hamiltonians under controlled conditions, rather than to assert convergence,
completeness, or equivalence with known spectra. In this sense, the probe occupies a position
analogous to experimental apparatus in physics: it enables observation prior to interpretation.
A further motivation arises from the distinction between operator-centric and function-centric
computation. Traditional numerical studies focus on analytic functions and their sampled values,
whereas the SMRK framework operates directly on operators acting on Hilbert space. This
shift demands new tools. Spectral properties such as rigidity, stability under perturbation, and
structural symmetry cannot be reliably inferred from function evaluation alone; they must be
measured at the operator level.
Finite-dimensional truncation introduces unavoidable artifacts, yet it also creates an opportunity.
By varying cut-offs and perturbations in a controlled manner, the SMRK Probe allows researchers
to distinguish persistent structural features from numerical or boundary-induced effects. Patterns
that survive such variation provide evidence of intrinsic operator structure, independent of
implementation details.
Finally, the motivation for formalizing the SMRK Probe as a versioned instrument lies in
reproducibility and discipline. By specifying what the probe measures, how measurements are
performed, and what claims are explicitly excluded, this whitepaper establishes a shared reference
point. It enables comparative study, critical evaluation, and future extension without conflating
exploratory results with mathematical proof.

2 Concept of a Spectral Probe
In the context of operator-theoretic arithmetic models, a spectral probe is defined as a controlled
instrument for exposing qualitative and quantitative features of an operator spectrum without

485



asserting completeness, convergence, or theoretical equivalence to a target conjecture or model.
Unlike numerical simulation, which typically aims to approximate solutions of explicit equations,
a spectral probe operates on operators themselves. Its primary function is not to compute
values, but to measure structural response. This includes sensitivity to perturbations, stability of
spectral ordering, and the persistence of symmetries under variation of construction parameters.
A spectral probe is also distinct from a proof-oriented framework. Proof seeks logical necessity
under exact assumptions, whereas a probe is designed to explore behavior under controlled but
imperfect conditions. The outputs of a probe are observables rather than implications. They
inform intuition, guide refinement, and constrain future theoretical development, but they do
not, by themselves, establish mathematical truth.
Formally, a spectral probe consists of three components:

• a well-defined operator assembly procedure,
• a finite execution or truncation regime,
• and a set of measurement protocols yielding reproducible observables.

Each component is specified explicitly to ensure that observed features can be attributed to
operator structure rather than implementation artifacts.
The necessity of finite truncation is not treated as a defect but as an integral aspect of probing.
By systematically varying truncation parameters and boundary conditions, a spectral probe
distinguishes intrinsic operator behavior from finite-size effects. Structural features that persist
across such variation are interpreted as candidates for genuine spectral invariants.
Within this framework, interpretation is deliberately restrained. The role of a spectral probe is
not to confirm conjectures, but to delineate the space of plausible operator behaviors. It serves
as an interface between abstract operator design and future formal analysis, providing empirical
guidance while preserving logical separation from proof.
The SMRK Probe is an instance of this general concept, specialized to arithmetic Hamiltonians
constructed from prime-indexed dynamics. However, the notion of a spectral probe introduced
here is intentionally broader and may be applied to other operator-theoretic contexts within and
beyond the QFC framework.

3 The SMRK Hamiltonian (Context Only)

The SMRK Hamiltonian provides the operator-theoretic object explored by the spectral probe
described in this document. It is introduced here solely to the extent necessary to define the
context of probing; a full mathematical treatment, including construction details and theoretical
motivation, is presented in dedicated SMRK and QFM publications.
At a high level, the SMRK Hamiltonian is an arithmetic operator acting on a Hilbert space
of square-summable sequences indexed by the natural numbers. Its structure is governed by
prime-indexed shift operations that implement multiplicative dynamics within the state space,
together with arithmetic weighting components that modulate spectral behavior.
Prime-shift operators map basis states according to multiplication by prime numbers, subject
to domain constraints imposed by finite truncation. These operators admit natural adjoint
counterparts corresponding to inverse multiplicative action when divisibility conditions permit.
The interaction between forward and adjoint shifts forms the dynamical backbone of the SMRK
construction.
The Hamiltonian is assembled as a structured combination of these shift operators and diagonal

486



arithmetic terms. The resulting operator is generally unbounded in the infinite-dimensional
setting and is therefore examined through controlled finite-dimensional realizations. Issues of
self-adjointness, domain specification, and closure are acknowledged but not resolved within the
scope of this probe-focused document.
From the perspective of the spectral probe, the SMRK Hamiltonian is treated as a black-box
operator with a well-defined assembly protocol. The probe does not modify the Hamiltonian’s
conceptual definition; rather, it subjects specific finite realizations to measurement procedures
designed to expose spectral structure, stability, and sensitivity.
By limiting discussion of the SMRK Hamiltonian to contextual essentials, this section preserves
a clear separation between operator design and instrumental analysis. The spectral observations
reported by the SMRK Probe are therefore to be interpreted as properties of instantiated operator
realizations, not as claims about the fully idealized infinite-dimensional object.

4 Architecture of the SMRK Probe

The SMRK Probe is structured as a modular spectral instrument whose architecture separates
operator construction, execution constraints, and measurement procedures. This separation
ensures that observed spectral features can be attributed to operator structure rather than to
implementation-specific coupling between components.
The architecture is defined independently of any particular programming language or numerical
backend. It specifies conceptual stages of probing that must be preserved across implementations
to maintain semantic consistency.

4.1 Hilbert Space Truncation

The probe operates on a finite-dimensional truncation of the underlying Hilbert space of square-
summable sequences indexed by the natural numbers. A truncation parameter N defines the
maximum index retained in the basis, yielding a computational state space of dimension N .
Truncation is treated as an explicit and variable parameter of the probe. Rather than fixing
N a priori, the probe is designed to examine spectral behavior across a range of truncation
scales. This enables differentiation between boundary-induced artifacts and persistent structural
features.
Boundary handling at the truncation limit is specified deterministically. Operator actions that
would map states beyond the truncated domain are either suppressed or projected according to
a consistent rule, ensuring reproducible spectral outcomes.

4.2 Operator Assembly

Within a given truncation regime, the SMRK Hamiltonian is assembled from its constituent
components following a fixed construction protocol. Prime-indexed shift operators and their
adjoints are instantiated as sparse linear operators acting on the truncated basis.
Diagonal arithmetic terms are incorporated to modulate spectral structure and ensure proper
scaling behavior. All components are combined into a single operator object representing a finite
realization of the SMRK Hamiltonian.
The assembly procedure is deterministic and fully specified. Given identical parameters and
truncation rules, independent implementations of the probe must produce equivalent operator
representations up to numerical precision.

487



4.3 Spectral Extraction

Spectral extraction constitutes the measurement phase of the probe. The assembled operator is
subjected to numerical eigenspectrum analysis appropriate to its size and structure. The probe
does not prescribe a specific eigensolver but requires that the chosen method provide consistent
ordering and reproducibility.
Extracted eigenvalues are treated as primary observables. Eigenvectors may be retained for
auxiliary analysis but are not required for core probe operation. Spectral data are recorded
together with truncation parameters and assembly metadata to enable comparative study.
The probe explicitly avoids post-processing steps that enforce expected spectral patterns. All
observed regularities must arise from the operator realization itself rather than from normalization
or filtering procedures applied after measurement.

5 Measurement Modes
The SMRK Probe supports multiple measurement modes, each designed to expose a distinct
aspect of spectral behavior of the instantiated SMRK Hamiltonian. These modes do not
constitute separate implementations, but rather distinct measurement protocols applied to the
same underlying operator architecture.
All measurement modes share a common principle: observed features are recorded as descriptive
spectral data without interpretive enforcement. Comparative analysis across modes enables
identification of structural regularities that are robust under variation.

5.1 Static Spectral Measurement

In static mode, the probe performs eigenspectrum extraction for a fixed truncation parameter
and fixed operator assembly. The resulting ordered set of eigenvalues provides a baseline spectral
profile for the given realization.
Static measurement is used to identify coarse spectral features such as spacing distributions,
clustering tendencies, and gross symmetry. No claims of spectral convergence are made on the
basis of static measurement alone.

5.2 Truncation Scaling Mode

In truncation scaling mode, the probe evaluates the spectrum across a sequence of increasing
truncation parameters. Spectral features are tracked as functions of the truncation scale, allowing
differentiation between boundary artifacts and persistent structural behavior.
Eigenvalues that exhibit stability under truncation scaling are identified as candidates for
intrinsic spectral features of the operator, whereas unstable or emergent modes are interpreted
as truncation-dependent effects.

5.3 Perturbative Sensitivity Mode

Perturbative mode introduces controlled variations to operator parameters or assembly weights
while preserving overall structural form. The resulting spectral drift is measured relative to the
unperturbed baseline.
This mode probes spectral rigidity and sensitivity. Small perturbations that produce dispropor-
tionate spectral changes indicate fragile structure, whereas gradual and coherent drift suggests

488



robust operator organization.

5.4 Prime-Shift Response Mode

In prime-shift response mode, the probe selectively activates or modulates prime-indexed compo-
nents of the Hamiltonian. The resulting changes in spectral behavior are recorded and compared
across prime subsets.
This mode isolates the contribution of multiplicative arithmetic dynamics to the overall spectrum.
Correlated responses across different prime activations provide evidence of structured arithmetic
coupling within the operator.

5.5 Comparative Mode

Comparative mode aggregates spectral data obtained from multiple probe runs with varying
parameters or construction variants. Rather than focusing on individual eigenvalues, this mode
emphasizes relational properties such as ordering consistency, symmetry persistence, and cross-run
correlations.
Comparative analysis serves as a synthesis layer, enabling structural inference without relying on
absolute spectral identification.

6 Observables and Outputs

The outputs of the SMRK Probe are defined as observables: descriptive quantities derived from
spectral measurement that characterize structural properties of instantiated operators. Observ-
ables are explicitly non-inferential; they do not imply convergence, equivalence, or theoretical
validation.
All observables are recorded together with metadata specifying truncation parameters, assembly
configuration, and measurement mode. This ensures that comparisons across probe runs remain
meaningful and reproducible.

6.1 Eigenvalue Distributions

The primary observable produced by the probe is the ordered set of eigenvalues of the instantiated
SMRK Hamiltonian under a given measurement mode. These distributions provide coarse
information about spectral density, spacing behavior, and large-scale structure.
Statistical summaries of eigenvalue distributions may be computed for descriptive purposes, but
no universal distributional assumptions are imposed.

6.2 Stability Indicators

Stability indicators quantify the sensitivity of spectral features to changes in truncation scale
or perturbation parameters. Eigenvalues that persist within bounded variation across multiple
probe runs are flagged as stable.
Stability is treated as a relative property, evaluated across controlled variation rather than as an
absolute criterion.

489



6.3 Spectral Drift Measures

Spectral drift observables capture the displacement of eigenvalues under perturbative or structural
modification of the operator assembly. Drift is recorded as a function of perturbation magnitude,
enabling qualitative classification of spectral response.
Coherent drift across eigenvalue subsets suggests organized operator structure, whereas irregular
drift patterns indicate fragile or incidental spectral features.

6.4 Rigidity and Correlation Metrics

Rigidity metrics describe the degree to which spectral ordering and relative spacing are preserved
across measurement modes. Correlation analysis between spectra obtained under different probe
configurations provides evidence of underlying structural coupling.
These metrics are comparative in nature and are not interpreted as invariant quantities.

6.5 Anomaly Detection

The probe records spectral anomalies such as isolated eigenvalues, unexpected degeneracies, or
abrupt structural transitions. Anomalies are documented without interpretation and serve as
prompts for further investigation rather than as evidence of theoretical significance.

7 Limitations
The SMRK Probe is intentionally limited in scope. These limitations are not treated as deficiencies,
but as intrinsic constraints of an instrumental framework operating at the boundary between
abstract operator theory and numerical realization.

7.1 Finite-Dimensional Truncation

All measurements performed by the SMRK Probe rely on finite-dimensional truncations of an
underlying infinite-dimensional Hilbert space. As a result, spectral features observed at any fixed
truncation level may reflect boundary effects rather than intrinsic operator properties.
While truncation scaling modes mitigate this limitation by enabling comparative analysis across
cut-off parameters, no finite probe can fully capture the behavior of the idealized operator.

7.2 Numerical Approximation

Spectral extraction is necessarily subject to numerical approximation. Floating point precision,
solver tolerances, and implementation-specific numerical behavior may influence measured spectra.
The probe does not attempt to eliminate numerical effects entirely, but instead treats them
as part of the measurement environment. Observed features must be robust under reasonable
numerical variation to be considered structurally meaningful.

7.3 Basis and Representation Dependence

Although the SMRK Hamiltonian is defined abstractly, its realization within the probe depends
on a chosen basis and representation scheme. Certain spectral features may therefore be sensitive
to representation choices.

490



The probe addresses this limitation through consistency and reproducibility requirements rather
than basis invariance. Interpretation is restricted to features that persist under controlled
representational variation.

7.4 Absence of Proof-Level Claims

The SMRK Probe does not establish self-adjointness, spectral completeness, or equivalence with
the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. No claim of verification or falsification of the
Riemann Hypothesis is made within this document.
Results obtained through the probe are descriptive and exploratory. They may inform conjecture
refinement or motivate formal analysis, but they do not constitute mathematical proof.

7.5 Interpretive Restraint

The probe deliberately avoids interpretive enforcement. Spectral patterns, correlations, or appar-
ent regularities are recorded without assigning theoretical significance beyond their descriptive
role.
This restraint is essential to maintaining a clear boundary between instrumentation and theory,
and to preventing overextension of exploratory results.

8 Role within QFC / QFM

Within the Quansistor Field Computing (QFC) framework, the SMRK Probe occupies the role
of an instrumental measurement layer. It does not define computational semantics, execution
models, or operator governance, but instead provides a means of empirically examining operator
structures prior to their integration into higher-level systems.
At the level of Quansistor Field Mathematics (QFM), the probe supports an operator-first
methodology. QFM emphasizes explicit operator construction, adjointness relations, and spectral
structure as primary mathematical objects. The SMRK Probe complements this perspective
by enabling controlled exploration of spectral behavior arising from such constructions, without
conflating observation with proof.
The probe serves as a bridge between abstract operator design and formal theoretical development.
Spectral features revealed through probing may inform refinement of operator definitions, guide
analytical investigation, or motivate reformulation of underlying assumptions. Conversely, the
absence of expected structure provides equally valuable feedback, constraining speculative models.
In the broader QFC stack, the SMRK Probe precedes execution-oriented components such as field
schedulers, operator governance layers, and QVM-native execution environments. Its function is
diagnostic rather than operational: it characterizes operator behavior without embedding it into
a computational pipeline.
By formalizing the SMRK Probe as a versioned and conceptually stable instrument, this document
establishes a reproducible reference point within the QFC corpus. Future probes may extend
this framework to other operator classes or execution contexts, but the role defined here remains
that of measurement, not adjudication.

491



9 Conclusion
This whitepaper has specified the SMRK Probe as a spectral measurement instrument for
arithmetic Hamiltonians, formalizing its conceptual basis, architectural structure, measurement
modes, observables, and limitations. By design, the probe operates at the interface between
abstract operator construction and empirical spectral observation.
The SMRK Probe does not assert mathematical proof, convergence, or equivalence to any
established conjecture. Its contribution lies instead in providing a disciplined and reproducible
framework for probing operator behavior under controlled conditions. In doing so, it enables
the identification of structural regularities and sensitivities that may inform future theoretical
development.
By clearly separating instrumentation from interpretation, this document establishes a stable
reference point for exploratory spectral analysis within the QFC and QFM ecosystem. The
versioned definition presented here ensures that subsequent extensions, refinements, or alternative
implementations can be evaluated against a common conceptual baseline.
The SMRK Probe therefore serves not as a conclusion to an inquiry, but as a starting instrument
for systematic exploration of operator-theoretic arithmetic models.

Abstract
This whitepaper defines the normative backbone of Vol. No. IV for
Enter Yourname: a suite of eight canonical operator artifacts intended as
reusable building blocks across the QFC stack. The objective is method-
ological. Instead of introducing a new operator object, this document
fixes the conventions that make subsequent artifacts comparable, au-
ditable, and interoperable across implementations and QVM execution
environments.
The core contribution is a shared specification grammar: common termi-
nology for operator objects, a canonical notion of specification identity
(SpecID) that binds a definition to its admissible classes, objectives,
constraints, tie-break rules, functional calculus, and numerical determin-
ism model, and a minimal set of invariants that each artifact MUST
satisfy. This establishes a standard interface between QFM-level operator
constructions and QVM-level validity enforcement, where reproducibility
and contract semantics are treated as first-class requirements.
This whitepaper also standardizes certificate semantics. Each artifact
in Vol. No. IV is designed to be re-derived or verified from public
inputs without trusting the producer, so this document fixes what a
certificate is allowed to contain, what a verifier MUST check, and how
failure modes are represented deterministically. In this framing, Validity
becomes an operator-level contract and auditability becomes a property
of the specification, not of a particular implementation.
