and clarifies their intended roles: canonical spectral probing, proof-carrying penalty operators,
audit-native evolution, compact program tokens, symmetry kernels, certified intertwiners across
regimes, coarse-graining with guaranteed invariants, and Koopman-style export of nonlinear
dynamics into spectral workflows. It explicitly delineates non-claims: Vol. No. IV does not assert
physical implementation, algorithmic advantage, or resolution of open conjectures by definitional
fiat; it defines the operator-law layer that makes later results comparable and falsifiable.

1 Scope, Intent, and What We Are Building

1.1 Why EY22 Exists

QFC treats operators as primary objects. In this viewpoint, a Hamiltonian H is not merely a
generator of time evolution; it is a definitional core from which meaning is extracted through



spectral action, constraints, and compositional operator laws. Yet in most workflows, the step
from “operator” to “interpretation” is performed by informal choices:

• a spectral probe f(H) is selected by taste,
• a validity rule is encoded procedurally rather than as an operator,
• distributed evaluation introduces hidden nondeterminism,
• comparisons across implementations degrade into incompatible conventions.

EY22 exists to eliminate this failure mode. It defines the shared normative conventions for
Vol. No. IV: a suite of canonical operator artifacts designed to be re-derivable, auditable, and
interoperable across QFC contexts.

1.2 What “Canonical” Means Here

In this volume, canonical does not mean “unique by theorem” and it does not mean “physically
privileged.” It means:

• the object is determined by a published specification, not by an informal choice,
• independent parties can reproduce the same artifact (or the same canonical equivalence

class),
• ambiguity is represented explicitly via tie-break rules or equivalence conventions.

Canonicality is therefore a property of the specification, not a property of the author.

1.3 The Deliverable of Vol. No. IV

Vol. No. IV is delivered as eight operator artifacts, each defined in a separate whitepaper. Each
artifact is required to ship with:

1. a normative definition (what the operator is),
2. a SpecID (a tuple binding the definition to admissible classes, objectives, constraints,

calculus, and numeric model),
3. a list of required invariants (properties that MUST hold),
4. a certificate format and verification semantics,
5. a deterministic protocol for evaluation and verification (including truncation and

aggregation rules).
EY22 provides the shared contract for these elements and acts as the registry of the suite.

1.4 The Eight Operator Artifacts

The operator suite consists of the following artifacts:

1. EY23 — Canonical Spectral Filter F⋆(H): an optimization-defined spectral filter
derived from a Hamiltonian H, not chosen ad hoc.

2. EY24 — Validity Penalty Operator V = C†C: a constructive validity object for
proof-carrying trajectories and enforceable constraints.

495



3. EY25 — Field Liouvillian Laudit: an audit-native dissipative evolution operator (dissi-
pation only into allowed subspaces).

4. EY26 — Floquet Program Operator UF : a compact program token defined by periodic
evolution with an auditable spectrum.

5. EY27 — Commutant Generator Set {Gi}: the symmetry kernel of a field: generators
commuting with a declared operator core.

6. EY28 — Intertwiner T1→2: a certified morphism between spectral regimes or layers,
preserving declared invariants.

7. EY29 — Coarse-Grain Operator R: a bucketing / aggregation operator with guaranteed
invariants under truncation and reduction.

8. EY30 — Koopman Field Operator K: a bridge from nonlinear dynamics to spectral
objects via a linear operator on observables.

1.5 Roles Within the QFC Stack

The suite is designed to cover the minimal operator-law layer needed for QFC-style work:

• Spectral probing and standardization (EY23, EY29): extraction and bucketing of
spectral meaning is made explicit and comparable.

• Validity as an operator object (EY24, EY25): constraints become constructive penalties
and audit-native evolution, not procedural checks.

• Programmability as evolution (EY26): programs are represented as auditable tokens
defined by controlled time dependence.

• Symmetry and regime mapping (EY27, EY28): invariants and bridges between layers
are explicit certified objects.

• Export of nonlinear dynamics to spectrum (EY30): nonlinearity is pulled into linear
spectral workflows via operator action on observables.

1.6 Non-Goals and Non-Claims

Vol. No. IV is methodological. It MUST NOT be interpreted as:
• a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis or any open conjecture by definitional fiat,
• a claim of quantum advantage or complexity separation,
• a hardware prescription for fabrication or implementation of a physical device,
• a replacement of established quantum field theory (“field” here is the QFC operator-

ecosystem sense).

1.7 How to Read This Volume

The recommended reading order minimizes forward references:
EY22 → EY23 → EY24 → EY25 → EY29 → EY26 → EY27 → EY28 → EY30.

EY22 fixes conventions; EY23 establishes canonicalization; EY24–EY25 define validity mech-
anisms; EY29 formalizes bucketing; EY26 introduces program tokens; EY27–EY28 handle
invariants and bridges; EY30 exports nonlinear dynamics.

496



1.8 What Comes Next in EY22

The remaining chapters of EY22 will specify:
• the normative language and threat model shared across the suite,
• the SpecID tuple and versioning rules,
• the determinism and numeric model (precision, rounding, tolerance, truncation),
• certificate formats and verification semantics,
• interoperability and composition rules between artifacts.

2 Normative Language, Core Objects, and Threat Model

2.1 Normative Keywords

This volume uses a strict normative vocabulary. The following keywords are binding:

• MUST / MUST NOT: absolute requirements.
• SHOULD / SHOULD NOT: strong recommendations; deviations require explicit

justification in the SpecID.
• MAY: optional behavior that must still be deterministic if exercised.

If a statement can affect reproducibility, auditability, or comparability across implementations, it
MUST be expressed using these keywords. Vague language (e.g. “typically”, “generally”) is not
sufficient for artifact definitions.

2.2 Core Object Model

Vol. No. IV treats every artifact as a specifiable operator object. The minimal shared model is:

Spaces

• H: a complex Hilbert space (often separable).
• B(H): bounded operators on H.
• Obs: a declared observable space when Koopman-style constructions are used (EY30).

Operator Core

• H: a (typically self-adjoint) operator on H, serving as a declared “core” operator.
• σ(H): spectrum of H.
• EH(·): spectral projection-valued measure when functional calculus is invoked.

Functional Calculus (Declared)

If an artifact uses f(H), it MUST declare which calculus is used (e.g. Borel functional calculus
for bounded f , holomorphic calculus, rational approximation protocol, etc.). The calculus choice
is part of the SpecID.

497



Artifacts

Each artifact is one of the following types:
• Operator filter: F (H) = f(H) (EY23).
• Penalty operator: V = C†C (EY24).
• Superoperator / generator: L acting on states or observables (EY25, EY30).
• Unitary token: UF (EY26).
• Symmetry kernel: generators {Gi} with [Gi, H] = 0 or analogous relations (EY27).
• Morphism / bridge: T1→2 satisfying intertwining relations (EY28).
• Coarse-graining: R mapping detailed objects to reduced/bucketed objects with invariants

(EY29).

2.3 The SpecID Principle (Preview)

In Vol. No. IV, an artifact is never referenced only by its symbol. It MUST be referenced by a
SpecID, a public tuple that binds meaning to the symbol.
Informally:

Symbol + SpecID = Unambiguous object.

The full SpecID schema is defined in Chapter 3. Here we only state the rule:

Rule (No-floating symbols). Any claim about F⋆(H), V , Laudit, UF , {Gi}, T1→2, R, or K
MUST be interpreted as a claim about that symbol under a declared SpecID.

2.4 Determinism Is a First-Class Constraint

QFC-style operator work becomes fragile when determinism is left implicit. Therefore:

• Any evaluation procedure MUST be deterministic under a declared numerical model.
• Any approximation MUST specify precision, rounding, and tolerance conventions.
• Any tie-breaking rule MUST be explicit and deterministic.
• Any optional randomness MUST be prohibited unless deterministically seeded from declared

public inputs.

The full determinism model is fixed in Chapter 4. Here we state the motivation:

Motivation. In Vol. No. IV, auditability is not a social promise. It is a property of the artifact
definition. If two parties cannot reproduce the same artifact from the same public inputs, the
artifact is not canonical.

2.5 Threat Model (What We Protect Against)

Each artifact is intended to survive adversarial and non-adversarial failure modes that commonly
appear in distributed, numeric, and multi-implementation contexts.

498



Threat Class T1: Parameter Smuggling

A producer can hide degrees of freedom in “minor” choices (filters, smoothing, truncation) and
tune them to fit expected outcomes.

Mitigation. Artifacts in this suite MUST move such degrees of freedom into SpecID-defined
admissible sets, objectives, constraints, and tie-break rules. If it is tunable, it must be declared.

Threat Class T2: Nondeterministic Replay

Two implementations compute “the same” artifact but differ due to numeric instability, ordering
dependence, or implicit randomness.

Mitigation. Artifacts MUST define a determinism model (precision, rounding, tolerance,
aggregation order) and provide certificates that can be verified deterministically.

Threat Class T3: Truncation Drift

Finite-dimensional truncations HN are used in practice. Without a declared truncation model,
results are incomparable and can be manipulated by choosing N .

Mitigation. Any artifact that depends on truncation MUST declare:
• how truncations are formed,
• which invariants must be preserved across N ,
• and how cross-N comparisons are performed (or forbidden).

Threat Class T4: Certificate Forgery or Ambiguity

A producer claims an artifact is canonical but provides no verifiable witness, or a witness that is
ambiguous.

Mitigation. Each artifact MUST define a certificate format and a verification procedure that
either accepts or rejects. Certificates MUST commit to all SpecID components relevant to
meaning.

Threat Class T5: Definition Drift Across Versions

A symbol is reused across revisions; the meaning changes but the name does not.

Mitigation. SpecID MUST include version identifiers (or hash commitments) to all normative
components. A change in meaning MUST imply a change in SpecID.

2.6 Non-Claims Boundary (Methodological Only)

The threat model is not a license to claim more than is defined.

• Canonical definitions do not imply physical realizability.

499



• Auditability does not imply scientific truth; it implies reproducible evaluation.
• Stability guarantees are only meaningful relative to declared perturbation classes.

2.7 Chapter Summary

This chapter fixed the normative language and the minimal shared object model for Vol. No.
IV. It also defined the threat classes that the suite is designed to address: parameter smuggling,
nondeterministic replay, truncation drift, certificate ambiguity, and definition drift.
Chapter 3 now formalizes the SpecID tuple and versioning rules that bind all subsequent
whitepapers to a common, auditable specification grammar.

3 Specification Identity: SpecID Tuples and Versioning

3.1 Why SpecID Exists

In Vol. No. IV, a symbol is not a definition. Symbols drift, implementations diverge, and “same
object” can silently become “similar object”. This volume therefore adopts a hard rule:

No artifact is valid unless it can be referenced unambiguously.

The mechanism is SpecID: a public tuple that binds an artifact symbol to the full set of
normative choices that determine its meaning.

3.2 Normative Rule: No Floating Artifacts

Rule (Binding). Any occurrence of an artifact symbol in Vol. No. IV MUST be interpreted
as:

Artifact Symbol + SpecID + Version ⇒ Unambiguous object.

If SpecID is missing, the reference MUST be treated as incomplete.

3.3 SpecID: The Canonical Tuple

Definition 3.1 (SpecID Tuple). A SpecID is a public tuple that uniquely identifies the
normative definition of an artifact.
All artifacts in Vol. No. IV MUST define a SpecID of the following canonical shape:

SpecID := (ArtifactType, Core, Calc, A, J , C, TieBreak, NumericModel, Cert, Interop, Version).

Each component is normative. If a component is not applicable for a given artifact type, it
MUST still be present and MUST take a declared null value (e.g. ∅ with explicit semantics).

3.4 SpecID Components (Normative Meanings)

This section fixes the meaning of each SpecID component.

500



ArtifactType

A required enumerated tag identifying the artifact class:

ArtifactType ∈ {CSF,VPO,LIOUV,FLOQ,COMM, INTW,CGR,KOOP}.

Where:
• CSF: Canonical Spectral Filter (EY23)
• VPO: Validity Penalty Operator (EY24)
• LIOUV: Field Liouvillian (EY25)
• FLOQ: Floquet Program Operator (EY26)
• COMM: Commutant Generator Set (EY27)
• INTW: Intertwiner (EY28)
• CGR: Coarse-Grain Operator (EY29)
• KOOP: Koopman Field Operator (EY30)

Core

The declared core object(s) the artifact is built from. Typical examples:
• Core = (H) for filter and commutant constructions,
• Core = (H,C) for validity penalty operators,
• Core = (H(t), T ) for Floquet objects,
• Core = (F,Obs) for Koopman objects.

Rule. If H is used, its self-adjointness / domain assumptions MUST be declared in the artifact
definition.

Calc

The declared evaluation calculus. Examples:
• Borel functional calculus (bounded f) for f(H),
• holomorphic/rational calculus for resolvent-like objects,
• explicit truncation protocol defining HN and f(HN ),
• superoperator calculus (action on density operators or observables).

Rule. Any two implementations claiming the same SpecID MUST use the same Calc semantics.

A (Admissible Family)

The admissible family of candidates over which the artifact is selected or constructed. For
different artifacts:

501



• EY23: admissible filter functions f ,
• EY24: admissible constraint operators C,
• EY25: admissible dissipators / Lindblad terms (or QFC-defined equivalents),
• EY27: admissible generator search space,
• EY29: admissible coarse-graining maps.

Rule. A MUST have a canonical representation form (see Appendix ?? in EY22, once filled).

J (Objective / Selection Functional)

The objective that canonically selects among admissible candidates.

Rule. If J ̸= ∅, it MUST be deterministically evaluable under the NumericModel.

C (Constraints)

The constraint predicates required for feasibility (boundedness, positivity, stability, implementabil-
ity, etc.).

Rule. Constraints MUST be explicit. “Reasonable constraints” MUST NOT be used.

TieBreak

A deterministic tie-breaking rule used when multiple candidates satisfy the same optimal score
or satisfy a canonical equivalence. Typical tie-breaks:

• lexicographic minimal canonical representation,
• minimal parameter norm,
• maximal smoothness subject to constraints,
• minimal operator norm among optimizers.

Rule. If tie-breaking is required, it MUST yield a unique canonical output given the same
public inputs.

NumericModel

The numeric determinism model: precision, rounding, tolerance rules, truncation scales, and
aggregation order.

Rule. NumericModel MUST be explicit whenever the artifact is evaluated approximately
(which is the default in practice). NumericModel is specified normatively in Chapter 4.

Cert

Certificate semantics: what must be published so that a verifier can accept the artifact.

502



Rule. Cert MUST include a verification procedure that deterministically accepts or rejects.

Interop

Interoperability constraints: how the artifact composes with others (e.g. R ◦ F⋆(H) allowed, or
T1→2 must preserve a declared invariant set).

Rule. If an artifact claims compatibility with another, the compatibility condition MUST be
stated in Interop and MUST be testable.

Version

A version identifier binding the entire SpecID to a stable reference.

Rule. Any change in meaning MUST change Version. Version MAY be a semantic version
string, but SHOULD be a cryptographic commitment when published in adversarial settings.

3.5 Canonical Naming and Referencing

To prevent ambiguity, this volume uses the following reference form:

Reference Form.

<ArtifactSymbol> @ <SpecID-Short> :: <Version>

SpecID-Short. For human readability, a short form MAY be used in text, provided it expands
to the full SpecID in the certificate. A recommended short form is:

SpecID_Short := (ArtifactType,CalcID,AID, JID,CID,NID,VID)

where each ∗ID is a stable label that resolves to a full canonical description.

3.6 Spec Drift and the “Same Symbol” Problem

Rule (Symbol reuse). A symbol MAY be reused across versions, but MUST NOT be assumed
to mean the same object without matching SpecID and Version. Therefore, any published artifact
MUST include SpecID and Version in:

• captions and figure annotations that rely on the artifact,
• experiment metadata,
• certificate headers,
• and machine-readable index entries.

3.7 Minimal SpecID for Each Artifact Type

This section provides minimal requirements by type. These are lower bounds.

• CSF (EY23) MUST specify: H, Calc, A, J , C, TieBreak, NumericModel, Cert, Version.

503



• VPO (EY24) MUST specify: C admissible family, V = C†C construction, constraints on
C, certificate of feasibility and canonical selection (if selection exists), NumericModel.

• LIOUV (EY25) MUST specify: the state space, generator form, allowed dissipators,
contract constraints, certificate and determinism.

• FLOQ (EY26) MUST specify: time-dependence model H(t), period T , time-ordering
convention, discretization protocol, certificate.

• COMM (EY27) MUST specify: commutation target(s), generator admissible class,
discovery/selection rule, certificate.

• INTW (EY28) MUST specify: source/target cores, intertwining relation, invariant
preservation, certificate.

• CGR (EY29) MUST specify: reduction target, invariants preserved, truncation interface,
certificate.

• KOOP (EY30) MUST specify: dynamical system F , observable space, operator action,
approximation protocol, certificate.

3.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter introduced SpecID as the unambiguous identifier of meaning for every artifact
in Vol. No. IV. It fixed a canonical tuple form and defined the normative semantics of each
component.
Chapter 4 now specifies the NumericModel: determinism rules for precision, rounding, tolerance,
truncation, and aggregation. This is where “canonical” becomes executable.

4 Determinism Model: Precision, Rounding, Tolerance, Trunca-
tion

4.1 Why a NumericModel Is Mandatory

Operator artifacts in Vol. No. IV are defined abstractly, but they are evaluated in practice by
truncation, approximation, and distributed aggregation. Without an explicit numeric model,
“the same artifact” becomes implementation-dependent. Therefore:

In Vol. No. IV, determinism is part of the definition.

Any artifact that can be evaluated approximately MUST bind itself to an explicit NumericModel
as part of its SpecID.

4.2 Normative Rule: Determinism Over Convenience

Rule. If a procedure has multiple implementation-equivalent choices (order of summation,
floating-point vs fixed-point, parallel reduction order, random sampling), then Vol. No. IV
requires:

• either a single canonical choice is specified,
• or the procedure MUST be reformulated to produce a deterministic result (e.g. sorting +

deterministic reduction),

504



• or the result MUST be rejected as non-canonical.

4.3 NumericModel Schema

Definition 4.1 (NumericModel Tuple). A NumericModel is a public tuple:

NumericModel := (NumberSystem, Precision, Rounding, Tolerance, Aggregation, Truncation, FailureModes).

All components are normative. If a component is irrelevant for a specific artifact, it MUST be
present and MUST be set to a declared null value with explicit semantics.

4.4 Number System and Precision

NumberSystem

The number system determines the determinism envelope.

Allowed (recommended).
• Fixed-point integers with declared scaling.
• Rational arithmetic with canonical normalization (exact but potentially expensive).
• IEEE floating point only if the remaining NumericModel components remove nondeter-

minism (see below).

Rule. If IEEE floating point is used, the NumericModel MUST additionally specify:
• the exact floating format (binary32, binary64, etc.),
• whether fused multiply-add is allowed,
• whether denormals are flushed to zero,
• and whether math-library functions are replaced by canonical approximations.

Precision

Precision MUST specify either:
• exactness (rational / integer scaling), or
• bit precision (e.g. 53-bit mantissa, or an explicit fixed-point scale), or
• decimal precision (only if conversion is canonical and deterministic).

Rule. Precision MUST be sufficient to make the tie-break and certificate verification determin-
istic. If precision is insufficient, the output MUST be rejected (not “accepted with warnings”).

4.5 Rounding

Rounding

Rounding MUST be specified as a global policy:

505



• round-to-nearest-even,
• round-toward-zero,
• floor/ceil,
• or exact reduction (no rounding).

Rule (Canonical rounding). Any conversion between representations (e.g. real → fixed-
point, or float → integer) MUST specify rounding and MUST be applied identically in all
implementations.

4.6 Tolerance Conventions

Tolerance

Tolerance is the contract used when equality cannot be exact.

Rule (Tolerance is part of meaning). Any acceptance criterion that depends on a tolerance
MUST include that tolerance in NumericModel. Two artifacts with different tolerances are
different artifacts.

Canonical tolerance form. Tolerance MUST be expressed as a tuple:

Tolerance := (εabs, εrel, εop, εspec),

where:
• εabs: absolute scalar tolerance,
• εrel: relative scalar tolerance,
• εop: operator-norm tolerance (or declared proxy),
• εspec: spectral tolerance (e.g. eigenvalue bin width).

Rule. At least one of εop or εspec MUST be specified for spectral artifacts, unless the artifact
is exact by construction.

4.7 Aggregation and Ordering

Aggregation

Distributed evaluation is a primary use-case for QFC-style work. Aggregation MUST therefore
be deterministic.

Canonical aggregation policy. If a procedure aggregates partial results {xi}, it MUST
specify:

• a canonical ordering key (e.g. lexicographic by shard ID, then by local index),
• a deterministic reduction operator,
• and a stable reduction strategy (e.g. pairwise reduction over a fixed binary tree).

506



Rule (No nondeterministic reductions). Parallel reductions that depend on runtime
scheduling MUST NOT be used unless the reduction order is fixed and provably equivalent under
the declared tolerance.

4.8 Truncation Model

Truncation

Most operator artifacts are evaluated via finite approximations. The truncation model MUST
define:

• how H is truncated to HN ,
• how auxiliary objects are truncated (e.g. C, L, observable bases),
• and which invariants must hold across N .

Canonical truncation tuple.

Truncation := (Basis, CutRule, BoundaryRule, ScaleSchedule, CrossNPolicy).

• Basis: declared basis / representation in which truncation is performed.
• CutRule: how indices are retained (e.g. first N , energy cutoff, weighted cutoff).
• BoundaryRule: how boundary terms are handled (Dirichlet/Neumann-like, padding, finite-

rank correction).
• ScaleSchedule: which N values are permitted or required.
• CrossNPolicy: rules for comparing results across different N (allowed / forbidden / must-

rescale).

Rule (Truncation drift is not “noise”). Differences due to truncation are meaningful unless
a CrossNPolicy explicitly defines them as negligible under declared tolerances.

4.9 Failure Modes

FailureModes

Every artifact MUST define deterministic failure behavior. A failure mode is a named outcome
that is returned instead of a numeric artifact when a rule is violated.

Required failure outcomes. At minimum, each artifact MUST support:
• FAIL_NONCONVERGENCE: numeric procedure fails to converge under the ScaleSched-

ule.
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM: repeated evaluation violates determinism checks.
• FAIL_CERT_INVALID: certificate verification fails.
• FAIL_OUT_OF_TOL: invariants violated beyond declared tolerance.

507



Rule (No silent fallback). Implementations MUST NOT silently change precision, tolerances,
truncation rules, or aggregation order to “make it work”. Any such change MUST change
NumericModel (hence SpecID) or trigger a failure mode.

4.10 Deterministic Tie-Break Under Approximation

Many artifacts rely on optimization or selection. Under approximate evaluation, ties may occur
due to tolerance.

Rule. If an objective produces candidate scores within tolerance, the TieBreak rule MUST
apply to canonical representations, not to approximate numeric values, unless a tolerance-aware
tie-break is explicitly specified.

4.11 Minimal NumericModel Profiles (Recommended)

For practical deployments, we recommend three standard profiles:

• NM-Exact: rational / fixed-point exact arithmetic, deterministic aggregation, explicit
truncation schedule.

• NM-Stable64: IEEE binary64 with fixed rounding, canonical reduction order, library-free
approximations for transcendentals.

• NM-Verified: NM-Stable64 plus interval bounds for certificate verification (accept only if
intervals prove invariants).

Artifacts MAY reference these profiles by ID, provided the full tuple is published in the certificate.

4.12 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the NumericModel as a mandatory component of SpecID. It fixed a canonical
schema for number systems, precision, rounding, tolerance, deterministic aggregation, truncation
models, and failure modes.
Chapter 5 now specifies certificate formats and verification semantics: what must be published,
what a verifier must check, and how artifacts are rejected deterministically.

5 Certificates: Format, Verification, Failure Modes

5.1 Why Certificates Exist

Vol. No. IV is designed for adversarial and multi-implementation settings. A canonical artifact
is not “whatever the author produced”; it is what any verifier can independently confirm from
public inputs.
Therefore, every artifact in EY23–EY30 MUST define a certificate and a verification proce-
dure. The certificate is the portable witness that binds:

• the artifact output,
• the SpecID that defines its meaning,
• and the deterministic protocol that makes it reproducible.

508



5.2 Normative Rule: No Certificate, No Canonical Status

Rule. An artifact instance MUST NOT be accepted as canonical unless:
1. a certificate is provided, and
2. the certificate verification procedure deterministically accepts under the declared Numeric-

Model.

5.3 Certificate Schema

Definition 5.1 (Certificate Object). A certificate is a structured artifact π with the following
canonical sections:
π := (Header, SpecID, Inputs, Protocol, Outputs, Checks, Commitments, Signatures, Metadata).
All sections MUST be present. Sections MAY be empty only if explicitly declared as null and
the semantics of null are defined.

5.4 Certificate Sections (Normative Semantics)

Header

The header MUST include:
• artifact symbol and ArtifactType,
• SpecID short form,
• Version identifier,
• creation timestamp (informational only; MUST NOT affect verification),
• producer identifier (informational; MUST NOT affect verification).

SpecID

The full SpecID tuple (Chapter 3) MUST be embedded in the certificate, not merely referenced.

Rule. A certificate that references SpecID externally (e.g. via a URL) MUST still include a
cryptographic commitment (hash) to the referenced content.

Inputs

Inputs are the public data required to re-derive the artifact. This includes:
• operator core definition(s) (e.g. H, C, H(t), the dynamical map F ),
• any admissible-class parameters A,
• objective weights J ,
• constraints C,
• tie-break parameters,
• NumericModel parameters,
• truncation schedule (if applicable).

509



Rule (No hidden inputs). If any information is required for reproduction and is not present
in Inputs or committed in Commitments, the certificate MUST be rejected.

Protocol

The protocol section MUST describe the deterministic procedure used to produce the artifact
instance. It MUST be specific enough that an independent implementation can re-run it under
the NumericModel.

Required content.
• the ordered list of steps,
• explicit aggregation and ordering rules,
• truncation procedure H 7→ HN ,
• stop conditions and failure triggers.

Outputs

The output section MUST contain the artifact instance in canonical representation. Examples:
• EY23: the canonical filter representation f⋆ (parameters / normal form) and optional

derived invariants,
• EY24: the operator C in canonical form (or its minimal description) and the resulting
V = C†C,

• EY26: a canonical representation of UF (e.g. time-slicing parameters + hash commitment
to evolution steps),

• EY27: the generator set {Gi} in a canonical ordering,
• EY29: the coarse-grain map R as an explicit matrix / rule set / basis mapping.

Rule. Numeric outputs MUST be normalized and serialized in a canonical encoding so that
equality checks are deterministic.

Checks

The checks section MUST enumerate what the verifier must test. Checks MUST be split into:
• Structural checks: well-formedness, canonical encoding, SpecID consistency.
• Constraint checks: C validity under the declared NumericModel.
• Optimality / canonicality checks: verification that the output is the canonical selection

(or an allowed canonical equivalence class) under J and TieBreak.
• Invariant checks: artifact-specific invariants claimed by the whitepaper.

Commitments

Commitments bind external or large objects without embedding them fully.

510



Required commitments.
• hash of any large input objects not embedded (e.g. large matrices, datasets),
• hash of reference implementations (optional but recommended),
• hash of the canonicalization objective definition text if not embedded in full.

Rule. Commitments MUST specify:
• hash algorithm,
• canonical byte encoding used prior to hashing.

Signatures

Signatures are optional. They MAY be included for provenance, but MUST NOT be required
for validity. Verification MUST be possible without trusting identities.

Metadata

Metadata MAY include:
• runtime logs,
• performance counters,
• environment descriptors.

Metadata MUST NOT affect acceptance; it is informational only.

5.5 Verification Semantics

Verifier Contract

A verifier takes (π) and deterministically returns one of:

{ACCEPT, REJECT} ∪ {FAIL_∗}.

Rule (Deterministic). Given the same certificate and the same NumericModel, the verifier
MUST return the same outcome.

Minimal Verification Algorithm

A compliant verifier MUST perform the following steps in order:

1. Parse & canonicalize: decode the certificate and confirm canonical encoding.
2. SpecID bind: confirm that SpecID is complete and internally consistent.
3. Input completeness: confirm no hidden inputs exist (or that missing objects are com-

mitted by hash).
4. Protocol feasibility: confirm protocol steps are well-defined under NumericModel.
5. Constraint checks: verify C deterministically.

511



6. Canonicality checks: verify optimality or tie-break selection as required.
7. Invariant checks: verify claimed invariants within declared tolerances.
8. Return outcome: ACCEPT or a deterministic failure/rejection code.

5.6 Failure Codes (Normative)

Certificates MUST use named failure codes. At minimum, the following codes are REQUIRED:

• REJECT_MALFORMED: certificate not parseable or violates canonical encoding.
• REJECT_SPECID_MISSING: SpecID incomplete or absent.
• REJECT_SPECID_MISMATCH: SpecID conflicts with embedded outputs or proto-

col.
• REJECT_HIDDEN_INPUT: reproduction requires uncommitted information.
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM: deterministic replay check fails under NumericModel.
• FAIL_NONCONVERGENCE: convergence criteria not met under declared truncation

schedule.
• FAIL_CONSTRAINT: constraints C violated.
• FAIL_CANONICALITY: output is not the canonical selection (objective/tie-break

violation).
• FAIL_INVARIANT: claimed invariants violated beyond tolerance.
• FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH: a committed external object does not match its hash.

Rule (No silent downgrade). A verifier MUST NOT accept an artifact by silently weakening
constraints, increasing tolerances, or switching NumericModel profiles. Any such change would
require a different SpecID and therefore a different certificate.

5.7 Certificate Minimalism vs Completeness

Certificates SHOULD be minimal but MUST be complete. This creates a design tension.

Normative guidance.
• Use Commitments for large objects; embed only the canonical hashes and canonical encoding

specs.
• Ensure Outputs are in a stable canonical representation (parameters, normal forms).
• Ensure Checks are explicit and short, but sufficient to force deterministic acceptance/rejection.

5.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the certificate as the audit object that binds artifact meaning to SpecID and
to a deterministic protocol. It fixed a canonical certificate schema, a minimal verifier algorithm,
and a set of required failure codes.
Chapter 6 next defines interoperability: how artifacts compose, what compatibility means, and
how a compatibility matrix is represented and verified.

512



6 Interoperability: Composition Rules and Compatibility Matrix

6.1 Why Interoperability Is a First-Class Topic

Vol. No. IV is not a collection of isolated definitions. The eight artifacts are intended to compose
into workflows: spectral probing, validity enforcement, bucketing, program tokens, regime bridges,
and Koopman export. If composition rules are left implicit, then the suite reintroduces the
ambiguity it was designed to remove.
Accordingly, interoperability is treated as a normative contract specifying:

• which compositions are permitted,
• which invariants MUST be preserved,
• how compatibility is certified and verified,
• and what failures are returned deterministically.

6.2 Interop Component in SpecID

Every artifact in EY23–EY30 MUST include an Interop component in its SpecID:

SpecID := (· · · , Interop, Version).

Interop is the formal statement of: (i) how the artifact composes with others, and (ii) which
compatibility predicates and invariants govern that composition.

Rule. If an artifact claims compatibility with another artifact, the compatibility condition
MUST be included in Interop, and MUST be checkable under the declared NumericModel.

6.3 Primitive Composition Forms

This section defines the primitive composition forms used throughout Vol. No. IV. Any higher-
level workflow MUST be reducible to these primitives (or declare additional primitives explicitly).

C1: Functional Composition

If an artifact produces an operator A ∈ B(H) and another consumes an operator, then the
composition MAY be operator multiplication or evaluation of a function of an operator:

AB, BA, f(A), f(A)B, Bf(A),

provided domains are compatible and the functional calculus is declared.

C2: Transport by a Morphism (Pushforward / Pullback)

If T1→2 is an intertwiner (EY28), then objects MAY be transported between regimes:

A2 := T1→2A1 T
−1
1→2 or A2 := T1→2A1 T

†
1→2,

depending on declared semantics (unitary / isometric / generalized mapping). The chosen
transport law MUST be part of Interop.

513



C3: Coarse-Grain Reduction

If R is a coarse-grain operator (EY29), then detailed objects MAY be reduced:

Ã := R(A),

where R MUST preserve the invariants explicitly declared as preserved (e.g. spectral classes,
positivity, trace, validity class), within the tolerances of the NumericModel.

C4: Superoperator Action

If L is a superoperator (EY25, EY30), it acts on states or observables:

ρ 7→ L(ρ), g 7→ K(g).

Composition is function composition at the superoperator level.

C5: Token Execution / Concatenation

If UF is a Floquet program token (EY26), it MAY compose by multiplication (time concatenation)
only if the same time-ordering and discretization semantics are used:

UF,2 UF,1.

Compatibility of periods, slicing, and ordering MUST be specified in Interop (or the composition
MUST fail).

6.4 Compatibility: What It Means

Definition 6.1 (Compatibility Predicate). A compatibility predicate is a boolean condition of
the form

Compat(A,B) ∈ {TRUE,FALSE},
where A,B are artifact instances (each with SpecID). A valid Compat predicate MUST be:

• deterministic under the declared NumericModel(s),
• explicit in terms of checkable invariants and protocol steps,
• stable under declared truncation policies (when truncation applies).

Rule (Compatibility is asymmetric by default). Unless explicitly stated, Compat(A,B) ̸=
Compat(B,A). The compatibility direction MUST be declared.

6.5 Required Interop Invariants

Interoperability is defined by preservation of invariants. Each artifact MAY define additional
invariants, but Vol. No. IV standardizes a minimal invariant vocabulary.

I1: Domain Compatibility

If A and B are composed, their domains MUST be compatible under the declared truncation
and calculus. If a domain mismatch occurs, the composition MUST fail deterministically.

514



I2: SpecID Consistency

If artifacts are composed in a workflow, their SpecIDs MUST not conflict on shared primitives.
In particular:

• if both use a NumericModel, either it MUST match or a declared coercion rule MUST
exist;

• if both use functional calculus, calculus choices MUST be compatible or explicitly bridged.

I3: Deterministic Replay

A composed workflow MUST produce the same result across verifiers given the same public
inputs. This includes deterministic aggregation order and deterministic tie-break behavior.

I4: Invariant Preservation Under Reduction

If R is applied (EY29), invariants marked as preserved MUST hold after reduction within
tolerance:

Inv(A) ⇒ Inv(R(A)),
as declared in the Interop component.

I5: Validity Propagation

If validity is enforced by V = C†C (EY24) or Laudit (EY25), then workflows MUST define how
validity propagates:

• whether filtering preserves validity,
• whether coarse-grain preserves or weakens validity,
• whether an intertwiner preserves validity constraints across regimes.

6.6 Compatibility Matrix

To make interoperability machine-readable and auditable, this volume standardizes a compatibility
matrix format.
Definition 6.2 (Compatibility Matrix). A compatibility matrix M is an 8× 8 matrix indexed
by artifacts (EY23, . . . ,EY30) such that each entry is one of:

• OK: composition is permitted under declared invariants and check procedures;
• OK∗: composition is permitted only under additional constraints (explicitly listed);
• NO: composition is forbidden (incompatible by design);
• N/A: composition is not defined / not meaningful for this pair.

For any entry marked OK or OK∗, the interoperability contract MUST reference:
• a compatibility predicate identifier,
• the required invariant list,
• and the verification routine (or certificate check ID).

515



Rule (No informal OK). A matrix entry MUST NOT be declared OK or OK∗ unless a verifier
can deterministically evaluate the referenced compatibility predicate under NumericModel.

6.7 Default Interop Policy (Vol. No. IV Baseline)

The following baseline policy is adopted unless overridden by an artifact:

• EY23 F⋆(H) MAY be applied before or after EY24 V only if domain and calculus match.
• EY29 R MAY be applied to outputs of EY23/EY24/EY25 only if invariant preservation

is certified.
• EY28 T1→2 MAY transport EY23/EY24/EY27 objects only if invariants are preserved

under the declared mapping law.
• EY26 UF MAY be used to generate inputs to EY23/EY27 only if time-slicing semantics

are compatible and declared.
• EY30 K MAY export workflows into observable-space only if correspondence of invariants

is declared.

This baseline is intentionally conservative. Artifacts may expand compatibility only by providing
explicit predicates and certificates.

6.8 Interop Certificates

Whenever a workflow depends on compatibility, it SHOULD produce an Interop Certificate.
Definition 6.3 (Interop Certificate). An interoperability certificate is a certificate πinterop that
attests:

1. the SpecIDs of all artifacts in the workflow,
2. the declared composition form(s) (C1–C5),
3. the compatibility predicates evaluated and their outcomes,
4. the invariants checked and their tolerances,
5. the deterministic aggregation and truncation schedule used for the workflow.

Rule. If a workflow outcome is published as an artifact-derived claim, an interop certificate
MUST be provided if the claim depends on cross-artifact composition.

6.9 Failure Modes for Interop

Interop verification MUST use deterministic failure codes, at minimum:
• FAIL_DOMAIN_MISMATCH: domains not compatible for composition.
• FAIL_CALC_MISMATCH: functional calculus semantics incompatible.
• FAIL_NUMERICMODEL_MISMATCH: numeric models conflict without declared

coercion.
• FAIL_INVARIANT_NOT_PRESERVED: required invariants fail after composition.
• FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE: compatibility predicate evaluates to FALSE.

516



6.10 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined interoperability as a normative contract. It introduced primitive composition
forms (C1–C5), compatibility predicates, required invariant vocabulary, a machine-readable
compatibility matrix, interop certificates, and deterministic failure codes for composition failures.
Chapter 7 next fixes the publication boundary and non-claims, and states the licensing intent for
Vol. No. IV in a QFC-consistent way.

7 Non-Claims, Publication Boundary, and Licensing Intent

7.1 Why This Chapter Exists

Vol. No. IV introduces a normative operator-law layer: definitions, certificates, and deterministic
protocols. This can look “stronger” than it is. Canonicalization is not a proof mechanism;
auditability is not a truth claim. This chapter draws an explicit boundary around what EY22
and the subsequent EY23–EY30 documents do not claim, and it clarifies the publication and
licensing intent for the suite.

7.2 Non-Claims (Hard Boundary)

The following statements are normative: they define what the suite MUST NOT be interpreted
as.

No Physical Realizability Claim

Nothing in Vol. No. IV asserts that any artifact is physically realizable on a quantum device,
nor that any Hamiltonian H corresponds to a realized quantum field theory.

Rule. The suite defines operator objects and contracts. Physical implementation is out of scope
unless a separate document explicitly provides an implementation claim with its own SpecID
and experimental protocol.

No Algorithmic Advantage Claim

No artifact in EY22–EY30 claims:
• quantum advantage,
• speedups over classical baselines,
• complexity separations,
• or cryptographic hardness assumptions.

Rule. If a future document claims advantage, it MUST be framed as a separate claim with
explicit benchmarks, threat models, and a reproducible measurement protocol.

No “Proof by Definition”

Canonical definitions are not proofs of conjectures.

517



Rule. Vol. No. IV MUST NOT be interpreted as proving the Riemann Hypothesis (or any
open conjecture) merely by defining a Hamiltonian, filter, penalty, or spectral extraction protocol.
Any future claim connecting an artifact to a conjecture MUST present falsifiable implications
and must survive independent reproduction.

No Hidden Authority

Canonical does not mean “authoritative because Enter Yourname says so.”

Rule. Canonization is only granted by the existence of:
• a published SpecID,
• a deterministic NumericModel,
• and a certificate verifiable by independent parties.

If these are missing, the artifact is not canonical in the Vol. No. IV sense.

7.3 Publication Boundary (What Counts as the Artifact)

The suite distinguishes between:
• Normative layer: the definitions, SpecID schema, NumericModel rules, certificate formats,

and verification semantics.
• Implementation layer: code, numerical experiments, simulation results, and performance

data.

Rule (Artifact identity). An artifact is defined by its SpecID and certificate semantics, not
by a specific codebase. Code MAY be published, and SHOULD be committed by hash, but is
not the definitional anchor.

Rule (Reproducibility). Any published numerical result based on these artifacts SHOULD
include:

• the full SpecIDs of the artifacts used,
• the NumericModel profile(s),
• truncation schedule(s),
• and an interop certificate if composition is involved.

7.4 Normative vs Informational Text

To keep the suite audit-friendly, the documents distinguish:
• Normative text: uses MUST/SHOULD/MAY and affects meaning.
• Informational text: intuition, motivation, examples, and non-binding commentary.

Rule. If a paragraph affects what a verifier must do, it MUST be normative. If it is not
normative, it MUST NOT be required for acceptance.

518



7.5 Licensing Intent (High-Level)

Vol. No. IV is written to be:
• publicly readable and referenceable,
• machine-readable in structure,
• and compatible with downstream implementation without forcing trust in any one

repository.

Intent. The intent is to allow broad use of the methodology while preserving clear attribution
and protecting the integrity of the specification layer.

Non-binding note. The concrete legal licensing text is typically maintained in the repository
and/or publication venue. This whitepaper states the intent: that the normative definitions
(SpecIDs, certificate formats, and verification semantics) are published as a stable reference, and
implementations may be licensed separately.

7.6 Attribution and Citation Form

Rule (Citation). Any reuse of Vol. No. IV artifacts in publications SHOULD cite:
• the artifact ID (EY22..EY30),
• the SpecID version,
• and the canonical publication location (e.g. DOI / hash commitment).

A recommended short form:

EY29 @ SpecID_Short :: VID-2026-02, Vol. No. IV (Enter Yourname).

7.7 Responsible Use Boundary

Although Vol. No. IV is methodological, it can be applied to security evaluation and adversarial
analysis contexts. This volume therefore states a boundary:

Rule (Responsible framing). If an artifact is used in a context that could reasonably
be interpreted as enabling wrongdoing, the publication MUST include a threat model and a
limitation statement, and MUST avoid procedural instructions intended to cause harm. This
suite is intended for auditable, responsible research and verification.

7.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter fixed the hard boundary of Vol. No. IV:
• no physical realizability claim,
• no algorithmic advantage claim,
• no proof-by-definition,
• and no hidden authority.

519



It also clarified what counts as the artifact (SpecID + certificate semantics), how normative
text is distinguished from informational text, and stated the licensing and attribution intent for
publication.

Appendices Reserved

Appendix A and Appendix B are reserved for canonical templates and checklists (to be filled
when we decide the exact serialization formats and repository layout conventions).

Appendix A

A.1 Reference Template: Canonical Representation and Hash
Commitments

A.1.1 Purpose

This appendix defines a canonical serialization template for certificates and a minimal set of
hash-commitment rules. The goal is to ensure that:

• certificates are byte-stable (the same content yields the same bytes),
• commitments are unambiguous (the same object yields the same hash),
• verifiers can deterministically reject malformed or ambiguous artifacts.

This appendix is normative. Any artifact in EY23–EY30 that claims conformance to EY22
MUST follow this template, unless it explicitly declares an alternative canonical encoding in its
SpecID.

A.1.2 Canonical Certificate Encoding (CCE)

CCE-1: Allowed Formats

A certificate MUST be encoded using exactly one of the following formats:
• Canonical JSON (preferred for machine verification),
• Canonical YAML (allowed only if transformed to Canonical JSON before hashing and

verification),
• CBOR (allowed only if a canonical CBOR profile is declared in SpecID).

Rule (single truth). If YAML is used for human readability, the certificate MUST still define
a Canonical JSON projection as the single source of truth for hashing and verification.

CCE-2: Canonical JSON Rules

The Canonical JSON projection MUST satisfy:

1. UTF-8: The document MUST be encoded in UTF-8 without BOM.
2. Key ordering: All object keys MUST be sorted lexicographically (byte-order of UTF-8).
3. No duplicate keys: Duplicate keys MUST cause REJECT_MALFORMED.
4. Numbers: Numbers MUST be represented deterministically:

• integers in base-10 with no leading zeros (except “0”),
• non-integers MUST NOT appear unless the NumericModel explicitly allows them and

defines their canonical string form.

521



5. No NaN/Inf : NaN, +Inf, -Inf MUST NOT appear; if needed, they MUST be represented
as strings with explicit tags.

6. Whitespace: No insignificant whitespace is permitted (minified JSON). Newlines are not
permitted inside tokens.

7. Arrays: Arrays preserve order; order is semantic and MUST be canonical where relevant
(see CCE-4).

8. Strings: Strings MUST be NFC-normalized Unicode and MUST escape characters using
standard JSON escaping only.

Rule. If any rule above is violated, verification MUST return REJECT_MALFORMED.

CCE-3: Canonical Section Layout

The Canonical JSON projection MUST include top-level keys in the following order (ordering
rule still applies, this is a schema requirement):

• "header"

• "specid"

• "inputs"

• "protocol"

• "outputs"

• "checks"

• "commitments"

• "signatures"

• "metadata"

Each key MUST exist. If a section is empty, it MUST exist as an empty object {} or empty
array [] as defined below.

Null policy. The literal null MUST NOT be used. Absence is represented only by empty
containers with explicit semantics.

CCE-4: Canonical Ordering Within Sections

Within sections where ordering could be arbitrary, ordering MUST be canonical:

• "outputs": lists of multiple objects MUST be sorted by a declared "id" field.
• "checks": check entries MUST be sorted by "check_id".
• "commitments": commitment entries MUST be sorted by "name".
• "protocol.steps": step lists preserve order and MUST be written in canonical execution

order.

If a whitepaper introduces a new list-like structure, it MUST define the canonical ordering key.

522



A.1.3 Certificate Schema Template (Normative JSON Skeleton)

The following is the normative skeleton for a certificate in Canonical JSON form.

{
"header": {
"artifact_symbol": "F_star(H)",
"artifact_type": "CSF",
"specid_short": "CSF:CalcID:AID:JID:CID:NID:VID",
"version": "VID-YYYY-MM",
"created_utc": "YYYY-MM-DDThh:mm:ssZ",
"producer": "informational"

},
"specid": {
"artifact_type": "CSF",
"core": {},
"calc": {},
"A": {},
"J": {},
"C": {},
"tiebreak": {},
"numeric_model": {},
"cert": {},
"interop": {},
"version": "VID-YYYY-MM"

},
"inputs": {
"core_objects": {},
"public_parameters": {},
"truncation_schedule": {},
"external_objects": []

},
"protocol": {
"steps": [],
"aggregation": {},
"stopping": {},
"failure_modes": []

},
"outputs": {
"canonical_representation": {},
"derived_invariants": {},
"output_hashes": []

},
"checks": {
"structural": [],
"constraints": [],
"canonicality": [],
"invariants": []

},
"commitments": {
"hash_alg": "sha256",
"byte_encoding": "utf-8",

523



"objects": []
},
"signatures": {},
"metadata": {}

}

Rule. Artifacts MAY extend this schema by adding keys inside existing section objects, but
MUST NOT add new top-level sections.

A.1.4 Hash Commitments

HC-1: Default Hash Algorithm

Unless otherwise specified, the hash algorithm MUST be:

HashAlg = sha256.

A different hash algorithm MAY be used only if:
• it is declared in "commitments.hash_alg",
• it is included in SpecID,
• and the verifier supports it deterministically.

HC-2: What Is Hashed

There are three categories of hash commitments:

1. Certificate hash: hash of the entire Canonical JSON byte string of the certificate.
2. Object commitments: hashes of external large objects (matrices, datasets, code snap-

shots).
3. Section commitments: hashes of specific sections if partial referencing is needed (op-

tional).

Rule. Any claim that references an external object MUST include an object commitment for
it.

HC-3: Canonical Byte Encoding Before Hashing

All hashes MUST be computed over a canonical byte encoding.

Default. For certificates and JSON sections: canonical byte encoding is the UTF-8 encoding
of Canonical JSON (CCE-2).

External objects. For external objects, the commitment MUST specify:
• "name": stable identifier,
• "media_type": e.g. "application/octet-stream", "application/pdf", "text/plain",

524



• "canonicalization": how the object was converted into bytes,
• "hash": the computed hash,
• "size_bytes": informational size.

If the object is a text file, canonicalization MUST specify:
• UTF-8 encoding,
• LF line endings,
• and whether trailing whitespace is preserved or stripped (default: preserved).

HC-4: Chunked Objects and Merkle Commitments (Optional)

For very large objects, a Merkle commitment MAY be used. If used, the commitment MUST
specify:

• chunk size in bytes,
• leaf hash algorithm,
• tree construction rules (ordering, padding),
• root hash.

Rule. Merkle commitments MUST be deterministic. Any ambiguity in chunking or ordering
MUST cause rejection.

A.1.5 Commitment Object Template

Each external commitment entry in "commitments.objects" MUST follow:

{
"name": "H_truncation_matrix_N1024",
"media_type": "application/octet-stream",
"canonicalization": {
"type": "raw-bytes",
"notes": "exact bytes as stored"

},
"hash_alg": "sha256",
"hash": "hex-string",
"size_bytes": 1234567

}

Rule. Hashes MUST be encoded as lowercase hexadecimal without prefixes.

A.1.6 Canonical IDs and Short References

To allow stable references inside and across certificates, the following IDs are standardized:

• artifact_type: one of CSF,VPO,LIOUV,FLOQ,COMM,INTW,CGR,KOOP.
• calc_id, A_id, J_id, C_id, nm_id: stable labels resolving to full definitions in "specid".

525



• check_id: unique string within "checks".
• step_id: unique string within "protocol.steps".

Rule. IDs MUST be ASCII and MUST be deterministic (no random UUIDs) unless derived
deterministically from public inputs.

A.1.7 Verifier Requirements (CCE/HC)

A compliant verifier MUST:
• reject non-canonical JSON encodings,
• recompute certificate hashes and compare against published commitments (if provided),
• verify each external object hash if the object is supplied,
• treat any canonicalization mismatch as FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH or REJECT_MALFORMED.

A.1.8 Appendix Summary

This appendix fixed a canonical certificate encoding (Canonical JSON projection) and standard-
ized hash commitment rules. Together, these rules ensure that Vol. No. IV artifacts can be
bound to deterministic bytes, enabling portable verification and eliminating ambiguity at the
serialization boundary.

Appendix B

B.1 Checklist: “QFC-Valid Whitepaper” Requirements

B.1.1 Purpose

This appendix provides a deterministic checklist for validating that a whitepaper in Vol. No. IV
(EY23–EY30) conforms to the EY22 conventions. The checklist is designed for:

• authors (before publication),
• reviewers (during audit),
• verifiers (as a quick failure triage map).

Rule. A whitepaper that fails any MUST item below MUST be treated as non-conformant to
Vol. No. IV.

B.1.2 A. Identity and Scope

□ MUST: The document has a stable ID (e.g. EY23) and the ID appears in the frontmatter.
□ MUST: ArtifactType is explicitly declared (CSF,VPO,LIOUV,FLOQ,COMM,INTW,CGR,KOOP).
□ MUST: Scope and Non-Claims are explicit (no proof-by-definition; no advantage claim;

no physical claim).
□ SHOULD: The document states intended role(s) within the QFC stack and references the

suite registry (EY22).

B.1.3 B. Normative Definitions

□ MUST: The artifact has a normative definition as an operator-level object (not a procedure-
only description).

□ MUST: All normative requirements use MUST/SHOULD/MAY; vague language does not
affect meaning.

□ MUST: Core objects are defined (e.g. H, C, H(t), Obs) with domain assumptions when
required.

□ MUST: If functional calculus is used, the calculus is explicitly declared.

B.1.4 C. SpecID Completeness

□ MUST: Full SpecID tuple is defined and embedded (not only referenced by name).
□ MUST: Any irrelevant SpecID component is present with an explicit null value and

semantics.
□ MUST: Version is specified and changes whenever meaning changes.
□ SHOULD: A SpecID short form is provided for human readability, with a deterministic

expansion rule.

527



B.1.5 D. Admissible Family, Objective, Constraints, Tie-Break

□ MUST: Admissible family A is explicitly specified and has canonical representation.
□ MUST: If selection/optimization is used, objective J is explicit and deterministically

evaluable.
□ MUST: Constraints C are explicit (no “reasonable constraints”).
□ MUST: TieBreak is defined and deterministic whenever non-uniqueness or tolerance ties

may occur.
□ SHOULD: The paper states minimal existence / well-posedness conditions or declares

failure modes.

B.1.6 E. NumericModel (Determinism)

□ MUST: NumericModel tuple is included in SpecID and specified explicitly.
□ MUST: Precision and rounding are specified; NaN/Inf behavior is forbidden or explicitly

encoded.
□ MUST: Tolerance conventions are explicit (εabs, εrel, εop, εspec).
□ MUST: Aggregation order is deterministic (ordering key + fixed reduction strategy).
□ MUST: Truncation model is specified (basis, cut rule, boundary rule, schedule, cross-N

policy).
□ MUST: Failure modes are defined and deterministic (no silent fallback).

B.1.7 F. Invariants

□ MUST: Required invariants are listed explicitly (what is preserved / enforced).
□ MUST: Each invariant has a check procedure (exact or tolerance-based) under Numeric-

Model.
□ SHOULD: Invariants are grouped as structural / spectral / validity / interop, for audit

clarity.

B.1.8 G. Certificates

□ MUST: The paper defines a certificate format π conforming to EY22 Chapter 5.
□ MUST: The paper defines a verifier procedure that deterministically returns ACCEPT/REJECT/FAIL_*.
□ MUST: The certificate binds to full SpecID and NumericModel.
□ MUST: Required failure codes are mapped (at least those in EY22 Chapter 5).
□ SHOULD: The certificate includes commitments to large external objects (hashes) and

canonicalization rules.

B.1.9 H. Canonical Encoding and Hash Commitments

□ MUST: Canonical JSON projection rules are adopted (EY22 Appendix A.1) or explicitly
overridden in SpecID.

528



□ MUST: Hash algorithm and canonical byte encoding are specified for all commitments.
□ MUST: Hashes are lowercase hex; duplicate-key JSON is rejected.
□ SHOULD: Merkle/chunking rules are specified if large objects require chunked commit-

ments.

B.1.10 I. Interoperability

□ MUST: Interop component exists in SpecID and states composition permissions and
requirements.

□ MUST: Compatibility predicates are explicit and checkable.
□ MUST: Composition failure codes exist (domain mismatch, calc mismatch, numeric model

mismatch, invariant failure).
□ SHOULD: A compatibility matrix entry (OK/OK*/NO/N/A) is declared for relevant

pairings.
□ SHOULD: Workflows that publish composed results define an interop certificate.

B.1.11 J. Protocol and Reproducibility Package

□ MUST: The paper defines a deterministic evaluation protocol (steps, ordering, stopping
conditions).

□ MUST: Protocol changes imply SpecID changes (version bump).
□ SHOULD: A minimal reproducibility bundle is described (inputs, commitments, how to

re-run verifier).

B.1.12 K. Final “Release Gate”

A paper is considered QFC-valid (Vol. No. IV) only if:
□ all MUST items in Sections A–J are satisfied, and
□ the certificate verifier accepts at least one reference certificate instance under the declared

NumericModel.

B.1.13 Appendix Summary

This appendix provided a deterministic, auditable checklist for ensuring that EY23–EY30
whitepapers are conformant to EY22 conventions. It functions as the suite’s “release gate” for
canonical operator artifacts.

Chapter 23

EY23: Canonical Spectral Filter
F⋆(H)

Canonical Operator Artifacts for QFC

Enter Yourname

Abstract
This whitepaper defines the Canonical Spectral Filter F⋆(H), a QFC
operator artifact that extracts a stable, audit-friendly spectral action
from a declared Hamiltonian H without hand-tuned filter design. Unlike
ad hoc choices of f(H), F⋆(H) is defined by an explicit admissible family
of filters, a canonical objective functional, constraint predicates, and a
deterministic tie-break rule, all bound into a SpecID as standardized in
EY22.
The central requirement is reproducibility: independent parties given the
same public inputs MUST derive the same canonical filter (or the same
declared canonical equivalence class) under the same NumericModel.
The whitepaper therefore specifies (i) the functional calculus semantics
used to interpret f(H), (ii) truncation and aggregation policies for
practical evaluation, (iii) stability and monotonicity invariants expected
of a spectral filter used for auditing and regime classification, and (iv)
certificate semantics and verifier checks that accept or reject F⋆(H)
deterministically.

F⋆(H) serves as the baseline spectral probing primitive in Vol. No. IV. It is designed to
compose with validity operators, audit-native evolution, coarse-graining, and intertwiners, pro-
viding a canonical interface between raw operator cores and higher-level QFC workflows where
comparability across implementations is mandatory.

1 Motivation, Scope, and Design Goals

1.1 Motivation: Why a Canonical Spectral Filter?

Given a self-adjoint operator H (the declared core Hamiltonian), a common operation across
spectral workflows is to apply a function f to H and interpret the result:

f(H).

In practice, the choice of f is often informal: a smoothing kernel is selected, a window is tuned,
or a polynomial is fitted until results “look stable.” This creates a systematic failure mode for
QFC-style work:

• Parameter smuggling: small filter choices become hidden degrees of freedom.



• Non-comparability: two parties claiming the same spectral conclusion may have used
incompatible f .

• Non-auditability: without a fixed selection rule, f(H) cannot be verified as canonical.

EY23 addresses this by defining a Canonical Spectral Filter F⋆(H): a filter action on H that
is not hand-designed, but selected by a published objective and constraints, with a deterministic
tie-break, all bound into a SpecID as standardized in EY22.

1.2 What This Whitepaper Defines

This whitepaper defines:
• the artifact F⋆(H) as a canonical instance of f(H) under a declared calculus,
• the admissible family A of filter candidates f ,
• the objective functional J that selects a canonical filter,
• the constraint set C that enforces stability and audit-friendly behavior,
• the tie-break rule ensuring determinism in the presence of non-uniqueness,
• and the certificate and verifier checks required for canonical acceptance.

All general conventions (SpecID, NumericModel, certificate schema, interop rules) are inherited
from EY22 unless explicitly overridden and recorded in the SpecID.

1.3 Scope

In-scope.
• Canonical selection of a spectral filter action derived from a declared H.
• Deterministic evaluation under truncation H 7→ HN using a declared truncation policy.
• Certificate semantics enabling third-party verification that the produced filter is canonical

under SpecID.
• Interoperability hooks: how F⋆(H) composes with validity and coarse-grain artifacts.

Out-of-scope.
• Any claim that H represents a physically realized system.
• Any claim of computational advantage (quantum or classical).
• Any claim that a particular spectral feature implies resolution of an open conjecture.
• Any attempt to standardize all possible filter families; this paper defines a canonicalizable

framework and a baseline profile.

1.4 Design Goals (Normative)

The Canonical Spectral Filter MUST satisfy the following design goals:

531



G1: Canonicality by Specification

F⋆(H) MUST be determined by public specification, not author preference. In particular, the
output MUST be uniquely determined by:

(H, Calc, A, J , C, TieBreak, NumericModel).

G2: Auditability

A verifier MUST be able to accept or reject the artifact using only:
• the certificate,
• the declared SpecID,
• and the public inputs (or their hash commitments).

The verifier MUST NOT require trusting the producer.

G3: Stability Under Declared Perturbations

The filter selection SHOULD be stable under the perturbation class declared in C (e.g. bounded
additive noise, small truncation changes). Stability is always relative to the declared Numeric-
Model and truncation schedule.

G4: Minimal Degrees of Freedom

The admissible family A SHOULD be chosen to minimize hidden degrees of freedom. If A is
broad, the objective J and tie-break MUST be strong enough to prevent parameter smuggling.

G5: Interoperability With Validity and Reduction

F⋆(H) SHOULD be composable with:
• validity penalties V = C†C (EY24),
• audit-native evolution Laudit (EY25),
• coarse-grain reduction R (EY29),

under the interoperability rules of EY22 Chapter 6. Any additional compatibility predicates
MUST be declared in the EY23 Interop component.

1.5 Interpretation: What F⋆(H) Is Used For

This artifact is intended as the baseline “spectral probe” in Vol. No. IV. Typical uses include:
• extracting stable spectral summaries for audit and classification,
• defining regime buckets by canonical spectral features,
• producing inputs to commutant discovery workflows (EY27),
• and serving as a standardized pre-processing operator prior to coarse-graining (EY29).

532



1.6 Chapter Summary

This chapter motivated the need for canonical spectral filtering and fixed the scope and design
goals for F⋆(H). Chapter 2 now introduces the normative definition of the artifact and the EY23
SpecID components that bind its meaning: calculus, admissible family, objective, constraints,
tie-break, and NumericModel profile.

2 Normative Definition and SpecID Binding

2.1 Conformance to EY22

EY23 conforms to the Vol. No. IV conventions defined in EY22. In particular:
• SpecID semantics are as defined in EY22 Chapter 3.
• NumericModel (determinism model) is as defined in EY22 Chapter 4.
• Certificate schema and verifier semantics are as defined in EY22 Chapter 5 and Ap-

pendix A.1.
• Interoperability rules are as defined in EY22 Chapter 6.

Any deviation MUST be explicitly declared in the EY23 SpecID.

2.2 Core Object and Assumptions

Core. The core object for this artifact is a (typically self-adjoint) operator H on a Hilbert
space H.

Assumptions (minimal). EY23 requires that:
• H is self-adjoint (or declared self-adjoint on a specified domain) so that spectral calculus is

meaningful;
• the truncation policy (if used) produces finite objects HN with a deterministic construction;
• the admissible family A is non-empty under the declared constraints C.

If these assumptions fail, the artifact MUST return a deterministic failure outcome (EY22
Chapter 4).

2.3 Artifact Definition

Definition 2.1 (Canonical Spectral Filter). Let H be the declared core operator. Let A be an
admissible family of filter candidates f , let J be an objective functional, and let C be constraint
predicates.
The Canonical Spectral Filter is defined as:

F⋆(H) := f⋆(H),

where f⋆ ∈ A is the canonical selection obtained by:

f⋆ ∈ arg min J (f ;H) subject to C(f ;H) = TRUE,
f∈A

533



with deterministic tie-breaking applied whenever the minimizer is not unique under the declared
NumericModel.
If the objective is a maximization, the above is interpreted with arg max (this choice MUST be
fixed in SpecID).

Rule (selection is part of meaning). The meaning of F⋆(H) is the entire selection procedure:
A, J , C, tie-break, calculus, and numeric model. Two filters with different selection rules are
different artifacts.

2.4 Functional Calculus Semantics

EY23 permits f(H) only under an explicitly declared calculus:

Allowed calculus classes.
• Borel functional calculus for bounded f ,
• holomorphic/rational calculus for resolvent-type families,
• truncation calculus defined by H 7→ HN and f(H) ≈ f(HN ) under a declared truncation

schedule.

Rule. The calculus choice MUST be encoded in Calc inside SpecID and MUST be compatible
with the NumericModel.

2.5 SpecID for EY23

ArtifactType. For EY23:
ArtifactType = CSF.

SpecID components (EY23 binding). The full SpecID tuple is:
SpecIDEY23 := (CSF, Core = (H), Calc, A, J , C, TieBreak, NumericModel, Cert, Interop, Version).

Each component MUST be specified as follows:

Calc (required)

Calc MUST declare:
• calculus class (Borel / holomorphic / truncation calculus),
• if truncation calculus: the truncation mapping H 7→ HN and evaluation of f(HN ),
• canonicalization of any numeric primitives used (e.g. matrix exponentiation or polynomial

evaluation).

A (required)

A MUST specify the admissible family of candidate filters f , including:
• function class (e.g. spline family, rational family, orthogonal expansion),

534



• parameter bounds (to avoid hidden degrees of freedom),
• canonical representation form (so tie-break can be deterministic on bytes).

J (required)

J (f ;H) MUST specify:
• whether the objective is minimized or maximized,
• the exact score function(s),
• any weights and normalization rules,
• any dependence on truncation schedule or spectral summaries.

C (required)

C(f ;H) MUST include constraint predicates. Typical constraints include:
• boundedness / Lipschitz constraints on f ,
• monotonicity constraints (if used for bucket ordering),
• positivity constraints (if f(H) is used as a penalty-like object),
• stability constraints across truncation levels N .

Rule. Constraints MUST be checkable deterministically under NumericModel, or the artifact
MUST fail.

TieBreak (required)

TieBreak MUST define a deterministic tie-breaking rule that yields a unique canonical f⋆ when:
• multiple f share equal objective score within tolerance,
• or multiple f satisfy a declared canonical equivalence.

Recommended tie-break. Lexicographic minimum of the canonical byte encoding of f ’s
parameterization (EY22 Appendix A.1).

NumericModel (required)

NumericModel MUST be included as defined in EY22 Chapter 4, including: precision, rounding,
tolerance, deterministic aggregation, truncation schedule, and failure modes.

Cert (required)

Cert MUST specify:
• the certificate payload required to verify f⋆,
• the verifier checks (structural, constraints, canonicality, invariants),
• and the failure codes used for rejection.

535



Interop (required)

Interop MUST specify:
• allowed composition forms (EY22 C1–C5),
• invariants that must be preserved under composition,
• compatibility predicates for advertised pairings (e.g. with EY24 validity penalty or EY29

coarse-grain).

Version (required)

Version MUST uniquely bind the meaning of the above components. Any change in: Calc,A,J , C,TieBreak,NumericModel,Cert, Interop
MUST change Version.

2.6 Deterministic Outcomes

EY23 verification MUST return one of:

{ACCEPT,REJECT} ∪ {FAIL_∗},

as defined in EY22. In particular, EY23 MUST support (at minimum):
• FAIL_NONCONVERGENCE

• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM

• FAIL_CONSTRAINT

• FAIL_CANONICALITY

• FAIL_INVARIANT

This chapter defined F⋆(H) as a canonical selection of f(H) bound by SpecID, and fixed

3 Admissible Family A: Canonical Filter Classes

3.1 Purpose of A

The admissible family A is the set of candidate filters f from which the canonical filter f⋆ is
selected. In EY23, A is not an implementation detail: it is a normative object and a primary
defense against parameter smuggling.

536



Rule. A filter f MUST be considered admissible only if:
• it belongs to a declared filter class,
• it has a canonical parameterization,
• its parameter bounds are explicit,
• and membership can be checked deterministically under the NumericModel.

3.2 Spectral Window Normalization

Most filter families require a declared spectral window in which the filter is interpreted.

Window. EY23 binds a window map:

W : σ(H) → [0, 1],

used to normalize the spectral coordinate. In practical truncation settings, W is defined from
truncation-level spectral summaries (e.g. extremal eigenvalues) under a deterministic rule.

Rule (window is part of A). The window map W MUST be specified as part of A (or Calc)
and MUST be reproducible under NumericModel.

Default window (Baseline CSF-0).( Unless overridden, the baseline window uses truncation-
level extrema: )

WN (λ) := clip λ− λmin(HN )
λmax(HN )− λmin(HN ) , 0, 1 ,

with deterministic handling of the degenerate case λmax = λmin (return FAIL_CONSTRAINT).

3.3 Canonical Representation Requirement

Rule (canonical encoding). Every f ∈ A MUST have a canonical representation that can
be serialized and compared lexicographically (EY22 Appendix A.1). This canonical encoding
MUST be used by the tie-break rule.

3.4 Admissible Filter Classes

EY23 defines three admissible filter classes. A SpecID MUST select exactly one of them as the
active A, or define an explicit union with deterministic tie-break across classes.

Class A1: Piecewise-Polynomial (Spline) Filters (Recommended Baseline)

Definition. A1 consists of piecewise-polynomial filters on the normalized coordinate x ∈ [0, 1]:

Admissibility constraints (structural). A filter is admissible in A1 only if:
• knots are strictly increasing and represented as rationals (or fixed-point) under Numeric-

• coefficients cj,k are represented in the declared NumberSystem,
• optional continuity constraints at knots are either enforced or explicitly not enforced (must

Why A1 is recommended. A1 avoids transcendental functions, admits deterministic evalua-

• n MUST be bounded by nmax to avoid hidden degrees of freedom.
• coefficients MUST be in the declared NumberSystem and bounded by explicit norms if

Canonical encoding. The encoding MUST serialize BasisID, then n, then a0, . . . , an in order,
using NumericModel number encoding.

3.5 Parameter Bounds (Anti-Smuggling Requirement)

Rule. Any admissible family MUST include explicit parameter bounds sufficient to prevent
unbounded tuning. At minimum:

• a complexity bound (e.g. m ≤ mmax, K ≤ Kmax, n ≤ nmax),
• a magnitude bound on coefficients (or a norm bound),
• and any smoothing / regularity bounds required by constraints.

If parameter bounds are omitted, the artifact MUST be treated as non-canonical.

3.6 Baseline Profile CSF-0 (Normative Default)

EY23 defines a baseline admissible family intended for Vol. No. IV defaults.

CSF-0. Unless the SpecID overrides A, the baseline family is:

ACSF-0 := A1 (Spline) with fixed (mmax, dmax) and rational knots.

Baseline constraints. The baseline profile MUST fix:
• mmax and dmax,
• a rational/fixed-point knot grid policy (e.g. knots drawn from a declared finite grid),
• coefficient bounds (e.g. |cj,k| ≤ B),
• and continuity policy (e.g. C0 continuity at knots enforced or not).

539



Rule (baseline must be fully specified). CSF-0 MUST be fully specified inside the SpecID
as concrete numeric values or as references committed by hash.

3.7 Membership Check Procedure

For any chosen admissible family, the certificate MUST include a membership check routine:
• parse the canonical encoding,
• verify bounds and ordering constraints,
• verify representation constraints (number system, precision),
• return deterministic failure if violated.

3.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the admissible family A as a normative object and introduced three canonical
filter classes (A1 spline, A2 rational, A3 orthogonal expansion). It also defined an anti-smuggling
requirement via explicit parameter bounds and established a baseline profile CSF-0 using the A1
spline class.
Chapter 4 now defines the objective functional J (f ;H): how the canonical filter is selected from
A under deterministic evaluation and tie-breaking.

4 Objective Functional J : Canonical Selection Principle

4.1 Purpose of J

The admissible family A (Chapter 3) provides candidate filters f . The objective J (f ;H) provides
the selection principle that turns candidates into a canonical choice f⋆. In EY23, J MUST be:

• explicit,
• deterministically evaluable under the NumericModel,
• and sufficiently strong to prevent parameter smuggling within A.

Rule. If J is under-specified (e.g. relies on informal smoothing goals), the artifact MUST be
treated as non-canonical.

4.2 Canonical Score Decomposition

EY23 standardizes J as a weighted sum of named score terms:

J (f ;H) := wstab Jstab(f ;H) + wsharp Jsharp(f ;H) + wsimp Jsimp(f) + wbias Jbias(f ;H),

with all weights w• ≥ 0 declared in SpecID.

Rule (deterministic weights). Weights MUST be explicit numeric values (or committed by
hash) and MUST NOT be tuned per instance unless the tuning rule is part of SpecID.

540



4.3 Jstab: Truncation Stability Term

A canonical spectral filter is expected to be stable under the declared truncation schedule.

Truncation schedule. Let N1 < N2 < · · · < NL be the truncation levels required by the
NumericModel.

Stability metric. Define a stability discrep(ancy between cons)ecutive truncations:

∆ℓ(f ;H) := D f(HN ), f(H ,
ℓ Nℓ+1)

where D(·, ·) is a declared deterministic discrepancy functional.

Default discrepancy (Baseline CSF-0). Unless overridden, the baseline discrepancy is a
normalized Frobenius proxy:

D(A,B) := ∥A−B∥F
max(1, ∥A∥F , ∥B∥F ) ,

with ∥ · ∥F computed deterministically under NumericModel and with deterministic aggregation
order.

Stability score.
