Chapter 30

EY30: Koopman Export Operator K
Canonical Operator Artifacts for QFC

Enter Yourname

Abstract
This whitepaper defines the Koopman Export Operator K, a canonical
artifact that maps state/operator-based workflows into observable-space
dynamics, enabling regime-agnostic comparison, reduced summaries, and
verifier-friendly export of Vol. No. IV pipelines. EY30 standardizes:
the observable function space declaration, the induced Koopman ac-
tion, finite-basis truncations, and deterministic certificates that bind
how an underlying evolution (EY25), token execution (EY26), or fil-
tered/operator workflow (EY23–EY24) is represented as a Koopman
operator.

K is treated as an export boundary: it does not claim physical equivalence of regimes or
completeness of observable spaces. Instead, it commits to a specific observable basis, sam-
pling/evaluation rules, and replayable construction routines. EY30 composes explicitly with
regime intertwiners (EY28) and coarse-grain reducers (EY29), and publishes interop declarations
so that Koopman-space statements remain auditable under QFC-style deterministic replay.

1 Motivation and Scope: Exporting Operator Workflows into
Observable Space

1.1 Motivation: Why an Export Operator Exists in Vol. No. IV

Vol. No. IV defines canonical operator artifacts that live naturally in “state/operator space”:
filters (EY23), validity penalties (EY24), audit-native evolution (EY25), tokens (EY26), commu-
tation constraints (EY27), regime intertwiners (EY28), and coarse-grain reducers (EY29). These
artifacts compose into workflows, but their outputs are often:

• high-dimensional,
• basis-dependent,
• regime-specific,
• and difficult to compare across implementations.

Koopman theory provides a complementary viewpoint: instead of evolving states, evolve ob-
servables (functions on state space). The induced operator (the Koopman operator) often
admits:

• linear structure even for nonlinear dynamics,
• representation-agnostic comparison via shared observable dictionaries,



• stable low-dimensional summaries (eigenfunctions, modes),
• and a natural interface for coarse-grain and classification.

EY30 exists to make this translation auditable. It defines a canonical export operator K that
binds:

• what the “observable space” is,
• how observables are evaluated/sampled,
• which finite-basis truncation is used,
• and how the induced Koopman action is constructed deterministically from upstream

artifacts.

1.2 What EY30 Defines

EY30 defines:
• an Observable Space Declaration (function class + basis/dictionary + evaluation rules),
• a Koopman Action specification (pullback by a declared evolution map),
• finite-basis truncation rules that produce a matrix/operator representation,
• deterministic construction routines and certificates that bind the export,
• interop rules for composing Koopman export with EY23–EY29 workflows.

1.3 Core Intuition: Koopman as Pullback of Observables

Let x be a state (in some regime-dependent representation) and let Φ be the evolution map:

xt+∆ = Φ(xt).

An observable is a function g of the state. The Koopman operator K acts by pullback:

(Kg)(x) := g(Φ(x)).

This is the export boundary:
• upstream artifacts define or constrain Φ (explicitly or implicitly),
• EY30 commits to how Φ is realized (via evolution/tokens/snapshots),
• and the resulting linear operator on observables is constructed deterministically.

1.4 Scope

In-scope.
• Export from EY25 evolution (generator- or trajectory-defined) to a Koopman operator on

a declared observable basis.
• Export from EY26 program tokens to a Koopman operator induced by token step execution.
• Export from general operator workflows (EY23/EY24) when an evolution map is provided

(by token or by explicit map artifact).

753



• Finite-basis Koopman representations (dictionary truncations) and their verification.
• Interop with EY28 (regime bridges) and EY29 (coarse-grain).

Out-of-scope.
• Claims of completeness of an observable dictionary (no “we span everything”).
• Unverifiable learned Koopman embeddings without committed parameters and deterministic

replay.
• Infinite-dimensional Koopman spectral claims inferred solely from finite truncations.

1.5 Why EY30 Matters for Registries and “Regime-Agnostic” Claims

Many “same phenomenon” claims are hard to justify directly in state/operator representations
because bases differ. Koopman export provides a unifying comparison layer:

workflow ⇒ K-representation ⇒ registry / bucket / invariant signatures.

But this only works if the export is auditable:
• the observable basis must be committed,
• sampling/evaluation rules must be deterministic,
• and the constructed Koopman operator must be replayable.

EY30 supplies exactly that.

1.6 Design Goals (Normative)

G1: Deterministic Export

Given the same upstream artifact commitments and the same EY30 SpecID, every verifier MUST
compute the same Koopman representation.

G2: Explicit Observable Space

The observable dictionary (basis) and evaluation rules MUST be explicit and hash-committed.

G3: Explicit Evolution Realization

EY30 MUST declare how Φ is realized:
• by generator evolution (EY25),
• by token execution (EY26),
• or by trajectory snapshots (committed).

G4: Interop by Construction

If Koopman export depends on regime transport (EY28) or coarse-grain (EY29), the workflow
MUST publish interop certificates binding:

754



• order of operations,
• truncation policies,
• and preserved/weakened invariants.

1.7 Chapter Summary

This chapter motivated EY30: Koopman export provides a regime-agnostic observable-space
layer for comparing and summarizing Vol. No. IV workflows, but only if export semantics are
explicit and replayable. It defined scope, core intuition (Koopman pullback), and the normative
design goals: deterministic export, explicit observable dictionary, explicit evolution realization,
and interop-by-construction.
Chapter 2 next defines the observable space declaration: function classes, dictionaries/bases,
sampling grids, evaluation rules, truncation policies, and the minimal invariant vocabulary used
to express correctness and stability in Koopman space.

2 Observable Space Declaration: Dictionaries, Evaluation Rules,
and Truncation

2.1 Purpose

Koopman export is meaningless without a precise statement of what an observable is and how it
is evaluated. This chapter defines the EY30 Observable Space Declaration:

• the observable function class,
• the dictionary/basis used for finite export,
• the sampling/evaluation rules (grids, measures, trajectories),
• truncation policies for finite-dimensional Koopman representations,
• and the invariant vocabulary for stability and verification in observable space.

Rule. Every EY30 instance MUST include an ObservableDecl component in its SpecID. If
ObservableDecl is missing, the export artifact is invalid.

2.2 ObservableDecl: Schema

An observable declaration is a tuple:
ObservableDecl := (StateRep, G, D, EvalRule, TruncObs, InnerProd, Canon).

StateRep (state representation reference)

StateRep is a reference that fixes how a state x is represented for evaluation:
• regime identifier (RegimeID or reference to EY28 RegimeSpec),
• state encoding type (vector, density, operator snapshot, reduced summary),
• coordinate/basis declaration (or a hash reference),
• normalization rule (if any).

755



Rule. If EY30 uses a regime bridge (EY28), StateRep MUST cite the target regime specification
and include INTW-Ref in Interop.

Function class G

G specifies the allowable observable functions. At minimum, EY30 supports the following classes
(choose one):

G1: Polynomial dictionary class.

G = POLY(d, p)
meaning: multivariate polynomials up to degree p on a d-dimensional state vector.

G2: Fourier/trigonometric dictionary class.

G = FOURIER(d,Ω)
meaning: trigonometric basis with frequency set Ω (explicitly enumerated or deterministically
generated).

G3: Kernel feature class (explicit parameters).

G = KERNEL(κ, θ)
meaning: kernel feature map with kernel type κ and committed parameters θ. (Learned
parameters are allowed only if committed and deterministic.)

G4: Operator-derived observables.

G = OP-FEAT(Ψ)
meaning: observables are features computed from operator/state objects (trace, norms, spectral
stats) via a committed feature map Ψ.

Rule. If G involves learnable parameters, those parameters MUST be committed and the
evaluation must be deterministic under NumericModel.

Dictionary/Basis D

Koopman export typically uses a finite dictionary D = {g1, . . . , gm} ⊂ G.

Schema.
D := (DictType, DictGen, DictParams, OrderSpec).

DictType options.
• explicit: the list of basis functions is explicitly enumerated.
• seeded: generated deterministically from a public seed + generator.
• reduced: derived from EY29 reduced summaries (must cite CGR-Ref).

756



Rule. A dictionary MUST be committed by explicit listing, hash, or deterministic seed+generator.
Omission is forbidden.

OrderSpec. Basis ordering must be fixed (lexicographic or committed order), because it
changes the Koopman matrix representation.

EvalRule (how observables are evaluated)

EvalRule binds the evaluation points and evaluation semantics.

Schema.

EvalRule := (EvalType, PointSet, MeasureSpec, TimeSpec, TieBreak).

EvalType options.
• trajectory: points are states along a committed trajectory (EY25 snapshots or EY26

token execution).
• grid: points are from a deterministic grid in state coordinates.
• sampled: points are sampled from a deterministic PRNG and a committed distribution

(seeded).

Rule. If trajectory is used, EvalRule MUST cite the upstream trajectory source (EY25
certificate or EY26 token transcript). If sampled is used, PRNGSpec and seed MUST be public
and deterministic.

TimeSpec. TimeSpec declares:
• discrete step ∆ or token period,
• time index set {tk},
• and whether Koopman is constructed per-step or per-period.

TruncObs (observable truncation policy)

Finite export requires choosing m, the dictionary size.

Schema.
TruncObs := (m, SelectRule, CrossMPolicy).

SelectRule examples.
• prefix: first m in canonical order,
• degree: all polynomials up to degree p (implies m),
• energy: select basis by a committed score and threshold.

Rule. Selection must be deterministic. If a score is used, the scoring routine must be committed.

757



InnerProd (how Koopman is projected)

Most practical Koopman constructions compute a finite operator by regression/projection in an
inner product:

⟨gi, gj⟩ := Ex∼µ[gi(x)gj(x)].

Schema.
InnerProd := (Type, µ, Estimator, Regularization).

Type options.
• empirical: empirical average over EvalRule point set,
• grid: weighted sum over grid,
• trajectory: time-average along trajectory (must bind window and weights).

Regularization. If regression is ill-conditioned, a deterministic regularization (e.g. ridge λI)
may be declared.

Rule. Any regularization MUST be explicit and committed; hidden conditioning fixes are
forbidden.

Canon (canonicalization rules)

Canon binds:
• numeric model for evaluation and regression,
• rounding/precision rules,
• canonicalization points (after evaluation, after regression, final).

2.3 Invariant Vocabulary in Observable Space

EY30 requires a minimal invariant vocabulary for export correctness and stability.

K1: Eval Determinism. Given the same EvalRule and NumericModel, all evaluators produce
identical observable values on all points.

K2: Dictionary Commitment. The dictionary D used is exactly the committed one (hash
or explicit list).

K3: Projection Stability. Koopman operator construction is stable under declared tolerances
(e.g. conditioning diagnostics are within bounds).

K4: Time-Step Semantics. The constructed operator corresponds to the declared ∆ or
period (no hidden time rescaling).

758



K5: Cross-M Stability (optional). If CrossMPolicy is used, the aggregated Koopman
representation is stable across dictionary sizes.

Rule. If a workflow uses Koopman eigenvalues/modes as registry keys, it MUST include K3
and K5 (if applicable) with explicit tolerances.

2.4 Deterministic Failure Codes (ObservableDecl Layer)

At minimum:
• REJECT_OBSDECL_MISSING
• REJECT_DICT_MISSING
• REJECT_EVALRULE_MISSING
• REJECT_TRUNCOBS_MISSING
• REJECT_INNERPROD_MISSING
• FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM
• FAIL_EVAL_SOURCE_MISSING
• FAIL_ILL_CONDITIONED

2.5 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the Observable Space Declaration (ObservableDecl): state representa-
tion reference, observable function class, finite dictionary/basis and ordering, evaluation rules
(trajectory/grid/sampled), observable truncation, inner product/projection estimator, and canon-
icalization. It also defined a minimal invariant vocabulary (K1–K5) for correctness and stability
of Koopman exports and fixed failure codes.
Chapter ?? next defines the Koopman construction semantics: how the evolution map Φ is realized
from EY25/EY26 pipelines, how the finite Koopman operator is computed (regression/projection),
and how the export is represented as a canonical operator artifact with SpecID.

3 Motivation and Scope: Exporting Operator Workflows into
Observable Space

3.1 Motivation: Why an Export Operator Exists in Vol. No. IV

Vol. No. IV defines canonical operator artifacts that live naturally in “state/operator space”:
filters (EY23), validity penalties (EY24), audit-native evolution (EY25), tokens (EY26), commu-
tation constraints (EY27), regime intertwiners (EY28), and coarse-grain reducers (EY29). These
artifacts compose into workflows, but their outputs are often:

• high-dimensional,
• basis-dependent,
• regime-specific,

759



• and difficult to compare across implementations.
Koopman theory provides a complementary viewpoint: instead of evolving states, evolve ob-
servables (functions on state space). The induced operator (the Koopman operator) often
admits:

• linear structure even for nonlinear dynamics,
• representation-agnostic comparison via shared observable dictionaries,
• stable low-dimensional summaries (eigenfunctions, modes),
• and a natural interface for coarse-grain and classification.

EY30 exists to make this translation auditable. It defines a canonical export operator K that
binds:

• what the “observable space” is,
• how observables are evaluated/sampled,
• which finite-basis truncation is used,
• and how the induced Koopman action is constructed deterministically from upstream

artifacts.

3.2 What EY30 Defines

EY30 defines:
• an Observable Space Declaration (function class + basis/dictionary + evaluation rules),
• a Koopman Action specification (pullback by a declared evolution map),
• finite-basis truncation rules that produce a matrix/operator representation,
• deterministic construction routines and certificates that bind the export,
• interop rules for composing Koopman export with EY23–EY29 workflows.

3.3 Core Intuition: Koopman as Pullback of Observables

Let x be a state (in some regime-dependent representation) and let Φ be the evolution map:

xt+∆ = Φ(xt).

An observable is a function g of the state. The Koopman operator K acts by pullback:

(Kg)(x) := g(Φ(x)).

This is the export boundary:
• upstream artifacts define or constrain Φ (explicitly or implicitly),
• EY30 commits to how Φ is realized (via evolution/tokens/snapshots),
• and the resulting linear operator on observables is constructed deterministically.

760



3.4 Scope

In-scope.
• Export from EY25 evolution (generator- or trajectory-defined) to a Koopman operator on

a declared observable basis.
• Export from EY26 program tokens to a Koopman operator induced by token step execution.
• Export from general operator workflows (EY23/EY24) when an evolution map is provided

(by token or by explicit map artifact).
• Finite-basis Koopman representations (dictionary truncations) and their verification.
• Interop with EY28 (regime bridges) and EY29 (coarse-grain).

Out-of-scope.
• Claims of completeness of an observable dictionary (no “we span everything”).
• Unverifiable learned Koopman embeddings without committed parameters and deterministic

replay.
• Infinite-dimensional Koopman spectral claims inferred solely from finite truncations.

3.5 Why EY30 Matters for Registries and “Regime-Agnostic” Claims

Many “same phenomenon” claims are hard to justify directly in state/operator representations
because bases differ. Koopman export provides a unifying comparison layer:

workflow ⇒ K-representation ⇒ registry / bucket / invariant signatures.

But this only works if the export is auditable:
• the observable basis must be committed,
• sampling/evaluation rules must be deterministic,
• and the constructed Koopman operator must be replayable.

EY30 supplies exactly that.

3.6 Design Goals (Normative)

G1: Deterministic Export

Given the same upstream artifact commitments and the same EY30 SpecID, every verifier MUST
compute the same Koopman representation.

G2: Explicit Observable Space

The observable dictionary (basis) and evaluation rules MUST be explicit and hash-committed.

761



G3: Explicit Evolution Realization

EY30 MUST declare how Φ is realized:
• by generator evolution (EY25),
• by token execution (EY26),
• or by trajectory snapshots (committed).

G4: Interop by Construction

If Koopman export depends on regime transport (EY28) or coarse-grain (EY29), the workflow
MUST publish interop certificates binding:

• order of operations,
• truncation policies,
• and preserved/weakened invariants.

3.7 Chapter Summary

This chapter motivated EY30: Koopman export provides a regime-agnostic observable-space
layer for comparing and summarizing Vol. No. IV workflows, but only if export semantics are
explicit and replayable. It defined scope, core intuition (Koopman pullback), and the normative
design goals: deterministic export, explicit observable dictionary, explicit evolution realization,
and interop-by-construction.
Chapter 2 next defines the observable space declaration: function classes, dictionaries/bases,
sampling grids, evaluation rules, truncation policies, and the minimal invariant vocabulary used
to express correctness and stability in Koopman space.

4 Artifact Structure and SpecID Schema

4.1 Purpose

Chapters 3–?? defined why EY30 exists, what observable space is, and how Koopman export is
constructed. This chapter defines EY30 as an auditable artifact with a precise SpecID schema:

• how ObservableDecl and EvolutionDecl are represented,
• how Koopman construction class and numeric routines are bound,
• how outputs (matrix K, spectral summaries) are committed,
• and what transcript/certificate payload is required for deterministic replay.

4.2 Koopman Export as a Typed Artifact

EY30 treats Koopman export as a typed map:

Kexport : (workflow commitments) → (observable-space operator artifact).

762



InputType and OutputType

Each EY30 instance MUST declare:

InputType ∈ {EVO,TOKEN,SNAP,WORKFLOW}, OutputType ∈ {KOOP_OP,KOOP_SPEC,KOOP_SUMMARY}.

Interpretation.
• InputType = EVO: export from EY25 generator-based evolution.
• InputType = TOKEN: export from EY26 token execution.
• InputType = SNAP: export from committed paired snapshots (xk, x′

k).
• InputType = WORKFLOW: export from a composed pipeline (must list upstream SpecIDs

in Interop).

4.3 KoopmanSpec

EY30 standardizes a Koopman export declaration:

KoopmanSpec := (ObservableDecl, EvolutionDecl, KoopClass, BuildSpec, DiagSpec).

KoopClass

KoopClass ∈ {KOP1,KOP2,KOP3}
as defined in Chapter ??.

BuildSpec

BuildSpec binds the deterministic construction routine:

BuildSpec := (RoutineID, LinAlgSpec, CanonPoints, TieBreaks).

LinAlgSpec (required). LinAlgSpec MUST bind:
• matrix multiplication order and accumulation,
• pseudo-inverse method (if used) and its truncation policy (threshold/grid),
• solver/inversion method and regularization (if used),
• eigensolver method and ordering (if eigenvalues/modes are published).

Rule (null discipline). Any BuildSpec component not used MUST be explicitly null. Omis-
sion is forbidden.

DiagSpec

DiagSpec binds required diagnostics and tolerances:

DiagSpec := {(DiagName, ValueType, TolSpec, RoutineID)}.

763



Rule. At minimum, DiagSpec MUST include:
• reconstruction error Lrec,
• a conditioning diagnostic,

unless explicitly justified as null (rare; generally non-acceptable for registry-grade exports).

4.4 NumericModel and Truncation Binding

Koopman export is only meaningful under declared numeric semantics and observable truncation.

TruncObs Binding

ObservableDecl.TruncObs binds:
• dictionary size m,
• selection rule and ordering,
• optional CrossMPolicy (if multi-m used).

NumericModel

EY30 NumericModel MUST bind:
• arithmetic type (float/fixed/exact),
• precision and rounding,
• deterministic evaluation rules for observables,
• deterministic linear algebra rules (as referenced in BuildSpec),
• canonicalization rules and points.

4.5 TranscriptSpec and Commitments

Export must be replayable. Therefore, transcript commitments MUST bind:
• all upstream references (EY25/EY26/SNAP dataset hashes, and/or workflow SpecIDs),
• dictionary commitments (hash/seed/generator, ordering),
• evaluation point set commitments (trajectory/window/grid/seeded samples),
• time semantics ∆ (or period) and per-step vs per-period choice,
• construction class and routine IDs,
• diagnostics and their computed values,
• output Koopman operator K (or its hash) and optional spectral summaries,
• deterministic tie-break decisions (SVD truncation, eigenvalue ordering, CrossM decisions).

Rule. If K is published as a matrix, its canonical serialization MUST be committed. If K is
published as a factorization, the factorization must be sufficient to reproduce K exactly under
NumericModel.

764



4.6 SpecID for EY30

ArtifactType. For EY30:
ArtifactType = KOOP.

SpecID components (EY30 binding). The full SpecID tuple is:

SpecIDEY30 := (KOOP, InputType, OutputType, KoopmanSpec, NumericModel, TranscriptSpec, Cert, Interop, Version).

Interop (Mini)

Interop binds intended compositions and references to upstream artifacts:
• UpstreamSpecIDs: list of EY23–EY29 artifacts used to generate the evolution or the

observables,
• INTW-Ref (if regime bridging is used),
• CGR-Ref (if coarse-grain reduction is used),
• Scope: what is exported (trajectory, token, filtered operator pipeline),
• CompatPredicates: identifiers of interop predicates (Koopman-layer + EY22 baseline).

Rule. If the export depends on reduction (EY29) or transport (EY28), Interop MUST declare
the order. If order is missing: FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE.

4.7 Schema-Layer Failure Codes

At minimum:
• REJECT_MALFORMED
• REJECT_SPECID_MISSING
• REJECT_OBSDECL_MISSING
• REJECT_EVODECL_MISSING
• REJECT_KOOPCLASS_MISSING
• REJECT_BUILDSPEC_MISSING
• REJECT_DIAGSPEC_MISSING
• REJECT_HIDDEN_INPUT
• FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM

4.8 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the EY30 artifact schema: InputType/OutputType, a KoopmanSpec binding
ObservableDecl, EvolutionDecl, KoopClass, construction routines (BuildSpec), and diagnostics
(DiagSpec); plus NumericModel and transcript commitments. It fixed the full SpecID tuple for

765



EY30 and required schema-layer failure codes and interop mini declarations (including order
binding for EY28/EY29).

spectral summaries are committed, how export replay is performed, and how Koopman exports
are accepted or rejected deterministically.

5 Certificate and Verifier: Replayable Export, Diagnostics, and
Acceptance Rules

5.1 Purpose

EY30 exports are meant to be used as:
• verifier-friendly operator artifacts K in observable space,

• registry keys (via bucket labels, spectral summaries, or Koopman signatures),

• and interop bridges between regimes and pipelines.
Therefore, every export must be replayable and must publish diagnostics that quantify how well
the finite K represents the declared Koopman action.
This chapter specifies:

• the certificate payload πKOOP,

• deterministic verifier checks for acceptance,

• transcript commitments for evaluation and construction,

• mandatory diagnostics (reconstruction error, conditioning),

• and required failure codes.

5.2 Certificate Object πKOOP

Rule. An EY30 publication MUST include a certificate πKOOP in canonical certificate encoding
(EY22-CCE).

Header (required)

• artifact type: KOOP

• artifact symbol: K

• InputType, OutputType

• KoopClass

• Version

• Certificate schema identifier (EY22-CCE)

766



SpecID (required)

The full SpecID tuple MUST be embedded:

SpecIDEY30 := (KOOP, InputType, OutputType, KoopmanSpec, NumericModel, TranscriptSpec, Cert, Interop, Version).

Committed Inputs (required)

πKOOP MUST commit to:
• ObservableDecl (StateRep, G, D, EvalRule, TruncObs, InnerProd, Canon),
• EvolutionDecl (Φ realization mode, source references, ∆, semantics, replay rules),
• KoopClass and BuildSpec (RoutineID, LinAlgSpec, thresholds, regularization, tie-breaks),
• DiagSpec (diagnostic names, routines, tolerances),
• NumericModel (evaluation + linear algebra determinism),
• all upstream references:

– EY25 πLIOUV or
– EY26 token transcript or
– SNAP dataset commitment,

• evaluation point set commitment (trajectory window/grid/seeded samples),
• any interop references used (INTW-Ref, CGR-Ref, upstream SpecIDs for WORKFLOW

input).

Committed Outputs (required)

πKOOP MUST commit to:
• Koopman operator representation K (or committed factorization) and its hash hK ,
• (optional) spectral summaries: eigenvalues/modes and their hashes,
• evaluation transcript commitment Txeval,
• construction transcript commitment Txbuild,
• diagnostics report commitment Txdiag,
• deterministic failure code if export fails.

5.3 Evaluation Transcript (Minimum Contents)

The evaluation transcript MUST bind enough information to replay the formation of X and Y :
• dictionary commitment resolution (explicit list/hash/seed+generator) and ordering,
• evaluation point set commitment:

– trajectory source and window indices (if trajectory),
– grid specification (if grid),
– PRNGSpec+seed+distribution (if sampled),

767



• time semantics: ∆ or period and per-step/per-period choice,
• pairing rule for (xk,Φ(xk)) (or (xk, xk+1)),
• canonicalization points and numeric evaluation rules,
• hashes of the resulting X and Y matrices (or their canonical encodings).

Rule. If X and Y are too large to publish, their canonical hashes MUST be published, and the
upstream commitments must allow reconstructing them exactly.

5.4 Construction Transcript (Minimum Contents)

The construction transcript MUST bind:
• KoopClass and BuildSpec resolution (including thresholds and regularization),
• linear algebra tie-breaks (SVD ordering, truncation choices),
• canonicalization points,
• intermediate matrix hashes as needed to replay deterministically,
• output K hash hK (or factorization hashes).

5.5 Diagnostics Report (Required Structure)

A diagnostics report is the canonical serialization of:

DiagReport := {(DiagName,Value,Tol,Result)}.

Mandatory diagnostics. At minimum:
• D1 Reconstruction error:

Lrec := ∥Y −KX∥F .
∥Y ∥F

• D2 Conditioning diagnostic: a committed estimate of κ(X) (or κ(G) for Galerkin).

Rule. If OutputType includes spectral summaries, a spectral solver diagnostic SHOULD be
included (e.g. residual norms of eigenpairs).

5.6 Verifier Contract

A verifier consumes πKOOP and returns:

{ACCEPT,REJECT} ∪ {FAIL_∗}.

Acceptance meaning. ACCEPT means: the export artifact is well-formed, replayable, K
matches replay under NumericModel, and mandatory diagnostics are computed and within
tolerances (if tolerances are declared). It does not claim that the dictionary is complete, that
the Koopman truncation is physically exact, or that any cross-regime equivalence holds beyond
declared interop.

768



5.7 Required Verifier Checks (Normative)

V1: Structural Validity (EY22-CCE)

Parse canonical certificate encoding and confirm required fields exist. Failure: REJECT_MALFORMED.

V2: SpecID Completeness

Confirm presence of:
• ArtifactType=KOOP,
• InputType, OutputType,
• KoopmanSpec (ObservableDecl, EvolutionDecl, KoopClass, BuildSpec, DiagSpec),
• NumericModel, TranscriptSpec, Cert, Interop, Version.

Failure: REJECT_SPECID_MISSING, REJECT_OBSDECL_MISSING, REJECT_EVODECL_MISSING,
REJECT_KOOPCLASS_MISSING, REJECT_BUILDSPEC_MISSING, REJECT_DIAGSPEC_MISSING.

V3: Commitment Integrity

Verify that all committed inputs resolve and match: dictionary, evaluation point set source,
upstream evolution source (EY25/EY26/SNAP), and any interop references (INTW-Ref, CGR-
Ref). Failure: FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH, REJECT_HIDDEN_INPUT.

V4: Evaluation Replay (X,Y )

Replay EvalRule deterministically:
• reconstruct points {xk},
• realize Φ per EvolutionDecl (generator/token/snap),
• evaluate dictionary ψ(xk) and ψ(Φ(xk)),
• construct X,Y in committed order and canonicalize.

Compare hashes to committedX,Y (or rebuild them directly if published). Failure: FAIL_NONDETERMINISM,
FAIL_EVAL_SOURCE_MISSING, FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH.

V5: Koopman Construction Replay (K)

Replay KoopClass construction under BuildSpec:
• compute K via KOP1/KOP2/KOP3,
• apply deterministic SVD/pseudo-inverse/inversion rules and thresholds,
• canonicalize K,
• compare hK to committed value.

Failure: FAIL_SVD_UNSPECIFIED, FAIL_PSEUDOINV_UNDEFINED, FAIL_ILL_CONDITIONED,
FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH.

769



V6: Diagnostics Replay

Replay all diagnostics in DiagSpec:
• compute Lrec,
• compute conditioning diagnostic,
• compute any optional diagnostics (CrossM stability, eigenpair residuals).

Compare to DiagReport commitments and tolerances. Failure: FAIL_RECONSTRUCTION_TOO_HIGH,
FAIL_ILL_CONDITIONED, FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH.

V7: Spectral Summary Replay (if published)

If eigenvalues/modes are published:
• replay eigensolver with committed algorithm and ordering,
• verify residual norms (if declared),
• compare to committed spectral summary hash.

Failure: FAIL_EIGEN_UNSPECIFIED, FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH.

V8: Interop Claim Consistency

If Interop declares EY28/EY29 dependencies:
• verify the order of operations is declared and consistent with transcripts,
• verify truncation policies do not conflict,
• verify that any reduction/transport obligations are satisfied by referenced certificates.

Failure: FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE.

5.8 Acceptance Rule

Rule. A verifier returns ACCEPT iff:
• V1–V5 pass,
• mandatory diagnostics are present and replay-match,
• and any declared tolerances are satisfied.

5.9 Required Failure Codes

At minimum:
• REJECT_MALFORMED
• REJECT_SPECID_MISSING
• REJECT_OBSDECL_MISSING
• REJECT_EVODECL_MISSING

770



• REJECT_KOOPCLASS_MISSING
• REJECT_BUILDSPEC_MISSING
• REJECT_DIAGSPEC_MISSING
• REJECT_HIDDEN_INPUT
• FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH
• FAIL_EVAL_SOURCE_MISSING
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM
• FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH
• FAIL_SVD_UNSPECIFIED
• FAIL_PSEUDOINV_UNDEFINED
• FAIL_ILL_CONDITIONED
• FAIL_RECONSTRUCTION_TOO_HIGH
• FAIL_EIGEN_UNSPECIFIED
• FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE

5.10 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined the EY30 certificate πKOOP and deterministic verifier checks: SpecID
completeness, commitment integrity, evaluation replay of X,Y , Koopman construction replay of

6 Interop Declarations (Mini): Koopman-Space Compatibility
and Registry Use

6.1 Purpose

EY30 sits at an export boundary: it converts Vol. No. IV workflows into observable-space
operator artifacts. This chapter instantiates EY22 interoperability rules for Koopman export:

• how EY30 is referenced by upstream and downstream artifacts,
• what it means for a workflow to be “Koopman-compatible”,
• a minimal set of compatibility predicates for Koopman export,
• and how interop certificates bind observable dictionaries, evaluation sources, and construc-

tion routines.

771



Rule. If a published claim depends on Koopman-space objects (Koopman matrix K, Koopman
eigenvalues/modes, Koopman signatures), the publication MUST include an interop certificate
πinterop referencing πKOOP and the upstream artifact(s) that define Φ, the evaluation points, and
any reduction/transport steps.

6.2 Interop Component Fields (Standard)

Any artifact that composes with EY30 MUST include an interop entry:

Interop ∋ (KOOP-Ref, InteropRole, Scope, DictObligations, EvalObligations, DiagObligations, CompatPredicates).

Required fields.
• KOOP-Ref: hash/SpecID reference to πKOOP (and hK).
• InteropRole: one of producer-export, consumer-koops, registry-key, signature-layer.
• Scope: what is exported (trajectory window, token period, workflow stage).
• DictObligations: required dictionary identity (DictType, ordering, truncation m, CrossM-

Policy if any).
• EvalObligations: required evaluation source identity (trajectory/token/dataset), time

semantics ∆, pairing rules.
• DiagObligations: required diagnostics and bounds (e.g. max Lrec, max conditioning).
• CompatPredicates: identifiers of compatibility predicates used (defined below).

Rule. If a workflow relies on Koopman comparability, it MUST bind dictionary identity and
ordering. Two Koopman operators are not comparable unless their ObservableDecl matches (or
a declared coercion exists).

6.3 Compatibility Predicates (EY30 Mini Set)

EY30 standardizes a minimal predicate set for Koopman export interop.

KOOP-C0: SpecID/Certificate Binding

KOOP-C0 := (EIF KOOP-Ref matches a valid πKOOP and SpecID hashes align).

KOOP-C1: Export Replay Closure

KOOP-C1 := (EIF evaluation and construction are replayable and hK matches replay).

KOOP-C2: Dictionary Identity

KOOP-C2 := (EIF ObservableDecl.Dictionary (type+hash/seed+order) matches exactly).

KOOP-C3: Evaluation Source Identity

KOOP-C3 := (EIF EvalRule point set source and pairing rules match; ∆ semantics match).

772



KOOP-C4: Diagnostics Present and Within Bounds

KOOP-C4 := (EIF mandatory diagnostics are present, replay-match, and satisfy DiagObligations).

KOOP-C5: CrossMPolicy Determinism (if used)

KOOP-C5 := (EIF CrossMPolicy is declared, deterministic, and transcript binds decisions).

KOOP-C6: Registry-Key Stability (if used)

KOOP-C6 := (EIF key material (eigenvalues/modes/signature) is canonically encoded with ordering+tie-breaks).

KOOP-C7: Upstream Interop Closure

KOOP-C7 := (EIF all upstream dependencies (EY25/EY26/EY28/EY29) referenced by KOOP are themselves verified).

6.4 Pairwise Interop Templates (EY23–EY29 → EY30)

This section lists intended composition semantics. These are templates; real workflows MUST
cite predicate IDs.

LIOUV (EY25) → KOOP (EY30): Generator-Based Export

Typical workflow.
Φ∆ from EY25 ⇒ K on dictionary D.

Compatibility template. OK if:

KOOP-C0 ∧KOOP-C1 ∧KOOP-C2 ∧KOOP-C3 ∧KOOP-C4 ∧KOOP-C7.

FLOQ (EY26) → KOOP (EY30): Token-Based Export

Typical workflow. Per-step or per-period Koopman:

xk+1 = UF (xk) ⇒ K.

Compatibility template. OK∗ if KOOP-C3 includes time-slicing semantics and KOOP-C7
confirms token transcript integrity.

INTW (EY28) ↔ KOOP (EY30): Regime-Bridged Export

Two options:
• Export-in-target: transport states first (EY28), then evaluate observables and build K.
• Export-in-source: build K in source regime, then map observable dictionary via a

declared observable-bridge.

Rule. The workflow MUST declare the order. Otherwise: FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE.

773



Compatibility template. Require:

INTW-C0..C4 ∧KOOP-C0..C4 ∧KOOP-C7,

and bind StateRep and dictionary identity in the target regime.

CGR (EY29) → KOOP (EY30): Reduced Dictionaries / Reduced Evaluation

If dictionary is reduced (derived from EY29 outputs), or if evaluation points are reduced
summaries, then KOOP-C7 must include a verified CGR-Ref and KOOP-C2 must bind the
reduced dictionary construction recipe.

Compatibility template. OK∗ iff:

CGR-C0..C3 ∧KOOP-C0..C4 ∧KOOP-C7.

CSF/VPO (EY23/EY24) → KOOP (EY30): Workflow Export

Filtering/validity alone do not define Φ. Therefore EY30 requires:
• Φ realized via EY25 or EY26, or
• committed snapshots derived from a verified workflow.

Compatibility template. NO unless EvolutionDecl cites EY25/EY26/SNAP with commit-
ments (KOOP-C3, KOOP-C7).

6.5 Interop Certificates for Koopman Workflows

Whenever a claim depends on Koopman export, the workflow SHOULD publish an interop
certificate:

πinterop := (UpstreamSpecIDs, KOOP-Ref, Scope, DictObligations, EvalObligations, DiagObligations, CompatPredicates, TranscriptRefs).

Rule (registry-grade Koopman keys). If Koopman eigenvalues/modes/signatures are used
as registry keys, πinterop MUST include:

• KOOP-C6 evidence (canonical key material + ordering/tie-breaks),
• KOOP-C4 evidence (diagnostics within bounds),
• KOOP-C2 and KOOP-C3 evidence (dictionary and evaluation source identity).

6.6 Deterministic Interop Failure Codes

At minimum:
• FAIL_COMPAT_PREDICATE
• FAIL_HASH_MISMATCH
• FAIL_NONDETERMINISM
• FAIL_EVAL_SOURCE_MISSING

774



• FAIL_TRANSCRIPT_MISMATCH

• FAIL_ILL_CONDITIONED

• FAIL_RECONSTRUCTION_TOO_HIGH

6.7 Chapter Summary

This chapter defined EY30 interoperability mini-declarations: how Koopman exports are refer-
enced (KOOP-Ref), how workflows state scope, dictionary/evaluation/diagnostic obligations,
and a minimal set of Koopman compatibility predicates (KOOP-C0..C7). It provided pairwise
interop templates for composing Koopman export with EY25/EY26/EY28/EY29, and fixed
interop certificate requirements for registry-grade Koopman keys.
Chapter 7 next provides a KOOP-0 reference SpecID template, fixes the publication boundary
and non-claims for EY30, and closes the artifact in a QFC-consistent way.

7 KOOP-0 Reference Instance, Publication Boundary, and Non-
Claims

7.1 Purpose

This chapter closes EY30 by:
• providing a concrete KOOP-0 reference SpecID template (a stable meaning of “Koopman

export artifact”),

• fixing what must be published for a valid EY30 export,

• stating explicit non-claims (what Koopman export does not guarantee),

• and recording licensing intent consistent with Vol. No. IV.

7.2 KOOP-0 Reference Instance (Template)

KOOP-0 is the conservative baseline profile for Koopman export. It aims to minimize ambiguity
and maximize verifier replayability.

KOOP-0 profile choices.
• KoopClass = KOP2 (ridge-regularized normal equation) as a conditioning-stable default,

• EvalType = trajectory using committed EY25 or EY26 trajectories,

• DictType = seeded or explicit (no hidden learned dictionary),

• mandatory diagnostics: reconstruction error Lrec and a conditioning estimate,

• no CrossMPolicy unless explicitly declared (non-baseline),

• optional spectral summaries only if eigensolver rules are fully committed.

Rule. All null fields MUST be explicit. Omitting them is not allowed.

7.3 Publication Boundary (Normative)

Rule (what must be public). An EY30 publication MUST include:
• full SpecIDEY30,
• ObservableDecl (dictionary commitments, evaluation rule, truncation m, ordering),
• EvolutionDecl (PhiType, PhiSource reference, declared time step ∆ semantics),
• KoopClass and BuildSpec (routine IDs, thresholds, regularization, tie-breaks),
• DiagSpec and computed DiagReport (including reconstruction error Lrec and conditioning),
• NumericModel (evaluation + linear algebra determinism),
• certificate πKOOP with transcript commitments: Txeval,Txbuild,Txdiag,
• output commitment hK (and optional spectral summary commitments),
• deterministic failure codes (or PASS) for all declared checks.

Rule (no hidden dictionary). A Koopman export is invalid if dictionary identity cannot be
reconstructed. Learned dictionaries are allowed only if parameters are committed and evaluation
is deterministic under NumericModel.

Rule (no hidden evaluation points). If EvalType is sampled, PRNGSpec and seed MUST
be public. If EvalType is trajectory, the trajectory source (EY25/EY26) MUST be cited and
committed.

Rule (no hidden time semantics). The declared time step ∆ MUST be bound as a value
in EvolutionDecl and EvalRule.TimeSpec. In code/spec blocks use ASCII (e.g. "delta=1"); in
math text use ∆ freely.

7.4 Non-Claims (Explicit)

EY30 explicitly does not claim:

NC1: Completeness of Observable Dictionaries

No claim is made that D spans a Koopman-invariant subspace or captures all dynamics.

NC2: Infinite-Dimensional Koopman Truth from Finite Truncations

Spectral claims about the true Koopman operator are not implied by finite K eigenvalues.
Finite-m eigenvalues are only export artifacts under a declared dictionary and evaluation rule.

778



NC3: Regime Equivalence

Using the same dictionary in two regimes does not imply those regimes are physically equivalent.
Any equivalence claim must be mediated by EY28 (transport) and explicit interop certificates.

NC4: Robustness Beyond Declared Diagnostics

Passing Lrec and conditioning thresholds does not guarantee robustness to adversarial pertur-
bations, sampling bias, or unmodeled dynamics. EY30 only certifies what it measures and
commits.

NC5: Comparability Without Shared ObservableDecl

Two Koopman exports are comparable only if ObservableDecl (dictionary, ordering, evaluation
source semantics) matches or a declared coercion/bridge exists. Otherwise they are different
objects.

7.5 Licensing Intent (Vol. No. IV)

The EY30 specification (schemas, baseline routines, diagnostics, verifier checks) is intended to
remain publicly readable. Implementations may be licensed under project-chosen terms, but:

dictionary commitments, evaluation determinism, and diagnostics may not be re-
moved.

Rule (no audit stripping). No distribution may claim EY30 compliance while omitting:
• explicit dictionary identity,

• explicit evaluation point set source semantics,

• reconstruction error and conditioning diagnostics,

• and replayable construction rules.

7.6 Chapter Summary

This chapter provided a KOOP-0 reference SpecID template (ASCII-safe), fixed the EY30
publication boundary (what must be committed and public), stated explicit non-claims (no com-
pleteness, no infinite-dimensional truth, no regime equivalence, no robustness beyond diagnostics,
no comparability without shared ObservableDecl), and recorded licensing intent consistent with
Vol. No. IV.

Next. Proceed to Chapter 8 for worked examples (non-normative), or close Vol. No. IV by
compiling the full EY22 compatibility matrix and publishing one canonical end-to-end reference
workflow with interop certificates.

8 Worked Examples (Non-Normative): Export Patterns and
Koopman Signatures

8.1 Purpose

This chapter is non-normative. It illustrates common EY30 usage patterns:
• generator-based Koopman export from EY25 (EDMD-style),
• token-based export from EY26 (per-step vs per-period),
• regime-bridged export using EY28 (export-in-target vs export-in-source),
• reduced dictionaries and reduced evaluation via EY29,
• and registry-grade Koopman signatures (bounded, canonical, replayable).

Reminder. Examples become valid only when ObservableDecl, EvolutionDecl, KoopClass,
BuildSpec, diagnostics, and transcripts are fully committed.

8.2 Example 1: Generator-Based Export (EY25 → EY30)

Setup. Assume EY25 provides a committed evolution routine that produces a trajectory:

xk+1 = Φ∆(xk),

with ∆ fixed.

ObservableDecl (sketch). Choose a polynomial dictionary on a d-dimensional state vector:

D = {1, x1, . . . , xd, x
2
1, x1x2, . . . },

ordered lexicographically, truncated to size m.

Construction. Form:

X = [ψ(x1) · · ·ψ(xn)], Y = [ψ(x2) · · ·ψ(xn+1)],

then compute K via KOP2 (ridge-regularized normal equation).

Diagnostics. Compute:
Lrec = ∥Y −KX∥F ,

∥Y ∥F
and a conditioning estimate. Publish both.

Interpretation. The export produces an auditable K that encodes how the chosen observables
behave under the EY25-evolution. It does not claim completeness of the dictionary.

8.3 Example 2: Token-Based Export (EY26 → EY30)

Setup. Assume EY26 defines a Floquet token UF and a step factorization UF = UJ · · ·U1.

780



Two exports.
• Per-step Koopman: Φ(x) = Uj(x) for a fixed j.
• Per-period Koopman: Φ(x) = UF (x) (one full period).

Rule reminder. EvolutionDecl MUST specify which one is used, including time-slicing seman-
tics.

Interpretation. Per-step Kj can reveal the internal structure of the token; per-period KF is a
compressed summary suitable for registries.

Interop requirement. The workflow MUST publish interop certificates that bind:
• the chosen order,
• the StateRep in the target regime,
• and dictionary identity in the target evaluation semantics.

Interpretation. This enables “same observable dictionary across regimes” comparisons without
claiming physical equivalence.

8.5 Example 4: Reduced Dictionary via EY29 (CGR → KOOP)

Setup. Suppose a high-dimensional operator/state yields a coarse-grain summary via EY29:

(BucketID, s) := R(trajectory summary),

where s is a bounded feature vector.

Dictionary construction. Define an OP-FEAT dictionary using coordinates of s as observ-
ables:

gi(x) := si(x), i = 1, . . . ,m,
with dictionary identity bound by CGR-Ref + SummarySpec.

Interpretation. This yields a Koopman export on a reduced, registry-friendly observable
space. But KOOP-C7 requires that the reduction certificate is verified.

Registry-grade usage requires bounded canonical signatures. Two examples:

Signature A: Spectral Window Summary

This avoids dependence on exact eigenvalue ordering beyond histogram bins.

Rule reminder. If signatures are used as keys:
• dictionary identity (KOOP-C2) and evaluation semantics (KOOP-C3) must match,
• diagnostics (KOOP-C4) must be within bounds,
• and the signature encoding must be canonical (KOOP-C6).

Interpretation. Signatures are designed for registry stability and comparison, not for claiming
analytic truth about the infinite-dimensional Koopman operator.

8.8 Chapter Summary

This non-normative chapter illustrated EY30 export patterns: generator-based export from EY25,
token-based export from EY26, regime-bridged export using EY28, reduced dictionary/evaluation
via EY29, registry-grade Koopman signatures, and CrossMPolicy stability.
